Section 00-01: Identification Codes

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) 

A 17-digit combination of numbers and letters form the vehicle 
identification number (VIN). The VIN is located in the center area of the 
Vehicle Rating Label. Refer to Vehicle Rating Label in this section for the 
label locations. 

By looking at the 17-digit VIN, a variety of information about the 
vehicle can be determined. The first three digits identify the manufacturer 
and the vehicle make and type. The fourth digit determines the type of brake 
system (air or hydraulic) and the gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) class for 
trucks (completed vehicles). For incomplete vehicles, the fourth digit 
determines the brake system only. Digits five, six and seven identify the 
model or line, series, chassis and cab type. The eighth digit points out the 
particular engine and type (gas or diesel) found in the vehicle. Digit nine is 
the VIN check digit. Digit 10 identifies the model year of a Ford-completed 
vehicle, or the model year of the incomplete vehicle, if sold by Ford as an 
incomplete vehicle. Digit 11 determines the assembly plant. Digits 12 through 
17 make up the sequential serial and warranty number. Digit 12 uses the letter 
A until the production or sequence of 99,999 units (digits 13 through 17) is 
reached. Letter A then becomes B for the next production sequence of vehicles. 

Refer to the code portion of this section for specific definitions of 
the numbers and letters of the vehicle identification number (VIN).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Chassis-Cab Certification Label 

The Chassis-Cab Certification Label is attached to the rear face of the 
driver's door or door pillar. The label contains the name of the manufacturer, 
the month and year of manufacture and the certification statement.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Rating Label 

The following illustration shows a typical Vehicle Rating Label. On 
cowl and windshield vehicles, the Rating Label is mounted on the right side of 
the cowl top panel under the hood. On incomplete vehicles, the rating label is 
attached to a booklet (incomplete vehicle manual) and secured to a suitable 
interior location. On all other vehicles, the rating label is mounted on the 
rear face of the left front door. 

The vehicle data appears on the Vehicle Rating Label on the two lines 
following the identification number. The code set (two numbers or a number and 
letter) above COLOR identify the exterior paint color (two sets of codes 
designate a two-tone). The first three digits under WB designate the wheelbase 
in inches. The letter and three digits under TYPE/GVW designate the truck 
model within a series and the gross vehicle weight rating. The letters and/or 
numeral under BODY designate the interior trim, seat and body type. The 
transmission installed in the vehicle is identified under TRANS by two 
letters, or a number and one letter. (If so equipped, a number is also stamped 
before the transmission code to identify the auxiliary transmission.) A letter 
and a number or two numbers or two letters under AXLE identify the rear axle 
ratio (when required, a letter is also stamped after the rear axle code to 
identify the front axle). 

A two-digit number is stamped above DSO to identify the district that 
ordered the vehicle. If the vehicle is built to special order (Domestic 
Special Order, Foreign Special Order, Limited Production Option or other 
special order), the complete order number will also appear above DSO. The 
vehicle model year appears in the lower right corner area of the decal under 
DSO. The charts that follow list the various vehicle data codes.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Build Date Stamp Location

The vehicle build date stamp is a four-digit number representing month 
and day of manufacture. The vehicle build date is stamped on the front surface 
of the radiator support on the passenger side of the vehicle.

For a build date of January 24, for example, the vehicle build date 
stamp reads 0124; for a build date of October 21, the vehicle date stamp reads 
1021.

Yellow ink is normally used for the date stamp. When the marking 
surface is painted the body color, the date stamp will be marked in red ink. 
Units from the Ontario Truck Plant (Code C) will be marked with silver ink.

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Noise 

Noise, defined as any unpleasant sound, can be described in a variety 
of ways, such as tapping, whistling, buzzing, humming, clunking or booming. 

All noises can be associated with a probable cause. Based on 
experience, these descriptions will assist in isolating the condition and 
correcting it. 

Generally recognizable concern areas are engine, driveline, wind and 
road surface noises. 

Other less obvious areas that should be considered as noise concern 
sources are any of the conditions that cause the vibrations described in this 
section. 

A gear driven mechanism, especially a drive axle, will produce a 
certain amount of noise. 

Some noise is acceptable and can be audible at certain speeds or under 
various driving conditions: for example, tire noise on a newly paved blacktop 
road or brake pedal noise associated with hydro-boost brake units. 

Such noise is in no way detrimental to the operation of the vehicle and 
must be considered normal.

================================================================================
PAGE 4136
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vibration 

Vibration, technically, is a high-frequency trembling, shaking or 
grounding condition, felt or heard, that is constant or variable in level and 
occurs during a portion of the total operating speed range. The types of 
vibrations that can be felt in the vehicle can be divided into three groups: 

Vibrations of various unbalanced rotating parts of the vehicle. 

Body and frame vibrations excited by powertrain, wind or road inputs. 

Tip-in moans or resonance vibrations from stressed engine or exhaust 
system mounts or driveline flexing modes. 

These vehicle vibrations can also be subdivided into those that occur 
at low speeds and those that are most noticeable at higher speeds. Since the 
dividing line between low and higher speed vibrations is not clear, there will 
be vibrations that overlap the two ranges. 

 Low-Speed Vibrations — Typical (Less Than 72 km/h [
45 mph]) 

Exhaust vibration 

Engine harshness 

Driveline vibration due to improper driveline angles

Improper installation of engine and transmission rear support 
insulators (void areas of insulators should be positioned at 12 o'clock and 6 
o'clock). Most noticeable at idle and low speeds.

Air conditioner compressor or drive belt vibrations 

Take-off shudder (clutch or driveline problems) 

Brake roughness or harshness 

Driveline roughness 

Clutch torsion vibration 

Driveline slip-yoke or U-joints, automatic transmission clutch slippage

 High-Speed Vibrations — Typical (Above 72 km/h [
45 mph]) 

Axle and companion flange runout or imbalance 

Driveshaft imbalance or improper angles

Excessive tire-wheel and drum assembly imbalance 

Tire roughness due to high nonuniformity (force variation) or 
out-of-balance condition

Rear axle pinion gear pitch line runout 

Excessive tire and wheel runout 

Worn suspension components 

Front end accessory vibrations 

Exhaust vibration (greatly reduced in exhaust systems decoupled by a 
flexible coupling and mounted with blade and block hangers)

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Harshness 

Harshness is the term commonly used to describe the ride quality of the 
vehicle. Hard ride or harshness is usually caused by the tires or suspension 
system, namely: 

Overinflated tire installed on the vehicle 

Worn suspension components 

Suspension components installed with preload on pivot points, bearings 
and bushings 

Units equipped with tires not specified by the manufacturer. (Different 
brand tires often give different ride qualities to vehicle.) 

Bent or bound-up shock absorbers 

Heavy-duty components installed on vehicle 

Improper installation of cab mounts (groundings) 

Improper installation of engine and transmission rear support 
insulators. (Void areas of insulators should be positioned at 12 o'clock and 6 
o'clock.) Most noticeable at idle and low speeds.

Other vehicle ride motions can be summarized as follows: 

Vehicle bounce — the vertical motion of a vehicle on 
its suspension system, front and rear in phase. A low frequency "float," an 
intermediate frequency "kick." 

Vehicle pitch — the out-of-phase vertical motion of the 
front and rear of the vehicle. A flat ride is considered the opposite of a 
pitch ride. 

Vehicle roll — the side-to-side rotation of the vehicle 
body about the front and rear axles.

================================================================================
PAGE 4138
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Weight Distribution

Weight properly distributed to front and rear axles gives the best ride 
and steerability, and eliminates premature failures due to overloaded axles, 
springs, tires, etc. 

Payload distribution has a definite bearing on vehicle performance. 
Even if the total vehicle is not loaded beyond the recommended maximum gross 
vehicle weight, this does not mean that individual components cannot be 
overloaded. 

Overloading can be due to the improper positioning of heavy materials 
so that the load is centered over one rear tire or so far forward in the body 
that the front axle and tires are overloaded. 

Unloaded or diminishing load type operations also affect the ride 
characteristics of a vehicle. Road vibrations and shock, for example, are not 
dampened in a light vehicle to the extent that they are under heavily loaded 
conditions.

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Noise, Vibration and Harshness

 Inspection and Verification 

The noise, vibration and harshness section is designed to give a 
working knowledge of the process of diagnosing noise and vibration situations. 
It is divided into several portions, each based on the description of a 
condition. If a condition occurs at high speed, for example, the most likely 
place to start is under High Speed Shake. The Vehicle Vibration Road Test 
portion will tell how to sort the conditions into categories and how to tell a 
vibration from a shake.

A gear-driven unit will produce a certain amount of noise. Some noise 
is acceptable and can be audible at certain speeds or under various driving 
conditions. The slight noise is in no way detrimental and must be considered 
normal. 

NVH usually occur in four areas: tires, engine accessories, suspension 
and drivetrain. It is important, therefore, that an NVH concern be isolated 
into its specific area as soon as possible. The easiest and quickest way to do 
this is to perform a road test. 

Make a visual inspection as part of the preliminary diagnostic routine, 
writing down anything that does not look right. Note tire pressures, but do 
not adjust them yet. Note leaking fluids, loose nuts or bolts, or bright spots 
where components might be rubbing against each other. Check cargo area for 
unusual loads. 

Do not make any repairs or adjustments until a road test and a thorough 
visual inspection of the vehicle have been performed. Do not change tire 
pressure or vehicle load. Adjusting tire pressures or vehicle load, or making 
some other adjustment, can reduce the condition's intensity to a point where 
it cannot be identified clearly. It can also inject a new condition into the 
system, preventing proper diagnosis. 

Make notes throughout diagnosis. It will help cover all bases when 
starting to compile data. Use a road test form that includes space for 
comments. Write down even the smallest bit of information, as it may turn out 
to be most important. 

Road test the vehicle, and define the condition by reproducing it 
several times during the road test. 

Perform the vehicle vibration road test as soon as the condition is 
reproduced. This will identify the proper section of the diagnostic procedure. 
Run through the test more than once to make sure a usable result is being 
obtained. Remember, the road test might not tell where the concern is, but it 
will tell where it is not.

 Vehicle Vibration Road Test 

24-80 km/h (15-50 mph): With light acceleration, a moaning noise is 
heard, and possibly a vibration is felt in the floorpan. It is usually worse 
at a particular engine speed and at a particular throttle setting during 
acceleration at that speed. It can also produce a moaning sound, depending on 
what component is causing it. 

High speed shake: With slow acceleration and deceleration, a shake is 
sometimes noticed in the steering wheel/steering column tube, seats, floorpan, 
trim panels, or front end sheet metal. It is a low frequency vibration (around 
9-15 cycles per second). It might or might not be increased by applying brakes 
lightly. 

High speed vibration: A vibration is felt in the floorpan or seats with 
no visible shake, but with an accompanying sound or rumble, buzz, hum, drone 
or booming noise. Coast with clutch depressed or transmission control selector 
lever in NEUTRAL and engine idling. If vibration is still evident, it can be 
related to wheels, tires, front disc brake rotors, front or rear brake drums, 
wheel hubs or wheel bearings. 

0-High speed: A vibration is felt whenever the engine reaches a 
particular rpm. It will disappear in NEUTRAL coast. The vibration can be 
duplicated by operating the engine at the problem rpm while the vehicle is 
parked. It can be caused by any component, from the accessory drive belt to 
the clutch or torque converter, which turns at engine speed when the vehicle 
is stopped. 

 Noise Diagnosis Procedure 

 Non-Axle Noises 

There are some noise conditions that sound like axle noise and have to 
be considered while performing road test diagnosis. The most common conditions 
are noise from the transmission, exhaust system and tires. Therefore, be sure 
that none of these non-axle noise conditions are the cause of the noise 
concern before proceeding with an axle teardown and diagnosis.

 Noise Conditions 

If noise is produced as part of a vibration condition, correcting the 
vibration will eliminate the noise. If the noise is related to a specific 
component or system, refer to the appropriate service manual section for 
further diagnosis.

 Vibration Conditions 

Engine or accessory vibration, all speeds — refer to Pinpoint Test B 
 and Pinpoint Test D in this section.

High-speed shake, 80 km/h (50 mph) and up:

Refer to Section 04-04 for tire conditions contributing to high-speed 
shake.

Refer to rotor and drum runout checks contained in Section 06-00 .

Tip-in moan — refer to Pinpoint Test C in this section.

Vibration, technically, is a high-frequency trembling, shaking or 
grounding condition, felt or heard, that is constant or variable in level and 
occurs during a portion of the total operating speed range. The types of 
vibrations that can be felt in the vehicle can be divided into three groups:

Vibrations of various unbalanced rotating parts of the vehicle.

Body and frame vibrations excited by powertrain, wind or road inputs.

Tip-in moans or resonance vibrations from stressed engine or exhaust 
system mounts or driveline flexing modes.

These vehicle vibrations can also be subdivided into those that occur 
at low speeds and those that are most noticeable at higher speeds. Since the 
dividing line between low and higher speed vibrations is not clear, there will 
be vibrations that overlap the two ranges.

 Leakage Conditions 

Most rear axle lubricant leakage conditions can be corrected without a 
teardown. However, it is important to clean up the leaking area enough to 
identify the exact source.

A plugged axle vent will cause excessive seal lip wear due to internal 
pressure buildup. When a leak occurs, check the vent located near the top of 
the differential housing. Make sure the vent hose is not kinked. Remove the 
vent hose from the vent nipple and make sure the hose is clear of dirt or 
other foreign materials. While hose is removed, pass a length of mechanics' 
wire or small diameter Allen wrench in and out of the vent nipple to clean it 
of any dirt or foreign materials. Install vent hose. If vent cannot be 
cleared, it must be replaced.

Make sure axle lubricant is within specified limits.

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveline 

For additional driveline adjustment procedures, refer to Section 05-00 . 

 Slip-Spline Coupling Binding 

If, while driving the vehicle, particularly during acceleration or 
deceleration, a ringing or grinding noise in the driveline is noted, or if the 
driveshaft center support bearing has been damaged, the driveshaft slip-spline 
coupling is a likely problem source. 

These noise conditions can be caused by the coupling shaft dust shield 
contacting the center support bearing insulator or bracket, as the result of a 
tight or binding slip-spline (between coupling shaft and driveshaft). When 
this condition exists, the coupling shaft, if pulled rearward into the center 
support bearing when the vehicle is being driven, causes the resultant noise 
or insulator damage. 

If this condition is verified, the following procedure should be 
followed:

Disconnect driveshaft universal joint from rear axle pinion flange. 

Push and pull driveshaft forward and rearward to work driveshaft to 
coupling shaft slip joint. 

If the slip joint has loosened up with the slipping action and is 
functioning satisfactorily, no replacement of the driveshaft or coupling shaft 
is necessary. Replace only damaged parts, such as the center support 
insulator. 

If after working the slip joint back and forth several times there 
still is excessive tightness or binding, the entire coupling shaft assembly 
(including the center support) should be replaced. 

Verify proper slip-spline action with the new coupling shaft and 
proceed with repairs. 

 NOTE: Check driveshaft for proper yoke phasing (90-degree phase angle shown). 

[FIGURE: E3745C.gif]

 Driveline Support Plate Position 

An adjustable driveline support plate is used on some applications. 
Although it can be mounted in any one of several positions, only one position 
is correct for a specific application. The correct position can be determined 
from the support plate part number shown on the Truck Specification List 
attached to each vehicle. 

The numerical digit in the adjustable support plate part number suffix 
indicates the hole set to be used. 

For example, support plate 4831 is bolted to crossmember (or bracket 
4691, some installations) through support plate hole set number 1. The hole 
sets are identified by the numbers stamped into the bracket 4691 or support 
plate 4831.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Body Sealer Types and Application

Since many sealers are used in the assembly of the vehicle, the 
following all-purpose sealers have been selected for service use. The method 
and points of application are shown in each applicable group.

 Liquid Butyl Sealer 

Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B (Black) or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G162-A does not run, is fast drying and remains 
semi-elastic. The sealer can be used for seam sealing in such areas as the 
floorpan, wheelhouse, dash panel, running board, door openings and drip rails. 
It can also be used to seal outside moulding clip holes and for windshield and 
rear window installation.

 Caulking Cord 

Caulking Cord D6AZ-19560-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESB-M4G32-A has a plastic base, is heavy-bodied and is commonly known as 
perma-gum. It is used on spotweld holes, around mounting clips and between two 
surfaces not sealed by a gasket. Apply the sealer with a putty knife.

 Weatherstrip Adhesive 

Weatherstrip Adhesive E8AZ-19552-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M2G14-A is designed to hold weatherstripping on doors, 
bodies, cowl ventilators and the surrounding metal. Windows and windshields 
that are set in rubber can be sealed effectively against leakage by flowing 
cement into the affected areas.

Clean all grease, dirt and old sealer from the surfaces to be cemented 
and apply a medium coat of cement to both surfaces. Immediately press both 
surfaces together.

 Silicone Lubricant 

Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M13P4-A can be used for lubricating rubber parts exposed to 
weather.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Dust and Water Leaks

The forward motion of the vehicle creates a slight vacuum within the 
body, particularly if a window or ventilator is partially open. Any unsealed 
crevice or small opening in the lower section of the body will permit air to 
be drawn into the body. If dust is present in the air, it will follow.

Under certain conditions, water can enter the body at any point where 
dirt or dust can enter. Any consideration of water leakage must take into 
account all points covered under dust leaks.

To determine the exact location of a dust leak, remove the following 
trim from the cab: cowl trim panel, kick pads, and floor mats.

Removal of the trim will reveal the location of most leaks. Seal these 
leaks and road test the vehicle on a dusty road to make sure all leaks are 
sealed. The entrance of dust is usually indicated by a pointed shaft of dust 
or silt at the point of entrance. After the road test, check for indications 
of a dust pattern around the door openings, cowl panel and cowl side panel.

Sometimes leaks can be located by putting bright lights under the 
vehicle, with the above components removed, and checking the interior of the 
body at joints and weld lines. The light will show through where leaks exist.

================================================================================
PAGE 4154
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 01-00: Body Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Wind Noise

Air entering or exiting the vehicle through small openings in the body 
can result in wind noise. Sources of wind noise are detected by driving the 
vehicle at highway speeds in four different directions. Listen for sources of 
wind noise with all windows closed, radio off, heater and air conditioner 
blower motor turned off and ventilation ducts open. A stethoscope can be used 
to pinpoint the source of the noise.

Most wind noise-producing leaks will occur at the door and window seals 
or at sheet metal joints in the door or the door opening in the body.

Seal all leaks with RTV sealant and foam tape or by repositioning or 
replacing the seals. Road test the vehicle to make sure all leaks have been 
adequately sealed.

An alternate method of verifying corrective actions involves the use of 
Rotunda Vacuum Leak Detector R164-R0256 or equivalent. After identifying the 
leak point through a drive evaluation, obtain a meter reading by using the 
leak detector. A check with the leak detector after repairing the leak will 
verify the effectiveness of the corrective action. A final test drive is 
advisable to check for additional leaks.

PAGE 4155
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 01-00: Body Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Rattle Elimination

Most rattles are caused by a loose bolt or screw. Foreign objects such 
as nuts, bolts, or small pieces of body deadener in the door wells and pillars 
are often the source of rattles. Door wells can be checked by carefully 
striking the underside of the door with a rubber mallet. The impact made by 
the mallet will indicate if loose objects are in the door well.

Tighten all bolts and screws periodically. In the event that tightening 
the bolts and screws located on such assemblies as the doors does not 
eliminate the rattles, the trouble is probably caused by misalignment. If this 
is the case, follow the adjustment and alignment procedures for these 
assemblies.

Rattles and squeaks are sometimes caused by weatherstripping and 
anti-squeak material that has slipped out of position. Apply additional cement 
or other adhesive, and install the material in the proper location to 
eliminate this difficulty.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Paint Damage from Airborne Materials

The following information gives a detailed description of paint damage 
caused by chemical or organic materials. If service is required, identify the 
source of the damage and follow the recommended service procedure.

 Chemical 

The effects of chemical airborne materials can be seen as follows:

dark blotches in the paint where the pigment in the paint surface has 
been attacked

irregular spots that are cracked or etched around the edges and dull in 
the centers

small orange colored spots caused by iron particles that appear on the 
paint surface

Generally, materials that attack a paint film are either acidic or 
alkaline in nature.

Sulfuric and nitric acids, in general, cause extreme damage to 
automotive paint finishes. Even very small concentrations of the same 
materials can cause chemical spotting damage. Due to evaporation and 
condensation, these acids can create severe etching that will eventually crack 
or lift the paint film after some time in service.

Although some automotive finishes are more resistant than others, none 
are completely immune to these chemicals. The most resistant paints used today 
are the urethanes because their resin system is least likely to react with 
chemicals. Air-dried coatings are more susceptible to attack only when they 
are fresh. The longer the paint dries, the more resistant it becomes.

Metallic colors are more intolerant to chemicals because aluminum flake 
is fairly reactive with either an acid or alkali. The following chart contains 
the most common acid materials found on automotive finishes.

 CHEMICAL SPOTTING DAMAGE OF AUTOMOTIVE FINISHES

 a Caustic refers to any alkaline substance that can be harsh
or corrosive, depending on strength or concentration.

 Organic 

Organic damage is generally easier to identify. Organic damage is 
mostly due to tree sap, bird and insect droppings, dead insects and pollen. 
Tree sap is easily identified by clear raised drops that can be hard or 
sticky. Bee or bug dropping spots appear brownish or yellow in color, about 
3.1 mm to 6.3 mm (1/8 to 1/4 inch) in diameter. Dead and decomposing insect 
bodies are readily visible to the eye. Pollen deposits are small yellow 
clusters.

Each of these items is potentially damaging to any currently available 
paint system. Other noticeable traits of organic damage are spots that are 
raised (swelling), micro-crazing (cracked) and pitting due to pollen eating 
into the paint film. The active ingredients in most organic contaminants are 
tannic and formic acids. These acids are found in berries and bodily fluids of 
insects and birds. Organic damage is accelerated by heat. During very hot 
weather conditions, it is important to wash vehicles more often.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Chemical or Organic Damage Repair

Iron dust particles or other industrial fallout can imbed themselves 
into the paint film. After some weathering, tiny dots of rust that feel rough 
to the touch or irregular discoloration begin to appear. This type of paint 
damage is difficult to repair. Use the following procedure to remove these 
particles and contaminants. Refer to the Specifications 
 portion of this 
section for product information necessary for this procedure.

 WARNING: THE TECHNICIAN MUST WEAR PROTECTIVE CLOTHING AND EYE PROTECTION TO 
PREVENT SKIN IRRITATION. 

 CAUTION: Any changes to this procedure will cause an incomplete or 
unsatisfactory repair and can result in possible damage to the painted 
surfaces and trim. 

 CAUTION: The use of any other product or procedure can cause damage to aluminum, 
flexible painted surfaces or other painted surfaces. Follow directions exactly 
and rinse thoroughly after each step. 

 NOTE: This procedure must be performed before any buffing, polishing, color 
sanding or refinishing is attempted. The materials in this procedure are 
alkaline, acidic and neutral. They must be used in the specified order.

 NOTE: This decontamination procedure is designed to remove surface 
contaminants from the paint on vehicles that have been contaminated up to 120 
days. Vehicles that have experienced the condition longer than this period 
might require an additional treatment to remove metal contaminants.

 NOTE: Ford does not recommend the use of oxalic acids or other fallout 
removal products. Use Finish Kare, Inc., products 1119, 883, and 118SC to 
decontaminate the paint surface.

Rinse off dust and debris with cold water. Be sure to start at the 
bottom of vehicle and work up.

Prepare product 1119 by mixing one part product 1119 with four parts 
cold water.

Use clean wash mitt and apply mixture to entire vehicle, starting at 
the bottom and working up to the top surface. Keep car wet with the solution 
for 5 to 10 minutes. Do not allow it to streak down the sides. Rewipe with 
mitt if necessary to avoid streaks.

Rinse vehicle with cold water.

Dry the flat surface of the vehicle hood and roof.

 NOTE: Product 883 is ready to use from the bottle. No mixing is necessary.

Apply product 883 directly to the contaminated surfaces using a clean, 
dry sponge, wash mitt, or soft truck brush. Keep the areas wet with product 
883 for 5 to 7 minutes. Do not allow to dry on vehicle. Wipe down to the body 
line on the sides.

Prepare product 118SC by mixing 0.03 liter (1 oz) with 3.7 liters (1 
gallon) of water.

 NOTE: Do not use the same mitt to apply shampoo that was used to apply 
product 883 or 1119. Always keep these mitts separate.

Shampoo the vehicle with product 118SC mixture using a clean wash mitt. 
Rinse with cold water.

Inspect the paint surface to see if rust particles have been removed. 
If rust particles have been on the vehicle for a long period of time, it may 
be necessary to repeat each of the previous steps. Acid rain discoloration or 
etching will require either buffing, color sanding or refinishing if etching 
is visible.

 Correction of Surface Following Decontamination 

Use the buffing products from only one manufacturer. Do not intermix 
products.

Always follow the manufacturer's product sequence. Use appropriate pads 
with each product as recommended by the manufacturer.

Use a dual action sander with a Velcro®-mount backing 
plate and appropriate foam pad for final polishing swirl removal.

Use an alcohol and water mixture (1:4 ratio) to clean buffed areas to 
verify removal of scratches and swirls before application of final protective 
glaze.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Repainting

 CAUTION: Some state and local governments have specific health and safety 
regulations that recommend the use of special breathing apparatus when using 
finishing materials containing toxic products. 

Before attempting repainting, determine the surface and overall 
condition of the existing paint. Horizontal surfaces usually show the greatest 
surface deterioration.

Carefully inspect the hood and roof panel to determine the overall 
condition of the paint.

Clean the areas being inspected and look carefully for any signs of 
surface deterioration or any other form of film breakdown such as checking, 
cracking or humidity blistering. In particular, note the gloss level. Low 
gloss indicates surface irregularities caused by such defects as checking or 
blistering.

Look for evidence of brittleness, poor adhesion or excessive chipping. 
If in doubt about the condition of the paint, scrape the finish slightly and 
examine further.

If a complete repaint job is necessary, plan a painting sequence, 
primarily for the sake of continuity so as to avoid dry joint overlaps and 
minimize unnecessary work, before beginning to spray.

Spray all locations that are not easily accessible (hood and hood 
edges, drain channels, door jambs). Keep doors slightly ajar to prevent 
sticking and to permit efficient drying. The purpose of this initial spraying 
is to remove dust that otherwise might be blown about and adversely affect the 
exterior finishing operation.

 Respray Sequence 

Once the difficult access areas have been sprayed, begin painting 
vehicle in the following sequence:

Paint the roof panel at the rear corner, along the drip rail to the 
front body pillar, then paint the rail inward toward the roof panel center.

Move to the opposite side of the body. Pick up the wet paint edge by 
applying the paint from the center of the roof panel. Continue outward and 
along the drip rail to the front body pillar and finish the roof panel by 
spraying the rear corner pillar.

Extend the coat application down the rear corner pillar, then paint the 
entire body side, including the door and vertical portion of the hood assembly.

Move across the front cowl and horizontal portion of the hood assembly.

Continue along the vertical portion of the opposite side of the hood 
assembly and along the body side including the door and the rear corner pillar.

Paint the back panel.

 Drying Paint Repair Work 

Following the painting procedure, dry vehicle paint thoroughly to 
ensure the best protection from organic and chemical elements.

 NOTE: If all openings caused by missing window frames, etc., are properly 
masked, it is not necessary to remove plastic parts from the interior of the 
vehicle.

Remove or cover the radiator grille. Cover the turn signal indicator 
lamps, headlamps, any lamps located on the roof panel, air horns and exterior 
mirrors.

Dry the vehicle at approximately 90°C (200°
F).

Monitor the temperature of the passenger compartment.

Latch doors in the first catch to avoid distortion of the weatherstrips.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Drain Holes

Drain holes are located on the underside of each door along the weld 
line of the inner and outer panels. If these holes become clogged with mud or 
road tars, water will collect inside the panels and rust the sheet metal from 
the inside. A sound of sloshing water in a door is an indication of this 
condition.

Check the drain holes regularly. Clean dirt and foreign material from 
the drain holes with a punch or screwdriver.

Section 01-00: Body Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Trim

The trim on the vehicles requires no special care. Periodic cleaning 
will preserve the beauty and life of the finishes. Wash with clear water or, 
if the parts are very dirty, use Multi-Purpose Cleaner Concentrate 
B8A-19523-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M14P4-A using a 
clean soft cloth or a sponge and water. Rinse and wipe the parts dry. Custom 
Bright Metal Cleaner 8A-19522-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESR-M5B194-B can be used sparingly to remove rust, salt and road chemicals 
from aluminum or stainless steel parts. Do not scour aluminum parts with steel 
wool or polish them with products containing abrasives. A wax will provide 
excellent protection for all bright metal parts.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Body Maintenance

Regular body maintenance preserves the vehicle's appearance and reduces 
the cost of maintenance during the life of the vehicle. The following steps 
are suggested as a guide for regular body maintenance.

Vacuum the interior thoroughly and wash the vehicle.

Check all openings for water leaks, and seal where necessary.

Inspect weatherstrip channel and crimp together as required to ensure 
retention on body opening flange.

Replace all door weatherstrips that are unfit for service.

Replace all cracked, fogged or chipped glass.

Align the hood and doors if necessary.

Inspect the windshield wiper blades and replace them if necessary.

Tighten the sill plate and garnish moulding screws.

Clean the seats, door trim panels and headlining.

Touch up or paint chipped or scratched areas.

Periodically clean drain holes located on the underside of each body 
panel and door.

SPECIFICATIONS

SPECIFICATIONS

 LUBRICANT/ADHESIVE/CLEANER SPECIFICATIONS

Description

 Removal 

 CAUTION: During disassembly, the hood hinges will support the open hood when the 
check cables are disconnected if the hood is not allowed to slam against the 
stop action of the hinge. During assembly, it is mandatory that the check 
cables be attached at the cowl end as soon as the hood is installed.

scratching the grille. Tilt the hood assembly forward.

attaching point on the hood and tilt the hood forward.

ADJUSTMENTS

Hood Alignment

The portion of the hinge assembly that attaches to the hood provides 
fore-and-aft and in-and-out adjustment; the portion attached to the chassis 
provides up and down adjustment. To correct a misaligned hood, use the 
following procedure. 

Loosen the three bolts retaining each hinge to the hood. Slide the hood 
fore or aft to establish a consistent 6.35-mm (0.25-inch) vertical margin 
between the hood and right and left cowl side panels. 

Slide the hood inboard or outboard, as required, to obtain a flush fit 
between the surfaces of the hood and right and left cowl side panels. 

Tighten the three hinge-to-hood retaining bolts to specification. 

If an upward or downward adjustment is needed to align the upper back 
edge of the hood with the cowl top panel, loosen the three hinge-to-chassis 
bolts and raise or lower the hood and hinge assembly as required. There is a 
3/8-inch diameter production tool hole that can be used to assist in 
alignment. Insert a 3/8-inch drill bit into the hole and pass it into the 
mating hole in the chassis-mounted hinge bracket. When the adjustment is 
completed, tighten the hinge retaining bolts to specification.

ADJUSTMENTS

Hood Latch 

The hood latch adjustment provides a means of increasing or decreasing 
hood latch tension. To increase latch tension, turn the head of the latch 
clockwise. Counterclockwise rotation decreases latch tension.

Section 01-03: Doors

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Doors 

 Removal 

Remove all usable hardware, trim, glass parts, and watershield, if so 
equipped.

Remove the upper and lower hinge access hole cover plates (if so 
equipped). Mark the location of the hinge on the door and body. 

Remove the door-to-lower hinge retaining bolts. 

Support the door, and remove the door-to-upper hinge retaining bolts. 
Slide the door off the hinges. 

If a hinge is to be replaced, remove the hinge-to-pillar bolts and the 
hinge. 

 Installation 

Install the door weatherstrip in proper position. 

If a hinge has been removed, install the hinge in the pillar in 
approximately the same position as the removed hinge. 

Position the door on the hinges, and install the retaining bolts snugly. 

Install the lock mechanism. Install the glass mechanism, glass, and 
vent window assembly. Make all necessary adjustments as these assemblies are 
installed. Refer to Section 01-14 for lock assembly adjustments and Section 01-11 for glass and window mechanism adjustments. 

Adjust the door, and tighten all hinge bolts securely. To provide a 
good weatherstrip seal, the upper front edge of the door must be 4.57 mm (0.18 
inch) inboard of the upper part of the pillar from the belt line to a point 
near the top of the door. The adjustment is made by adjusting the upper 
striker of the right door inboard 4.57 mm (0.18 inch). 

Install the watershield, if so equipped. Cement the top edge to the 
inside surface of the inner panel. 

Install the hinge access hole cover plates and the door access hole 
cover plate.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Trim Panel, Roof, High Level Interior 

 Removal 

Remove four screws retaining radio speaker housing. Disconnect speaker 
wire, and remove speaker. 

Peel off front and rear plastic retaining strips. 

Remove air horn lanyard forward retaining screw. 

Remove air horn valve cover (left side) screws. 

Starting from either side, pull the edge of the headliner from beneath 
the door weatherstrip. 

Pull the headliner gently down until all eight Velcro®
 fasteners retaining the center disengage. 

Remove the headliner from the vehicle. 

 Installation 

Position the headliner between the doors and metal retainers, letting 
the center droop so as not to engage the Velcro® fasteners. 

Make sure the headliner is centered front to rear and side to side. 

Push up the center of the headliner engaging the eight Velcro®
 fasteners. 

Position air horn valve cover and secure with retaining screws. 

Install air horn lanyard forward retaining screw. 

Install front and rear plastic retaining strips. 

Connect speaker wires. Position radio speaker housing and four 
retaining screws.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

 Removal

wire, and remove speaker.

the door weatherstrip.

Pull the headliner gently down until all eight Velcro®
 fasteners retaining the center disengage.

Remove the headliner from the vehicle.

 Installation 

Position the headliner between the doors and metal retainers, letting 
the center droop so as not to engage the Velcro® fasteners.

Make sure the headliner is centered front to rear and side to side.

Push up the center of the headliner engaging the eight Velcro®
 fasteners.

Secure the headliner with the retainer screws. Position the roof vent 
retainer and fasten with screws.

Position air horn valve cover and secure with retaining screws.

Install air horn lanyard forward retaining screw.

Install front and rear plastic retaining strips.

Connect speaker wires. Then position radio speaker housing and four 
retaining screws.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Cowl Assembly

 Hood Cowl Alignment 

Do not attempt to align the cowl to the hood by elongating or modifying 
the hood hinge mounting holes if the hood-to-cowl gap is 19.05 mm (3/4 inch) 
or less and even side-to-side. (For LLS, LTLS, LLA and LTLA, margin is 9.52 mm [
.375 inch]). No attempt should be made to decrease the 
(design) gap.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Airshield, Roof, Aeromax

 Removal 

Remove side air deflector fasteners and vertical muffler heat shield 
mounting brackets, if so equipped.

Remove body side deflectors.

Remove eight roof-mounted brackets and remove roof airshield. Clean old 
sealer from roof.

Remove grab handle reinforcing brackets from side trim panels and 
remove grab handles.

 Installation 

Open manufacturer's kit. Refer to installation instructions and read 
instructions thoroughly.

Refer to parts listing and make sure all parts are present.

 NOTE: Skip Step 3 if vehicle was already equipped with airshield or side 
deflectors.

Remove fasteners covering holes in roof and side trim panels.

Attach grab handles to side trim panels with reinforcing brackets.

[FIGURE: N6067C.gif]

Install eight roof-mounted brackets. Use fasteners supplied with kit, 
and attach to roof using Ford Threadlock and Sealer EOAZ-19554-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G315-A5 to ensure the fasteners are installed 
securely and to prevent noise and vibration from entering the cab.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Spare Tire Carrier

 WARNING: DO NOT ALLOW ANY PORTION OF YOUR BODY TO BE UNDER THE CARRIER WHILE 
REMOVING THE TIRE. THE TIRE IS HEAVY AND CAN CAUSE PERSONAL INJURY IF DROPPED. 

 Removal 

Loosen both hinge bolt nuts (do not remove completely).

While supporting the channel assembly, slide the left hinge bolt/nut 
assembly out of the channel assembly.

Slowly lower the channel assembly to the floor/ground.

Remove the spare tire.

 Installation 

Reverse Steps 1 through 4. 

Install stop bar using last hole toward rear of frame.

 Removal

lower support.

mounting support and remove the mirror assembly.

Section 01-10B: Seat, Cush-N-Aire

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Seat Support and Base Assembly 

 Removal 

Remove the protective covering (if so equipped) from the seat base. 

Press switch until all air is exhausted from the air spring. 

Disconnect the air hose from the air hose fitting, then remove the 
fitting from the air spring. Plug the hose and fitting to prevent dirt or 
other matter from entering. 

Remove the nuts, washers and bolts retaining the base and upright 
assembly to the cab deck. Remove the seat assembly from the cab. 

Remove the lock nuts and bolts retaining the track bar and upper seat 
assembly to the seat support assembly. Remove the track bar and upper seat 
assembly. 

Raise the seat assembly to maximum height, then place a wood block 
between the lower arm and the base and upright assembly. 

Remove the retaining ring from the air spring. 

Remove the pin clip retaining the air spring to the lower arm assembly. 
Remove the air spring. 

Remove the nuts and bolts retaining the shock absorber to the upper arm 
and to the base and upright assembly. Remove the shock absorber from the seat 
assembly. 

Using snap ring pliers, remove the snap rings from the shaft assembly. 

 NOTE: The two shafts to be driven out are connected at the opposite end. To 
prevent binding, drive shafts evenly and a little at a time.

Using a drift punch, drive out the shafts from the base assembly and 
the seat support assembly.

Remove the sleeves from the base assembly and seat support assembly. 
Remove the seat support, upper arm and lower arm from the base. 

Remove the bearings from the upper and lower arm shafts. 

 Installation 

Place the lower end of the shock absorber in the mounting bracket of 
the base and upright assembly. Using a new spacer and bushings, install the 
bolt and nut. Tighten the nut to 34 Nm (25 lb-ft). 

Install the bearings in the upper and lower arm shafts. 

Place the lower and upper arms on the base, aligning the arm tubes and 
bearings with the holes in the base. Install the sleeves into the holes of the 
base. 

Install the shaft assembly through the base and the arm assembly tubes. 
Using snap ring pliers, install the snap rings and secure the shaft and arm 
assemblies to the base. 

Using new spacers and bushings, position the shock absorber so the 
extended arm end is in the mounting bracket of the upper arm. 

Install the bolts and nuts to retain the shock absorber to the upper 
arm. Tighten the nuts to 34 Nm (25 lb-ft). 

Position the air spring in the lower arm assembly. Install the pin clip. 

Install the retaining ring on the air spring. 

Align the lower and upper arm tubes and bearings with the holes in the 
seat support assembly, then install the sleeves into the seat support holes. 

Insert the shaft assembly through the seat support and through the 
upper arm and lower arm tubes. Using snap ring pliers, install the snap rings 
to secure the shaft and arm assemblies to the seat support. 

Align the top of the air spring with the hole in the seat support 
assembly. Unplug the air hose and fitting. Install the fitting on the air 
spring. 

Place the track bars and upper seat assembly on the seat support 
assembly. Unplug the air hose and fitting. Install the fitting on the air 
spring. 

Place the seat assembly on the cab deck. 

Install the bolts through the seat base, upright assembly and the cab 
deck. Install the washers and nuts. Tighten the nuts to 34 Nm 
(25 lb-ft).

Connect the air hose to the fitting on the air spring. 

Install the protective covering (if so equipped) on the seat base. 
Adjust the seat base as needed.

================================================================================
PAGE 4209
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 01-10B: Seat, Cush-N-Aire

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Spring 

 Removal 

Remove the protective covering (if so equipped) from the seat base. 

Raise the seat assembly to maximum height, then place a wood block 
between the lower arm and the base and upright assembly. 

Press switch until all air is exhausted from the air spring. 

Remove the plastic tie strap retaining the lower seat cushion to the 
lower frame assembly. 

Remove the capscrews retaining the seat cushion to the front cushion 
brackets. Remove the seat cushion. 

Disconnect the air hose from the air hose fitting on the air spring. 
Remove the fitting from the air spring. Plug the hose and fitting to prevent 
dirt or other matter from entering. 

Remove the retaining ring from the air spring. 

Remove the pin clip retaining the air spring to the lower arm assembly. 
Remove the air spring. 

 Installation 

Position the air spring in the lower arm assembly. Install the pin clip. 

Install the retaining ring on the air spring. 

Unplug the air hose and fitting. Install the fitting on the air spring, 
then connect the air hose to the fitting. 

Position the seat cushion, then install the front cushion brackets and 
capscrews. 

Install a new plastic tie strap to secure the seat cushion to the lower 
frame assembly. 

Remove the wood block from between the lower arm and the base and 
upright assembly. 

Install the protective covering (if so equipped) on the seat base. 
Adjust the seat as needed.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Chugger Bearing Kit 

 Removal 

Cut plastic tie strap and raise seat cushion. 

Make sure chugger isolator handle is in the up position. 

Remove two lock nuts. 

While holding seat, slide bearings support rail up and off track studs. 
Two bearings will fall off. 

Move seat frame to the opposite side to expose the two bearings. Remove 
bearings. 

If only bearings are being replaced, stop at this point and replace 
with new bearings after inspecting bearing studs for wear. 

If entire chugger kit is to be replaced, remove the other two lock nuts 
on the bearing support assembly and remove the welded assembly. 

 Installation 

Use a good grade of grease such as Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or 
-K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to thoroughly 
lubricate the bearing and cups. 

Install the welded frame bearing support onto the track studs and 
tighten lock nuts. 

Install two bearings on round posts and align lower seat frame bearing 
cups over bearings. 

While holding one side in place, assemble the loose bearing rail and 
the two remaining bearings. Tighten two lock nuts. Do not overtighten lock 
nuts; bearings must turn freely. 

Push chugger assembly fore and aft to determine the position of the 
bearing rail before tightening lock nuts. It should be tight enough to 
eliminate side play without interfering with the fore and aft movement of the 
seat. 

Lower seat cushion, and replace plastic tie strap at rear of seat.

Section 01-10C: Seat, Bostrom Air-915

1997 L-LTL-Series Vehicles Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Seats, Front

 WARNING: SERIOUS INJURY CAN OCCUR IF HEAD CLEARANCE IS NOT ADEQUATE. BEFORE 
DRIVING OR RIDING IN VEHICLE, MAKE SURE THERE IS ADEQUATE HEAD CLEARANCE AT 
MAXIMUM UPWARD TRAVEL OF SEAT. 

 NOTE: Refer to Section 01-10A for passenger seat service procedures.

 NOTE: Safety belts should be worn at all times when operating the vehicle.

To check for adequate head clearance, sit in the seat and slowly raise 
it to its maximum upward position using proper comfort adjustment. 

The Bostrom Air-915 seat provides five adjustments to accommodate the 
size, weight, and proportions of the driver. 

The seat air suspension system uses a rolling lobe air spring, with air 
supplied by the vehicle's air system.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Shock Absorber 

 NOTE: Seat need not be removed from vehicle.

 Removal 

Be sure suspension is at maximum height. Add air if needed. 

Move channel assembly full rearward to gain working room. 

Use pliers or screwdriver to twist off push-on fasteners (not reusable). 

Remove damper assembly. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: A 1/2-inch box end wrench works well to push fasteners on. 

Install new damper with flanges of bearings to the outside of the 
suspension. 

Add thrust washers and install push-on fasteners until seated.

Section 01-10C: Seat, Bostrom Air-915

1997 L-LTL-Series Vehicles Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Spring 

 NOTE: Seat need not be removed from vehicle.

 NOTE: Seat/back assembly and channel assembly need not be removed. Move 
channel assembly to rearmost position to gain working room. 

 Removal 

Fill air spring assembly so seat is at maximum height. 

Block suspension up with a spacer placed between the base riser and the 
upper frame. 

Release air pressure from air spring so seat is supported by spacer. 

Disconnect air line from air spring assembly by pushing in collar of 
fitting while pulling air line out of fitting. 

Remove top screw and loosen bottom screw through rear opening in base 
riser. Remove air spring assembly from suspension. 

 Installation 

Assemble bottom screw to new air spring assembly. Install air spring 
with screw into keyhole opening in bottom of base riser. Position air spring 
so that fitting at bottom of air spring is toward front of seat. 

Tighten screw at bottom of air spring assembly to 13-14 Nm
 (10-11 lb-ft). 

Install screw at top of air spring assembly and tighten to 21-25 Nm
 (16-18 lb-ft). 

Reconnect air line to fitting in air spring assembly by pushing tube 
into fitting. 

Fill air spring assembly and remove spacer block.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Seat, Bucket, Back 

 Disassembly 

Move fore and aft isolation channel assembly with seat back assembly to 
most rearward position. Remove two screws and flatwashers from underside of 
channel assembly. 

Remove two shoulder bolts from channel assembly. 

Move seat/back assembly forward to disengage seat tilt cam assembly 
from sleeve bearings on channel assembly. 

 Assembly 

Follow disassembly procedure in reverse order.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Cover and Pad 

 Disassembly 

Remove upper seat assembly from the suspension, exposing bottom side of 
seat. 

Remove seat cover and pad from seat frame assembly. Note location of 
fasteners on existing seat cover. Do not remove small vinyl patch from seat 
tilt handle unless it needs replacement. 

 Assembly 

Place new pad over seat frame, making sure back edge of pad is hooked 
over rear support tube. If seat is equipped with a seat tilt adjustment, make 
a cut in the bottom edge of pad (RH side) to fit around the handle. 

Place cover over seat tilt and position it over pad. Fold rear half of 
cover forward to expose the three tie-down tabs. Push tabs through the holes 
in foam. Reposition cover and turn seat over. 

Pull tie down tabs tight and attach to the center support wire (third 
wire from rear). Use one hog ring per tab. 

Insert the longest wire into looped material sewn to bottom of cover. 
Place shorter wire into rear flap of cover. 

Pull rear corners of side panels rearward around back corners of frame. 
Attach material with one hog ring per side. 

Starting at the front of the seat cover and working rearward, hog ring 
the wire through the holes in seat frame. Ten hog rings required for frame. 
Fold rear flap down and toward front of seat. Pull tightly and fasten with 
three hog rings to most rearward foam support wire. 

Remount seat.

Section 01-10C: Seat, Bostrom Air-915

1997 L-LTL-Series Vehicles Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Backrest Cover and Pad 

 Disassembly 

Remove upper seat assembly from the suspension. Remove armrests and 
fasteners if seat assembly has armrests. 

Remove back cover and pad from seat frame assembly. Note location of 
fasteners on existing back cover. 

 Assembly 

Place new pad over back frame. If seat has lumbar adjustment, make a 
cut in the edge of pad (LH side) to fit around the handle. 

 NOTE: There will be two sets of tie-down tabs (six total with two wires) to 
be pulled through the back pad and wired. 

Place cover (inside out) over top of back pad. Pull down cover until 
three tie-down tabs are even with three slots in pad. Pull tie-down tabs 
through slots in pad and run short wire through all three tabs. Work cover 
around lumbar adjustment handle (if seat has lumbar) and continue to pull 
cover down completely over pad. Tuck front flap of back cover between seat 
cushion and bottom of back pad. Insert two long wires into looped material 
sewn to bottom of cover. (One in rear flap and one in front flap.) Starting at 
top, pull cover down tight and hog ring the two wires at bottom of cover 
together behind seat pad with three hog rings. 

Remount seat. 

When ordering replacement components, order by color and material as 
follows: black vinyl, brown vinyl, gray vinyl, black cloth and vinyl, brown 
cloth and vinyl, gray cloth and vinyl, blue cloth and vinyl, red cloth and 
vinyl, cocoa cloth and vinyl, red velour and vinyl, cocoa velour and vinyl. 
Some components are not available separately. Order the kit that includes the 
parts required.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Channel Roller 

 NOTE: Removal of seat/back assembly will make channel removal easier, but is 
not necessary. 

 Disassembly 

Adjust channel assembly to rearmost position. 

With isolator handle on channel assembly in isolation position, push 
channel assembly forward to expose screw and nut. Remove screw and nut and 
save for reassembly. 

Move isolator handle on channel assembly to fore and aft release 
position. Slide channel assembly forward past both sets of rollers. 

Be careful not to lose parts. Either remove and save for reassembly or 
replace with new parts from roller assembly kit. 

 Assembly 

Follow disassembly procedure in reverse order. See lateral side play 
adjustment procedure, if required. 

If seat/back assembly was removed, reassemble.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Isolator Springs 

 Disassembly 

Remove seat/back assembly and channel assembly. 

Remove two isolator springs by carefully extending and disengaging from 
mounting points. 

Slide latch bar until retaining ring can be seen through hole in 
channel assembly. Remove retaining ring and keep for reassembly. 

Pull latch bar free of pivot block. 

 NOTE: Pivot block can be removed by removing screw and lockwasher, and screw 
and lock nut. 

Rubber isolation bumpers are now accessible and can be replaced if 
necessary. 

 Assembly 

Follow disassembly procedure in reverse order.

Section 01-10C: Seat, Bostrom Air-915

1997 L-LTL-Series Vehicles Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Suspension 

 Disassembly 

Bleed all air from supply line. Disconnect air supply line to seat. 
Using air valve, exhaust all air from air spring. Remove complete seat 
assembly from vehicle. 

Remove seat/back assembly and channel assembly from suspension. Be 
careful not to lose parts for reassembly. 

If seat assembly has a suspension cover, remove along with fasteners, 
after removing ICP bracket and capscrews. 

Block suspension up with a spacer placed between the base riser and the 
upper frame. 

Remove air valve by loosening nut on valve and removing from bracket on 
upper frame assembly. 

Remove capscrews from upper front bearing blocks. 

Remove upper frame assembly by sliding it forward off bearing blocks 
and slide blocks. 

Remove air spring screws. Disconnect air line from fitting and remove 
air spring assembly. Mark air line for reassembly. 

Remove damper assembly by removing push-on fasteners (not reusable) and 
washers. 

Remove capscrews from lower front bearing blocks and slide lever 
assemblies forward until bearing blocks are removed from channel on base 
riser. Then slide lever assemblies rearward until slide blocks are removed 
from channel. Be careful not to pinch fingers in lever assemblies. 

Remove shoulder bolts and nuts from pivots of lever assemblies and 
inspect. Replace if worn. 

 Assembly 

Replace bearings at pivots on lever assembly by pushing the old out and 
pressing in new. Flange of bearings should be on outside of lever assembly. 
Tighten pivot shoulder bolts to 25-29 Nm (19-21 lb-ft). 

Put new bearing blocks and slide blocks on levers with beveled surfaces 
outward and slide levers with blocks into channel on base riser. Tighten 
screws to 37-44 Nm (28-32 lb-ft). 

Slide upper frame assembly over blocks. Line up screws with bearing 
blocks and tighten screws to 37-44 Nm (28-32 lb-ft). 

Manually move suspension up and down to make sure there are no 
clearance problems. Be careful not to pinch fingers in linkage. 

Block up suspension and reinstall air spring assembly. Tighten upper 
screw to 21-25 Nm (16-18 lb-ft) and lower screw to 13-14 Nm
 (116-123 lb-in). 

Reinstall damper assembly with washer and push-on nuts. 

Remove any blocks, remount air valve to bracket on upper frame.

Reinstall suspension cover and ICP brackets if removed previously. 

Install channel assembly and seat/back assembly. Make sure parts are 
installed correctly on roller pins. If necessary, adjust lateral side play. 
Refer to Lateral Side Play in the Adjustments portion of this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Operator Seat Adjustments 

 Driver's Weight 

The seat level weight adjustment is controlled by the air control push 
button valve at the left front corner of the seat cushion. Pushing the valve 
button in after sitting on the seat, automatically adjusts the seat for the 
driver's weight. 

 Seat Back Angle 

Lean forward slightly to remove pressure from seat back. Hold handle 
rearward to adjust to any position within range. 

 Seat Height 

 WARNING: SERIOUS INJURY CAN OCCUR IF HEAD CLEARANCE IS NOT ADEQUATE. BEFORE 
DRIVING OR RIDING IN VEHICLE, MAKE SURE THERE IS ADEQUATE HEAD CLEARANCE AT 
MAXIMUM UPWARD TRAVEL OF SEAT. 

 NOTE: Safety belts should be worn at all times when operating the vehicle.

To check for adequate head clearance, sit in the seat and slowly raise 
it to its maximum upward position using proper comfort adjustment. 

To adjust, push valve knob in to raise seat and pull out to lower it. 
When adjusted properly, the seat should not top or bottom against the end 
limits of the vertical travel under normal driving conditions. Adjustment 
position should also provide for driving visibility and vehicle control. 

 Seat Cushion Tilt Adjustment 

Move seat tilt handle downward to decrease or upward to increase seat 
tilt to one of five possible positions. 

 Lumbar Adjustment 

Rotate handle forward to increase or rearward to decrease the support 
in the lumbar area to one of the three positions provided. 

 Fore and Aft Isolator 

Hold lever to left to adjust seat position forward or backward a total 
of six inches (150 mm). 

Isolation is provided when lever is in center (straight forward) 
position. To lock out, move lever to right. 

 Lateral Side Play 

Remove seat/back assembly from channel assembly. 

Reposition channel assembly until Allen head adjusting screws in right 
isolator roller shafts on upper frame are visible in cutouts on right hand 
side of channel assembly. 

Use a 3-mm Allen wrench (do not use a 1/8-inch Allen wrench) to adjust 
the screws. Turn screws in until resistance is felt plus 1-1/2 turns. 

 NOTE: To ensure best performance, make certain parts are assembled correctly. 

Move channel assembly through entire fore and aft adjustment range to 
check lateral clearance for binding. Isolator springs should return channel to 
neutral position for best ride.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Door Window Glass, Front

 Removal 

Remove the access panel from the door.

Remove the vent window division bar retaining screw at the belt line. 

Remove the four screws retaining the vent window assembly to the door 
frame.

Remove the bolt retaining the glass run retainer and bracket to the 
division bar lower bracket.

Remove the vent window assembly from the door.

Lower the glass to the full down position and disconnect the regulator 
arms from the channel brackets (Views A and B in the following illustration).

Remove the regulator retaining screws and regulator handle. Remove the 
regulator assembly from the door.

Remove door glass, channel bracket and equalizer bracket.

Lay glass on flat surface and check flatness with straightedge from 
forward edge to rear edge. Glass must be flat within 1.52 mm (0.06 inch) from 
front to back. If not within this specification, replace glass.

retaining the glass run retainer and bracket to the division bar lower bracket.

Install the regulator handle.

channel and regulator assembly rollers with a generous amount of Multi-Purpose 
Grease D7AZ-19584-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M1C106-B.

COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M13P4-A to all side 
glass weatherstripping. Run glass up and down through full travel, and adjust 
run retainers if necessary.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Window Regulator

 Removal 

Remove door trim panel and access cover, if so equipped.

Support the glass in the full up position.

 CAUTION: Be careful not to damage sheet metal holes during drilling. 

Remove the center pin from the regulator retaining rivets with a drift 
punch. Drill the head from each rivet using a 6.35-mm (1/4-inch) drill, and 
remove the rivet.

Disengage the regulator arm from the glass bracket and remove the 
regulator.

 Installation 

Position the regulator in the door and insert the arm into the glass 
bracket channels.

Position regulator to the inner panel and install rivets using Rotunda 
Blind Fastener Installation Tool 107-R0600 or equivalent to attach the 
regulator to the inner panel. If hand tool for installing the pop rivets is 
not available, use a 1/4-20 x 1/2-inch screw and washer assembly and a 1/4-20 
nut and washer assembly.

Check the operation of the window mechanism and install the door trim 
panel.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Windshield Glass

 Removal 

Remove the windshield wiper arms and blades.

Loosen the weatherstrip around the windshield opening.

Push the windshield glass and mouldings, if so equipped, out of the 
windshield opening from inside the vehicle.

Remove the mouldings, if so equipped, from the weatherstrip.

Remove the weatherstrip from the glass.

Clean the glass and weatherstrip of all old sealer if either is to be 
reused.

 Installation 

Clean the windshield opening flange to remove all old sealer or other 
foreign material. Make sure drain slots are clean.

Apply Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G162-A to the windshield opening flange.

Position the weatherstrip on the windshield glass.

Insert a draw cord in the pinch weld opening all around the 
weatherstrip. Overlap the cord about 457 mm (18 inches) at the lower center of 
the glass. Tape the ends of the cord to the inside of the glass.

[FIGURE: N11271B.gif]

Coat the weatherstrip mounting surfaces with a rubber lubricant meeting 
Ford specification ESA-M1B6-A. Position the mouldings on the weatherstrip.

Position the windshield and weatherstrip to the windshield opening.

With an assistant applying hand pressure to the outside of the 
windshield, pull the draw cord from the inside to pull the lip of the 
weatherstrip over the windshield opening flange. Draw the lip of the 
weatherstrip over the lower flange, each side of the flange, and then over the 
upper flange.

Clean the glass and surrounding area.

Install the windshield wiper arms and blades.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Window Glass, Back

 Removal 

With a helper outside, loosen the weatherstrip and push the glass inward.

Remove the weatherstrip from the glass.

Clean the back window opening flange, and check the flange for wavy 
areas and service as necessary.

Clean the weatherstrip with cleaning solvent to remove all the old 
sealer and cement.

 Installation 

Apply Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G162-A in the glass crevice of the weatherstrip, and 
install it on the glass.

Run a bead of Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification ESB-M4G162-A around the opening flange and in the flange 
crevice in the weatherstrip.

Install a draw cord all around the weatherstrip in the flange crevice. 
Let the draw cord overlap at the bottom center. Apply rubber lubricant to the 
lip of the weatherstrip.

Position the glass assembly in the opening. With a helper applying hand 
pressure from the inside, draw the lip of the weatherstrip over the window 
opening lower flange, each side flange, and then over the upper flange.

Water test the installation for leaks. If leaks exist, apply caulk and 
additional sealer.

Clean the window and the surrounding area.

LUBRICATION

Window Regulator

The window glass mechanism should be properly lubricated whenever the 
glass channel or front door window regulator assembly is removed or excessive 
effort is required to operate the windows. To lubricate a door window 
regulator, apply an even coating of Multi-Purpose Grease D7AZ-19584-AA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M1C106-B to the window regulator 
rollers, shafts and the entire length of the roller guides.

ADJUSTMENTS

Window Glass, Door

Secure loose door glass by performing the following adjustment procedure.

Lower glass to full down position.

Using blunt tools, remove door glass run at rear of door frame from top 
of door to bolt.

Install a piece of two-sided Vinyl Foam Tape C6AZ-19627-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESB-M3G77-A 12.7 mm (1/2 inch) wide x 3.18 mm (1/8 
inch) thick x 355.6 mm (14 inches) long as a shim in the run retainer.

Install run and cycle glass up and down to check for smooth operation.

[FIGURE: N1896C.gif]

 Longitudinal Adjustment 

If, after performing above adjustment procedure, glass tilts or comes 
out of glass runs approximately two-thirds of the way up, perform the 
following steps.

Remove door trim panel and watershield.

Lower glass to full down position.

Loosen self-tapping screws retaining vent window to door frame. Loosen 
retainer screw for vent window division bar.

Raise vent window as high into door frame as it will go and tighten 
self-tapping screws. Tighten lower retaining screw.

Cycle glass up and down to check for smooth operation.

Install door trim panel and watershield.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Latch, Door

 Removal 

Remove the door trim panel or door access hole cover.

Disconnect the remote control link and the push-button rod from the 
latch assembly. 

Remove the outer handle-to-latch rod and clip. 

Remove the lock cylinder-to-latch rod and clip. 

Remove three screws retaining the latch to the door and remove the 
latch assembly. 

 Installation 

Lubricate the latch assembly with Multi-Purpose Grease Spray 
D7AZ-19584-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M1C106-B.

Position the latch assembly to the door and install the three retaining 
screws. 

Connect the push-button rod and the remote control link to the latch 
assembly. 

Connect the lock cylinder-to-latch rod and clip. 

Connect the outer handle-to-latch rod and clip. 

Check the operation of the latch and install the door trim panel and 
door access hole cover.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Lock Cylinder, Door

 Removal 

When a lock cylinder is replaced, both door lock cylinders and the 
ignition lock cylinder should be replaced in a set. This will prevent the need 
to carry an extra key that will fit only one lock. If a key is to be replaced, 
the new key code number is stamped on a metal tag attached to the key. 

Position the window all the way up. 

Remove the access hole cover and trim panel and pull away the 
watershield (if so equipped). 

Disconnect the lock actuating rod from the lock control link clip. 

Slide the lock cylinder retainer away from the lock cylinder. 

Remove the lock cylinder. 

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order. 

Attach watershield (if equipped) using Weatherstrip Adhesive 
E8AZ-19552-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M2G14-A.

ADJUSTMENTS

Striker, Door Latch

Use Torx® Drive Bit Set D79P-2100-T or equivalent 
where required to loosen or tighten striker. 

The striker pin can be adjusted laterally and vertically as well as 
fore and aft. Do not adjust the latch striker to correct door sag. The latch 
striker should be shimmed to get the clearance shown, between the latch 
striker and the latch.

To check door latch clearance:

Clean latch jaws and striker.

Apply a thin layer of dark grease, such as Premium Long-Life Grease 
XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to striker 
pin.

Open and close door several times until a measurable pattern is visible 
in grease on striker.

 NOTE: Do not use more than two shims.

Loosen striker and install or remove shims as needed to bring striker 
contact pattern within specification of 2.38-3.97 mm (3/32-5/32 inch) from top 
of striker pin head and align door with cab. 

Tighten striker screws to 14-27 Nm (10-20 lb-ft).

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Wiper and Washer Systems

 Inspection and Verification 

Verify the customer concerns by operating the wiper and washer systems.

Visually inspect the components of the systems.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Electrical

Binding wiper pivot arms

Damaged wiper motors

Wiper mounting arm and pivot shaft improperly connected to wiper motor

Low washer fluid level

Plugged or damaged washer hoses and/or washer nozzle jet

Loose or corroded connectors

Check the windshield wiper pivot arms for proper adjustment and proper 
connection to the windshield wiper motor output arm.

Check washer hoses for proper routing and connections.

Inspect the wiper or washer system wiring harnesses and connectors for 
obvious signs of damage.

If the fault is not visually evident, determine the symptom and proceed 
to the symptom chart.

 Symptom Chart — Wiper and Washer Systems 

Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for the 
connector numbers in the pinpoint tests.

 NOTE: Use Rotunda Digital Volt-Ohmmeter 014-00407 or equivalent to perform 
electrical pinpoint tests.
