REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Windshield Wiper

 Pivot Arm 

 Removal 

Remove pivot arm retaining nut and lockwasher.

Disconnect windshield washer hose and remove pivot arm.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten the retaining nut to 9-11 Nm (80-97 lb-in).

[FIGURE: K22978B.gif]

 Pivot Shafts and Linkage 

 Removal 

Open the hood and disconnect the battery ground cable. 

Remove windshield wiper pivot arms with wiper blades attached.

Remove 16 screws retaining the cowl top vent grille to the body. Remove 
grille from vehicle. 

Remove clip from linkage and motor. 

Remove three screws retaining wiper pivot shafts to body. 

Remove linkage. 

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten pivot arm and blade assembly nut to 9-11 Nm 
(80-97 lb-in). 

 Wiper Motor, Electric 

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable. 

Remove cowl grille. 

Disconnect linkage from motor output arm crankpin by removing retaining 
clip. 

Disconnect wiring at motor. 

From engine side of dash panel, remove three bolts that retain motor to 
dash. 

 NOTE: An output shaft seal of moulded rubber is installed on the casting neck 
below the output arm. A 15.875-mm (5/8-inch) thick expanded rubber flat seal 
is used for sealing the motor to the body sheet metal. 

Remove motor.

[FIGURE: K17795C.gif]

 Installation 

If motor is being replaced, transfer output arm and moulded rubber 
shaft seal to the new motor. Install the flat expanded rubber seal before 
installing to body. 

Install motor and three retaining bolts. Tighten to 7-9 Nm
 (62-79 lb-in). 

Connect wiring at motor. 

Connect linkage to motor output arm. Install retaining clip. 

Install cowl grille. 

Connect battery ground cable. 

 Wiper Motor, Air 

 Removal 

Open two air tank petcocks to allow system air pressure to exhaust. 

Disconnect two plastic air lines from the wiper motor. 

Remove cowl grille.

Disconnect linkage from motor output arm crankpin by removing retaining 
clip.

Remove the wiper motor retaining screws and remove motor.

Transfer the fittings. 

 Installation 

Position the motor to the mounting bracket. Install retaining screws. 
Tighten screws to 4-9 Nm (36-79 lb-in).

Position the arms to the motor and install the retaining clip. 

Install cowl grille.

Connect two nylon air lines to the motor. 

Close the two air tank petcocks. 

Start the engine and check the wiper operation.

ADJUSTMENTS

Park Position 

Remove the arm and blade assemblies from the pivot shafts.

Turn on the wiper switch, allow the motor to move the pivot shafts 
three or four cycles, and then turn off the wiper switch. This will place the 
pivot shafts in PARK position.

Install the arm and blade assemblies on the pivot shafts to Dimension X 
as shown. Dimension X is the distance between the centerline of the blade 
saddle and the windshield lower moulding or weatherstrip. The value of 
Dimension X is given in the illustration.

Section 01-20: Restraints, Active

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Occupant Restraint System

 WARNING: BELT ASSEMBLIES MUST BE INSTALLED IN MATCHED SETS AS RECEIVED AND MUST 
NOT BE INTERCHANGED BETWEEN VEHICLE MODELS. IF A COMPONENT PORTION (BUCKLE 
PORTION, RETRACTOR PORTION, ETC.) OF A SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLY IS NONFUNCTIONAL 
OR DAMAGED, THE ENTIRE ASSEMBLY MUST BE REPLACED. 

 WARNING: THE REPLACEMENT ASSEMBLY MUST BE INSTALLED AS A MATCHED SET AND THE 
IDENTIFICATION LABELS ON ALL PORTIONS MUST BEAR EXACTLY THE SAME CODE, DATE OF 
MANUFACTURE AND MANUFACTURER'S NAME. UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCES ARE SAFETY BELT 
COMPONENTS TO BE REPLACED AS INDIVIDUAL COMPONENTS. 

The safety belts are factory-installed in their proper locations. If 
the safety belts are removed for any reason, they must be installed as shown 
in the illustrations in this section. Sealer is placed around all safety belt 
anchor bolt holes in the floorpan. Tighten the anchor bolts to 30-40 Nm
 (22-30 lb-ft).

================================================================================
PAGE 4262
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 01-20: Restraints, Active

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Restraints, Active

 Inspection and Verification 

 NOTE: The passenger belt can be tested with a driver only, providing the 
driver has the ability to grasp the right front shoulder belt and extend it 
approximately 660 mm (26 inches) with no compromise to safe driving.

 NOTE: If test is to be performed by driver only, do not extend passenger side 
safety belt fully. False indication of lockup will result.

 NOTE: This method applies to the 8 km/h (5 mph) test only.

Driver will buckle up and proceed to a safe test area. If the passenger 
safety belt must be tested, a passenger can be buckled into the right front 
seat. 

After reaching a safe area to perform sudden stops, the driver will 
attain a speed of approximately 8 km/h (5 mph). The driver will inform the 
passenger, if applicable, that he is preparing to make a severe brake 
application. At this time, both driver and rider will grasp their respective 
shoulder harnesses and prepare to lean slightly forward at the moment the 
brake application is made. 

 WARNING: THE DRIVER AND PASSENGER MUST BE PREPARED TO BRACE THEMSELVES IN THE 
EVENT THE SAFETY BELT RETRACTOR DOES NOT LOCK. 

The driver will make a maximum brake application (approximately 9.7 
m/sec. [32 ft./sec.]) without tire skid. (The maximum brake 
application should be on dry concrete or equivalent hard road surface, never 
on a wet or gravel road.) The driver and passenger will lean slightly forward 
into the shoulder harness. At this instant, the belts should lock up without 
webbing payout.

If there is a lockup of both shoulder straps, the safety belt 
assemblies are functioning properly. Should either or both retractors fail to 
lock up at the 8 km/h (5 mph) speed, repeat the test at a constant 24 km/h (15 
mph). (This test must be performed with a passenger if the right front belt is 
to be tested.) 

 WARNING: IF THE RETRACTOR OF A NEW SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLY HAS BEEN BOLTED INTO A 
DAMAGED OR DISTORTED MOUNTING AREA, THE NEW RETRACTOR COULD BE WARPED AND WILL 
NOT FUNCTION. IF THIS IS THE CASE, REWORK THE SHEET METAL BACK TO ITS ORIGINAL 
SHAPE AND STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY, AND INSTALL ANOTHER NEW COMPLETE SAFETY BELT 
ASSEMBLY. 

If either or both shoulder belts do not lock up at the 24 km/h (15 mph) 
test, the vehicle is to be returned for service of the malfunctioning safety 
belts. Remove the retractor and rework the sheet metal in the retractor's 
mounting surface back to its original shape and structural integrity. Install 
the retractor assembly and test the safety belt assembly(s) as previously 
stated.

 Symptom Chart — Active Restraints 

 ACTIVE RESTRAINTS 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Excessive Pressure on Occupant During Normal Wear. Webbing Cannot Be 
Extracted. Excessive Slack in Webbing Does Not Retract.

Safety belt retractor.

PERFORM Functional Test Procedure . REFER to the Service Procedures 
portion of this section. CHECK and REPLACE if necessary.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Safety Belts

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Safety Belt Bolt Bit (No. 50 Torx®)

T77L-2100-A

 Removal 

Remove the shoulder belt retractor trim cover.

 NOTE: Use Safety Belt Bolt Bit T77L-2100-A to remove or replace all safety 
belt assembly anchorage bolts.

 NOTE: The buckle end of the front safety belt can be removed by removing the 
safety belt anchor bolt from the floor. Driver side buckle contains an 
electrical switch. Disconnect before removing the anchor bolt. 

Remove the shoulder belt retractor anchor bolt, the floor anchor bolt, 
the D-ring cover and retaining bolt.

Remove affected safety belt assembly from the vehicle.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Safety belt and shoulder harness anchor bolt torque might fall below 30 Nm
 (22 lb-ft) after installation. A minimum established 
static audit torque of 27 Nm (20 lb-ft) must be maintained, 
but safety belt anchor bolts must be capable of being retightened to 50 Nm
 (37 lb-ft.) Place sealer around all safety belt anchor 
holes in the floorpan. 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order to install the replacement 
safety belt assemblies in the vehicle. 

Check for sealer around each removed floor anchor bolt hole. Add Ford 
Caulking Cord D6AZ-19560-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M4G32-A.

Tighten all bolts to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft) with bolts 
securely seated. 

Replace all covers where applicable. 

Install all washers and spacers in same location from which they were 
removed.

Check belts for proper routings.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Safety Belt with Anchor Plate Thread Damage 

 Removal 

Remove the broken or stripped bolt and discard. 

Drill out the internal threads in the safety belt anchor plate with a 
27/64-inch drill. 

Rethread the safety belt anchor plate with a 1/2-13 tap. 

Blow out the chips. 

 Installation 

Install the attachment parts. Tighten the replacement bolt to 30-40 Nm
 (22-30 lb-ft). Original parts are to be replaced with the 
repair parts indicated in the safety belt parts replacement chart 

at the end of this section. Unless specified in the chart, use original parts. 

When repairing a multiple belt and attachment, install nut (382599) to 
the bolt in the tunnel area from the underside of the floorpan. Tighten to 
30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Safety Belt Procedure After a Collision

 WARNING: ALL SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLIES INCLUDING RETRACTORS AND ATTACHING HARDWARE 
MUST BE INSPECTED AFTER ANY COLLISION. FORD RECOMMENDS THAT ALL SAFETY BELT 
ASSEMBLIES IN USE DURING A COLLISION BE REPLACED UNLESS THE COLLISION WAS 
MINOR AND A QUALIFIED TECHNICIAN FINDS THAT THE BELTS SHOW NO DAMAGE AND 
CONTINUE TO OPERATE PROPERLY. SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLIES NOT IN USE DURING A 
COLLISION MUST ALSO BE INSPECTED AND REPLACED IF EITHER DAMAGE OR IMPROPER 
OPERATION IS NOTED. 

Safety belt assemblies must be periodically inspected to ensure that 
they have not become damaged and that they remain in proper operating 
condition, particularly if they have been subjected to severe stress.

Safety Belt Tongue Rotated on Belt 

The following procedure can be used to correct a rotated tongue on the 
safety belt. 

Grasp the safety belt tongue and pull down on the belt webbing closest 
to you to form a loop through the upper narrow, longer slot in the tongue as 
shown in the illustration. 

Working within the upper slot, rotate and fold the belt webbing over 
itself as required to remove the twist. 

Pull the excess belt webbing back through the upper slot in the tongue. 

Repeat this procedure to complete the removal of the twist at the 
lower, wider and larger slot in the tongue as shown in the illustration. 

When finished, the belt should hang properly as shown in the 
illustration.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Functional Test Procedure

 NOTE: The passenger belt can be tested with a driver only, providing the 
driver has the ability to grasp the right front shoulder belt and extend it 
approximately 660 mm (26 inches) with no compromise to safe driving.

 NOTE: If test is to be performed by driver only, do not extend passenger side 
safety belt fully. False indication of lockup will result.

 NOTE: This method applies to the 8 km/h (5 mph) test only.

Driver will buckle up and proceed to a safe test area. If the passenger 
safety belt must be tested, a passenger can be buckled into the right front 
seat. 

After reaching a safe area to perform sudden stops, the driver will 
attain a speed of approximately 8 km/h (5 mph). The driver will inform the 
passenger, if applicable, that he is preparing to make a severe brake 
application. At this time, both driver and rider will grasp their respective 
shoulder harnesses and prepare to lean slightly forward at the moment the 
brake application is made. 

 WARNING: THE DRIVER AND PASSENGER MUST BE PREPARED TO BRACE THEMSELVES IN THE 
EVENT THE SAFETY BELT RETRACTOR DOES NOT LOCK. 

The driver will make a maximum brake application (approximately 9.7 
m/sec. [32 ft./sec.]) without tire skid. (The maximum brake 
application should be on dry concrete or equivalent hard road surface, never 
on a wet or gravel road.) The driver and passenger will lean slightly forward 
into the shoulder harness. At this instant, the belts should lock up without 
webbing payout.

If there is a lockup of both shoulder straps, the safety belt 
assemblies are functioning properly. Should either or both retractors fail to 
lock up at the 8 km/h (5 mph) speed, repeat the test at a constant 24 km/h (15 
mph). (This test must be performed with a passenger if the right front belt is 
to be tested.) 

 WARNING: IF THE RETRACTOR OF A NEW SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLY HAS BEEN BOLTED INTO A 
DAMAGED OR DISTORTED MOUNTING AREA, THE NEW RETRACTOR COULD BE WARPED AND WILL 
NOT FUNCTION. IF THIS IS THE CASE, REWORK THE SHEET METAL BACK TO ITS ORIGINAL 
SHAPE AND STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY, AND INSTALL ANOTHER NEW COMPLETE SAFETY BELT 
ASSEMBLY. 

If either or both shoulder belts do not lock up at the 24 km/h (15 mph) 
test, the vehicle is to be returned for service of the malfunctioning safety 
belts. Remove the retractor and rework the sheet metal in the retractor's 
mounting surface back to its original shape and structural integrity. Install 
the retractor assembly and test the safety belt assembly(s) as previously 
stated.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Safety Belt Webbing

The following procedure is recommended for the removal of spots and 
stains from safety belt webbing. It is important that proper cleaning 
techniques and cleaning agents be used to prevent setting the stain or 
affecting the color and flame resistance of the safety belt webbing. Avoid 
bleaching or redyeing the webbing as this could affect belt strength and 
performance. 

 WARNING: DO NOT BLEACH OR DYE THE WEBBING. THIS CAN WEAKEN THE BELT. 

The following materials are needed to clean safety belts: 

clean, undyed cotton fabric

medium hard bristle brush

Ford Spot and Stain Remover F3AZ-19521-WA or equivalent commercial 
product

Extra Strength Upholstery Cleaner E8AZ-19523-AA or equivalent 
commercial product

Prior to selecting a cleaning method, perform the following steps.

Remove excess staining material from fabric by scraping or wiping with 
a clean cloth. 

Identify the staining material if possible. 

Clean the fabric as described in the following Methods A, B or C. 

 Spot Cleaning Method A 

For stains from grease, oil, tar, water spotting, crayon and lipstick.

 CAUTION: Care should be used in application of the spot lifter to prevent it 
from contacting vinyl trim. 

 NOTE: Using other than recommended cleaners or procedures may affect 
flammability or fabric appearances. 

Spray stain with Extra Strength Upholstery Cleaner E8AZ-19523-AA or 
equivalent commercial product from a distance of 204-254 mm (8-10 inches) as 
directed by instructions on can. 

Allow spot lifter to dry completely, until it forms a white powder on 
surface of fabric. 

Brush and vacuum white powder from fabric. 

If soiled spot is not removed from fabric, repeat as necessary. 

Wipe cleaned area with damp cloth to remove any residual cleaner. 

 General Cleaning Method B 

For stains such as grease, oil, tar, adhesive, crayon and lipstick. 

If stain is still visible after spot cleaning procedure (Method A), 
blot soiled area with a clean cotton cloth saturated with Ford Spot and Stain 
Remover F3AZ-19521-WA or equivalent commercial product. 

Rub in a circular motion while continuously exposing clean portion of 
cloth. 

Gradually widen area of application onto edges of belts. 

Repeat as necessary. 

Wipe cleaned area with clean, damp cloth to remove any residual cleaner. 

 General Cleaning Method C 

For stains from dirt, soil, food and beverages. 

 NOTE: Spot cleaning as described in Method A will be sufficient when the 
soiled area is not excessive. In the event of severe soiling or staining, 
clean the entire belt to avoid a ring condition. 

Apply Rosenthal or Bissell or equivalent commercial upholstery cleaner 
with cloth or brush as directed by instructions on container. 

Rub in a circular manner until stain is removed. 

Gradually widen area of application to edges of belts. 

Repeat as necessary. 

Rub cleaned area with a damp cloth to absorb residual cleaner. 

Allow belts to dry at room temperature.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Frame Inspection 

Frame misalignment is the result of damaged or loose frame components. 
It can affect front wheel alignment and cause improper operation and abnormal 
wear of chassis parts. 

Before checking frame alignment, inspect the frame for damage and loose 
parts. Inspect all frame members for cracks, twists or bends. Check all welded 
connections for cracks. Inspect all rivets, bolts and body support brackets 
for looseness. Make all necessary service or replacements. 

Refer to the Body Builders Book for dimensional data when performing 
service operations on the body cab or frame.

================================================================================
PAGE 4275
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 02-01: Frame

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Diagonal or X-Frame Checking Method 

Frame alignment can be checked without removing the body from the frame 
by using the diagonal or X-frame checking method. 

Use this method to identify misalignment prior to any attempt to 
straighten a frame. 

Place the vehicle on a clean level floor and set the parking brake. 

Select several points along one frame sidemember and carefully transfer 
these points with a plumb bob to the floor. If desired, paper can be taped on 
the floor along both sides of the vehicle below the frame. Accurately mark the 
points on the floor. 

Locate the corresponding points along the opposite frame sidemember and 
carefully transfer these points to the floor in the same manner as in the 
previous step. 

Move the vehicle away from the marks on the floor, and measure between 
diagonal points. Both corresponding measurements should be equal within 6.35 
mm (1/4 inch). Measure diagonally between all points on the floor. 

Measure between corresponding points parallel to the frame sidemembers. 
These measurements should be within 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) of each other. 

The squareness of the frame sidemember web and the lower flanges at the 
spring hangers should be within 1.59 mm (1/16 inch). The squareness of the 
sidemember web at the steering gear mounting location should be within 1.59 mm 
(1/16 inch). The web and flange should be square at all other points within 
3.18 mm (1/8 inch). 

Any point on one sidemember should be within 3.18 mm (1/8 inch) ahead, 
behind, above, or below the corresponding point on the opposite sidemember. 
The frame sidemember should not be bowed more than 3.18 mm (1/8 inch) for each 
2540 mm (100 inches) of frame length. The overall width of the frame should 
not vary more than 3.18 mm (1/8 inch). 

An alternate method of checking frame alignment is to use a frame gauge 
such as Rotunda Laser Measuring System 190-01025 or equivalent.

================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 02-01: Frame

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Frame Service 

 Drilling Precautions 

Do not drill holes in the frame flanges. This tends to reduce the frame 
strength.

 Welding Precautions 

 CAUTION: These vehicles are equipped with 50,000 and 110,000 psi frames. Do not 
apply heat to or weld the frames. 

 Frame Strength Identification 

The code symbol is punched in side rails near the front spring rear 
hangers. The following illustration shows the symbol for 50,000 and 110,000 
psi frames. Absence of the 50,000 psi triangular code symbol implies a 110,000 
psi frame.

[FIGURE: N5911C.gif]

 Frame Straightening 

Correct frame misalignment by straightening the out-of-line parts or by 
replacing the crossmembers, braces or brackets if they are badly damaged. 

Straightening should be attempted on frames that fail to meet 
specifications of the diagonal checking method, or where damage is visually 
apparent. 

 CAUTION: Do not apply heat to 50,000 and 110,000 psi frames. 

To prevent internal stresses in the metal, limit frame straightening to 
parts that are not severely bent. 

 Frame Reinforcing 

After straightening a bent frame member, inspect the member closely for 
cracks. If any cracks show, the frame member must be replaced. Do not weld 
reinforcements to the frame.

Reinforcements can be made from channel, angle, or flat stock. The 
reinforcement stock should be the same material and thickness as the frame 
member being reinforced. It also should extend a minimum of six inches to 
either side of the crack. 

 Frame Member Replacement 

If a damaged frame member is to be replaced, new bolts must be used. 
Grade 8 fasteners are required for replacement of frame parts.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support Insulator, Front Engine

 Removal 

Support the engine under the flywheel housing with a jack.

Remove the sound panels. Refer to the appropriate engine section in 
Group 03 for procedures.

Loosen the two through-bolts under the front crossmember holding the 
front insulator assembly. Remove the lower insulator, plate and spacers.

Raise the engine slightly and remove the upper insulator.

Remove bolts retaining the support bracket to the engine and remove 
bracket (if so equipped).

 Installation 

Install support bracket and tighten the bolts to 102-142 Nm
 (75-105 lb-ft) on Caterpillar 3176 and 3406 engines.

Install support bracket and tighten the bolts to 64-72 Nm
 (47-53 lb-ft) for L10 engine and 68-95 Nm 
(50-70 lb-ft) for NTC engine.

Position the upper insulator under the front engine support bracket and 
lower the engine, making sure the holes in the support bracket, top insulator 
and frame crossmember are lined up.

Assemble the lower insulator assembly and spacers to the through-bolts. 
Push these through the two holes in the frame crossmember.

Install the through-bolt nuts and tighten the retaining nuts to 204-277 Nm
 (150-205 lb-ft).

Remove the jack.

================================================================================
PAGE 4280
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 02-03: Engine and Transmission Mounting

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support Insulator, Front Engine, Single Front Type, FD-1460 Engine

 Removal 

Remove the front engine support lower insulator bolts and washers. 
Remove insulators.

Remove the front engine support upper insulator-to-front engine support 
bolts and washers.

Loosen the engine rear support insulator nuts approximately 1/4 turn.

Raise the engine about 25.4 mm (1 inch) with a jack and block of wood 
placed under the oil pan; then, remove the upper insulator.

To remove the engine front support from the engine, remove the 
retaining bolts.

 Installation 

If the engine front support was removed from the engine, position it on 
the cylinder front cover, and install the retaining bolts. Tighten the bolts 
to specifications.

Position upper insulator to engine front support and install retaining 
bolts and washers. Tighten bolts securely.

Lower the engine and install the lower insulator and retaining bolts 
and washers and tighten bolts to specification.

Tighten the engine rear support insulator nuts to 112 Nm
 (82 lb-ft).

================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 02-03: Engine and Transmission Mounting

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support Insulator, Rear Engine, Double Rear Type

 Removal 

Remove the nuts, bolts and washers from the engine mount cap at each 
engine support-to-frame bracket.

Raise the rear of the engine with a jack and wood block placed under 
the transmission.

Remove the insulator from each engine support bracket.

 Installation 

Position the insulators on the engine support brackets.

Lower the engine until the engine support-to-frame brackets touch the 
insulators. Install the engine mount cap, bolts, nuts and washers.

Remove the jack. Tighten the nuts to specification.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support Insulator, Rear Engine, Caterpillar 3176 and 3406

 Removal 

Remove the engine noise panels. Refer to the appropriate engine section 
in Group 03 for procedures.

Loosen the engine front insulator assembly, permitting the engine to 
raise slightly.

Remove the two through-bolts holding the lower support cap on both 
sides of the rear of the engine. Remove both lower support caps. The engine 
can now be raised away from the rear support brackets.

Remove the bolts and nuts attaching the rear engine supports to the 
frame and remove insulator assemblies.

Remove the insulators from the assemblies.

 Installation 

Install the insulators on the insulator assemblies and install the 
assemblies on the frame. Tighten the retaining nuts to 204-277 Nm
 (150-205 lb-ft).

Lower the engine onto the two rear engine frame supports.

Install the two lower insulator support caps with the two through-bolts 
for each cap. Tighten to 102-142 Nm (75-105 lb-ft).

Lower the front of the engine and tighten the front insulator assembly. 
Remove the jack. Tighten to 204-277 Nm (150-205 lb-ft).

Install engine noise panels. Refer to the appropriate engine section in 
Group 03 for procedures.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support, Rear Engine, Cummins M11 and N14

All Cummins diesel installations use a similar rear engine support 
insulator. It is basically a sleeve that slides over a stub shaft on the 
frame-mounted side support. This sleeve is clamped to the engine rear side 
supports.

 Removal 

Remove the right and left engine support cap retaining bolts and remove 
caps.

Remove front engine mount retaining nuts to loosen mount.

Place a wooden block on a floor jack and raise the rear of the engine 
approximately 152 mm (6 inches).

Remove the nuts and bolts retaining the left engine support bracket to 
the frame rail.

Remove the left mounting bolt retainer, and remaining mounting bolts.

Lower the support bracket and slide rearward along frame rail to 
remove. Remove insulator from mount.

Move engine toward the left frame rail. Remove the nuts and bolts and 
right mounting bolt retainer.

Remove the engine support bracket and insulator. Remove the insulator 
from the support bracket.

 Installation 

Install the insulator on the support bracket (RH) and install the 
engine support bracket and insulator.

Install the right mounting bolt retainer and install retaining nuts and 
bolts.

Install insulator to support brackets (LH). Raise the support bracket 
and slide forward along frame rail.

Install the left mounting bolt retainer and install the retaining bolts.

Position the left engine support bracket to the frame rail and attach 
the retaining nuts and bolts.

Lower the rear of the engine approximately 152 mm (6 inches) and remove 
the wooden block from the floor jack.

Install the front engine mount and tighten the retaining nuts to 
specifications.

Install right and left engine support cap and retaining bolts, then 
install support caps.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Support Insulator, Engine and Transmission 

 Removal 

Position Rotunda Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or equivalent under 
the transmission. Raise the transmission to relieve the pressure from the 
transmission mount that requires service.

Remove the bolts retaining the transmission support to the frame rail 
brackets and transmission case bolts. Remove any other necessary fasteners. 
Remove the transmission support from the vehicle.

 Installation 

With proper support, position the transmission assembly for 
installation of the support.

Position the support. Replace all components and fasteners and secure 
with lockwire, if so equipped. Tighten to specification.

Lower transmission and remove jack from the vehicle.

1997 L-Series Equipped with Ford FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Introduction

This section covers various engine tests, adjustments, service 
procedures and cleaning/inspection procedures. Engine assembly and service 
specifications appear at the end of Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 
(FD-1460). 

For engine removal, disassembly, assembly, installation, adjustment 
procedures and specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 

When performing tests, adjustments or service to the engine system or 
fuel ignition system, it is essential to follow the procedures and 
specifications in the appropriate repair group in this manual, and in the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual
.

Before replacing damaged or worn engine components such as the 
crankshaft, cylinder heads, valve guides, valves, camshafts or cylinder block, 
make sure that part(s) is not serviceable.

 WARNING: TO AVOID THE POSSIBILITY OF PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE, 
DO NOT OPERATE THE ENGINE WITH THE HOOD OPEN UNTIL THE FAN HAS FIRST BEEN 
EXAMINED FOR POSSIBLE CRACKS AND SEPARATION.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Engine Oil Leaks 

When diagnosing engine oil leaks, the source and location of the leak must be identified prior to service.

 Fluorescent Oil Additive Method 

Add Rotunda Gas Engine Dye 164-R3705 or equivalent to the engine oil. Use 29.6 ml (1 ounce) of fluorescent additive in all engines.

Clean engine with a suitable solvent to remove all traces of oil.

Run engine for 15 minutes.

Stop engine and inspect all seal, gasket and galley plug areas for leaks using Rotunda Oil Leak Detector 164-R0756 or equivalent. A clear bright yellow or orange area will identify leak. For extremely small leaks, several hours may be required for the leak to appear.

 NOTE: For minor gasket leaks tightening the retaining bolts may resolve the problem. 

Service all leaks as required.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Leakage Points

 NOTE: Should oil be found in the engine coolant or coolant in the lubricating 
oil, the oil cooler must be checked as a possible source of contamination. 
This can be done by pressurizing the cooler to 483 kPa (70 psi) and submerging 
in clean liquid. Cooler core or gaskets may have to be replaced.

 Underhood

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Compression Test

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Impact Slide Hammer

T50T-100-A

 Compression Gauge Check 

Be sure battery is charged to specifications. Refer to Section 14-01 
for specifications. 

Clean the engine, especially the area around the injectors. 

Warm up the engine by operating for a minimum of 30 minutes at 1200 rpm. 

 NOTE: The lines must not be capped until the residual fuel has been removed 
from them. Otherwise, when the engine is cranked during the compression test 
the fuel remaining in the lines will blow the caps off. 

Stop the engine and remove the high-pressure fuel lines and fuel 
leak-off line from the engine. Cap all of the openings in the fuel system and 
fuel injection pump. 

 CAUTION: Do not crank the engine to remove stuck injectors. If an injector is 
stuck in the head and will not pull straight out, first soak the injector with 
penetrating fluid for three minutes. Strike the side of the injector body with 
a brass drift to loosen. If the injector still won't come out, use Injector 
Removal Kit D92T-9000-B or Injector Remover Adapter D92T-9000-A or equivalent 
and Impact Slide Hammer T50T-100-A. If the injector is allowed to turn in the 
head, damage to the head will occur, resulting in the need to replace the 
cylinder head. 

Remove the injector and seat washer from each cylinder. Cap the 
injector and line to prevent the entry of dirt into the system. Place the 
injectors in a rack to protect them from being damaged while they are removed 
from the engine and to keep them in order. 

Disconnect the electrical harness to the fuel shutoff solenoid. This 
must be done to shut off the flow of fuel to the engine during cranking.

[FIGURE: A17614A.gif]

Crank the engine to blow out any loose carbon particles from the 
injector bores. 

Install Rotunda Diesel Engine Pressure Test Adapter Kit 014-00742 or 
equivalent into the bore of cylinder No. 1, using a new seat washer and the 
injector mounting studs and nuts. 

Connect the Rotunda Engine Cylinder Leak Detection/Air Pressurization 
Kit 014-00708 or equivalent and hose to the adapter. 

Crank the engine (speed must be at least 250 rpm) and observe the gauge 
reading. Allow about 6-8 "puffs" per cylinder. 

Repeat above four steps for each cylinder. 

After completing the compression check, reinstall the injectors (use 
new washers) and lines. Connect the plug to the fuel shutoff solenoid. 

 Test Results 

Compression test results are very sensitive to cranking speeds. 
Compression from cylinder to cylinder must be within 689 kPa (100 psi) of each 
other. 

If any of the readings do not meet the above specifications, this 
indicates that there is a possible leak at the cylinder head gasket, piston 
rings or valves. 

 Compression Readings, Interpreting 

To determine if the rings or valves are at fault, squirt the equivalent 
of a tablespoon of heavy oil into the combustion chamber. Crank the engine to 
distribute the oil and repeat the compression test. The oil will temporarily 
seal leakage past the rings. 

If approximately the same reading is obtained, the rings are 
satisfactory, but the valves are leaking. If the compression has increased 
over the original reading, there is leakage past the rings. 

During a compression test, if the pressure fails to climb steadily and 
remains the same during the first two succeeding strokes, or fails to climb 
during the entire test, suspect a sticking valve. 

A low, even compression in two adjacent cylinders indicates a cylinder 
head gasket leak. Check head gasket area before rejecting the rings or valves.

If, after checking the compression pressures in all cylinders, it was 
found that the highest reading obtained was 2413 kPa (350 psi) and the lowest 
pressure reading was 1862 kPa (270 psi), the engine is within specification 
and the compression is considered satisfactory.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cylinder Leakage Detector

When a cylinder produces a low reading, the use of a cylinder leakage 
detector will be helpful in pinpointing the exact cause.

The leakage detector is inserted in the fuel injector hole, the piston 
is brought up to top dead center on the compression stroke, and compressed air 
is admitted.

While the air pressure is retained in the cylinder, listen for the hiss 
of escaping air. A leak by the intake valve will be audible in the air intake 
duct system. A leak by the exhaust valve can be heard at the exhaust pipe. 
Leakage past the rings will be audible at the crankcase ventilation tube. If 
air is passing through a blown gasket to an adjacent cylinder, the noise will 
be evident at the fuel injector hole of the cylinder into which the air is 
leaking. Cracks in the block or gasket leakage into the cooling system can be 
detected by a stream of bubbles in the radiator.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Oil Leak and Valve Guide Seal Test

The cylinder leakage detector can be used to test for engine oil leaks 
and to check the valve seals for leakage.

Plug all crankcase openings except the one used for connecting the 
leakage detector.

Connect the detector to a crankcase opening (oil dipstick tube is 
convenient) and adjust the air pressure to approximately 34 kPa (5 psi).

Using a solution of liquid soap and water, brush the solution along the 
gasket sealing surfaces and bearing seals. Look for bubbles or foam.

Remove the fuel injectors and rotate the engine slowly with a wrench. 
Check for large amounts of air escaping into the cylinders as each intake and 
exhaust valve opens.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Engine Oil Consumption, Excessive

The amount of oil an engine uses will vary with the way the vehicle is 
driven in addition to normal engine-to-engine variation. This is especially 
true during the first 12,000 km (7,500 miles), when a new engine is being 
broken in or until certain internal engine components become conditioned. 
Vehicles used in heavy-duty operation (severe service) may use more oil. 
Following are examples of heavy-duty operation: 

trailer towing applications 

severe loading applications 

sustained high speed operation 

Engines need oil to lubricate the following internal components: 

engine block cylinder walls 

pistons and piston rings 

intake and exhaust valve stems 

intake and exhaust valve guides 

all internal engine components 

When the pistons move downward, a thin film of oil is left on the 
cylinder walls. The thin film of oil is burned away on the firing stroke 
during combustion. If an engine burned a drop of oil during each firing 
stroke, oil consumption would be about one quart for every mile traveled. 
Fortunately modern engines use much less oil than this example. However, even 
efficient engines will use some oil or they would quickly wear out. 
Additionally as the vehicle is operated, some oil is drawn into the combustion 
chambers past the intake and exhaust valve stem seals and burned. 

Many different conditions can affect oil consumption rates. A partial 
list of those conditions includes the following:

operator driving habits 

ambient temperature 

quality and viscosity of the oil 

vehicle load and driving terrain 

Operation under certain conditions can create a false impression of 
excessive oil consumption. Most commonly, this happens when the vehicle has 
been operated for repeated short trips at low ambient temperatures. Under 
these conditions, substantial amounts of condensed water and fuel can build up 
in the oil. If the vehicle is then run for a significant time at highway 
speeds and/or at heavy loads, much of the accumulated water and fuel can be 
removed by the engine ventilation system. Removing the water and fuel in a 
relatively short time will often create the appearance of an excessive 
consumption rate for the customer. In this situation, the customer can be 
assured that these events are normal for the conditions noted. The customer 
might also be advised to change oil and filter more frequently, especially 
prior to starting a long trip in cold weather, if unduly concerned about this 
condition. 

Make sure the selected engine oil meets the recommended API performance 
category "SG" and SAE viscosity grade as shown in the vehicle Owner Guide. It 
is also important that the engine oil is changed at the intervals specified 
for the typical operating conditions.

 Oil Consumption Test 

The following diagnostic procedure is intended to be used to determine 
the source of excessive internal oil consumption. 

Determine what the customer considers excessive oil consumption to be. 
Note vehicle mileage and the following observations: 

How many miles are typically driven per quart of oil used? 

How is the vehicle being used? For example, sustained high speed 
operation, heavy loads, trailer towing, high ambient temperature. 

What does the customer expect normal oil consumption to be? 

Verify that the engine has no external oil leak as described under 
Engine Oil Leaks in the Service Procedures portion of this section. 

Verify that the engine has the proper engine oil dipstick by comparing 
the part number stamped on it against the Ford Master Parts Catalog. Verify 
that the dipstick and tube are unmodified and in good condition. Verify that 
the tube is properly seated in the block, and the dipstick seats properly in 
the tube. 

Verify that the engine is not being run in an overfilled condition. 
Check the oil level at least 20 minutes after a hot shutdown with the vehicle 
parked in a level area. Under no circumstances should the oil level be above 
the letter F in the word FULL. If a significant overfill is indicated, perform 
Steps 5a through 5d to verify the dipstick calibration. If the dipstick 
calibration checks OK, instruct the customer to avoid overfilling the engine 
and return the vehicle to service. To verify the vehicle's actual oil 
consumption, perform Step 5a and Step 5f only after the dipstick has been 
calibrated. 

[FIGURE: DA0874A.gif]

Perform engine oil consumption test as follows: 

Drain engine oil. Remove and replace oil filter. Refill crankcase with 
recommended quality of oil. 

Run the engine for three minutes (ten minutes if cold) then turn engine 
off. Allow oil to drain into the oil pan for an additional 20 minutes (vehicle 
should be on level ground). 

Remove engine oil dipstick and wipe clean. Do not wipe with anything 
contaminated with silicone compounds. Reinstall dipstick, making sure to seat 
the dipstick firmly in the tube. Remove the dipstick and scribe a mark on the 
back (unmarked) surface at the indicated oil level. This should be in the full 
range.

Add one U.S. quart of oil. Restart the engine and allow it to idle for 
at least two minutes. Shut down and allow oil to drain back for at least five 
minutes. Mark the dipstick using the procedure above. This level should be at 
the top of the FULL range.

[FIGURE: DA0874A.gif]

Instruct the customer to drive the vehicle as usual and perform the 
following steps:

Check the oil level regularly at intervals of 160 to 240 km (100 to 150 
miles). 

Return to the service facility when the oil level drops below the ADD 
mark scribed on the dipstick by the technician. 

In an emergency, add only full quarts of the same oil and note the 
mileage at which the oil was added. 

Check the oil level under the same conditions as in Step 5c and Step 
5d, reading the back of the dipstick where the scribe marks are located. 

Measure the distance from the oil level to the upper scribe mark on the 
dipstick and record. 

Measure the distance between the two scribe marks and record. 

Divide the first measurement by the second. Add one to this total for 
every quart added by the customer as instructed in Step 5e. 

Divide the distance driven during the oil test by the result. This 
quantity is the approximate oil consumption rate in miles per quart (MPQ). 

If the calculated oil consumption rate is unacceptable, proceed to Step 
6.

Check crankcase ventilation tube. Make sure tube is not plugged.

Check for plugged oil drain-back holes in cylinder head(s), and 
cylinder block. 

If condition still exists, perform a cylinder compression test as 
outlined and/or perform a cylinder leak detection test. This can be helpful in 
determining source of oil consumption, i.e., valves, piston rings, etc. 

Check valve guides for excessive guide clearance. Replace all valve 
stem/guide seals after correct valve guide clearance has been verified. 

 NOTE: After checking for worn parts, if it is determined parts should be 
replaced, make sure correct replacement parts are used. 

Worn or damaged internal engine components can cause excessive oil 
consumption. If internal oil consumption still persists, proceed as follows: 

Remove engine from vehicle and place it on an engine work stand. Remove 
intake manifold(s), cylinder head(s), oil pan and oil pump. Refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 

Check piston ring clearance, ring gap and ring orientation. Service as 
required. 

Check for excessive bearing clearance. Service as required. 

Perform Step 5 again to confirm oil consumption concern has been 
resolved.

Valve Train Analysis, Static (Engine Off)

 Rocker Arm Cover Removed 

 NOTE: For the removal and installation of the engine rocker arm cover, refer 
to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 

Check for damaged and/or severely worn parts, for correct assembly, and 
make sure correct parts are used by proceeding as follows with the static 
engine analysis. 

 Rocker Arm Assemblies 

Check for loose mounting bolts.

Check for plugged oil feed in the rocker arm or cylinder head. 

 Push Rods 

Check for bent push rods and restriction in oil passage. 

 Valve Springs 

Check for broken or damaged parts. 

 Valve Spring Retainer and Valve Spring Retainer Keys 

Check for proper seating of keys on valve stem and in retainer. 

 Valves and Cylinder Head 

Check the cylinder head gasket for proper installation. 

Check for plugged oil drain back holes. 

Check for worn or damaged valve tips. 

Check for missing or damaged guide-mounted valve stem oil seals. 

Check installed spring height. 

Check for missing or worn valve spring seats, if equipped. 

Static checks (engine off) are to be made on the engine prior to the 
dynamic procedure.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Valve Train Analysis, Dynamic

Start the engine and, while running at idle, check for proper operation 
of all parts. 

 Rocker Arm Assemblies 

Check for plugged oil feed in rocker arm or cylinder head. 

Check for proper overhead valve train lubrication. 

If a condition of insufficient oiling is suspected, accelerate the 
engine to 1200 rpm ± 100 rpm with the transmission in 
neutral and the engine at normal operating temperature. Oil should spurt from 
the rocker arm oil holes so that valve tips and rocker arm are well oiled 
and/or, with the rocker arm cover off, oil splash may overshoot rocker arm. If 
oiling is insufficient for this condition to occur, check oil passages for 
blockage. 

 Push Rods 

Check for bent push rods and restriction in oil passage. 

Check for proper rotation of push rod (non-roller tappets).

 Valves and Cylinder Head 

Check for plugged oil drain back holes. 

Check for missing or damaged valve stem oil seals or guide mounted oil 
seals. 

If a condition of insufficient oiling is suspected, check oil passages 
for blockage, then accelerate the engine to 1200 rpm with the transmission in 
neutral and the engine at normal operating temperature. Oil should spurt from 
the rocker arm oil holes so that valve tips and rocker arms are well oiled. 
With the rocker arm cover off, some oil splash may overshoot rocker arm.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Camshaft Lobe Lift 

 NOTE: If lift on any lobe is below specified service limits, camshaft and 
tappet operating on worn lobe(s) must be replaced, as well as any tappet 
showing pitting or having contact face worn flat or concave. 

Check the lift of each lobe in consecutive order and make a note of the 
readings. Remove rocker arm cover(s). 

Remove rocker arm seat, bolt, seat and rocker arm. 

Make sure tappet is seated against cam. Install Dial Indicator with 
Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or equivalent in such a manner as to have ball socket 
adapter of indicator on top of push rod and in same plane as push rod 
movement. 

Remove fuel injectors. 

Connect an auxiliary starter switch in starting circuit. Crank engine 
with ignition switch in off position. "Bump" crankshaft over until tappet is 
on base circle of camshaft lobe. At this point, tappet will be in its lowest 
position. If checking during engine assembly, turn crankshaft using a socket 
and ratchet. 

Zero dial indicator. Continue to rotate crankshaft slowly until tappet 
is in fully raised position (highest indicator reading).

Compare total lift recorded on indicator with specifications. Refer to 
 Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 

To check accuracy of original indicator reading, continue to rotate 
crankshaft until indicator reads zero.

Remove dial indicator and auxiliary starter switch.

Install rocker arm cover. 

Install fuel injectors. 

[FIGURE: A21124C.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Camshaft End Play

 CAUTION: Prying against the camshaft gear with the valve train load on the 
camshaft can break or damage the gear. Therefore, the rocker arm adjusting 
nuts must be backed off sufficiently to free the camshaft. After checking the 
camshaft end play, adjust the valve clearance. 

Push camshaft toward rear of engine. Install Dial Indicator with 
Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or 
equivalent so indicator point is on camshaft sprocket attaching screw.

Zero dial indicator. Pull camshaft forward and release it. Compare dial 
indicator reading with specifications. If end play is excessive, replace 
camshaft thrust plate. 

Remove dial indicator. 

After replacing thrust plate, check end play again. If it is still out 
of specified range, inspect camshaft and cylinder head/cylinder block for 
excessive wear.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Crankshaft End Play

Measure the end clearance of the crankshaft as follows: 

Install Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator 
with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent onto the oil pan flange. 

Put the tip of the gauge against the crankshaft counterweight. 

Push the crankshaft toward the rear of the cylinder block. 

[FIGURE: A18246A.gif]

Set the dial indicator at zero. 

Push the crankshaft toward the front of the cylinder block. If the end 
clearance is less than 0.16 mm (0.006 inch), complete the following steps: 

Loosen the main bearing capscrews one turn. 

Push the crankshaft toward the front and then toward the rear of the 
cylinder block. 

Tighten the capscrews in three steps following the illustrated sequence. 

Step 1 — 50 Nm (37 lb-ft)

Step 2 — 119 Nm (88 lb-ft)

Step 3 — 176 Nm (129 lb-ft) 

[FIGURE: A18230A.gif]

 NOTE: Crankshafts that have been reground on the thrust bearing surfaces are 
marked for oversize thrust bearings on the No. 4 journal crankshaft 
counterweight. If the crankshaft counterweight is marked, check the thrust 
bearing part number to make sure the correct bearing size is used. 

Example: 0.010 = 0.25 mm (0.010 inch). Measure the crankshaft end 
clearance. The end clearance specification for a new or reground crankshaft 
with new thrust bearings is 0.16-0.33 mm (0.006-0.013 inch). 

[FIGURE: A18247A.gif]

If the crankshaft end play is more than 0.54 mm (0.021 inch), the 
crankshaft must be removed from the engine and repaired.

Connecting Rod Side Clearance

Install Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator 
with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent so that the contact points rests 
against the connecting rod cap. 

Pull connecting rod cap toward front of engine and zero the dial 
indicator. 

Push the cap toward rear of engine and observe amount of side clearance 
on dial indicator. 

If side clearance exceeds specification, replace connecting rod and 
cap. Refer to Section 03A-01 or Section 03B-01 for specifications. 

If side clearance is less than specification, remove connecting rod and 
cap and inspect for scratches, burrs, nicks or dirt between crankshaft and 
connecting rod.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Flywheel Runout, Manual Transmission 

To measure flywheel runout, perform the following procedure. 

Disconnect the fuel injection pump shutoff solenoid. 

Push the flywheel all the way in to prevent crankshaft end play from 
having an effect on flywheel runout. 

Install a Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator 
with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent so that the indicator point bears 
against the flywheel face, one inch in from the edge of the flywheel.

 NOTE: Loosen the injectors so that the engine is easier to rotate. 

Turn the engine over in the direction of rotation (clockwise from the 
front) and observe the movement of the needle on the dial indicator. 

Flywheel clutch face runout must not exceed 0.13 mm (0.005 inch). 

If the flywheel clutch face runout exceeds specification, remove the 
flywheel and check for burrs between the flywheel and the face of the 
crankshaft mounting flange. If no burrs exist, check the runout of the 
crankshaft flywheel mounting face; it must not exceed 0.0381 mm (0.0015 inch). 
If the crankshaft mounting flange face is the cause of the excess runout, 
machine the mounting flange or replace the crankshaft. If the crankshaft 
mounting flange is not the cause of the runout, reface or replace the flywheel.

[FIGURE: A8816D.gif]

 Flywheel Housing Bore Alignment, FD-1060 Engine 

 NOTE: Loosen the injectors so the engine is easier to rotate. 

To measure flywheel housing bore, perform the following procedure: 
Disconnect the injection pump fuel shutoff solenoid. 

Attach Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator with 
Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent to the crankshaft. The dial indicator 
can be mounted by any method that holds the extension bar of the indicator 
rigid so it does not sag. If the bar sags or the indicator slips, the readings 
obtained will not be accurate.

[FIGURE: A17615A.gif]

Position the indicator in the 6 o'clock position and zero the gauge. 

Prepare a worksheet with four columns marked A, B, C and D to record 
concentricity readings. 

Slowly rotate the crankshaft. Record the readings obtained at the 9 
o'clock, 12 o'clock, and 3 o'clock positions as A, B and C respectively on the 
concentricity worksheet. Recheck zero at the 6 o'clock position. 

The values for A, B and C can be positive or negative. Refer to the 
accompanying figure to determine the correct sign when recording these values.

[FIGURE: A17616A.gif]

Rotate the crankshaft until the dial indicator is at the 12 o'clock 
position and zero the gauge.

 CAUTION: Do not force the crankshaft beyond the point where the bearing 
clearance has been removed. Do not pry against the flywheel housing. These 
actions can cause false bearing clearance readings. 

Using a pry bar, raise the rear of the crankshaft to its upper limit. 
Record the value as D on the concentricity worksheet. This is the vertical 
bearing clearance adjustment and will always be positive.

[FIGURE: A17617A.gif]

Using the concentricity worksheet, determine the values for the total 
vertical and total horizontal values. 

The total horizontal is equal to the 9 o'clock reading (A), minus the 3 
o'clock reading (C). 

The total vertical is equal to the 12 o'clock reading (B), plus the 
bearing clearance (D). 

Example:

6 o'clock = ref. = 0

9 o'clock = A = 0.004 inch

12 o'clock = B = 0.003 inch

3 o'clock = C = 0.002 inch

Bearing clearance = D = 0.002 inch

TOTAL HORIZONTAL A - C = 0.002

Using the worksheet and the numbers from the example, the total 
horizontal value = 0.002 inch and the total vertical value = 0.005 inch. 

Mark the total horizontal value on the horizontal side of the following 
chart and the total vertical on the vertical side of the chart. 

Using a straightedge, find the intersection point of the total 
horizontal and total vertical values. The intersection point must fall within 
the shaded area for the flywheel housing concentricity to be within 
specification. 

Using the total horizontal and total vertical values from the previous 
example, the intersection point falls within the shaded area. Therefore, the 
flywheel housing concentricity is within specification.

[FIGURE: A23688A.gif]

 NOTE: The ring dowels are not required to maintain concentricity of the 
housing; the clamping force of the capscrews holds the housing in place. 

If the intersection point falls outside the shaded area, the ring 
dowels must be removed and the housing repositioned.

[FIGURE: A17618A.gif]

After the ring dowels are discarded, install the flywheel housing on 
the engine. 

To position the housing, tighten the capscrews enough to hold the 
flywheel housing in place, but loose enough to enable small movement when 
struck lightly with a mallet. 

Recheck the concentricity. When concentricity is within specification, 
tighten the capscrews to 60 Nm (45 lb-ft). Follow torque 
sequence as illustrated.

[FIGURE: A23690A.gif]

 Flywheel Housing Face Alignment, FD-1460 Engine 

To measure flywheel housing face alignment, perform the following 
procedure.

Disconnect the injection pump fuel shutoff solenoid.

 CAUTION: The dial indicator tip must not enter the capscrew holes or the gauge 
will be damaged. 

 NOTE: The extension bar for the indicator must be rigid for an accurate

Adjust the dial until the needle points to zero. 

Install Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator 
with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent as illustrated.

[FIGURE: A17619A.gif]

 NOTE: Loosen the injectors so that the engine is easier to rotate.

the crankshaft end clearance each time a position is measured. 

Slowly rotate the crankshaft. Record the readings at the 3 o'clock, 6 
o'clock and 9 o'clock positions.

[FIGURE: A17620A.gif]

Continue to rotate the crankshaft until the indicator is at the 12 
o'clock position. Check the indicator to make sure the needle points to zero. 
If it does not, the readings will be incorrect.

 Flywheel Bore Runout Measurement, FD-1460 Engine 

To measure flywheel housing bore runout, perform the following procedure: 

Disconnect the injection pump fuel shutoff solenoid. 

Attach Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial Indicator with 
Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent to the flywheel housing. The dial 
indicator can be mounted by any method that holds the extension bar of the 
indicator rigid so it does not sag. If the bar sags or the indicator slips, 
the readings obtained will not be accurate. 

Position the contact tip of the indicator against the inside diameter 
of the flywheel bore, and zero the gauge. 

[FIGURE: A19058A.gif]

 NOTE: Loosen the injectors so the engine is easier to rotate.

crankshaft one complete revolution (360 degrees), and note reading on dial 
indicator. The total indicator reading (TIR) must not exceed 0.127 mm (0.0050 
inch). 

[FIGURE: A19059A.gif]

inspect the mounting surface for dirt or damage. 

Also, inspect the mating surface of the crankshaft for dirt or damage. 
If necessary, replace the crankshaft. Refer to Section 03B-01 .

Install the flywheel, and inspect the bore runout again. Replace the 
flywheel if the runout does not meet specifications.

Service Limit Specifications 

Service limit specifications are intended to be a guide only, to be 
used when overhauling or reconditioning an engine or engine component. A 
determination can be made whether a component is suitable for continued 
service or should be replaced for extended service while the engine is 
disassembled.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cylinder Block

 Cleaning and Inspection 

If the engine is disassembled, thoroughly clean the block with solvent. 
Remove old gasket material from all machined surfaces. Remove all pipe plugs 
that seal oil passages and clean out all the passages. Blow out all passages, 
then bolt holes, with compressed air. Make sure threads in the cylinder head 
bolt holes are clean. Dirt in the threads may cause binding and result in a 
false torque reading. Use a tap to true-up threads and to remove all deposits. 

After the block has been thoroughly cleaned, check it for cracks. Tiny 
cracks not visible to the naked eye can be detected by coating the suspected 
area with a mixture of 25 percent kerosene and 75 percent light engine oil. 
Wipe the part dry and immediately apply a coating of zinc oxide dissolved in 
wood alcohol. Do not use rubbing alcohol as a substitute. If cracks are 
present, the coating will become discolored at the damaged area. Replace the 
block if it is cracked. 

Check all machined surfaces for burrs, nicks, scratches and scores. 
Remove minor imperfections with an oil stone. 

Check the cylinder block for flatness of the cylinder head gasket 
surface following the procedure and specifications recommended for the 
cylinder head. The cylinder block can be machined to bring the cylinder head 
gasket surface within the flatness specifications listed in the specific 
engine section, but not to exceed 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) stock removal from the 
original gasket surface. Use of an over-thick service gasket is required if 
stock is removed.

Replace all plugs that show evidence of leakage.

 Cylinder Block Distortion 

Visually inspect the cylinder block head surface for damage.

Using a straightedge and feeler gauge, check the surface for flatness. 
Maximum out-of-flat is 0.075 mm (0.003 inch) side to side.

[FIGURE: A24343A.gif]

 Sand Holes or Porous Engine Castings, Service 

Porosity or sand hole(s), which will cause oil seepage or leakage, can 
occur with modern casting processes. A complete inspection of engine and 
transmission should be made. If the leak is attributed to the porous condition 
of the cylinder block or sand hole(s), service can be made with Devcon 
Aluminum Liquid F2 or equivalent (for ferrous casting repair) meeting Ford 
Manufacturing Standard M-3D35A(E). Do not service cracks with this 
material. Service with Aluminum Liquid F2 or equivalent must be 
confined to those cast iron engine component surfaces where the inner wall 
surface is not exposed to engine coolant pressure or oil pressure. For 
example: 

Cylinder block surfaces extending along the length of the block, upward 
from the oil pan rail to the cylinder water jacket, but not including machined 
areas. 

Lower rear face of the cylinder block. 

Intake manifold casting. Service is not recommended to the intake 
manifold exhaust crossover section, since temperatures can exceed the 
recommended temperature limit of 260°C (500°
F).

Cylinder head, along the valve rocker arm cover gasket surface. 

Use the following procedure to service porous areas or sand holes in 
cast iron. 

Clean surface to be serviced by grinding or rotary filing to a clean 
bright metal surface. Chamfer or undercut hole or porosity to a greater depth 
than rest of cleaned surface. Solid metal must surround hole. Openings larger 
than 6.35 mm (0.25 inch) should not be serviced using Devcon Aluminum Liquid 
F2 or equivalent. Openings in excess of 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) can be drilled, 
tapped and plugged using common tools. Clean service area thoroughly. Devcon 
Aluminum Liquid F2 or equivalent will not stick to a dirty or oily surface. 

Mix Devcon Aluminum Liquid F2 or equivalent and hardener as directed on 
container. Stir thoroughly until uniform. 

Apply service mixture with a suitable clean tool (putty knife, wood 
spoon, etc.) forcing Devcon Aluminum Liquid F2 or equivalent into hole or 
porosity. 

Allow service mixture to harden. This can be accomplished by two 
methods. Heat cure with a 250-watt lamp placed 254 mm (10 inches) from 
serviced surface, or air-dry for 10-12 hours at temperatures above 10°
C (50°F). 

Sand or grind serviced area to blend with general contour of 
surrounding surface. 

Paint the surface to match the rest of the block.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cylinder Walls, Refinishing, FD-1060 Engine

 CAUTION: Before any cylinder is refinished, all main bearing caps must be in 
place and tightened to the proper torque so that the crankshaft bearing bores 
will not become distorted from the refinishing operation. 

Cylinder walls that are severely marred or worn beyond the specified 
limits must be refinished. Hone only the cylinder or cylinders that require 
refinishing. If the cylinder will not clean up, the engine block must be bored 
to the next oversize.

Refinish cylinders that are deeply scored, out-of-round, or taper 
exceeds specification. If the cylinder walls have minor surface imperfections, 
but the out-of-round and taper are within limits, it may be possible to remove 
the imperfections by honing the cylinder walls and installing new service 
piston rings, providing the piston clearance is within specification. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 .

Use of a ball-type hone is recommended for refinishing cylinder walls 
when no cross-hatch pattern is visible on cylinder walls.

 Cleaning 

 CAUTION: If the following steps are not followed, rusting of the cylinder 
bore(s) can occur. 

After any cylinder bore service operation, such as honing or deglazing, 
clean the bore(s) with soap or detergent and water. Then thoroughly rinse the 
bore(s) with clean water to remove the soap or detergent, and wipe the bore(s) 
dry with a clean lint-free cloth. Finally, wipe the bore(s) with a clean cloth 
dipped in engine oil. 

If the engine is disassembled, thoroughly clean the block with solvent. 
Remove old gasket material from all machined surfaces. Remove all pipe plugs 
that seal oil passages and clean out all the passages. Blow out all passages, 
then bolt holes, etc., with compressed air. Make sure threads in the cylinder 
head bolt holes are clean. Dirt in the threads can cause binding and result in 
a false torque reading. Use a tap to true-up threads and to remove all deposits.

 Inspection 

After the block has been thoroughly cleaned, check it for cracks. Tiny 
cracks not visible to the naked eye can be detected by coating the suspected 
area with a mixture of 25 percent kerosene and 75 percent light engine oil. 
Wipe the part dry and immediately apply a coating of zinc oxide dissolved in 
wood alcohol. Do not use rubbing alcohol as a substitute. If cracks are 
present, the coating will become discolored at the damaged area. Replace the 
block if it is cracked.

Inspect the cylinder walls for scoring, roughness or other signs of 
wear. Check the cylinder bore for out-of-round and taper.

 Cylinder Bore 

 CAUTION: All cylinder bores must be the same. If you elect to overbore, all 
cylinders must be overbored to the same dimension. Oversize pistons and rings 
cannot be intermixed in any combinations. 

Cylinder bore(s) can be repaired by the following two methods: 

overboring and use of oversize pistons and rings

boring and installing a repair sleeve to return the bore to standard 
dimension

Oversize pistons and rings are available in two sizes: 0.50 mm (0.0197 
in.) and 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.).

If more than 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.) overbore is needed, a repair 
sleeve(s) is required. It is permissible to install sleeves into individual 
cylinders as required. Repair sleeves can be replaced by using a boring bar to 
bore out the old sleeve. Do not cut the cylinder bore beyond the oversize 
limit. 

Block cylinder bores can be rebored twice before use of a repair sleeve 
is required. The first rebore is 0.50 mm (0.0197 in.) oversize. The second 
rebore is 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.) oversize. 

Boring diameter dimensions: 

A = 102.469 mm (4.0342 inches) 1st rebore 

102.969 mm (4.0539 inches) 2nd rebore 

Honing diameter dimensions: 

B = 102.020 ± 0.020 mm (4.0165 ± 0.0008 in.) standard bore 

102.520 ± 0.020 mm (4.0362 ± 0.0008 in.) 1st rebore 

103.020 ± 0.020 mm (4.0559 ± 0.0008 in.) 2nd rebore 

After boring, use a honing stone to break the edge of the bore to 
Dimension C, approximately 1.25 mm (0.049 inch) x 15 degrees. 

[FIGURE: A17851A.gif]

A correctly honed surface will have a cross-hatched appearance with the 
lines at 15- to 25-degree angles with the top of the cylinder block. 

Rough hone: use 80 grit honing stones 

Finish hone: use 280 grit honing stones 

A maximum 1.2 micrometer (48 micro-inch) surface finish must be 
obtained. 

Immediately after finish honing is complete, clean the cylinder bores 
with a strong solution of laundry detergent and hot water. 

Rinse and blow the block dry. 

Check bore cleanness by wiping with a white, lint-free, lightly oiled 
cloth. If grit residue is still present, reclean. 

If the block is not to be used right away, coat with a rust-preventive 
solvent. 

 Cylinder Bore Taper 

To determine cylinder taper, measure at point A at the top and bottom 
of the cylinder. The difference between the two measurements is the amount of 
cylinder taper.

[FIGURE: A21988A.gif]

 Cylinder Out-Of-Round 

To determine if the cylinder is out-of-round, measure at points A and B 
as shown. The difference between the measurements is the amount the cylinder 
is out-of-round. 

[FIGURE: A21988A.gif]

 Cylinder Bore Diameter 

Measure the bore with an accurate bore gauge following the instructions 
of the manufacturer. Measure the diameter of each cylinder bore at the top, 
middle and bottom with the gauge placed at right angles and parallel to the 
centerline of the engine to determine if cylinder is out-of-round. Use 
only the measurements obtained at 90 degrees to the engine centerline when 
calculating the piston-to-cylinder bore clearance. 

 Cylinder Wall Honing 

 CAUTION: Before any cylinder is refinished, all main bearing caps must be in 
place and tightened to the proper torque so that the crankshaft bearing bores 
will not become distorted from the refinishing operation. 

 CAUTION: All cylinder bores must be the same. If you elect to overbore, all 
cylinders must be overbored to the same dimension. Oversize pistons and rings 
cannot be intermixed in any combinations. 

Cylinder walls that are severely marred or worn beyond the specified 
limits must be refinished. Hone only the cylinder or cylinders that require 
refinishing. If the cylinder will not clean up, the engine block must be bored 
to the next oversize. 

Cylinder bore(s) can be repaired by two methods. 

Methods: 

Overboring and use of oversize pistons and rings. 

Boring and installing a repair sleeve to return the bore to standard 
dimensions. 

Oversize pistons and rings are available in two sizes: 0.50 mm (0.0197 
in.) and 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.).

If more than 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.) overbore is needed, a repair 
sleeve(s) is required. It is permissible to install sleeves into individual 
cylinders as required. Repair sleeves can be replaced by using a boring bar to 
bore out the old sleeve. Do not cut the cylinder bore beyond the oversize 
limit. 

Block cylinder bores may be rebored twice before use of a repair sleeve 
is required. The first rebore is 0.50 mm (0.0197 in.) oversize. The second 
rebore is 1.00 mm (0.0393 in.) oversize. 

Boring diameter dimensions: 

A = 102.469 mm (4.0342 inches) 1st rebore 

102.969 mm (4.0539 inches) 2nd rebore 

Honing diameter dimensions: 

B = 102.020 ± 0.020 mm (4.0165 ± 0.0008 in.) standard bore 

102.520 ± 0.020 mm (4.0362 ± 0.0008 in.) 1st rebore 

103.020 ± 0.020 mm (4.0559 ± 0.0008 in.) 2nd rebore 

After boring, use a honing stone to break the edge of the bore to 
Dimension C, approximately 1.25 mm (0.049 inch) x 15 degrees. 

[FIGURE: A17851A.gif]

A correctly honed surface will have a cross-hatched appearance with the 
lines at 15- to 25-degree angles with the top of the cylinder block. 

Rough hone: use 80 grit honing stones 

Finish hone: use 280 grit honing stones 

A maximum 1.2 micrometer (48 micro-inch) surface finish must be 
obtained. 

Immediately after finish honing is complete, clean the cylinder bores 
with a strong solution of laundry detergent and hot water. 

Rinse and blow the block dry. 

Check bore cleanness by wiping with a white, lint-free, lightly oiled 
cloth. If grit residue is still present, reclean. 

If the block is not to be used right away, coat with a rust-preventive

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Repair Sleeve Installation, FD-1060 Engine

If more than a 1.00 mm (0.03937-in.) diameter oversize bore is 
required, the block must be rebored and a repair sleeve installed. The sleeve 
bore must be refinished after installation to a 102.020 ± 
0.020 mm (4.0165 ± 0.0008 in.) diameter. A standard 
diameter piston and a service piston ring set must be used.

Block rebore for repair sleeve.

A = 104.500 + 0.015 mm (4.1142 + 0.0006 
in.) 

B = 6.35 mm (0.250 in.) 

After boring thoroughly, clean the bore of all metal chips, debris and 
oil before installing the repair sleeves. 

[FIGURE: A17852A.gif]

Freeze the repair sleeve(s) for a minimum of one hour at a temperature 
at or below -12°C (+10°F). 
Remove the sleeves one at a time and install in the block using the following 
procedure. 

Apply a coat of Loctite® 620 or equivalent to the 
bore one at a time as the sleeve is installed. 

Using protective gloves, push the frozen sleeve into the bore as far as 
possible by hand. 

Using a sleeve driver, press or drive the sleeve in until it contacts 
the step in the bottom of the bore. 

[FIGURE: A17853A.gif]

Set up a boring bar and machine to the following dimensions. 

A = 101.956 mm (4.014 in.) 

B = Minimum — flush with block 

Maximum — 0.050 mm (0.0019-in.) protrusion 

After removing the boring bar, use a honing stone to break the edge of 
the repair sleeve(s) to Dimension C, approximately 1.25 mm (0.049 in.) x 15 
degrees. 

[FIGURE: A17854A.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Engine Block Plugs

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Impact Slide Hammer

T59L-100-B

Impact Slide Hammer

T50T-100-A

 Removal and Installation 

To remove a large engine block plug, drill a 12.70 mm (0.5-inch) hole 
in the center of the plug and remove with Impact Slide Hammer T59L-100-B or 
T50T-100-A or pry it out with a large drift punch. On a small engine block 
plug, drill a 6.35 mm (0.25-inch) hole in the center of the plug and pry it 
out with a small pin punch. Clean and inspect the plug bore. 

Prior to installing an engine block plug, the plug bore must be 
inspected for any damage that would interfere with the proper sealing of the 
plug. 

Coat the plug and bore lightly with an oil-resistant sealant such as 
Perfect Seal Sealing Compound B5A-19554-A or F2AZ-19554-AA or equivalent 
meeting Ford specifications ESR-M18P2-A and ESE-M4G115-A and install it 
following the procedure for cup-type or expansion-type below. 

 Engine Block Plugs, Expansion-Type 

 CAUTION: It is imperative to push or drive the plug into the machined bore using 
a properly designed tool. Under no circumstances is the plug to be driven 
using a tool that contacts the crowned portion of the plug. This method will 
expand the plug prior to installation and can damage the plug and/or plug 
bore. 

 CAUTION: If the engine block plug replacing tool has a depth seating surface, do 
not seat the tool against a non-machined (casting) surface. 

Expansion-type engine block plugs are installed with the flange edge 
inward. The maximum diameter of this plug is located at the base of the flange 
with the flange flaring inward.

When installed, the trailing (maximum) diameter must be below the 
chamfered edge of the bore to effectively seal the plugged bore. 

 Engine Block Plugs, Cup-Type 

 CAUTION: It is imperative to pull the plug into the machined bore by using a 
properly designed tool. Under no circumstances is the plug to be driven into 
the bore using a tool that contacts the flange. This method will damage the 
sealing edge and will result in leakage and/or plug blowout. 

 CAUTION: If the engine block plug replacing tool has a depth seating surface, do 
not seat the tool against a nonmachined (casting) surface. 

Cup-type engine block plugs are installed with the flanged edge 
outward. The maximum diameter of this plug is located at the outer edge of the 
flange. The flange on cup-type plugs flares outward with the largest diameter 
of the outer (sealing) edge.

The flanged (trailing) edge must be below the chamfered edge of the 
bore to effectively seal the plugged bore.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Crankshaft Main and Connecting Rod Bearings 

 Cleaning 

Bearings that are to be reused must be identified so they can be 
installed in their original locations. 

Clean the bearing inserts and caps thoroughly in solvent, and dry them 
with compressed air. Do not scrape gum or varnish deposits from the bearing 
shells.

 Inspection 

Inspect each bearing carefully. Bearings that have a scored, chipped or 
worn surface must be replaced. Typical examples of unsatisfactory bearings and 
their causes are shown in the illustration. The copper lead bearing base may 
be visible through the bearing overlay. If the base showing is less than 20 
percent of the total area, the bearing is not excessively worn. It is not 
necessary to replace the bearing if the bearing clearance is within 
recommended limits. Check the clearance of bearings that appear to be 
satisfactory with Plastigage® D81L-6002-B or equivalent as 
outlined below.
