SERVICE PROCEDURES

Crankshaft Main or Connecting Rod Bearings, Fitting

 Plastigage® Method 

Clean crankshaft journals. Inspect journals and thrust faces for nicks, 
burrs or roughness that would cause premature bearing wear. When replacing 
standard bearings with new bearings, it is good practice to fit bearing to 
minimum specified clearance. If desired clearance cannot be obtained with a 
standard bearing, try a 0.050 mm (0.002 inch) undersize bearing set to obtain 
proper clearance. 

 CAUTION: Do not position the jack under the crankshaft pulley. Crankshaft post 
damage will result. 

If fitting main bearing in vehicle, position a jack under counterweight 
adjoining bearing which is being checked. Support crankshaft with jack so its 
weight will not compress Plastigage® and provide an 
erroneous reading. 

Place a piece of Plastigage® D81L-6002-B or 
equivalent on bearing surface across full width of bearing cup and about 6.35 
mm (0.25 inch) off-center. 

[FIGURE: A23339A.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

D81L-6002-B

Plastigage®

2

Plastigage® Scale
(Part of D81L-6002-B)

A

—

Check Width of Plastigage®

B

—

Location of Plastigage® Prior to Tightening

Install cap and tighten bolts to specification. Do not turn crankshaft 
while Plastigage® is in place. 

Remove cap. Using Plastigage® scale, check width of 
Plastigage® at widest point to get minimum clearance. Check 
at narrowest point to get maximum clearance. Difference between reading is 
taper of journals. 

If bearing clearance exceeds the specified limits, try using one of the 
various combinations of undersize bearings as directed by the accompanying 
table. Use of any other bearing combination is not recommended. Bearing 
clearance must be within specified limits. Refer to appropriate section under Specifications 
 for main and connecting rod bearing clearance limits. If use of 
these bearing combinations does not bring clearance to the desired limits, 
refinish the crank journal to 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) undersize, and use the 
appropriate bearing. 

After bearing has been fitted and cleaned, apply a light coat of engine 
oil to journal and bearings. Install bearing cap. Tighten cap bolts to 
specification. 

Repeat procedure for remaining bearings that require replacement.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Crankshaft 

 Cleaning 

 CAUTION: Handle the crankshaft with care to avoid possible damage to the 
finished surfaces. 

Clean the crankshaft with solvent, then blow out all oil passages with 
compressed air. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the crankshaft main journals and connecting rod journals for 
scores, nicks, burrs, signs of overheating, deep scratches or other damage. If 
damage is found, refinish journals as outlined.

[FIGURE: A100941A.gif]

On an engine used with a manual transmission, check the fit of the 
clutch pilot bearing in the bore of the crankshaft. A needle roller bearing 
and adapter assembly is used as a clutch pilot bearing. It is press-fit 
directly into the engine crankshaft and should not be loose.

Inspect the inner surface of the bearing for wear or a bell-mouth 
condition. Check the inside diameter of the bearing to see if it is worn or 
damaged. The bearing and adapter assembly cannot be serviced separately. The 
needle bearing clutch pilot can only be installed with the seal end of the 
bearing facing the transmission. The bearing and seal are pregreased and do 
not require additional lubrication. A new bearing must be installed whenever a 
bearing is removed. 

Inspect the pilot bearing, when used, for roughness, evidence of 
overheating or loss of lubricant. Replace if any of these conditions are 
found. 

 Crankshaft End Play 

Measure the end clearance of the crankshaft as follows:

Install Dial Indicator with Bracketry D78P-4201-F or Dial Indicator 
with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent onto the oil pan flange.

Put the tip of the gauge against the crankshaft counterweight.

Push the crankshaft toward the rear of the cylinder block.

[FIGURE: A18246A.gif]

Set the dial indicator at zero.

Push the crankshaft toward the front of the cylinder block. If the end 
clearance is less than 0.16 mm (0.006 in.) for the FD-1460 or less than 0.13 
mm (0.005 in.) for the FD-1060, do the following steps:

Loosen the main bearing capscrews one turn.

Push the crankshaft toward the front and then toward the rear of the 
cylinder block.

Tighten the capscrews in three steps following the illustrated sequence:

Step 1 — 50 Nm (37 lb-ft)

Step 2 — 119 Nm (88 lb-ft)

Step 3 — 176 Nm (129 lb-ft)

[FIGURE: A18230A.gif]

 NOTE: Crankshafts that have been reground on the thrust bearing surfaces are 
marked to oversize thrust bearings on the rear crankshaft counterweight. If 
the crankshaft counterweight is marked, check the thrust bearing part number 
to make sure the correct bearing size is used.

Example: 0.010 = 0.25 mm (0.010 inch).

Measure the crankshaft end play. The end play specification for a new 
or reground crankshaft with new thrust bearings can be found in Specifications 
 in Section 03A-01 
(FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A18247A.gif]

If the crankshaft end play is greater than 0.33 mm (0.013 in.) for the 
FD-1460 or 0.36 mm (0.014 in.) for the FD-1060, the crankshaft must be removed 
from the engine and repaired.

 Crankshaft Main Journal and Connecting Rod Journals 

Measure the diameter of each journal in at least four places to 
determine an out-of-round, taper or undersize condition. For specifications, 
refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

 Journals, Refinishing 

Dress minor imperfections such as scores, nicks or burrs with an oil 
stone. If the journals are severely marred or exceed the service limit, they 
must be refinished to size for the next undersize bearing. 

If required, machine the journals to give the proper clearance with the 
next undersize bearing. If the journals will not clean up to maximum undersize 
bearing available, replace the crankshaft. 

Always reproduce the same journal shoulder radius that existed 
originally. Too small a radius will result in fatigue failure of the 
crankshaft. Too large a radius will result in bearing failure due to radius 
ride of the bearing. 

After refinishing the journals, chamfer the oil holes. Polish the 
journal with a No. 320 grit polishing cloth and engine oil (crocus cloth can 
also be used as a polishing agent) to obtain a smooth finish.

================================================================================
PAGE 4312
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-00: Engine Service, Diesel

1997 L-Series Equipped with Ford FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Pistons, Piston Pins and Piston Rings 

 Cleaning 

Remove deposits from the piston surfaces. Clean gum or varnish from the 
piston skirt, piston pins, and rings with solvent.

 CAUTION: Do not use a caustic cleaning solution or a wire brush to clean pistons. 

Clean the ring grooves with Piston Ring Groove Cleaner D81L-6002-D or 
equivalent. Make sure oil ring slots (or holes) are clean. 

[FIGURE: A21327A.gif]

 Inspection 

Carefully inspect the pistons for fractures at the ring lands, skirts, 
oil ring slot corners, and pin bosses, and for scuffed, rough or scored 
skirts. If the lower inner portion of the ring grooves have a high step, 
replace the piston. The step will interfere with ring operation and cause 
excessive ring side clearance. 

Spongy, eroded areas near the edge of the top of the piston are usually 
caused by detonation or preignition. A shiny surface on the thrust surface of 
the piston, offset from the centerline between the piston pin holes, can be 
caused by a bent connecting rod. Replace pistons that show signs of excessive 
wear, wavy ring lands or fractures or damage from detonation or preignition. 

Check the piston-to-cylinder bore clearance by measuring the piston and 
bore diameters. For specifications refer to Section 03A-01 or Section 03B-01 
for the proper clearance. Refer to Cylinder Block in the Service Procedures 
portion of this section for the bore measurements procedure. Measure the 
outside diameter of the piston and micrometers at the centerline of the piston 
pin bore and at 90 degrees to the pin bore axis. Check the ring side 
clearance. Refer to Piston Rings, Fitting in the Service Procedures portion of 
this section. 

Replace piston pins showing signs of fracture, etching or wear. Check 
the piston pin fit in the piston and rod. 

Check the outside diameter of the piston pin and the inside diameter of 
the pin bore in the piston. Replace any piston pin or piston that is not 
within specifications. For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 or Section 03B-01 . 

Replace all rings that are scored, broken, chipped or cracked. Check 
the end gap and side clearance. Rings must not be transferred from one piston 
to another, regardless of mileage.

 Pistons, Fitting 

 NOTE: Pistons are available for service in standard size and the oversize 
shown in Specifications in Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 
(FD-1460). 

 NOTE: Cylinder bore must be clean and dry, and engine block must remain at 
room temperature (21°C [70°
F]) for eight hours before taking cylinder measurements. 

Measure the cylinder bore and select the piston to make sure the proper 
clearance is obtained. 

A — At right angle to centerline of engine

B — Parallel to centerline of engine

 Top Measurement: Take a measurement 12.70 mm (0.5 inch) 
below top of block deck.

 Bottom Measurement: Take a measurement within 12.70 mm 
(0.5 inch) above top of piston — when piston is at its lowest 
travel (B.D.C).

 Bore Service Limit: Equals the average of A and B when 
measured at the center of the piston travel.

 Taper: Equals difference between A top and A bottom.

 Out-of-Round: Equals difference between A and B when 
measured at the center of piston travel.

[FIGURE: A4165H.gif]

Measure the piston diameter to make sure the specified clearance is 
obtained. It may be necessary periodically to use another piston (within the 
same grade size) that is either slightly larger or smaller to achieve the 
specified clearance.

If none can be fitted, refinish the cylinder to provide the proper 
clearance for the piston. 

When a piston has been fitted, mark it for assembly in the cylinder to 
which it was fitted. 

If the taper, out-of-round and piston-to-cylinder bore clearance 
conditions of the cylinder bore are within specified limits, new piston rings 
will give satisfactory service. 

If new rings are to be installed in a used cylinder that has not been 
refinished, remove the cylinder wall glaze using only a ball-type hone and 
only if there is no visible sign of cross-hatch markings on the cylinder 
walls. Refer to Cylinder Walls, Refinishing , in the Service Procedures portion 
of this section. Always clean the cylinder bore thoroughly with detergent and 
water solution. 

Calculate size piston to be used by taking a cylinder bore check. 
Follow procedures outlined previously. 

Select proper size piston to provide desired clearance. Measure piston 
diameter in line with centerline of piston pin and at a 90-degree angle to 
piston pin axis. 

 NOTE: After any refinishing operation, allow cylinder bore to cool, and make 
sure piston and bore are clean and dry before piston fit is checked.

Make sure piston and cylinder block are at room temperature, 21°
C (70°F). 

[FIGURE: A8793F.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Cylinder Bore Micrometer — Typical

2

—

Centralizing Plungers — Part of Cylinder Bore Micrometer

3

—

Gauging Plunger — Part of Cylinder Bore Micrometer

4

—

Range Extension — Part of Cylinder Bore Micrometer

A

—

Extensions Furnished with Each Size Bore Gauge

 Piston Rings, Fitting 

 NOTE: Always use a piston ring expanding tool to install rings on a piston. 

Select proper ring set for size of cylinder bore. 

Position ring in cylinder bore in which it is going to be used. 

Push ring down into bore area where normal ring wear is not encountered. 

 CAUTION: Use care to avoid damage to ring or cylinder bore. 

Position ring in bore so ring is square with cylinder wall.

Measure gap between ends of ring with a feeler gauge. If ring gap is 
less than or greater than specified limits, try another ring set. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A21326A.gif]

Use a micrometer and piston ring groove gauge to measure the wear of 
the top ring groove keystone angle. Use a piston ring groove gauge to measure 
the wear of the intermediate ring groove keystone angle. For specifications 
refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

Check ring side clearance of rectangular intermediate and oil control 
ring grooves with a feeler gauge inserted between ring and its lower land. For 
specifications refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 
Gauge should slide freely around entire ring circumference without binding. 
Any wear that occurs will form a step at inner portion of lower land. If lower 
lands have high steps, piston should be replaced.

[FIGURE: A8514B.gif]

 Piston and Piston Pin Fit 

Measure the piston pin bore when the piston temperature is at 20°
C (68°F). Piston bore ID limits are 
45.006-45.025 mm (1.7719-1.7726 inch). Add 0.013 mm (0.0005 inch) to the bore 
inside diameter per 5°C (10°F) temperature 
rise up to 32°C (90°F).

Measure the piston pin outside diameter. Piston pin OD limits are 
44.993-45.003 mm (1.7714-1.7718). Discard the piston pin if it is more than 
0.03 mm (0.001 inch) out-of-round.

 Piston Pin-to-Piston Clearance 

Measure the piston pin bore inner diameter.

[FIGURE: A24344A.gif]

Measure the piston pin outside diameter.

[FIGURE: A24345A.gif]

Subtract the piston pin outside diameter from the piston bore inner 
diameter. The value obtained is the piston pin-to-piston pin bore clearance. 
Tolerance for piston pin-to-piston pin bore is 0.003-0.032 mm (0.0001-0.0016 
inch) for the FD-1460 and 0.003-0.035 mm (0.0001-0.0014 inch) for the FD-1060.

 Piston Outer Diameter 

Measure the piston diameter using a micrometer. Measure the piston 
skirt diameter 90 degrees to piston pin center axis, 12 mm (0.48 inch) from 
the bottom of the piston skirt for FD-1060 engines or 11 mm (0.43 inch) from 
the bottom of the piston skirt for FD-1460 engines.

[FIGURE: A17534B.gif]

Subtract the piston diameter from the bore diameter. The resultant 
figure should be within the clearance tolerances specified at the end of each 
engine section.

 Piston Rings 

Remove the piston rings from the piston.

Worn piston rings will have vertical lines. The chromium plate is worn 
through and the face of the ring has a brighter finish when compared to the 
dull satin finish of a new ring.

[FIGURE: A24346A.gif]

Scuffing and scoring are indicated by heavy scratches, metal 
discoloration and voids. This damage indicates a breakdown of the oil film on 
the liner wall causing transfer of material from the ring face to the liner.

[FIGURE: A24347A.gif]

Oil ring plugging is indicated by the deposits in the oil ring grooves. 
Plugging of the ring drains restricts oil drainback, which floods the ring 
belt area resulting in a loss of oil control.

[FIGURE: A24348A.gif]

 Piston Pin Hole Diameter 

Measure the piston pin bore inner diameter. The tolerance for the inner 
diameter is 45.006-45.025 mm (1.7719-1.7726 inches) for the FD-1460 and 
40.006-40.025 mm (1.5750-1.5758 inches) for the FD-1060.

 Piston Pin Diameter 

Measure the piston pin outside diameter. The pin diameter tolerance is 
44.993-45.003 mm (1.7710-1.7718 inches) for the FD-1460 and 39.990-40.003 mm 
(1.5744-1.5749 inches) for the FD-1060.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Connecting Rods 

 Piston Pin Clearance 

Measure the connecting rod piston pin bushing inside diameter. 
Connecting rod pin bore specifications are 45.023-45.060 mm (1.7726-1.7740 
inch) with bushing installed.

If the pin bore measurements are not within specifications, replace the 
rod assembly.

 Cleaning 

Remove the bearings from the rod and cap. Identify each bearing 
location if they are to be used again. Clean the connecting rod in solvent, 
including the rod bore and the back of the inserts. Do not use a caustic 
cleaning solution. Blow out all passages with compressed air. 

 Inspection 

The connecting rods and related parts must be carefully inspected and 
checked for conformance to specifications. For specifications, refer to 
 Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). Various forms of engine 
wear caused by these parts can be readily identified. 

A shiny surface on either pin boss inside of the piston usually 
indicates that a connecting rod is bent. 

Abnormal connecting rod bearing wear can be caused by either a bent 
connecting rod, worn or damaged crankpin, or a tapered connecting rod bore. 

Twisted connecting rods can create an identifiable piston skirt wear 
pattern, but badly twisted rods will disturb the action of the entire piston, 
rings, and connecting rod assembly and may be the cause of excessive oil 
consumption. 

Check the connecting rods for bend or twist on a suitable alignment 
fixture. Follow the instructions of the fixture manufacturer. If the bend or 
twist exceeds specification, the connecting rod must be replaced. 

Inspect the connecting rods for signs of fractures and the bearing 
bores for out-of-round and taper. If the bore exceeds the recommended limits 
or if the connecting rod is fractured, it should be replaced. Check the inside 
diameter of the connecting rod piston pin bore. If the pin bore in the 
connecting rod is larger than specification, the connecting rod must be 
replaced. 

 Connecting Rod Bushing Inner Diameter 

Measure the connecting rod piston pin inner diameter. Tolerances are 
45.023-45.060 mm (1.7726-1.7740 inches) for the FD-1460 and 40.019-40.042 mm 
(1.5755-1.5765 inches) for the FD-1060.

[FIGURE: A24350A.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Camshaft 

 Cleaning 

Clean the camshaft in solvent and wipe it dry. 

Remove light scuffs, scores or nicks from the camshaft machined 
surfaces with a smooth oil stone.

If camshaft journals are excessively worn or scored, the camshaft must 
be replaced. Camshaft journals can be refinished to accommodate 0.38 mm (0.015 
inch) undersize bearing. If the journals do not "clean up," the camshaft must 
be replaced. 

 Inspection 

Check camshaft bores for size, taper, roundness, alignment and finish. 
If any of these exceed the limits given in Specifications 
, install new 
camshaft bearings. 

 Cam Lobes 

Inspect the camshaft lobes for scoring and signs of abnormal wear. Lobe 
pitting except in the general area of the lobe toe is not detrimental to the 
operation of the camshaft; therefore, the camshaft should not be replaced 
unless the lobe lift loss has exceeded specification or pitting has occurred 
in the lobe lift area. 

The lift of the camshaft lobes can be checked with the camshaft 
installed in the engine or on centers. 

 Cam Lobe Lift 

To measure the cam lobe lift, proceed as follows: 

Measure distance between major (A-A) and minor (B-B) diameters of each 
cam lobe with a Vernier caliper and record readings. The difference in 
readings on each cam diameter is lobe lift. 

If readings do not meet specification, replace camshaft. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A21328A.gif]

 Camshaft Journal Diameters 

Measure the diameter of the camshaft bearing journals as shown. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). 
If any of the measurements are not within specification, replace the camshaft 
and verify the camshaft bearing journal diameters are within specification.

[FIGURE: A17576A.gif]

 Camshaft Bearing Diameter 

Measure the camshaft bearing inside diameter of each camshaft bearing 
installed in the cylinder block. For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 
(FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). If any of the measurements are not 
within specification, replace all camshaft bearings and verify the bearing 
inside diameters are within specification.

[FIGURE: A17593A.gif]

 Camshaft End Play 

Measure camshaft end play with a dial indicator. For specifications, 
refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

End play is controlled by the thickness of the thrust plate and the 
groove in the camshaft. If the camshaft end play is greater than the stated 
limit, the thrust plate must be replaced.

 Camshaft Gear 

Check the camshaft gear for scores or nicks, and the condition of the 
teeth wear pattern. Minor gear teeth imperfections can be removed using a 
carborundum stone. If tooth wear or damage is severe, replace the camshaft gear.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Valve Tappets, Solid Lifters

 Cleaning 

 CAUTION: Any time a new camshaft is installed, new tappets must also be installed. 

Clean the valve tappets with solvent and dry with compressed air.

 Inspection 

Inspect the socket, stem and face for excessive wear, cracks, concavity 
and other damage. Maximum allowable tappet face concavity for reuse is 0.025 
mm (0.001 inch).

[FIGURE: A17570C.gif]

Measure the valve tappet stem. Tappet stem diameter limits are 
15.925-15.98 mm (0.627-0.6291 inch).

Pit marks on the tappet face are acceptable. The following criteria 
define the size of the pits allowed.

A single pit cannot be greater than 2 mm (0.078 inch).

Interconnection of pits is not allowed.

Total pits when added together must not exceed 6 mm (0.236 inch) 
diameter or a total of 4 percent of the tappet face.

No pitting is allowable on the edges of the wear face of the tappet.

[FIGURE: A17571A.gif]

1997 L-Series Equipped with Ford FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Oil Pump 

 Cleaning 

Wash all parts in a solvent and dry them thoroughly with compressed 
air. Use a brush to clean the inside of the pump housing and the pressure 
relief valve chamber. Make sure all dirt and metal particles are removed. 

 Inspection 

 NOTE: Internal components are not serviced. If any component is out of 
specification, the pump assembly must be replaced. 

For specifications and clearance limits, refer to Section 03A-01 
(FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). Check the inside of the pump housing 
and the inner and outer gears for damage or excessive wear. 

Check the mating surface of the pump cover for wear. Minor scuff marks 
are normal, but if the cover, gears or housing surfaces are excessively worn, 
scored or grooved, replace the pump. Inspect the rotor for nicks, burrs or 
score marks. Remove minor imperfections with an oil stone. 

 Tooth Tip Clearance 

Measure the inner to outer rotor tip clearance with feeler gauge 
inserted 13 mm (0.5 in.) minimum.

[FIGURE: A17877A.gif]

 Rotor End Play 

With the rotor assembly installed in the housing, place Straightedge 
D83L-4201-A or equivalent over the rotor assembly and the housing. 

Measure the vertical clearance (rotor end play) between the 
straightedge and both the inner rotor and the outer race. Maximum clearance 
must not exceed 0.13 mm (0.005 inch).

[FIGURE: A17878A.gif]

 Outer Rotor-to-Pump Body Clearance 

Measure clearance between outer rotor and pump body in several areas 
around the circumference of the outer rotor.

[FIGURE: A23432A.gif]

================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-00: Engine Service, Diesel

1997 L-Series Equipped with Ford FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Oil Pan 

 Cleaning 

Scrape any dirt or metal particles from the inside of the pan. Scrape 
all old gasket material from the gasket surface. Wash the pan in a solvent and 
dry it thoroughly. Make sure all foreign particles are removed. 

 Inspection 

Check the pan for cracks, holes or damaged drain plug threads. Check 
the gasket surface for damage caused by overtightened bolts. Replace with a 
new oil pan if repairs cannot be made.

================================================================================
PAGE 4318
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-00: Engine Service, Diesel

1997 L-Series Equipped with Ford FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cylinder Heads 

 CAUTION: Do not plane or grind more than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) from original 
cylinder head gasket surface. 

Replace the head if it is cracked. Remove all burrs or scratches with 
an oil stone. 

 Cleaning 

With the valves installed to protect the valve seats, remove deposits 
from the combustion chambers and valve heads with a scraper and a wire brush. 
Be careful not to damage the cylinder head gasket surface. After the valves 
are removed, clean the valve guide bores. Use cleaning solvent to remove dirt, 
grease and other deposits from the valves with a fine wire brush or buffing 
wheel. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the cylinder heads for cracks or excessively burned areas in 
the exhaust outlet ports. 

Check the gasket surface for burrs and nicks. Small imperfections of 
this type can be dressed down using an oil stone. Replace the head if it is 
cracked. 

The following inspection procedures are for a cylinder head that is to 
be completely overhauled. For individual repair operations, use only the 
pertinent inspection procedure. 

 Cylinder Head Flatness 

Use a straightedge and feeler gauge to measure the overall flatness of 
the cylinder head deck. The overall flatness, side to side, must not exceed 
0.075 mm (0.003 in.). The overall flatness, end to end, must not exceed 0.305 
mm (0.012 inch). 

Visually inspect for any localized dips or imperfections. If present, 
the cylinder head deck must be reground.

[FIGURE: A17624A.gif]

 Valve Seat Runout 

Check the valve seat runout with a valve seat runout gauge. Follow the 
instructions of the gauge manufacturer. If the runout exceeds the wear limit, 
reface the valve. For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or 
 Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: DA0873A.gif]

 Valve Stem-to-Valve Guide Clearance 

Check the valve stem-to-valve guide clearance of each valve in its 
respective valve guide with Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or Dial 
Indicator with Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent and Valve Stem 
Clearance TOOL-6505-E or equivalent. Use a flat-end indicator point. 

Install the tool on the valve stem until it is fully seated, and 
tighten the knurled setscrew firmly. Permit the valve to drop away from its 
seat until the tool contacts the upper surface of the valve guide. 

Position the dial indicator with its flat tip against the center 
portion of the tool's spherical section at approximately 90 degrees to the 
valve stem axis. Move the tool back and forth in line with the indicator stem. 
Take a reading on the dial indicator without removing the tool from the valve 
guide upper surface. Divide the reading by two, the division factor for the 
tool. If valve stem-to-valve guide clearance exceeds the wear limit, ream the 
valve guide for the next oversize valve stem as outlined under Valves, Select 
Fitting in the Service Procedures portion of this section. 

[FIGURE: A10707D.gif]

 Valves, Select Fitting 

If valve stem-to-guide clearance exceeds the service limit, the guide 
can be bored out to accept an oversize valve guide. Once the guide is 
installed in the cylinder head, it must be reamed to specifications. 

In the case of valve stem-to-valve guide clearance, the service 
clearance is intended as an aid to diagnosing engine noise only, and does not 
constitute a failure or indicate need for service. However, when overhauling 
or reconditioning a cylinder head, the service clearance should be regarded as 
a practical working value, and used as a determinant for installing the 
oversize valve guide. 

[FIGURE: A21329A.gif]

If the valve face runout is excessive or to remove pits and grooves, 
reface the valves to a true 45-degree angle. Remove only enough stock to 
correct the runout or to clean up the pits and grooves. If the edge (or 
margin) of the valve head is less than 0.794 mm (1/32 inch) thick after 
grinding, replace the valve as the valve will run too hot in the engine. 
Remove all grooves or score marks from the end of the valve stem, and chamfer 
it as necessary. Do not remove more than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) from the end of 
the valve stem.

If the valve or valve seat has been refaced, it will be necessary to 
check the clearance between the rocker arm pad and the valve stem with the 
valve train assembly installed in the engine. 

 Valve Seats, Refacing 

Exhaust valve seats and intake valve seats are induction hardened and 
can be refaced. 

[FIGURE: A14139D.gif]

 Valves 

The critical inspection points of the valve are illustrated below. 
Refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

 Valves, Inspection 

Inspect the valve stem for bends, and the end of the stem for grooves 
or scoring. 

Inspect the valve face and the edge of the valve head for pits, grooves 
or scores. Inspect the stem for a bend condition and the end of the stem for 
grooves or scores. Check the valve head for signs of burning or erosion, 
warpage and cracking. Minor pits, grooves, etc., may be removed. Discard 
severely damaged valves. 

Inspect the valve spring assembly, valve spring retainers, locks and 
sleeves and discard any visually damaged parts. 

 Valves, Refacing 

Minor pits or grooves may be removed. Discard valves that are severely 
damaged if the face runout cannot be corrected by refinishing, or stem 
clearance exceeds specification. Refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460) for specifications. Discard any excessively worn or damaged 
valve train parts.

Refer to Engine Service in the Rotunda Tool catalog for a description 
of the various types of valve resurfacing equipment. 

The valve refacing operation must be closely coordinated with the valve 
seat refacing operations so that the finished angles of the valve face and 
valve seat will be to specifications and provide a compression-tight fit. 

Make sure refacer grinding wheels are properly dressed. Refer to the 
following illustration and to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 
(FD-1460) for critical valve dimensions.

 Valve Guide Height 

Use a depth micrometer to measure the valve guide installed height. 
Measure from the top of the valve guide to the bottom of the recess area. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

If damage is found or the valve guide(s) do not meet the limits 
specified, the valve guide(s) must be replaced.

[FIGURE: A18330A.gif]

 Valve Guide Inner Diameter 

Visually inspect the valve guides for scuffing or scoring.

Using a small bore gauge to measure the inside diameter of the valve 
guides in locations 13 mm (1/2 inch) from each end and the center as shown. 
For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 
(FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A18329A.gif]

If the inspection reveals damaged valve guides, replace the valve guides.

 Valve Stem Diameter 

Measure the outside diameter of the valve stem as shown. For 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A17521A.gif]

Replace any valve with a valve stem that is worn below specifications.

 Valve Head Margin Thickness 

Measure the valve head margin thickness as shown to determine if there 
is enough stock to grind the valve. For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A17524A.gif]

If margin is less than specification, replace valve.

 Valve Spring Length Inspection 

Measure the length of the valve spring. For specifications, refer to 
 Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460).

[FIGURE: A23470A.gif]

If valve spring length is not with specifications, replace spring.

 Valve Spring Tension 

Inspect the valve spring, valve spring retainers, and keys for wear or 
damage. Discard any damaged parts. 

Check the springs for proper pressure at the specified spring lengths 
using Valve/Clutch Spring Tester TOOL-6513-DD or equivalent. Weak valve 
springs cause poor engine performance. Replace any spring not within 
specification. For specifications, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or 
 Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). Manually rotating the valve spring assemblies while 
installed in the engine will not determine condition of valve springs.

[FIGURE: A21330A.gif]

 Valve Spring Squareness 

Check each spring for squareness using a steel square and a flat 
surface. Stand the spring and square on end on the flat surface. Slide the 
spring up to the square. Revolve the spring slowly and observe the space 
between the top coil of the spring and the square. Refer to the illustration 
below.

[FIGURE: A8517A.gif]

For out-of-square limits, refer to Section 03A-01 (FD-1060) or Section 03B-01 (FD-1460). Follow the same procedure for new valve springs before 
installation.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Rocker Arm/Shaft Assembly 

 Cleaning 

Clean all parts thoroughly. Make sure all oil passages are open. 

 Inspection 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to true this surface by grinding. On pedestal-mounted 
rocker arms, check the rocker arm pad, side rails and fulcrum seat for 
excessive wear, cracks, nicks, or burrs. Check the rocker arm bolt for 
stripped or broken threads. 

Inspect the shaft and the rocker arm bore for nicks, scratches, scores 
or scuffs. Replace any damaged parts. 

Inspect the pad at the valve end of the rocker arm for indications of 
scuffing or abnormal wear. If the pad is grooved, replace the rocker arm. 

[FIGURE: A17508A.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Rocker Arm-to-Rocker Arm Shaft Clearance

Measure the inner diameter of the rocker arm.

[FIGURE: A24454A.gif]

Measure the outside diameter of the rocker arm shaft.

[FIGURE: A24455A.gif]

Subtract the rocker arm shaft measurement from the inner diameter 
measurement of the rocker arm. This is the clearance measurement. Tolerances 
are 0.025-0.102 mm (0.0010-0.0040 inch) for the FD-1460 and 0.025-0.113 mm 
(0.0010-0.0044 inch) for the FD-1060.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Valve Clearance Adjustment, Solid Lifters

 CAUTION: To prevent damage to the timing pin, make sure to disengage the pin 
after locating top dead center. 

Locate top dead center (TDC) for cylinder No. 1 by rotating the 
crankshaft slowly while pressing on the engine timing pin.

When the pin engages the hole in the camshaft gear, cylinder No. 1 is 
at top dead center on the compression stroke.

[FIGURE: A23434A.gif]

Valves are adjusted with the engine cold (below 60°C [
140°F]).

Clearance is correct when slight resistance is felt as the feeler gauge 
is moved between the valve stem and rocker arm pad.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Push Rods 

 Cleaning 

Clean the push rods in a suitable solvent. 

 Inspection 

Check the ends of the push rods for nicks, grooves, roughness or 
excessive wear. Replace damaged push rods. 

The push rods can be visually checked for straightness while they are 
installed in the engines by rotating them with the valve closed. They also can 
be checked with a dial indicator. 

If the push rod is bent beyond specifications, it must be replaced. Do 
not attempt to straighten push rods.

[FIGURE: A10196C.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Intake Manifold

 Cleaning 

Remove all gasket material from the machined surfaces of the manifold. 
Clean the manifold in a suitable solvent and dry it with compressed air. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the manifold for cracks, damaged gasket surfaces, or other 
problems that would make it unfit for further service.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Exhaust Manifold 

 Cleaning 

Remove all gaskets or foreign material from all inlet and outlet 
sealing surfaces of the manifold. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the cylinder head joining flanges of the exhaust manifold for 
evidence of exhaust gas leaks. 

Inspect the manifold for cracks, damaged surfaces, or other damage that 
would make them unfit for further service. Warped or cracked exhaust manifolds 
must be replaced.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Flywheel Inspection

 Transmission, Automatic 

Inspect the flywheel for cracks or other damage that would make it 
unfit for further service. Inspect the flywheel ring gear for worn, chipped or 
cracked teeth. If the teeth are damaged, replace the ring gear and flywheel 
assembly. 

With the flywheel installed on the crankshaft, check the gear face 
runout. 

 Transmission, Manual 

Inspect the flywheel for cracks, heat check, or other damage that would 
make it unfit for further service. Machine the friction surface of the 
flywheel if it is scored or worn. If it is necessary to remove more than 1.0 
mm (0.040 inch) of stock from the original thickness, replace the flywheel. 

Inspect the ring gear for worn, chipped or cracked teeth. If the teeth 
are damaged, replace the ring gear. 

With the flywheel installed on the crankshaft, check the flywheel face 
runout. Refer to Flywheel Housing Face Alignment under Flywheel 
Runout in the Service Procedures portion of this section.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Flywheel Clutch Surface Machining

 CAUTION: If more than 1.0 mm (0.040 inch) is removed from the flywheel, the 
flywheel must be discarded. If after removal of the 1.0 mm (0.040 inch), 
material heat or surface cracks are apparent, the flywheel must be discarded. 
If after removal of the 1.0 mm (0.040 inch), grooves are apparent in the 
surface, the flywheel must be discarded. 

Inspect the flywheel for cracks, heat check or other damage that would 
make it unfit for further use. Acceptable flywheels can be repaired by 
polishing with fine grade (400 grit) sandpaper. Flywheels can be resurfaced to 
remove scratches or grooves. After resurfacing, the flywheel thicknesses must 
not be less than the dimensions noted in the illustration. 

Flywheel resurfacing machining requirements are as follows. 

To measure the flywheel thickness, place the flywheel on a straight 
edge or flat surface. Measure from the clutch face or flat surface to the 
surface that the flywheel mounting contacts to the end of the crankshaft. 

The maximum material removal allowed is 1.0 mm (0.040 inch). 

Minimum flywheel thickness is 32.00 mm (1.260 inches). Discard the 
flywheel if final machined thickness is less than 32.00 mm (1.260 inches).

 NOTE: The illustration is an example only; each flywheel thickness may be 
different. 

Clutch contact surface finish must be 2.0 micrometers (40 rms).

Inspect the ring gear for worn, chipped or cracked teeth. If the teeth 
are damaged, replace the ring gear. 

[FIGURE: A17626C.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Viscous Vibration Damper

Near the end of the useful life of a viscous damper, the fluid inside 
the damper can gel and expand. This expansion can cause either an overall 
increase in damper thickness or a variation in thickness. Measuring the 
thickness can indicate whether a damper has exceeded its useful life and must be replaced.

The following is the inspection schedule for viscous vibration dampers:

Engine Model

Inspection Interval

FD-1060

77,000 km (48,000 miles), 2,000 hours, or 2 years

FD-1460

77,000 km (48,000 miles), 2,000 hours, or 2 years

Clean the damper with a solvent cleaner.

Check the mounting area for cracks. Check the housing for dents or 
raised surfaces. Replace the damper if any of these defects are identified.

[FIGURE: A22299A.gif]

Examine the damper and record the vendor identification, date code, and 
part number.

[FIGURE: A22300A.gif]

Using the date code, determine the type of bearing material in the 
damper. Date codes followed by a P represent dampers with P.T.F.E. (Teflon®
) bearing material. Date codes that are not followed by a P 
represent dampers with nylon bearing material.

[FIGURE: A23051A.gif]

[FIGURE: A23052A.gif]

Determine whether the damper is a cast type or fabricated type. 
Fabricated vibration dampers are the most common type and can be identified by 
a weld bead on the front center section of the damper where the housing joins 
the mounting flange.

[FIGURE: A23053A.gif]

Remove the paint on both sides of the damper in four 
locations spaced 90 degrees apart.

[FIGURE: A23054A.gif]

 NOTE: This procedure will result in a total of eight measurements.

Measure and record the thickness at two points at each of the four 
locations.

Measure the thickness at 3.18 mm (0.125 inch) from the outer lip.

Measure thickness at 25.4 mm (1.0 inch) from the outer lip.

[FIGURE: A23055A.gif]

If the variation between any of the eight measurements exceeds 0.25 mm 
(0.010 inch), or if the thickness at any point exceeds the maximum thickness 
dimensions indicated in the following chart, replace the damper.

 VIBRATION DAMPER THICKNESS SPECIFICATIONS

Engine Model

Part No.

Housing Type

Bearing Material

Maximum Thickness Allowable

Fabricated

Teflon®

38.10

1.500

Spray the rolled lip of the damper with crack detection developer, Part 
No. 3375434 or its equivalent. Heat the damper in an oven (rolled lip side 
down) at 93°C (200°F) for two hours.

[FIGURE: A23056A.gif]

 WARNING: WEAR PROTECTIVE GLOVES WHEN HANDLING PARTS THAT HAVE BEEN HEATED TO 
PREVENT PERSONAL INJURY. 

Remove the damper from the oven and check for fluid leakage around the 
rolled lip. If there is leakage, replace the damper.

[FIGURE: A23057A.gif]

 NOTE: Always replace the vibration damper after a camshaft nose failure. 
Camshaft nose breakages are primarily caused by excessive torsional activity.

Dampers that have exceeded their useful life will not function properly 
and can cause engine damage due to excessive torsional vibration in the 
engine. Viscous vibration dampers must be replaced when a major overhaul has 
been performed.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Filter Element, Luber-Finer 

 Removal 

Open drain cock. Refer to the illustration in the Description and 
Operation portion of this section.

Remove clamp screws and filter cover. 

Unscrew filter element hold-down (wing bolt and spring) assembly. 

Withdraw and discard filter element. 

 Installation 

Clean housing and element retainer in solvent. 

Check orifice plug. Blow out with air jet. 

Check cover gasket for damage. 

Install new element in housing. 

Install element hold-down assembly in filter and tighten to shoulder 
stop. 

Install cover gasket and cover clamps. Secure clamps with alternate 
tightening of clamp screws to make sure cover and gasket sealing is uniform. 

 NOTE: The engine oil pan has sufficient capacity for the 11-liter 
(3.0-gallon) filter requirements. 

Add oil to filter at vent plug. Add remainder of 11-liter (3.0-gallon) 
filter oil capacity to the crankcase. 

Start engine and check for oil leaks.

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling System

Coolant is drawn from the radiator by the integrally mounted water 
pump. The output from the water pump empties into the bottom of the oil cooler 
cavity in the cylinder block.

From the cooler cavity, the coolant flows into the upper water 
manifold. A portion of the coolant flows through the coolant filter and 
returns to the lower manifold. The remainder flows through six cast openings 
up to the cylinder head.

A portion of the coolant flowing into the cylinder head is directed to 
the liner cavity and, by means of a diffuser plate cast into the cavity, is 
circulated around the top portion of the liners.

The remainder of the coolant flows across the valve bridges around the 
injector bores and down into the liner cavities through two orificed holes per 
cylinder. The orificed holes control the coolant flow around the liners.

From the liner cavities the coolant flows through cast openings into 
the lower manifold and on to the thermostat cavity.

================================================================================
PAGE 4333
================================================================================

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Coolant Recovery System

 NOTE: Walter C. Avrea, the owner of patents 3,601,181 and RE27,965, has 
granted Ford Motor Company rights with respect to cooling systems covered by 
these patents.

 CAUTION: The use of a winter front or other air flow restriction device mounted 
in front of the radiator is not recommended on vehicles equipped with chassis 
mounted air-to-air after cooling. Airflow restriction causes high exhaust 
temperatures, power loss, excessive fan usage, and a reduction in fuel 
economy. If a winter front or other airflow restriction device is used, it 
must have a permanent opening directly in line with the center of the fan 
drive. The minimum opening size must be 120 square inches. 

 CAUTION: Coolant recovery systems are used on some vehicles. Do not remove the 
radiator cap on these vehicles when system is hot — add 
coolant to the plastic bottle only. Maintain level at the specified cold or 
hot fill mark. Check coolant level in the radiator periodically by removing 
the radiator cap only when the system is cold. 

Correct coolant level is essential for maximum circulation and adequate 
cooling. In addition, for the cooling system to perform its function, it must 
receive proper care. This includes keeping the radiator fins clean and a 
periodic inspection of the cooling system for leakage.

When cooling system is drained, fill supply tank with coolant. Refer to Cooling System, Draining, Filling and Bleeding 
 in the Cleaning and Inspection 
portion of this section.

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Coolant

 Approved Coolant and Concentration 

Whenever engine coolant is added to the radiator, use equal parts of 
water and Ford Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid (low silicate) 
E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M97B18-C. Also, add 
Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System Additive FW-15 or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESN-M99B169-A, at a strength of 4 ounces per gallon of engine 
coolant being added. If coolant must be added more than once a month, or if 
more than one quart at a time must be added, have your dealer check the 
cooling system for leaks.

Ordinary tap water can be used in an emergency except in areas where 
the water is known to be exceptionally hard or to have a high alkali content. 
The cooling system should be drained and flushed and the proper mixture of 
coolant added as soon as possible. With only water in the system, do not let 
the engine run hot.

To avoid possible overheating in very hot weather, do not use mixtures 
with more than 50 percent antifreeze except in areas where antifreeze 
protection below -37°C (-35°F) is required. 
In this case, refer to the coolant mixture chart on the Ford Cooling System 
Fluid container.

For vehicles equipped with other than Ford diesel engines, refer to the 
diesel engine manufacturer operator's manual for cooling system maintenance 
procedures.

 Unsatisfactory Coolant Materials 

 CAUTION: Do not add any radiator sealers containing water-soluble oil to the 
cooling system of diesel engines, as it will make the corrosion resistor 
inoperative. 

A standard ethylene glycol hydrometer can be used to check the 
protection level of the long-life coolant or Rotunda Battery Anti-Freeze 
Tester 021-00046 or equivalent.

When water or coolant is added to the supply tank, operate the engine 
at fast idle for 30 minutes before letting the vehicle stand with the engine 
off for prolonged periods to prevent damage to the cooling system during 
periods of below freezing temperatures. This will allow a uniform mixture 
throughout the cooling system and prevent damage by freezing, when sufficient 
antifreeze is used.

Do not use alcohol or methanol antifreeze, or mix them with the 
specified coolant.

Some engine coolant recycling manufacturers have claimed to have the 
ability to recycle engine coolant. Ford Motor Company has not authorized the 
use of recycled engine coolant nor have they sanctioned the use of any 
machines or devices that recycle engine coolant. Recycled coolant is not 
equivalent to the Ford Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid (low 
silicate) E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M97B18-C.

 Coolant Disposal 

The disposal of all used engine coolant must always be done in 
accordance with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations.

 NOTE: For information on the warning and shutdown system, refer to Section 13-09 .

PAGE 4335

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Coolant Conditioner

 CAUTION: Inadequate concentration of the coolant conditioner can result in major 
corrosive damage to engine cooling system components. Overconcentration can 
cause formation of gels that can cause coolant flow restriction, plugging of 
passages and overheating. 

With Ford diesel engines, always use engine cooling system conditioner 
as specified in the maintenance schedule.

Changing engine coolant filter/conditioner as specified in the 
maintenance schedule will help keep engine coolant properly conditioned.

Engine coolant conditioner provides additional long-term protection 
against cavitation erosion and corrosion beyond that provided by the engine 
coolant solution.

Do not add any radiator sealers containing water-soluble oil to the 
cooling system of diesel engines; it will make the corrosion resistor 
inoperative.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Radiator

All heavy-duty trucks use radiators of the tube and serpentine 
fin-type. On the L-7000 through L-9000 series radiators, tubes are arranged 
for horizontal flow of coolant. Other models are arranged for vertical flow of 
coolant.

On L-7000 through L-9000 horizontal flow radiators, there are two 
header tanks, one on either side of the radiator. The header tanks provide 
uniform distribution of coolant to the tubes. The radiator outlet port is 
connected to the water pump inlet port. The radiator inlet port is connected 
to the coolant outlet fitting of the engine, which permits coolant circulation 
through the radiator when the thermostat is open.

The radiator tanks are molded glass-filled nylon and are secured to the 
core header by crimp strips. If damaged, replace the tank. Do not attempt to 
repair or reseal it.

 Copper/Brass Core 

Valeo radiators are a modular design, featuring copper-brass core and 
header assemblies combined with plastic tanks. The plastic tank is sealed to 
the header with an oval gasket seal and is held in place with removable crimp 
strips. Radiator core replacements and tank replacements can be performed in 
the dealership with suitable repair equipment.

================================================================================
PAGE 4337
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling Fan and Fan Clutch

The fan and viscous or on-off clutch assembly are used to cool the 
engine. The fan is driven by the engine through the use of drive belts.

The viscous fan clutch is a temperature-sensitive and torque-limiting 
fluid drive that provides the engine cooling and fuel savings by operating the 
engine cooling fan in a controlled manner. The viscous fan clutch is a 
self-contained unit that requires no additional connections of air, oil or 
coolant lines.

If it has been determined that the viscous fan clutch is worn or 
damaged because it failed to engage or disengage at the correct temperature, 
or failed to operate the fan at the specified speed, then replacement of the 
viscous clutch assembly is required.

The viscous clutch components cannot be serviced in the field.

If the fan drive belt(s) is noisy, check the tension of the belt(s) to 
make certain it is within specifications. Refer to Specifications in Section 03A-05 , Section 03B-05 or Section 03C-05 . Also, check for misaligned pulleys. 
If the drive belt(s) is worn or frayed, replace it.

================================================================================
PAGE 4338
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Thermostat, Water

 CAUTION: Never operate the engine without a thermostat. If operated without a 
thermostat, the path of least resistance for the coolant is through the bypass 
to the pump inlet. This will cause the engine to overheat. 

The thermostat controls the coolant temperature. When the coolant 
temperature is below operating temperature, the thermostat closes, and coolant 
is bypassed to the water pump inlet. As the coolant temperature increases to 
the intermediate range, the thermostat will start to open, and coolant flow to 
the bypass will start to be restricted. At engine operating temperature the 
thermostat will be open and the bypass will be closed.

================================================================================
PAGE 4339
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Block Heater

The engine block heater consists of an electrical heating element 
installed in one or more of the core plug openings in the engine block and an 
electrical cable that plugs into a standard 110-volt AC electrical outlet. It 
is designed to keep the engine coolant warm during cold weather to aid in 
cold-weather starting.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Engine Cooling

 Inspection and Verification 

Verify the original concern by operating the engine cooling system to 
duplicate the condition.

Check for leaks at the following locations:

all hoses and hose connections

radiator seams, radiator core, and radiator drain petcock

all block core plugs and drain plugs

edges of all other cooling system gaskets

transmission oil cooler

vehicle heating system components

water pump

Examine oil dipstick for evidence of engine oil contaminated with 
coolant.

Check radiator for evidence of oil in coolant (leakage at transmission 
oil cooler).

Overtemp Warning Activates Before Fan Engages

Defective overtemp warning switch.

Air solenoid valve may be plumbed incorrectly.

Fan Engages at Low Engine Temperatures While Vehicle Is Moving

Temperature gauge.

REPLACE temperature gauge or sender.

A/C system overcharged or condenser covered with debris.

CHECK A/C system.

Refrigerant pressure switch.

REPLACE pressure switch if necessary.

Fan temperature switch (if fan engages at low engine temperature and 
A/C is off).

Normal condition in extremely hot weather or at slow vehicle speeds in 
warm weather.

REPLACE fan temperature switch.

Fan Will Not Run Under Any Condition

Air line may be leaking (Horton/Evans air-on fan drives).

CHECK air lines. SERVICE as necessary.

Wiring may be shorted and/or fuses, circuit breakers blown.

CHECK wiring, fuses and circuit breakers.

Air solenoid may be faulty. Test air solenoid valve by shorting across 
the terminals of the temperature switch to energize the air solenoid valve and 
to activate the fan drive.

If solenoid does not activate, REPLACE solenoid.

Fan Runs All the Time When the Air Conditioning Is Off

Manual override switch is on.

TURN manual override off.

Air solenoid valve may be faulty or plumbed incorrectly.

CHECK air solenoid valve plumbing, REPLACE valve as necessary.

Air line to clutch may be leaking (Bendix/Kysor air-off fan drives).

CHECK air lines. SERVICE as necessary.

Fan temperature switch may be stuck open; with engine temp below 180°
F short across terminals. If fan turns off, switch is faulty.

REPLACE fan temperature switch.

Pressure switch may be stuck open; turn off A/C system. If fan 
continues to run, short across pressure switch. If fan stops, pressure switch 
is defective.

REPLACE pressure switch.

Fan Runs All the Time When the Air Conditioning Is On

This is a normal condition in extremely hot weather; spray water on A/C 
condenser (fan should disengage for a short period of time and then re-engage 
after water evaporates.)

Normal condition in hot weather.

Air conditioning system may be overcharged or condenser covered with 
debris.

SERVICE A/C system. CHECK A/C pressure and condenser.

Pressure switch may have drifted out of calibration; use pressure gauge 
to compare actual fan-on and fan-off pressures vs. specified pressures.

If out of calibration, REPLACE pressure switch.

Fan Operation Is Erratic

Loose electrical connection.

CHECK wiring and SERVICE as necessary.

Fan temperature or pressure switch may be faulty.

If other system components and connections check out OK, (a) REPLACE 
pressure switch if erratic fan operation is associated with A/C at idle or (b) 
REPLACE fan temperature switch if the erratic operation occurs primarily when 
the engine is hot.

Fan Cycles Frequently When Engine Is Hot

The fan should remain engaged long enough to reduce temperature 7-10°
F; the fan temperature switch is defective if the fan 
disengages after only a 3-4°F reduction.

REPLACE fan temperature switch.

Fan Cycles Frequently When Vehicle Is Stationary with A/C On

Up to 4 cycles per minute is a normal condition for conventional 
control systems; turn off A/C system and cycling should stop.

To reduce cycling by up to 90%, INSTALL an Index K7 fan control system.

Fan Turns On Whenever Ignition Is On (Turns Off When Engine Gets Hot)

Air solenoid valve plumbed backwards.

CHECK solenoid installation instructions and plumb correctly.

Control System Fuses Blown

If fuse blows whenever the ignition is turned on, the problem is most 
likely related to a concern in the wiring.

CHECK wiring and SERVICE as necessary.

If the fuses blow only when the fan engages, the concern is probably 
associated with the solenoid valve.

USE an ohmmeter to check for a shorted solenoid coil (the coil 
resistance should be greater than 14 ohms). If shorted, REPLACE air solenoid 
valve.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Water Temperature Sending Unit

 Removal 

Drain coolant from radiator.

Disconnect the temperature sending unit wire at the sending unit.

Prepare the new temperature sending unit for installation by applying 
Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting 
Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-A2.

 Installation 

Remove the temperature sending unit from the cylinder head and 
immediately install the new temperature sending unit. Tighten to 14-20 Nm
 (10-15 lb-ft) for 3.18-mm (1/8-in.) pipe thread senders or 
20-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft) for 9.53-mm (3/8-in.) pipe thread 
senders.

Connect the wire to the temperature sending unit.

Refill cooling system.

Start the engine and check the sending unit operation.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Radiator Core, Valeo

 CAUTION: Unless the plastic tank is removed from the radiator core, heat must be 
kept away from the header/gasket/tank area. Do not attempt to clean Valeo 
radiator core using caustic cleaning solutions unless the plastic tanks are 
removed first. Immersing the plastic tanks in a caustic cleaning solution can 
damage the tanks and oval gaskets. 

The Valeo radiator core is of copper-brass construction and can be 
serviced by using the usual radiator shop procedures for this type of radiator 
core.

================================================================================
PAGE 4354
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Radiator, Valeo

 Disassembly 

 NOTE: This procedure applies only to L-7000, L-8000 Series.

Disassemble the module by removing the four bolts (manual) or two 
bolts/two nuts (automatic), spring packs, steel plates and Teflon®
 pads that hold the CAC to the radiator support frame.

Remove the charge air cooler (CAC).

Remove the nuts holding the gusset to vertical support at each corner.

Remove the drain cock and de-aeration fitting as required.

The steel support members can now be removed by light tapping in a 
horizontal direction on the two vertical support members.

 NOTE: Always use new crimp strips and gaskets when servicing these assemblies.

Service heat exchangers as required. Mount radiator in a crimp machine 
(Plastech by Rad-Pal or similar machine), compress gasket and uncrimp 
retaining tabs by approximately 90 degrees (facing straight up) starting near 
the center of the tank and working toward the ends. Remove crimp strips, tank 
and gasket.

Invert radiator and repeat procedure for remaining tank.

Surface preparation for service and refinishing can be accomplished 
through a boil-out procedure. This will remove any detrimental contaminants 
and allow proper soldering.

Number of blocked tubes allowed: two tubes can be soldered shut if 
required for service, providing they are not in line from front to back.

 Assembly 

Mount radiator core in the crimp and compress machine, install 
lubricated (glycol) gasket in header and compress gasket with tank.

Precrimp the four end tabs at each end of tank. Also precrimp three 
tabs located near the center of the tank on both sides. Precrimp remaining 
tabs beginning near the center of tank and work outward to the ends of the tank.

Final crimp tabs beginning at the center of the tank and work outward. 
Finish with the end tabs.

Invert radiator and repeat procedure for remaining tank.

Proper gasket compression is vital to proper tank-to-header seal. 
Compression is controlled by proper crimp height of crimp strip tabs.

[FIGURE: Q4248B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

Crimp Height

Remove clamping device before taking crimp height measurement.

Use vernier calipers or similar accurate measuring device to check for 
ideal crimp dimension of 11.9-12.0 mm (0.470-0.475 inch) measured between tabs 
from top of tank foot to the bottom of crimp strip. Tabs bent 90 degrees 
indicate proper crimp.

Pressure leak test to 124 kPa (18 psi).

Install four corner rubber shock mounts on radiator.

Install radiator core to the lower frame.

Install upper radiator frame.

 NOTE: Do not tighten strut nuts at this time.

Install vertical strut rods and two Nyloc nuts.

Install two radiator side frames by lightly tapping in a horizontal 
direction.

Loosely install the fifteen nuts for the side, upper and lower frames. 
Using a 6.4-mm (0.25-inch) drift, align frames. Tighten nuts to 34 Nm
 (25 lb-ft).

Tighten the vertical strut support nuts.

If removed, install the drain cock and de-aeration fitting.

Install the charge air cooler.

 NOTE: Threadlock® and Sealer EOAZ-19554-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G315-A5 is recommended on all threads.

Assemble the module by installing the four bolts (manual) or two 
bolts/two nuts (automatic), spring packs, steel plates and Teflon®
 pads that hold the charge air cooler to the radiator 
support frame. Tighten 3/8-inch shoulder bolts to 47 Nm (35 
lb-ft). Tighten 3/8-inch nuts to 20 Nm (15 lb-ft).

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Radiator Coolant Level Check

Check coolant level in the radiator coolant recovery reservoir at least 
once a month.

With a cold engine, the level must be maintained at or above the FULL 
COLD mark.

At normal engine operating temperature, the coolant level should be at 
the FULL HOT mark. If coolant level in the radiator coolant recovery reservoir 
is less than the above indicated levels, a 50/50 mixture of Heavy-Duty Diesel 
Engine Cooling System Fluid E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESE-M97B18-C or equivalent and water should be added to the 
radiator coolant recovery reservoir to the specified levels. Also add 
Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System Additive FW-15 or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESN-M99B169-A (for FD-1060 and FD-1460 only) at a strength of 4 
ounces per gallon of engine coolant being added.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System Hoses and Clamps

Inspect cooling system hoses and clamped hose connections for leaks or 
excessive deterioration. Service or replace as required.

required.

Inspect cooling system hose routing to ensure sufficient clearance to 
engine compartment components. Reposition hoses if required.

Check radiator supports and brackets for firm radiator retention. 
Correct as required. The radiator is installed with rubber isolation mounts.

1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Draining, Filling and Bleeding

To prevent loss of antifreeze when draining the radiator, attach a hose 
to the radiator drain cock and drain the coolant from the radiator into a 
clean container.

Open the drain cock and remove the radiator or supply tank cap.

Close drain cock.

 CAUTION: Never operate an engine with the cooling system filled solely with 
water. Severe engine corrosion can result. Refer to the owner guide 
maintenance schedule for proper cooling system additives. Do not operate 
engine without additive. 

Always use the specified mixture of water and Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine 
Cooling System Fluid E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESE-M97B18-C. Also add Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System Additive FW-15 or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESN-M99B169-A (for FD-1060 and FD-1460 
only) at a strength of 4 ounces per gallon of engine coolant being added. In 
areas where protection against freezing is not required (hot climates), it is 
advisable to use a concentration of antifreeze to make sure of protection 
against corrosion. The approved antifreeze agents contain corrosion-inhibiting 
properties. 

Refer to the Coolant Mixture chart in the Specifications portion of 
this section to establish correct proportions of water and antifreeze to be 
used in cooling system.

Place heater temperature control in maximum HEAT position.

 NOTE: Add required amount of cooling system additive for FD-1060 and FD-1460 
diesel engines only.

Fill supply tank or the radiator to bottom of filler neck with the 
recommended permanent antifreeze mixture. Leave the radiator cap off.

 WARNING: DO NOT STAND IN LINE WITH OR NEAR COOLING FAN WHEN REVVING ENGINE. 

Start engine. Vary rpm between idle and 1500 rpm for three minutes.

Increase rpm to maximum (governed) and run engine until the thermostat 
opens (upper radiator hose becomes hot) and an additional ten minutes to allow 
air to escape from the cooling system.

Throttle back to idle and fill the system with coolant to the bottom of 
the filler neck. Install the radiator cap. During subsequent operation of the 
engine, some coolant may be disposed of through the overflow nipple. This is 
normal. After extended operation of the vehicle, when the engine has cooled 
off to ambient temperature, the coolant level should be stabilized at a level 
approximately in line with the mounting tabs of the tank.

If the vehicle is equipped with a coolant recovery reservoir, fill to 
the HOT mark.

================================================================================
PAGE 4358
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Cleaning

 Cooling System Flush Procedure, Radiator Installed 

Slowly fill cooling system with a mixture of clean water and a suitable 
flushing agent (mixed according to manufacturer's recommendations). If cooling 
system is still hot, either fill with hot water or allow system to cool, then 
fill with cold water.

Start engine and allow it to idle until normal operating temperature is 
reached. Run engine for ten minutes, and then switch off.

Drain cooling system, fill, and run engine. Repeat procedure until 
water draining from radiator is clean.

Reverse-flush radiator as follows:

Disconnect radiator top and bottom hoses.

Insert a hose in radiator lower tank, and pack around hose with cloth.

Back-flush radiator until clean water flows freely from top connection. 
If difficulty is experienced in back-flushing, remove radiator from vehicle. 
Turn radiator upside down, and then back-flush.

Back-flush cylinder block and cylinder head as follows:

Remove thermostat housing cover, and remove thermostat(s). Refer to 
 Section 03A-03 (FD-1060 engine), Section 03B-03 (FD-1460 engine) or Section 03C-03 (Cummins, CAT or DDC engine).

Insert a hose into thermostat housing, and back-flush engine until 
clean water flows freely from radiator bottom hose.

Install thermostat(s) and housing cover. Refer to Section 03A-03 
(FD-1060 engine), Section 03B-03 (FD-1460 engine) or Section 03C-03 (Cummins, 
CAT or DDC engine). Connect radiator top and bottom hoses. Tighten securely.

After flushing system replace coolant filter.

 Heater Core Back-Flushing 

All engine cooling system flushing and back-flushing procedures must 
include a separate back-flushing of the heater or air conditioning system 
heater core after the back-flushing of the engine cooling system. This will 
prevent engine cooling system particles from clogging the heater core tubes 
and reducing (or eliminating) coolant flow through the heater core. The heater 
core must be back-flushed separately from the engine cooling system for proper 
back-flush water flow direction through the heater core.

Disconnect the heater core outlet heater hose from the water pump 
fitting. Install a female garden hose-end fitting adapter in the end of the 
outlet heater hose. Secure with a hose clamp.

Connect the female garden hose-end of the outlet heater hose to the 
male end of a water supply garden hose.

Disconnect the heater core inlet heater hose from the engine block 
fitting and allow to drain onto the ground or into a floor drain.

Check to be certain the water valve is open (no vacuum) if a water 
valve is installed in the heater core inlet heater hose.

Turn the water supply valve on and off several times so the surge 
action will help to dislodge larger stubborn particles from the heater core 
tubes. Allow full water pressure to flow approximately five minutes.

If a water valve is installed in the heater core inlet heater hose, 
apply vacuum to the water valve vacuum motor to ensure proper operation of the 
water valve and proper closure with no water leakage. Replace the water valve 
if required.

Remove the hose clamp and female garden hose-end adapter from the end 
of the outlet heater hose and connect the outlet heater hose onto the water 
pump fitting.

Connect the inlet heater hose onto the engine block fitting.

Fill the cooling system. 

Test the system for proper heater performance with the specified engine 
cooling system conditions.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Radiator Cap

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CONDITIONS WHILE THE ENGINE IS 
OPERATING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THESE INSTRUCTIONS CAN RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AND DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE.

TO AVOID HAVING SCALDING HOT COOLANT OR STEAM BLOW OUT OF THE RADIATOR, 
USE EXTREME CARE WHEN REMOVING THE CAP FROM A HOT RADIATOR. IF POSSIBLE, WAIT 
UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, THEN WRAP A THICK CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP 
AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK WHILE THE PRESSURE IS RELEASED 
FROM THE COOLING SYSTEM. WHEN YOU ARE SURE ALL THE PRESSURE HAS BEEN RELEASED, 
PRESS DOWN ON THE CAP (STILL USING A CLOTH), TURN AND REMOVE IT. 

Inspect the areas under the vacuum valve and rubber seal for rust or 
dirt particles.

 NOTE: If paint is observed on the filler neck sealing surface, remove it

replace with new cap.

If seal surface on fill neck is damaged or distorted, replace.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Radiator

 External 

The radiator core can be cleaned externally with a soft bristle brush, 
warm water and a mild household liquid detergent, being careful not to bend or 
damage the fins. Rinse with clear water.

 Internal 

 NOTE: Do not use caustic cleaning solutions. Internal cleaning of the 
radiator core can be accomplished by removing one radiator tank to gain access 
to tubes. Then, clean the tubes with a mild household liquid detergent. Rinse 
the core with clean water when completed. Do not use a metal brush to clean 
the core. Use only horsehair, bristle or nylon brushes. A boil-out tank may be 
used to clean the radiator core only if both end tanks and gaskets are removed 
first. Do not "rod out" the core tubes. This can damage the tube "dimples" and 
harm the heat transfer performance of the radiator.

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter System

The function of the starting system is to crank the engine at a speed 
fast enough to permit the engine to start.

The system consists of the following components:

starter motor

flywheel ring gear

starter relay

ignition switch and push-button switch

battery and interconnecting wiring

neutral switch

 WARNING: WHEN SERVICING THE STARTER MOTOR OR PERFORMING OTHER UNDERHOOD WORK IN 
THE VICINITY OF THE STARTER MOTOR, BE AWARE THAT THE HEAVY-GAUGE BATTERY INPUT 
LEAD AT THE STARTER SOLENOID IS ELECTRICALLY HOT AT ALL TIMES.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Motor

The 28-MT, 37-MT and 42-MT starter motors are of the same basic 
construction and function essentially the same. Electrically, the motors 
consist of an armature, field coils and a brush assembly.

The field coils are mounted in the starter frame and are held in 
position by the pole shoes. Current flow through field coils generates 
magnetic fields that are concentrated by the pole shoes.

The armature consists of insulated wire loops connected to the segments 
on the commutator. Battery current supplied to the armature wires through the 
brushes and commutator generates magnetic fields in the armature. The 
repelling action between the magnetism generated in the armature loops and 
field coils forces the armature to rotate. The rotating armature is supported 
on bronze bushings located in the brush end housing, lever housing and drive 
end housing.
