DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Solenoid

The starter solenoid performs two functions. It shifts the starter 
drive pinion into engagement with the engine flywheel and connects the starter 
motor to the positive side of the battery.

The drive pinion is shifted through a lever that is connected to the 
solenoid plunger. The electrical circuit between the starter B- and 
M-terminals is closed by a contact disc that is also attached to the solenoid 
plunger.

Movement of the plunger is the result of a magnetic field generated by 
the pull-in and hold-in windings contained in the solenoid.

When the ignition switch is turned to START, current flows through both 
solenoid windings. This creates a magnetic field strong enough to pull in the 
plunger, shifting the overrunning clutch and drive pinion into mesh with the 
flywheel. As the plunger nears bottom, it strikes the contact disc and forces 
the disc against the starter motor contacts. This completes the battery 
circuit, and the starter motor operates.

When the contact disc closes the contacts, the pull-in winding loses 
its effect due to the voltage being equal at both ends of the winding. The 
hold-in coil continues to hold the plunger in the closed position and reduces 
the current needed by the solenoid. When the ignition switch is released, the 
current to the solenoid stops. The springs within the solenoid open the 
starter motor circuit contacts and shift the clutch and pinion assembly to the 
at-rest position.

 NOTE: The 28-MT and the 37-MT hold-in coil is internally grounded to the 
solenoid case. The 42-MT hold-in coil is connected to ground through an 
external terminal and wire.

[FIGURE: J6403A.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 4367
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Overrunning Clutch

During engine cranking, the drive pinion is locked to the armature 
shaft through an overrunning clutch. When the engine starts and picks up 
speed, the overrunning clutch allows the pinion to spin freely on the cranking 
motor driveshaft, preventing the engine from driving the cranking motor. This 
protects the armature from excessive speed during the brief period that the 
starter drive pinion gear remains enmeshed and the engine has started.

[FIGURE: J6465A.gif]

PAGE 4368
================================================================================

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Relay

The starter relay is an electrically operated switch used to connect 
the windings in the starter motor solenoid to the battery. The relay consists 
of a coil, plunger and contact disc. When the coil is connected to battery 
power through the ignition or push-button switch, it becomes an electromagnet. 
The magnetic force draws the plunger into the coil core. A disc connected to 
the plunger contacts the relay terminal, completing the battery-to-solenoid 
circuit. When the key or button is released, the magnetic field in the coil 
collapses and spring pressure returns the plunger and contact disc to the open 
circuit position.

[FIGURE: DJ0147A.gif]

PAGE 4369
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Sequence of Operation

On an automatic transmission-equipped vehicle, shift lever is 
positioned in NEUTRAL (N) to close neutral switch. On a manual transmission 
equipped-vehicle, clutch pedal is pressed to disengage engine from transmission.

Ignition switch is turned to START or ON position and starter 
push-button is pressed.

Battery voltage is connected to starter relay coil through ignition 
switch/push button. Current flow through relay coil generates magnetic field.

Iron core is drawn into relay coil. Disc connected to core closes 
electrical contacts inside relay.

Electrical contacts and disc complete circuit between relay battery 
feed terminal and starter solenoid S-terminal.

Starter solenoid is energized, creating a magnetic field in solenoid 
pull-in and hold-in windings.

Iron plunger core is drawn into solenoid coil.

Lever connected to drive assembly engages drive pinion gear with 
flywheel ring gear.

When iron plunger core is all the way into the coil, its contact disc 
closes circuit between battery and motor terminals. As current flows to 
starter motor, solenoid pull-in coil is bypassed. Hold-in coil keeps drive 
pinion gear engaged with flywheel.

Current flow through field coils generates magnetic field.

Current flow through brushes and armature wires generates magnetic 
field. Repelling magnetic fields cause armature to rotate.

Starter remains engaged until ignition switch is released from START 
position. Overrunning clutch in drive assembly protects starter motor from 
excessive speeds during brief period before ignition switch is released from 
START position (as the engine starts).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starting Aid, Ether

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE WHEN INSTALLING, MAINTAINING, TESTING OR TROUBLESHOOTING 
AN ETHER START SYSTEM. MAKE SURE YOU ARE IN A WELL-VENTILATED AREA AWAY FROM 
HEAT, OPEN FLAMES OR SPARKS. WEAR GOGGLES WHEN TESTING TO AVOID EYE INJURY. 
MAKE SURE OPENINGS IN THE VALVE, TUBE OR NOZZLE ARE POINTED AWAY FROM YOU 
WHILE TESTING. 

 CAUTION: Do not use the ether cold start system for purposes other than cold 
starting. When high engine temperatures are expected, such as during warm 
weather or when carrying a heavy load in a mountainous or hilly area, remove 
the cylinder to avoid activation of the cylinder's safety relief valve. The 
safety relief valve is set to activate at approximately 93°C 
(200°F), causing a loss of starting fluid. 

In cold weather starting, the heat of piston compression is dissipated 
into the cold cylinder walls, reducing the chamber's ability to attain 385°
C (725°F) temperature required for diesel 
fuel combustion.

The reduced 180°C (360°F) ignition 
temperature of the injected ether supplies the external starting aid fuel and 
heat source for the rapid increase in the combustion chamber temperature 
required for fuel oil combustion.

This system consists of an ether supply cylinder, an actuator valve, a 
temperature-sensitive switch and an atomizer orifice located in the intake 
manifold and the connecting tubing.

The ether cold start system is a fully automatic engine starting fluid 
system designed to spray a controlled amount of starting fluid into the air 
intake system of an engine during and immediately after cranking.

The system's engine temperature sensor (ETS) switch determines when the 
system should function. When needed, the solenoid valve is activated 
automatically during engine cranking. Starting fluid is released from the 
pressurized cylinder, flows through the valve, through the vaporizing fitting, 
through the nylon tubing, and out of an injector nozzle located in the 
engine's air intake system. A reservoir in the valve maintains a flow of 
starting fluid after cranking to prevent the just-started engine from 
faltering or dying.

[FIGURE: J6408A.gif]

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starting Aid, Intake Air Heater

The intake air heater system improves cold weather startability and 
reduces white smoke after a cold engine start. The system is activated by an 
electronic controller when engine temperature is below 7°C (45°
F). Intake air is heated by burning a small amount of diesel 
fuel in the intake manifold. The fuel is ignited by a pair of glow plugs 
installed in the intake manifold.

The system operates in two cycles — pre-heat and 
post-heat. During pre-heat, the wait-to-start light is on while the glow plugs 
reach operating temperature. After the engine starts, the controller maintains 
the post-heat cycle for two to three minutes, depending on engine temperature.

If a system fault occurs, the controller has self-test capabilities. 
Refer to Inspection and Verification, Starting Aid, Intake Air 
Heater for further details on system self test.

[FIGURE: DJ0148A.gif]

 Controller Inputs 

Engine temperature sensor: installed in engine block; provides engine 
temperature signal. Based on this input, system will activate when engine 
temperature is below 7°C (45°F).

Oil pressure switch: closed by engine oil pressure; provides engine 
running signal. When controller receives engine running signal, it switches to 
post-heat cycle.

Engine cranking: spliced into starter relay circuit; provides engine 
cranking signal. Based on this input, controller will open fuel valve.

 Controller Outputs 

Wait-to-start light: length of time light remains on depends on engine 
temperature. Waiting period allows glow plugs to reach operating temperature. 
In self-test mode, the controller will output system flash codes that can be 
used to isolate a system fault.

Glow plug relay: controller provides battery power to relay coil. When 
relay contacts close, glow plugs are connected to battery power.

Fuel solenoid valve: fuel from injection system enters glow plugs when 
fuel valve opens. Controller opens valve by providing battery power to 
solenoid attached to valve.

 Intake Air Heater System

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Jump-Starting 

The following instructions for starting the vehicle with jumper cables 
contain precautions that should be observed to avoid possible injury or damage 
to the vehicle.

 WARNING: HYDROGEN AND OXYGEN GASES ARE PRODUCED DURING NORMAL BATTERY OPERATION. 
THIS GAS MIXTURE CAN EXPLODE IF FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED TOBACCO ARE BROUGHT 
NEAR THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR USING A BATTERY IN AN ENCLOSED SPACE, 
ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION AND SHIELD YOUR EYES. DO NOT DISCONNECT THE BATTERY 
OF THE VEHICLE TO BE STARTED. DISCONNECTING THE BATTERY COULD DAMAGE THE 
VEHICLE'S ELECTRONIC SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: TO AVOID ANY POSSIBILITY OF INJURY, USE PARTICULAR CARE WHEN CONNECTING 
A BOOSTER BATTERY TO A DISCHARGE BATTERY. 

 CAUTION: Headlamp filament failures can occur when vehicle with a dead battery 
is jump-started with the headlamp switch on. 

 CAUTION: Use only a 12-volt jumper system. A 12-volt starting motor and other 
vehicle components can be damaged beyond repair by connecting it to a 24-volt 
power supply (two 12-volt batteries in series, or a 24-volt motor generator 
set). 

 NOTE: Battery top has warnings. 

 NOTE: To prevent any damage to electrical or lighting components during 
jump-starting, follow procedure in exact sequence. 

Position vehicles so jumper cables will reach, being careful that 
vehicles do not touch.

Turn all lights off before and during jump-starting. 

Turn on heater blower motor to remove transient voltage. 

Avoid contact with any moving engine parts. 

Make connections in numerical order. Disconnect in reverse order.

Connect ends of one cable to the positive (+) terminal 
of each battery starting with the discharged battery (1 in the following 
illustration) and going to the booster battery (2 in the following 
illustration).

[FIGURE: J2704C.gif]

 WARNING: MAKING THE FINAL CABLE CONNECTION CAN CAUSE AN ELECTRICAL SPARK NEAR 
THE BATTERY, RESULTING IN AN EXPLOSION. REFER TO WARNING AT THE BEGINNING OF 
THE JUMP-STARTING PROCEDURE. 

Connect one end of other cable to negative (-) terminal of good battery 
(3 in preceding illustration). Connect other end of the same cable to engine 
block on vehicle being started (4 in preceding illustration), NOT TO NEGATIVE 
(-) TERMINAL OF BATTERY.

Make sure jumper cables are not in the way of moving engine parts.

Start engine of vehicle with good battery. Do not crank engine 
continuously for more than 30 seconds at a time. Allow two minutes for starter 
motor to cool between cranking. Run engine at a moderate speed.

Start engine of vehicle with discharged battery. Follow starting 
instructions in the Owner Guide.

Leave all switches off except heater blower motor. Reduce engine speed 
to idle on both vehicles to prevent possible damage to vehicle electrical 
system.

Make sure engines are at idle speed before disconnecting jumper cables. 

Remove cable from engine block first, then other end of negative cable. 

Remove ends of positive cable.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Starting System

Wipe field coils, armature, commutator and armature shaft with a clean 
cloth. Wash springs, shims, thrust washer, trip collar, locking collar, and 
brush end housing assembly in solvent. Dry the parts. 

Examine contacts on starter solenoid assembly and, if necessary, clean 
them with very fine sandpaper or crocus cloth. 

The starter solenoid windings can be tested for internal shorts or open 
circuits with an ohmmeter. Connect instrument across windings and note 
reading. Resistance of pull-in winding should be 0.14-0.16 ohms, while 
resistance of hold-in winding should be 0.65-0.70 ohms. A low reading will 
generally indicate an internal short circuit, while no reading at all 
indicates an open circuit. 

If starter solenoid contacts are badly burned or starter solenoid 
winding is shorted, replace solenoid assembly, then adjust drive travel.

================================================================================
PAGE 4385
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Armature, Starter Motor

Inspect armature for broken or burned insulation and unsoldered 
connections. Inspect commutator surface for grooves, and check for runout. 

If surface of commutator is rough or more than 0.051 mm (0.002 inch) 
out of round, turn it down. Do not undercut the mica. 

Check armature windings with a growler tester.

================================================================================
PAGE 4386
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bushings

The armature shaft is supported on three sintered bronze bushings 
installed in the drive end housing, lever housing and brush end plate.

These bushings have a dull finish, as compared to the early-type 
machined, cast bronze bushings, which had a shiny finish. 

Press or tap the bushings out of their housing using a suitable puller 
or driver of the appropriate size. Make sure the housing is well supported.

Saturate all bushings, wicks and oil reservoirs with SAE No. 20 oil.

 NOTE: Before pressing the bushing into place, dip it in SAE No. 20 oil. Also, 
soak tangent wicks with SAE No. 20 oil.

 NOTE: DO NOT DRILL, REAM OR MACHINE sintered bushings in any way. These 
bushings are supplied to size. If drilled or reamed, the ID (inside diameter) 
will be too large; also, the bushing pores will be sealed over. 

 NOTE: It is not necessary to cross-drill a sintered bushing when used with a 
tangent wick. Because the bushing is so highly porous, oil from the wick 
touching the outside bushing surface will bleed through and lubricate the 
shaft. 

 NOTE: The lever housing bushing prevents starter motor armature deflection 
during cranking. As compared to end frame bushings, the clearance between the 
lever housing bushing and shaft is large and the clearance provides a loose 
fit when assembled. 

Insert the wick into place first, and then press in the bushing.

Field Coil Inspection

With starter motor disassembled, check field coil windings with a

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Brush and Brush Holder

Check brushes for free movement in brush holders. Inspect brushes for 
excessive wear. Where brush leads are insulated, make sure insulation is not 
burned or worn. 

The brushes must be well seated to commutator; that is, contacting 
commutator over at least 60 percent of brush contact area. If not, fit brushes 
to commutator with fine sandpaper until desired seating area is obtained. Do 
only one brush at a time. Clean brushes and commutator with compressed air. 
Make sure no abrasive particles from sandpaper are embedded in the contact 
area of brushes. 

New brushes are not ground to fit the commutator; therefore, they must 
be seated as described. 

Mark each brush and brush holder with which it was seated to permit 
assembly in the same position.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Alignment, Front

Wheel alignment measurements describe the angular orientation of the 
wheel/tire assembly and the steering axis.

Caster, camber and toe are the three major, measurable alignment 
parameters.

================================================================================
PAGE 4395
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Caster

 NOTE: Keep in mind that if the caster is changed, the toe adjustment must be 
rechecked.

Caster is the amount in degrees that the top of the spindle pin is 
inclined toward the front or rear of the vehicle as viewed from the side of 
the vehicle. The caster angle can range from a positive angle to a negative 
angle.

Positive caster is the tilting of the top of the spindle pin toward the 
rear of the vehicle, while negative or reverse caster is the tilting of the 
spindle pin toward the front of the vehicle.

Positive caster imparts a trailing action to the front wheels, while 
negative or reverse caster causes a leading action. The correct amount of 
caster helps to keep the front wheels in the straight-ahead position. When in 
a turn, caster acts as a lever, assisting the driver to return the front 
wheels to the straight-ahead position.

Caster specifications are based on vehicle design load (no payload) 
which will usually result in a level frame. Because of this, raising (or 
lowering) the rear without changing front ride height will subsequently 
decrease (or increase) the caster angle by the same amount the frame angle 
changes. If the frame is not level when alignment checks are made, this must 
be considered in determining whether the caster setting is correct.

[FIGURE: F9180A.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Caster Angle

2

—

Tapered Wedge

3

—

4

—

Centerline of Spindle Pin

================================================================================
PAGE 4396
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Camber

Camber is the amount in degrees that the wheel inclines away from the 
vertical at the top, as viewed from the front of the vehicle.

Positive camber is an outward tilt or inclination of the wheel at the 
top.

Negative or reverse camber is an inward tilt of the wheel at the top.

The amount of camber used depends on the amount in degrees the spindle 
pin is inclined. An incorrect camber angle causes the side of the tread to 
wear, resulting in abnormal tire wear.

Unequal camber in the front wheels can cause the vehicle to lead to the 
right or left on a level road. The vehicle will lead to the side that has the 
most positive camber.

Spindle pin inclination (angle) is the amount in degrees that the top 
of the spindle pin inclines away from the vertical toward the center of the 
vehicle as viewed from the front of the vehicle.

[FIGURE: F9181A.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Camber Angle

2

—

Vertical Angle

3

—

Spindle Pin Inclination

4

—

Level of Spring Pad

5

—

Centerline of Tire

Spindle pin inclination working together with the camber angle puts the 
approximate center of the tire tread in contact with the road. Spindle pin 
inclination has the effect of reducing steering effort and improves 
directional stability in the vehicle.

There is no means of adjusting this angle; therefore, it will not 
change unless the front axle has been bent. Corrections or changes to this 
angle are accomplished by replacement of broken, bent or worn parts.

================================================================================
PAGE 4397
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Toe

Toe-in is the amount in millimeters (or fractions of an inch) that the 
front wheels are closer together at the front than at the back as viewed from 
the top of the vehicle. With camber on the front wheels, the left front wheel 
tries to steer to the left and the right front wheel tries to steer to the 
right. This is due to the wheels wanting to turn in the same direction each 
wheel leans. To overcome this condition, the wheels are given a certain amount 
of toe-in.

No change should be made in toe-in until the other factors of front 
wheel alignment are known to be within specifications.

PAGE 4398
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Load Effect

Truck front end alignment settings change between loaded vehicle and 
unloaded vehicle conditions. The amount of this change will depend on vehicle 
suspension and front axle design, as well as the actual amount of load on the 
front axle.

================================================================================
PAGE 4399
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tandem Drive Axle Alignment 

Vehicle alignment (axle alignment) is the process of setting the axles 
of the vehicle into a position to establish true rolling action of the tires 
on the ground.

[FIGURE: F9182A.gif]

Drive axle alignment affects the overall wear rate and wear patterns of 
steering axle tires as well as tires on the drive axles. Proper drive axle 
alignment should be confirmed before making final front end alignment 
settings. 

The two primary objectives in setting drive axle alignment are, first, 
that the drive axles be positioned perpendicular to the chassis centerline and 
second, that the two axles be parallel to one another. Most drive axle tandem 
suspensions have provisions for setting alignment.

Although single rear axles are not specifically addressed, the 
procedures in this section are applicable to both single and tandem rear axle 
vehicles. The procedure for aligning the axles with respect to squareness to 
the frame is the same. The portions discussing rear drive axle-to-forward rear 
drive axle alignment (parallelism) can be ignored for single rear axle 
vehicles. 

 Axle Alignment Procedure Example 

The tractor should be on a level surface and positioned so that all 
suspension joints are free. This can be done by moving the vehicle slowly 
backward and forward several times in a straight line. Release all brakes and 
chock the front wheels. 

Securely clamp a 9-foot section of angle iron or straight bar stock to 
both frame rails. Use a carpenter's square to ensure a 90-degree 
(perpendicular) relationship between the angle iron and frame rails. Locate 
the angle iron as far forward as practical.

[FIGURE: F45971B.gif]

Using a trammel gauge or other suitable device, measure from the angle 
iron to the center of the rear drive axle on both sides (A 1 and A 2 
 in the illustration). If these measurements differ by more than 
5 mm (3/16 inch), reposition the rear axle so that A 1 = A 2 
. Depending on the particular suspension, this adjustment can be 
made by changing the length of the torque rod(s), turning an eccentric or 
adding or removing shims. 

Similarly measure from rear rear drive axle centers to forward rear 
drive axle centers on both sides (B 1 and B 2 in the 
illustration). If these measurements differ by more than 3 mm (1/8 inch), 
reposition the forward rear drive axle so that B 1 = B 2 
. After repositioning axles, move the vehicle backward and forward several 
times in a straight line to allow suspension joints to return to their neutral 
settings. Recheck measurements to confirm A 1 = A 2 
and B 1 = B 2 with a tolerance of no more than 3 mm 
(1/8 inch).

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Suspension

 Inspection and Verification 

 Tire Wear 

Verify the operator's original concern regarding the tires to duplicate 
the condition.

 NOTE: Tires that show irregularities and definite roughness must be replaced.

Inspect to determine if the following conditions apply:

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Incorrect mounting

Misalignment

Loose wheel bearings

Bent wheels

Cupping or scalloping of tires from imbalance

Possible loose or worn steering connecting rod, drag link and pitman arm

Underinflation or mechanical irregularities such as out-of-balance
condition of wheel or tire and bent or damaged wheel

Loose, damaged or worn front suspension parts

 Tire Wear 

[FIGURE: F8903A.gif]

 Vibration and Roughness 

Vibration, roughness, tramp, shimmy and thump can be caused by 
excessive tire or wheel runout, worn or cupped tires, or wheel and tire 
unbalance.

These conditions can also be caused by rough or undulating road 
surfaces. Driving the vehicle on different types of road surfaces will 
indicate if the road surfaces are actually causing the condition.

Do not immediately suspect the tires when attempting to diagnose a 
vibration concern. Other sources of vibration include:

loose or worn wheel bearings

loose or worn suspension or steering components

brake hub and rotor runout

loose engine or transmission supports

engine driven accessories

This section covers those vibrations related to the tires and wheels.

For diagnostic procedures and service for non-tire related vibrations, 
refer to Section 00-04 .

 Road Test 

A tire vibration diagnostic procedure always begins with a road test. 
The road test and customer interview (if available) will provide much of the 
information needed to find the source of a vibration.

During the road test, drive the vehicle on a road that is smooth and 
free of undulations. If vibration is apparent, note and record the following:

the speed at which the vibration occurs

what type of vibration occurs in each speed range — 
mechanical or audible

how the vibration is affected by changes in vehicle speed, engine speed 
and engine torque

type of vibration sensitivity — torque sensitive, 
vehicle speed sensitive or engine speed sensitive

If the road test indicates the vibration is related to the tires or 
wheels, refer to Tire Wear in the Diagnosis and Testing portion of this 
section or refer to Section 00-04 . If the road test indicates that there is 
tire whine, but no shake or vibration, the noise originates with the contact 
between the tire and the road surface.

A thumping noise usually means that the tire has flat or soft spots 
making a noise as they slap the roadway. Tire whine can be distinguished from 
axle noise because axle noise diminishes or changes according to load or 
speed. Tire noise remains the same over a range of speeds.

To verify that tire noise is not associated with shake or vibration, 
inflate the tires one at a time and check for a change in the sound. The pitch 
or whine will change as the increased pressure changes the tire frequency.

Be sure to deflate tires to their proper pressures after this check is 
completed.

Use the following explanation of terms to help isolate the source of 
the vibration.

 Torque Sensitive 

The condition can be improved or worsened by accelerating, 
decelerating, coasting, maintaining a steady vehicle speed and applying engine 
torque.

 Vehicle Speed Sensitive 

The vibration always occurs at the same vehicle speed and is not 
affected by engine torque, engine speed or transmission gear selection.

 Engine Speed Sensitive 

The vibration occurs at varying vehicle speeds when a different 
transmission gear is selected. It can sometimes be isolated by increasing or 
decreasing engine speed with the transmission in NEUTRAL, or by stall testing 
with the transmission in gear. If the condition is engine speed sensitive, the 
condition is not related to tires.

 Front End 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to adjust front wheel alignment without first making a 
preliminary inspection of the front end parts, and correcting where necessary. 

Fill all fluids to specification.

Remove any excessive accumulation of mud, dirt or road deposits from 
the chassis and underbody.

Retain all normal loads in the vehicle. Inflate all tires to the 
pressure specified on the Safety Compliance Certification Label (usually 
located on the inside driver's door pillar).

Check both front tires and make sure they are the same size, ply rating 
and load range.

Check for excessive front wheel bearing end play. Adjust or replace the 
front wheel bearings. Refer to Section 04-01 .

Check for worn or damaged spindle pin bushings and loose spindle pin 
lock pins. Refer to Spindle Pin Bushing Wear Check in the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of this section.

Check for bent steering linkage or excessively worn joints. Refer to 
 Section 11-03A .

Check the steering gear mounting bolts and tighten to the specified 
torque. Refer to appropriate section in Group 11.

Check other suspension components for damage.

Check for aftermarket changes to steering, suspension, wheel and tire 
components (i.e., competition, heavy-duty, etc.). Specifications in this 
manual do not apply to vehicles with aftermarket changes.

 Shock Absorber Checks 

The hydraulic shock absorbers are of the direct-acting type. This type 
of shock absorber is non-adjustable and non-refillable and cannot be repaired.

 Vehicle Inspection 

Before replacing a shock absorber, check the action of the shock 
absorbers according to the following procedures.

Check the shock absorber to be sure it is installed securely and 
properly. Check shock absorber insulators for damage and wear. Replace any 
worn or damaged insulators. Tighten attachments to specification.

 CAUTION: Replace the shock absorber if leakage is severe. 

Inspect shock absorber for evidence of fluid leakage. A light film of 
fluid is permissible. Make sure any fluid observed is not from sources other 
than shock absorber.

Disconnect lower end of shock absorber. Extend and compress shock 
absorber as fast as possible, using as much travel as possible. Action should 
become smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Higher resistance on 
extension than on compression is a normal condition. Faint swish noises are 
also normal.

If action is smooth but shock absorber is suspected of being weak, 
repeat Step 3 on mating shock absorber installed on opposite side of vehicle. 
Compare results of both tests. If action is similar, it is unlikely that 
either shock absorber is worn or damaged. Connect both shock absorbers.

 CAUTION: Make sure the part number of the replacement is the same as that of the 
original shock absorber. 

If there is a difference between the two, replace shock absorber having 
lower resistance. The replacement shock absorber resistance will appear to be 
higher than either original, due to initial friction of rod seal.

 Hoist Check 

 Noise: Noise can be caused by loose suspension or shock 
attachments. Verify that all attachments, suspension components, front springs 
and front shock absorbers are tight. Replace any worn or damaged upper mount 
insulators. Check springs and shock absorbers for external damage.

 Bottom/Hopping: Check condition of the rubber suspension 
travel stops (front suspension bumpers). Replace if worn or missing. Examine 
for evidence of previous overload or damaged components.

 Force-Check: Support axle and remove lower shock 
attachment. Stroke shock body using as much travel as possible. The action 
should be smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Damping forces should be 
equivalent on both sides of the vehicle.

Replace only the worn or damaged shock absorber.

In the past it was recommended that shock absorbers be replaced in 
pairs if one unit became unserviceable. Improved sealing, new materials, 
design and improved rod machining and hardening techniques have added to the 
reliability of shock absorbers. Therefore, shock absorbers no longer need to 
be replaced in pairs when only one unit is not serviceable.

 Bench Test 

Place the shock absorber right side up in a vise. Hand-stroke the shock 
absorber as fast as possible using as much travel as possible. Action should 
be smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Higher resistance on extension 
than on compression is normal.

The following conditions are abnormal:

a lag or skip at reversal of travel near mid-stroke when shock absorber 
is properly primed and in the installed position

seizing

noise, other than a faint swish, such as a clicking upon fast stroke 
reversal

excessive fluid leakage

with rod fully extended, any lateral motion of rod in relation to outer 
cylinder

If shock absorber action remains erratic after purging air, install a 
new shock absorber, replacing only the damaged one. Shock absorbers do not 
need to be replaced as sets.

 Suspension, Rear 

Check for leaks on shock absorbers.

Check shock absorber operation for stiff, rough or spongy operation.

Check condition of rear suspension bushings and rear suspension springs.

If the above checks reveal evidence of excessive wear, deterioration or 
improper operation, replace damaged components.

 Spindle Pin Inspection 

These procedures are for determining if front axle spindle pin bushing 
wear (side play) and spindle vertical end play measurements exceed the maximum 
wear limits for normal service and if maintenance is necessary.

 Spindle Pin Bushing Wear Check 

Spindle pin and bushings must not have been lubricated shortly before 
making this check. Measurements must be made before lubrication.

The simplest method for checking spindle pin looseness is to use a 
camber gauge. Instructions for the use of the camber gauge in this particular 
operation are as follows:

Block the rear wheels.

Raise and support the axle on two jack stands. If the axle is supported 
on only one jack stand, a false reading will be obtained.

Apply brakes to eliminate wheel bearing play and to ensure a correct 
reading. Failure to do so will result in a false reading.

Mark the tire at 444.5-mm (17.5-inch) radius (A in the following 
illustration) from the center of the spindle. Position a dial indicator at the 
444.5-mm (17.5-inch) mark to measure tire movement. Accurate results depend 
upon measurement at specified radius.

[FIGURE: F9183A.gif]

Push the wheel inward at the top and measure the movement obtained on 
the dial indicator (B in the illustration) at the 444.5-mm (17.5-inch) radius 
mark on the tire. If more than 3.175 mm (1/8 inch) is obtained at the 444.5-mm 
(17.5-inch) mark, the spindle pin bushings should be replaced.

 Measuring Spindle Vertical End Play 

Block the rear wheels prior to performing this procedure.

Raise and support the axle.

Lift the wheel and tire (spindle only if wheel is removed) so that all 
clearance is taken up between the steering knuckle and the axle spindle pin 
boss.

[FIGURE: F9184A.gif]

Using a feeler gauge, measure clearance between steering knuckle and 
spindle pin boss. If more than 1.524 mm (0.060 inch) is measured, add shims as 
needed to reduce clearance to 0.1270-0.3810 mm (0.005-0.015 inch).

ADJUSTMENTS

Axle Alignment, Front 

As a first step in aligning the front suspension system, the front axle 
must be squared to the frame. If axle-to-frame alignment is not square, loosen 
the U-bolts (which attach the front springs to the front axle) on both sides 
of the vehicle. Shift the axle to the proper square-to-frame position, and 
retighten all U-bolts.

================================================================================
PAGE 4404
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Wheel Alignment, Front

Prior to any alignment check, the vehicle tires must be inspected for 
the following: 

correct tire inflation pressure (with respect to tire temperature and 
vehicle load as specified in the Tire and Rim Association yearbook) 

tire condition (tread uniformity, balance, runout, etc.) 

correct tire matching and selection (same tire brand, tread depth, 
tread design, ply rating and construction type on both ends of axles) 

correct wheel bearing adjustment

Check the frame for straightness. The frame rails must be straight 
within 3 mm (1/8 inch) per 2540 mm (100 inches) of length. If the rails are 
not within this specification, they can be straightened by qualified frame 
straightening technicians. 

Check for loose or missing frame crossmember and suspension bracket 
mounting fasteners, which can allow the frame assembly to parallelogram 
(deviate from true rectangular shape). If loose fasteners are found, check for 
egg-shaped holes. If holes have been enlarged, redrill for the next size bolt, 
and retighten all fasteners to the appropriate torque. 

Inspect chassis/suspension systems for worn or damaged components 
(bushings, spring leaves, tie rods, brackets, etc.) and replace prior to the 
alignment check. 

On tandem axle vehicles, check and set the alignment of the drive axles 
before the front axle alignment is performed. 

 Caster 

The caster angle is controlled by the angle of the front spring pads, 
and changes as the load on the front axle increases or as the springs sag. The 
spring pads must be parallel to each other. Any change in the caster angle 
results from a twisted axle or spring sag. 

Caster specifications are based on the assumption that the frame is 
level front to rear. Caster should be checked with the vehicle at empty load.

Measure the frame angle with a bubble protractor or inclinometer.

If the frame is low at the front, add the frame angle to the caster 
angle shown on the checking equipment.

If the frame is high in front, subtract the frame angle from the caster 
angle reading on the checking equipment to get the true caster angle.

[FIGURE: F30091A.gif]

If the springs have sagged, adjust the caster angle by replacing the 
springs or by installing tapered wedges between the springs and the spring 
pads. Use only one wedge per side. The wedges are available in different 
thicknesses. Position the thick edge of the wedge toward the rear of the 
vehicle to increase the caster, or toward the front to decrease the caster. 
When installing wedges, make sure the front spring tie bolts extend through 
the wedge and into the axle pilot hole.

[FIGURE: F30101B.gif]

 Camber 

Camber is built into the axle and cannot be changed. If the camber 
measurement is not within specifications, the axle must be replaced.

 Toe 

If the toe is out of specification, loosen the clamp bolts at each end 
of the spindle connecting rod tube.

Rotate the tube until the correct toe is obtained, and tighten to 43-56 Nm
 (32-41 lb-ft) for 1/2-20 clamp bolts or 68-95 Nm
 (50-70 lb-ft) for 5/8-18 clamp bolts.

Recheck the toe to make sure no changes occurred when the bolts were 
tightened.

[FIGURE: F30111A.gif]

Clamps that are not fixed should be positioned with the tab against the 
end of the rod. The clamp bolt must be vertical and rearward, with the clamp 
facing forward.

[FIGURE: G3428D.gif]

Alignment for Clear Vision

Set wheels in straight-ahead position by driving vehicle a short 
distance and mark the steering wheel relationship to steering column with a 
chalk mark.

If the steering wheel is more than 9 degrees off center, remove the 
steering wheel. Refer to Section 11-04A or Section 11-04B , then perform Step 3.

 NOTE: The steering wheel has serrations equally spaced and can be installed 
in any position.

With the front wheels in the straight-ahead position, install the 
steering wheel on the column so that the spokes are in a horizontal position 
(plus or minus 9 degrees from horizontal).

Install the steering wheel. Refer to Section 11-04A or Section 11-04B .

ADJUSTMENTS

Alternate Alignment Procedures

 Bee Line Method 

The Bee Line method for aligning tandem axles uses the chassis or frame 
as a primary reference and a laser to measure the perpendicularity 
(squareness) of the rear rear drive axle to the centerline of the vehicle. 

The centerline is established by shooting through a centered target at 
the rear rear drive axle to a second centered target at the front of the 
chassis. 

Measure the distance the laser dot is either left or right of the 
centerline of the forward target.

[FIGURE: F8229A.gif]

 NOTE: The acceptable distance of the laser dot to the left or right of center 
on the Bee Line target increases as the distance between the laser and forward 
target increases.

 NOTE: The axle error value is half the maximum value of 5 mm (3/16 inch) 
because it is measured from axle tip to centerline rather than axle tip to 
axle tip.

Using the following conversion chart, compute the amount of error at 
the rear rear drive axle. Axle error is the amount the axle tip is forward or 
rearward of square from the centerline of the vehicle. Computing axle error 
greater than 2.5 mm (3/32 inch) indicates that the axle is out of square and 
needs adjustment.

For example, on a particular vehicle, the distance measured between the 
laser and the forward target is 306 inches (25.5 ft.). The measured distance 
between the laser dot and the forward target centerline is 1/2 inch. Rounding 
25.5 ft. up to 26 ft., the chart gives an error of 1/16 inch, which is less 
than 3/32 inch and is acceptable. If the measured distance between the laser 
dot and the forward target centerline is 1 inch, the error at the axle is 5/32 
inch, indicating the axle needs adjustment.

Depending on the alignment condition, axle position adjustments can be 
made for each suspension.

 Hunter Method 

The Hunter method aligns axles with each other, without reference to 
chassis or frame. Computerized alignment systems use sensors containing 
calibrated devices and microprocessors attached to individual wheels with 
lines connecting one adapter to the others to measure tandem axle alignment 
angles. The thrust angle is determined for the rear rear drive axle to measure 
perpendicularity (squareness) to the frame. Thrust angle is the resultant 
direction of travel for an axle due to the relative toe setting for the wheel 
at both ends of the axle. An acceptable thrust angle on Hunter alignment 
equipment is within ±0.12 degrees on the rear rear drive 
axle. Refer to the previous illustration. 

Depending on the alignment condition, axle position adjustments can be 
made for each suspension. 

For either Bee Line or Hunter methods, a trammel gauge or other 
suitable device can be used to set the forward rear drive axle parallel to the 
rear rear drive axle. Measure from rear rear drive axle centers to forward 
rear drive axle centers on both sides. If these measurements differ by more 
than 3 mm (1/8 inch), reposition the forward rear drive axle so that B 1 
 = B 2 . 

[FIGURE: F45971B.gif]

ADJUSTMENTS

Vehicle Lean Correction

 CAUTION: Frame twisting should not be attempted to correct vehicle lean because 
it can cause frame damage. 

Before attempting any correction, the cause for excessive lean must be 
determined. The following measurements must be made without payload on the 
vehicle and with all vehicle fluid levels at full.

Place the vehicle on a flat surface, and fill all tires to the 
recommended inflation pressures. Measure and record the ride height (ride 
height is the perpendicular distance between the top of the axle and the 
bottom of the frame rail). Measure and record the distance between the lower 
flange of the bumper ends and ground for both the left side and right side of 
the vehicle.

Corrections should not be attempted on vehicles with a bumper-to-ground 
right-to-left height variation of 25.4 mm (1 inch) or less. Corrections should 
not be made if the ride height variation is 12.7 mm (1/2 inch or less).

If a front spring spacer is needed to correct a vehicle lean condition, 
use the following procedure.

Raise the vehicle by the frame until the tire comes off the ground and 
place a jack stand under the frame to retain that height. 

Raise the axle slightly with a jack to remove the weight from the 
spring. 

Remove the U-bolt nuts and the U-bolts. 

Lower the axle slightly to allow enough clearance between the bottom of 
the spring and the top of the axle so the spacer can be installed. 

 NOTE: If a spacer 25.4 mm (1 inch) thick or less is in place, remove the 
spacer on the opposite side to eliminate the lean condition. 

Install the spacer between the spring and axle, making sure the 
locating pin is facing down.

[FIGURE: F8228B.gif]

Raise the axle to the spring and reinstall the applicable U-bolts with 
hardened flatwashers and attaching nuts. Refer to the following chart.

ADJUSTMENTS

Drive Axle Adjustments 

 Hendrickson Walking Beam Suspension 

Misalignment of Hendrickson Walking Beam Suspension must be checked. 
Although no single point for alignment adjustment is currently provided, frame 
attachment brackets, axle attachments and spring-to-saddle location are all 
items to be checked. 

Correct a misalignment condition through the following procedures: 

Loosen the frame bracket retaining bolts and the spring-to-saddle bolts 
to allow freedom of movement. 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to move the off-axle hanger brackets with respect to the 
axle housing. The welds at this interface are critical to the structural 
integrity of the axle housing. If axle misalignment cannot be corrected by 
this procedure and is determined to be caused by the off-axle brackets, review 
the condition with the service manager and contact the axle manufacturer's 
representative. 

Move the axles to achieve squareness to frame (within 5 mm [
3/16 inch]) and parallelism to each other (within 3 mm [
1/8 inch]). 

Retighten all fasteners to original torque specifications.

 NOTE: The following procedure should be performed after all service has been 
completed and all suspension fasteners have been tightened to specified torque 
values. 

Begin alignment by checking rear rear drive axle. Use a trammel bar or 
its equivalent to measure from straightedge to centerline of rear rear drive 
axle on both sides of vehicle (Ll and Lr in the illustration). If both sides 
measure within 5 mm (3/16 inch) of each other, alignment of rear rear drive 
axle is acceptable.

[FIGURE: F37051A.gif]

If Ll and Lr differ by more than 5 mm (3/16 inch), adjust rear rear 
drive axle by loosening up torque rod bar pin lock nuts on center spring 
hanger and add drop-in shims. Torque rod bar pin must always be mounted 
adjacent to forward face of spring hanger legs. No more than four shims can be 
used (1/4 inch maximum total thickness). Snug torque rod bar pin lock nuts, 
but do not tighten to specification yet.

[FIGURE: F3706F.gif]

 Hendrickson HAS-Series Air Suspensions 

Make sure all suspension system fasteners are tightened to the 
specified torque. 

Drive the vehicle back and forth several times on a flat, level surface 
without using the brakes. Driving the vehicle in this manner frees all 
suspension joints and puts the suspension joints in the center position. 

Put blocks under the front wheels to prevent the vehicle from moving. 
Make sure the parking brakes are released. 

Use C-clamps to securely fasten a 2743-mm (9.0-foot) straight bar stock 
or angle iron across the frame as shown previously in this section. Put the 
bar in a location as far forward of the forward rear axle as possible. Make 
sure that brackets, rivets, fasteners or any other items do not prevent the 
bar from being installed flat against the frame. If possible, install the bar 
on the lower flange of the frame. 

Use a carpenter's square to make sure the bar is installed in a flat 
and straight position on the frame. 

Begin alignment by checking the rear rear drive axle first. Use a 
trammel bar or equivalent to measure from the straightedge to the centerline 
of the rear rear drive axle on both sides of the vehicle (Ll and Lr in the 
illustration). If both sides measure within 5 mm (3/16 inch) of each other, 
the alignment of the rear rear drive axle is acceptable.

If Ll and Lr differ by more than 5 mm (3/16 inch), adjust the rear rear 
drive axle by loosening the lock nuts on the torque rod bar pin on the center 
spring hanger and add drop-in shims. The torque rod bar pin must always be 
mounted next to the forward face of the spring hanger legs. Do not install 
more than four shims with a 6-mm (1/4-inch) maximum thickness each. Snug the 
lock nuts on the torque rod bar pin but do not tighten to the specified torque 
at this time. 

[FIGURE: F37051A.gif]

With the rear rear drive axle properly aligned, the alignment of the 
forward rear drive axle can then be checked by measuring forward from the 
center of the rear rear drive axle using a trammel bar. If the forward rear 
drive axle measurements (Sl and Sr) differ by more than 3 mm (1/8 inch), make 
adjustments at the forward spring hangers in a similar manner. Snug the lock 
nuts on the torque rod bar pin but do not tighten to the specified torque at 
this time. 

When both axles are aligned, move the vehicle back and forth several 
times before removing the bar from the frame. Recheck the alignment to confirm 
the adjustments. Tighten the lock nuts on the torque rod bar pin to 204-277 Nm
 (150-205 lb-ft).

SPECIFICATIONS

SPECIFICATIONS

 Tire Zone Description 

Specified wheelcuts and turning diameters are based on the tire zone 
concept. Tire zones are determined by the combination of tire and rim. Any 
tire by itself does not fall into a particular zone and, in fact, the same 
tire can be in more than one zone. Only a tire and rim combination uniquely 
determines the tire zone.

The main reason for using the tire zones is to take advantage of 
greater wheel offsets on certain rims, which allows increased wheelcuts and, 
therefore, tighter turning diameters.

To determine wheel turn angle, first determine the tire zone for the 
rim/tire combination installed on the vehicle using the tables below and then 
use the corresponding column in the Front Wheel Turn Angle Specifications 
chart that follows the tire zone tables.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suspension

The front suspension consists of the following major components:

axle

leaf springs

shock absorbers

When servicing the front axle, wheel hubs or suspension, replace any 
component that is damaged or out of specification. All major axle and 
suspension components are heat treated and, therefore, cannot be bent, 
twisted, welded, heated or reconditioned without experiencing a strength or 
fatigue life reduction.

Following are examples of specific prohibited operations:

hot or cold bending or twisting of I-beam, tie rod assemblies, 
spindles, steering arms or tie rod arms for any reason

welding of, or to, steering arms, tie rod arms, I-beams, steering 
spindles, spindle pins or tie rod assemblies

redrilling or reboring of I-beam spindle pin holes for a bushing

milling or machining of any component

spray welding of bearing diameters or other machined surfaces

redrilling or reboring of draw keyholes

relocation or removal of tie rod clamps

================================================================================
PAGE 4413
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-01: Suspension and Wheel Hubs, Front

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Components

Spindle

Provides steering pivot point. The spindle pivots on a pin installed 
through the end of the axle. Bushings provide bearing surface between spindle 
and pin. The front wheel and brake drum are mounted on the spindle. Opposed 
tapered roller bearings are installed in the wheel hub to support the weight 
of the vehicle on the spindle.

Shock absorber

Hydraulic, direct-acting type. Provides continuous damping effect 
under compression and extension. Connected to frame and bracket located below 
the leaf spring. Rubber bushings are used to isolate the shock absorbers from 
their attaching points.

Leaf spring

 Multi-leaf unsymmetrical or parabolic taper leaf springs are used to 
support the front of the vehicle. The leaf spring is an over-the-axle 
installation with U-bolts used to attach the spring to the axle. The spring is 
attached to the frame by a single pivot and bracket at the front, and a 
shackle and bracket arrangement at the rear.

Axle

I-beam, non-driving type axle is attached to the frame through leaf 
springs and stabilizer bar. Spindle pin and camber angles are built into axle 
and are not adjustable.

================================================================================
PAGE 4414
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-01: Suspension and Wheel Hubs, Front

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Component Replacement

Shock absorbers must be replaced as an assembly. They are not 
serviceable. It is not necessary to replace shock absorbers in pairs. Replace 
only the worn or damaged shock absorber.

Leaf springs can be replaced individually. Bushings in spring eyes and 
spring pins are serviceable as separate components.

Spindle assembly can be replaced as an assembly. Since spindle pin 
bushings are serviceable items, it is not necessary to replace the spindle 
assembly.

Spring, shock and stabilizer mounting brackets are serviceable as 
separate components.

PAGE 4415
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fasteners, Suspension

 CAUTION: All front suspension fasteners are important retaining parts in that 
they affect the performance of vital parts and systems and result in major 
service expense. Any part must be replaced with one of the same part number or 
with an exact equivalent part if replacement becomes necessary. Do not use a 
replacement part of lower quality or substitute design. Torque values must be 
used as specified during assembly to ensure proper retention of suspension 
parts. 

Never attempt to heat, quench or straighten any front suspension part. 
Replace with a new part.

================================================================================
PAGE 4416
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 04-01: Suspension and Wheel Hubs, Front

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Bearing and Wheel Hub

 CAUTION: Wheel seals on front axles must be replaced any time the axle 
lubricants on that axle are changed from the factory installed mineral lube to 
synthetic lube or vice versa. 

Each front wheel and tire assembly is bolted to its respective front 
hub and brake drum or hub and rotor assembly. Two opposed tapered roller 
bearings are installed in each hub. A grease or oil seal is installed at the 
inner end of the hub to prevent lubricant from leaking into the drum or onto 
the rotor. The entire assembly is retained to its spindle by an adjusting nut 
and cotter pin.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Spring

 Removal 

Raise the vehicle until the weight is off the front springs, with the 
wheels still touching the floor.

Remove the shock absorber.

Remove lock bolts that secure the spring pin in the front bracket. 

Remove the spring pin from the front bracket. 

Remove the four lock bolts and two shackle pins securing the shackle 
assembly. Remove the shackle from the spring and rear bracket. 

Remove the two U-bolts attaching the spring to the axle. 

Lift the spring from the axle, noting the position of any caster wedges 
or spacer.

 Installation 

Position the spring on the spring seat and align the spring front eye 
with the spring bracket. 

Remove the lube fitting from the retaining pin. Position the pin with 
the notches aligned with the attaching bolt holes in the front bracket, and 
the lubricator opening facing outward (inward on LS and LTS models). Drive the 
pin through the bracket and spring, then install lock bolts, lockwashers and 
nuts. Install the lube fitting in the pin. 

Align the shackle assembly upper holes with the rear bracket holes and 
the shackle lower holes with the spring eye. Drive one shackle pin through the 
upper hole and bracket and the other pin through the lower hole and spring 
eye. 

 NOTE: Make sure the notches in the shackle pins are aligned with the lock 
bolt holes in the shackle and that lube openings face outward. 

Install the lock bolts and nuts, and tighten to 43-56 Nm
 (32-41 lb-ft). 

On vehicles equipped with a spacer, place it on the axle. 

On vehicles equipped with a caster wedge, place it on the axle with the 
thick edge in the same position as it was originally. 

Position the spring bolt spacer on top of the spring. Install the 
U-bolts over the spacer and through the holes in the axle. Make sure the 
spring tie bolt is centered in the recess of the axle, spacer or caster wedge. 
Install the flatwashers and lock nuts on the U-bolts. 

 NOTE: To ensure complete distribution of the grease around the spring pins, the load must be removed from the front suspension before lubrication.

Lubricate bushing pins with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C 
or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Lower the vehicle to the floor and tighten the U-bolt nuts to 299-406 Nm
 (220-300 lb-ft). Lubricate all pins with Premium Long-Life 
Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Wheel Spindle

 Removal 

Loosen the front wheel hub bolt nuts. Raise the front of the vehicle 
and remove the wheel. 

If equipped with disc brakes, remove the caliper. To prevent damage to 
the brake hose, use a length of wire to hang caliper from the frame.

Remove the hub and drum/rotor assembly. 

Remove the retaining bolts and backing plate/adapter from the spindle. 
To prevent damage to the drum brake hose, hang the backing plate from the 
frame. 

Remove cotter pin and retaining nut from steering linkage drag link and 
connecting rod.

Disconnect drag link from steering spindle arm and connecting rod from 
steering arm.

Remove nut from upper and lower lock pins.

Remove lock pins using brass drift and hammer. Strike threaded end of 
pin. Note direction of threaded ends before removing lock pins.

If spindle is to be replaced, remove spindle and steering arms.

 Installation 

Front cast spoke wheels are now made of nodular iron instead of steel 
and are mounted on phosphate and oil coated studs. Tighten wheel clamp nuts to 
299-352 Nm (220-260 lb-ft). 

Place the spindle in position on the axle. Insert pin thrust bearing 
between the bottom of the axle and the spindle.

Pack the thrust bearing and coat all mating surfaces of spindle and 
axle parts with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B prior to assembly. The thrust bearing 
must be installed with the retainer lip facing down. Install the spindle pin 
seals and end play shim(s). The shim(s) are placed between the top of the axle 
and the spindle. A 0.076-0.254-mm (0.003-0.010-inch) axle-to-spindle clearance 
must be maintained on all axles.

Line up the notches in the spindle pin with the lock pin holes in the 
axle. Drive the spindle pin through the axle with a drift until the notches 
and holes are aligned. Install the lower (longer) lock pin first and seat by 
striking prior to installing nut. Install upper (shorter) lock pin and seat by 
striking prior to installing nut. Tighten nuts to 68-95 Nm 
(50-70 lb-ft). Do not install both lock pins from same side of axle.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Grease Seal and Bearings 

 CAUTION: Sodium-base grease is not compatible with lithium-base grease and 
should not be intermixed. Therefore, do not lubricate wheel bearings without 
first determining the type of original wheel bearing lubricant. Mixing 
incompatible bearing lubricants can result in premature lubricant breakdown. 

 CAUTION: If bearing adjustment does not eliminate looseness or rough and noisy 
operation, the hub and bearings should be cleaned, inspected and repacked or 
filled with specified wheel lubrication. If the bearing cups or the cone and 
roller assemblies are worn or damaged, they must be replaced. 

 CAUTION: Wheel seals used on front axles must be replaced any time the axle 
lubricant is changed from factory installed mineral lube to synthetic lube or 
vice versa. 

 NOTE: Wheel bearing lubricant is a lithium-base grease such as Motorcraft 
Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-MIC75-B.

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Impact Slide Hammer

T50T-100-A

Driver Handle

T80T-4000-W

Seal Replacer

T73T-1190-B

 Removal 

Raise the vehicle until the tires clear the floor and install safety 
stands to support the front axle.

Remove wheel. Remove the hub cap and gasket from the hub. 

If equipped with disc brakes, remove the caliper. To prevent damage to 
the brake hose, use a length of wire to hang the caliper from the frame.

Remove the cotter pin, adjusting nut and flatwasher from the spindle. 

Inspect the condition of the spindle and nut threads to ensure a free 
turning nut when reassembling. 

Remove the outer bearing cone and roller assembly. Using Rotunda 
Heavy-Duty Wheel Dolly 014-00030 or equivalent to support the hub and drum 
rotor assembly, pull the hub and drum/rotor assembly off the spindle. 

Remove inner bearing cone and wheel seal using Impact Slide Hammer 
T50T-100-A and Seal Remover TOOL-1175-AC or equivalent. Be careful not to 
damage bearing cone cage.

[FIGURE: F7553B.gif]

 Installation 

Remove all traces of old lubricant from the bearings, hubs and axle 
spindle. Inspect bearing cups for pitting, spalling or unusual wear. If either 
cup is worn or damaged, remove both cups. It is recommended that bearings and 
cups be replaced in sets. If cups are worn or damaged, install the inner and 
outer bearing cups in the hub with an appropriate bearing cup driver tool. 
Check for proper seating of new bearing cups by trying to insert a 0.038-mm 
(0.0015-inch) feeler gauge between bottom face of cup and wheel hub seat. You 
should not be able to insert feeler gauge.

[FIGURE: F31301A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not spin the bearings dry with compressed air. 

Clean the inner and outer bearing cone and roller assemblies with 
solvent and dry thoroughly.

Inspect bearing cones and rollers for pitting, spalling or unusual 
wear. Closely inspect rollers for end wear and flat or rough spots. Replace 
all worn or damaged assemblies. It is recommended that bearings and cups be 
replaced in sets. 

If equipped with drum brakes, cover the spindle with a clean cloth and 
brush all loose dust and dirt from the brake assembly. Remove the cloth from 
the spindle carefully to prevent dirt from falling on the spindle. 

Remove all burrs from the shoulder of the spindle and seal bore in the 
hub with emery cloth. Remove any nicks or scratches from the seal bore or 
spindle with emery cloth.

Scratches in the hub seal bore may be too deep to be dressed out by 
light polishing with an emery cloth. In this case, apply a thin layer of 
non-hardening sealer such as Silicone Rubber D6AZ-19562-AA or -BA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M5G92-A or ESE-M4G195-A to the 
colored outside diameter of the new seal prior to installation.

If bearing lubricant is oil, dip inner and outer bearing in SAE 90 
Premium Rear Axle Lubricant C6AZ-19580-E or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESW-M2C105-A. If bearing lubricant is grease, proceed as follows.

Pack the inside of the hub with lithium-base wheel bearing grease such 
as Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1C75-B. Fill the hub until the grease is flush with the 
inside diameters of both bearing cups. 

Pack the bearing cone and roller assemblies with wheel bearing grease. 
Use a bearing packer for this operation. If a packer is not available, work as 
much lubricant as possible between the rollers and cages. Lubricate the cup 
surfaces with grease. 

Place the inner bearing cone and roller assembly in the inner cup and 
install the wheel seal using Seal Replacer T73T-1190-B and Driver Handle 
T80T-4000-W. Be sure the seal is fully bottomed in the hub.

[FIGURE: F7554A.gif]

Bearing Rollers (Part of 1201)

On all synthetic-type seals, coat the seal lips with wheel bearing 
grease such as Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B before installing the hub and 
drum/rotor assembly. On seals not coated on the outside diameter with sealer 
by the manufacturer, coat the grease seal bore in the hub with a thin coat of 
non-hardening sealer prior to installing the grease seal. 

 CAUTION: Keep the hub centered on the spindle to prevent damage to the grease 
retainer or the spindle threads. 

Install hub and drum/rotor on wheel spindle using Rotunda Wheel Dolly 
014-00030 or equivalent.

Install the outer bearing cone and roller assembly and the flatwasher 
on the spindle. Then, install the adjusting nut. Make the final bearing 
adjustment. Refer to <a hre

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Shock Absorber

 Removal 

Remove the self-locking nut, steel washer, and rubber bushings at the 
upper and lower ends of the shock absorber. 

Remove the shock absorber. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: When installing a new shock absorber, use new rubber bushings. 

Position the shock absorber on the mounting brackets with the large 
diameter at the top. 

Install the rubber bushing, steel washer, and self-locking nut. 

Tighten the nut until it rests against the shoulder of the stud. 
Tighten to 68-95 Nm (50-70 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Bushing, Spindle

 Removal 

On a spindle with bronze or low friction (Garlock) bushings, press the 
bushing out of the spindle with a tool that is slightly smaller than the 
spindle bore.

[FIGURE: F14531B.gif]

Clean the spindle bores thoroughly, and make certain lubricating holes 
are not plugged.

 Installation 

Position a new bushing in the spindle bore with the lubricating hole in 
line with the lubricating fitting and the open end of the oil groove toward 
the axle. Press bushing into the spindle with a driver that pilots in the 
bushing.

Press the bushing until there is 3.4-4.1 mm (0.133-0.161 inch) between 
the bottom of the bushing and the bottom of the top bore. See following 
illustration.

[FIGURE: F9372A.gif]

[FIGURE: F14541B.gif]

Turn the spindle over and install the remaining bushing in the same 
manner.

Ream bronze or low friction (Garlock) bushings 0.025-0.076 mm 
(0.001-0.003 inch) larger than the diameter of a new spindle pin.

[FIGURE: F56401A.gif]

Clean all the shavings from bushings after reaming, and coat the 
bushing and pin with lubricant prior to assembly.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Bushing, Spring Eye and Shackle

If vehicle owner/operator feels the front spring bushings have not 
provided the expected service life, it should be explained that the cause of 
premature bushing wear is the use of non-specified or incompatible grease.

As part of the following repair procedure, the bushings are lubricated 
with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. If this grease is not readily available, 
comparable greases are available from retail outlets. Refer to the Ford Lube 
Approved Source List in the Specifications portion of this section.

These greases are formulated to maintain their lubrication qualities 
under high load applications. They also are compatible with one another. If 
mixed, they will not break down or deteriorate.

 Removal 

 WARNING: THE TOOLS SPECIFIED IN THIS PROCEDURE MUST BE USED WITH A PRESS. USE OF 
A HAMMER CAN RESULT IN DAMAGE TO THE SPRING EYES, BUSHINGS AND TOOLS. EYE 
INJURY OR OTHER PERSONAL INJURY IS ALSO A POTENTIAL HAZARD IF A HAMMER IS USED 
WITH THESE TOOLS. 

If portable press is not available, remove spring and shackle bracket. 
If necessary, refer to Spring in the Removal and Installation portion of this 
section.

If portable press is available, proceed as follows:

Disconnect lower ends of shock absorbers.

Raise front of vehicle until vehicle weight is removed from springs. 
Wheels must be touching floor and body must be supported on safety stands.

Support weight of axle using floor jack.

Remove spring and shackle pin lock bolts.

Remove spring pins and rear shackles.

Lower axle until eyes of front springs clear mounting brackets.

 CAUTION: Use care when removing bushing to prevent gouging or other damage to 
shackle bracket bushing bore. 

Press bushings from shackle brackets using Non-Expanding Arbor 
D94T-3110-B or equivalent. 

 CAUTION: Use care when removing bushings to prevent gouging or other damage to 
spring eye. 

Press bushings from spring eyes using Expanding Arbor D94T-3110-C or 
equivalent. 

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B must be used as the bushing lubricant. Failure 
to observe this caution or later lubrication of the bushing with an 
incompatible grease can result in breakdown of the grease and premature 
bushing wear. 

For a list of equivalent, compatible lubricants, refer to the Ford Lube 
Approved Source List in the Specifications portion of this section.

 CAUTION: Use care when installing bushing to prevent gouging or other damage to 
shackle bracket bushing bore. 

Press replacement bushings into shackle brackets using Non-Expanding 
Arbor D94T-3110-A or equivalent. 

 CAUTION: Use care when installing bushing to prevent gouging or other damage to 
spring eyes. 

Press replacement bushings into spring eyes using Expanding Arbor 
D94T-3110-C or equivalent. 

Lubricate the bushing pins with a light coating of Motorcraft Premium 
Long Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M1C75-B.

 CAUTION: Do not ream a bushing. Reaming can result in damage to lubricant 
grooves in bushing. Press Broach D94T-3110-A or equivalent through bushing. 
Cutting edge of broach will properly size bushing in single pass without 
damage or oversizing. 

Test fit the bushing pins. The pin should slide through the bushing 
using hand pressure. Do not use a hammer to force the pin through the bushing.

If removed, install spring and shackle bracket. If portable press was 
used, proceed as follows:

Raise axle until spring eyes and shackles are aligned.

Install bushing pins.

Install bushing pin lock bolts. Tighten attaching nuts to 102-142 Nm
 (75-105 lb-ft).

Install lubrication fittings in bushing pins.

Lubricate bushing pins with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C 
or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. Advise customer 
that bushing will provide expected service life if lubricated at recommended 
6,000-mile intervals.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Axle, Front

 Removal 

Loosen wheel retaining nuts.

Raise and support vehicle at frame rails.

Remove wheels.

If equipped with disc brakes, remove the caliper. To prevent brake hose 
damage, use a length of wire to hang the caliper from the frame.

Remove hub and brake drum/rotor.

Remove retaining bolts and brake backing plate/adapter. To prevent 
damage to drum brake hose, hang backing plate from frame.

Disconnect drag link from steering spindle arm.

Support axle on suitable jack.

Remove U-bolt attaching nuts.

Lower axle and remove from vehicle.

 Installation 

Position axle in vehicle and install U-bolt retaining nuts. Tighten 
3/4-inch nuts to 299-406 Nm (220-300 lb-ft), 5/8-inch nuts to 
204-277 Nm (150-205 lb-ft).

Connect drag link. Use new cotter pin and tighten attaching nuts to 
149-203 Nm (110-150 lb-ft).

Install brake backing/adapter plate. Tighten the retaining nuts to 
245-325 Nm (180-240 lb-ft).

Install hub and drum/rotor assembly. Adjust wheel bearings.

Install wheels and lower vehicle.

Tighten wheel nuts to specified torque. Refer to Specifications 
at the end of this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Wheel Bearings, Front

 CAUTION: Wheel seals on front axles must be replaced any time the axle 
lubricants are changed from the factory-installed mineral lube to synthetic 
lube or vice versa. 

 CAUTION: If bearings are adjusted too tightly, they will overheat and wear 
rapidly. An adjustment that is excessively loose can cause pounding and 
contribute to uneven tire wear, steering difficulties and inefficient brakes. 
Check bearing adjustment at regular inspection intervals. 

Wheel bearings are adjustable to correct for bearing and spindle 
shoulder wear. Satisfactory operation and long bearing life depend on proper 
adjustment and correct lubrication. If bearings are adjusted too tightly, they 
will overheat and wear rapidly. An adjustment that is excessively loose can 
cause pounding and contribute to uneven tire wear, steering difficulties and 
inefficient brakes.

Periodically check the oil level on oil-lubricated front axle bearings. 
Keep oil level between ADD and FULL marks shown on the hub cap. Do not 
overfill. Overfilling can result in oil on brake linings.

[FIGURE: F2633D.gif]

Front hub assemblies and bearings must be cleaned, inspected and 
lubricated whenever the hub assemblies are removed or at the mileage/time 
periods indicated in the maintenance schedule. 

New wheel seals must be installed when the hub is removed. A damaged or 
worn seal can permit bearing lubricant to reach the brake linings, resulting 
in ineffective brake operation and necessitating premature replacement of 
linings.

To check wheel bearing adjustment, raise the front of the vehicle. 
Grasp the tire at the sides, and alternately push inward and pull outward on 
the tire. If any looseness is felt, adjust the front wheel bearings as 
follows. 

Remove the hub cap and gasket from the hub.

Remove cotter pin.

While rotating the wheel, tighten the adjusting nut to 108-162 Nm
 (80-120 lb-ft) to seat the bearings. 

Back off the adjusting nut until loose. 

Finger-tighten the adjusting nut. Final bearing adjustment must provide 
0.000-0.125 mm (0.000-0.005 inch) end play. The final adjustment must not 
result in a preloaded bearing.

Install washer and cotter pin. If the cotter pin hole lines up with a 
slot in the nut, insert and secure a new cotter pin. If it does not, advance 
the adjusting nut to align a slot with the first available cotter pin hole.

Install the gasket and grease or oil hub cap, and adjust the brakes.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suspension

Semi-elliptic, leaf-type rear springs are used on all vehicles. The 
springs are mounted to the frame sidemembers and are held in place on the axle 
by spring clips (U-bolts).

The front ends of the springs are mounted on the frame side rails by 
spring hanger brackets connected to a radius leaf. The rear ends of the 
springs are mounted with a supporting slipper bracket and rebound pin.
