Tighten to 6-9 Nm (50-80 Lb-In)

E

—

Tighten to 7-9 Nm (60-80 Lb-In)

F

—

Install with Outlet Hole Pointing Down. Tighten Pipe Threaded Fittings 
a Minimum of Two Turns Past Finger-Tight. Position Directional Fittings in the 
Tightening Direction Only.

 CAUTION: Do not use any clamping device to hold the end cover as damage can 
occur. The end cover can be held by installing a pipe nipple into the supply 
port and clamping the nipple in a vise. 

Using a machinist's scribe, matchmark the air dryer housing and end 
cover. Remove the three self-tapping screws retaining the purge valve assembly 
to the end cover. Remove the purge valve assembly from the end cover. 

Remove the three O-rings from the exterior of the purge valve assembly.

Remove the six 3/8-inch air dryer housing bolts, air dryer housing nuts 
and twelve special washers and remove the end cover and desiccant cartridge 
assembly.

Remove and discard the end cover O-ring. 

Place a strap or chain wrench around the desiccant cartridge 
approximately two to three inches away from the end cover. Rotate the 
desiccant cartridge counterclockwise and separate it from the end cover. 

Remove the desiccant cartridge O-ring from the end cover. 

 NOTE: Do not remove the heater and thermostat assembly unless proven damaged. 
Refer to Air Dryer in Component Tests in the Diagnosis and Testing portion of 
this section. 

 NOTE: A Torx® head socket or a twelve point 1/4-inch socket 
is required.

Disassemble the purge valve assembly. 

Remove the 1/4-inch purge piston nut from the bottom of the purge valve 
assembly with a socket wrench and one of the sockets mentioned above to hold 
the purge piston bolt head. Remove the exhaust diaphragm, diaphragm (if used) 
and purge valve. 

Remove the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt, 
purge piston, spring and the O-rings; one from the inside and one from the 
outside of the purge piston.

 Assembly 

Wash all parts thoroughly in a quality commercial solvent such as 
mineral spirits. Make sure that all parts are thoroughly dry before assembly.

Inspect all components for wear and damage. Replace as necessary. 

Lubricate the new O-rings and bores with a barium-base lubricant. 

Install the O-rings in the purge piston inside and outside O-ring 
grooves. 

Install the spring into the top inside diameter of the purge valve 
housing. Install the purge piston in the inside diameter of the spring. 
Install the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt in the 
purge piston. Depress the purge piston into the exhaust cover. 

Hold the purge piston and, from the opposite end of the exhaust cover, 
install the purge valve, rubber side up on the purge piston bolt. Install the 
diaphragm and diaphragm washer (if used) or the flatwasher and purge piston 
nut. Tighten the purge piston nut to 7-9 Nm (60-80 lb-in). 

Install the three O-rings on the exhaust cover and install the exhaust 
cover into the end cover aligning the scribe marks. Install the three 1/4-inch 
self-tapping exhaust cover screws and tighten to 6-9 Nm 
(50-80 lb-in). 

Install the O-ring on the check valve assembly and install the assembly 
in the end cover. Tighten to 23-28 Nm (17-21 lb-ft). 

Install the desiccant cartridge sealing ring in the end cover. 
Lubricate the bottom of the cartridge at the O-ring seal and end cover contact 
area with a light coating of barium grease. 

Screw the desiccant cartridge into the end cover until it contacts the 
O-ring. With a strap or chain wrench positioned two to three inches from the 
bottom of the cartridge, turn the cartridge clockwise 180-225 degrees. Do not 
overtighten. 

Install the end cover O-ring on the end cover, place the housing over 
the cartridge and align the holes. 

 NOTE: The longer 3/8-inch capscrews are used to secure the dryer assembly to 
its support bracket. 

Install the six 3/8-inch capscrews, lock nuts and 12 special washers 
making sure they are in proper position as removed. Tighten the capscrews 
using a cross pattern. Tighten to 31-43 Nm (23-32 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Delivery System 

The air delivery system delivers the air brake pressure from the air 
supply system to the brake chambers. It controls the amount of air pressure 
that is delivered to the brake chambers, and controls the amount of braking 
during a stop. It consists of the foot control valve, the relay valve, quick 
release valve and the brake air chamber.

================================================================================
PAGE 4854

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Foot Control Valve 

The E-7 foot control valve is mounted to the dash panel and uses a 
suspended brake pedal. The foot control valve is the dual brake valve type 
which provides two separate circuits to control the primary and secondary 
systems of the dual (or split) systems.

[FIGURE: H3758C.gif]

The foot control valve is connected to each of the air supply systems. 
The air from supply tanks is metered by the foot control valve as the driver 
applies the brake pedal during a brake stop. The metered air pressure is then 
delivered to a rear axle relay valve which controls the amount of air to the 
brake air chambers. This amount of air is proportional to the air delivered 
from the foot control valve. 

The front brakes are supplied directly from the foot control valve.

The circuits in the foot control valve are identified as follows: 

The number one (primary) circuit is the portion of the valve between 
the primary piston and the secondary piston.

The number two (secondary) circuit consists of the area between the 
secondary piston and the exhaust cavity. 

The supply, delivery and exhaust ports of the foot control valve are 
identified by designations cast into the valve body next to the port. The 
primary supply and delivery ports are located in the valve's primary body. The 
secondary supply and delivery ports are located in the secondary body. 

The primary circuit of the foot control valve is similar in operation 
to a standard single circuit air brake valve. Under normal operating 
conditions the secondary circuit is similar in operation to a relay valve. 

Both the primary and secondary circuits use a common exhaust, protected 
by an exhaust diaphragm.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Relay Valve 

The R-12 relay valve speeds up the application and release of the air 
at the rear brake air chambers. The valve is constantly supplied with air 
pressure from the air reservoir to its supply port. As an application is made 
to the foot control valve, air pressure is delivered to the relay valve 
service port. The air supply to the relay valve is then metered to the rear 
brakes from the valve delivery port proportional to the air pressure at the 
service port.

[FIGURE: H5840C.gif]

Air pressure delivered to the service port enters the small cavity 
above the piston and moves the piston down. The exhaust seat moves down with 
the piston and seats on the inner or exhaust portion of the inlet/exhaust 
valve and seals off the exhaust passage. At the same time, the outer or inlet 
portion of the inlet/exhaust valve moves off its seat, permitting supply air 
to flow from the reservoir, past the open inlet valve and into the brake air 
chambers. 

The air pressure being delivered by the open inlet valve also is 
effective on the bottom area of the relay piston. When air pressure beneath 
the piston equals the service air pressure from above, the piston lifts 
slightly and the inlet spring returns the inlet valve to its seat. The exhaust 
remains closed as the service line pressure balances the delivery pressure. 
The R-12 relay valve is equipped with a piston return spring which will assist 
the lifting of the piston. As delivered air pressure is changed, the relay 
valve reacts instantly to the change and holds brake application at that 
level. 

When air pressure is released from the service port as the foot control 
valve is released, and air pressure in the cavity above the piston is 
exhausted, air pressure beneath the piston lifts the piston and the exhaust 
seat moves away from the exhaust valve, opening the exhaust passage. With the 
exhaust passage open, the air pressure in the brake air chambers is permitted 
to exhaust through the exhaust port and releases the brakes.

================================================================================

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brake Air Chamber 

A brake air chamber converts the energy of air pressure into mechanical 
force. This force is used to push a lever to rotate a brake camshaft, forcing 
the brake shoes against the brake drum. Air pressure delivered to the brake 
air chambers (delivered through the inlet port) acts on the diaphragm, moving 
the push rod and plate. The amount of force coming from the brake air chamber 
is equal to the air pressure multiplied by the effective area of the 
diaphragm. This force is proportional to the air pressure delivered to the 
brake air chambers.

When air pressure is released from the brake air chamber, the push rod 
return spring and the brake shoe return spring return all the affected 
components (push rod and plate, diaphragm, brake camshaft) to their released 
position, releasing the brakes. 

Spring brake air chambers also have an integral service chamber which 
applies the spring brakes the same as the service chamber above. Refer to 
 Section 06-05A for spring brake air chamber operation.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Quick Release Valve 

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. Its function is to speed up the exhaust of air from a particular part 
of the brake system. It is used to exhaust air from brake air chambers, front 
and rear, near the brake air chamber, to speed up the release of air without 
the air traveling all the way back to the source of air. It is used in 
tractors to release air pressure in the service line to the trailer. It is 
used in the parking brake system to provide a faster brake application and to 
eliminate the undesirable exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H4959E.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

2A095

Quick Release Valve

2

—

Supply Port (Part of 2A095)

3

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2A095)

4

—

Exhaust Port (Not Threaded) (Part of 2A095)

When a brake application is made, air pressure enters the supply port. 
The diaphragm moves down and seals the exhaust port. At the same time, air 
pressure forces the edges of the diaphragm down and air flows out the delivery 
port. 

When the air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals 
the pressure being delivered by the foot control valve (above the diaphragm), 
the diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm. When the foot control 
valve application is released, the air pressure above the diaphragm is 
released back through the foot control valve exhaust. Air pressure beneath the 
diaphragm forces the diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust and allowing air 
to exhaust.

Section 06-08B: Brake, Air Delivery

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brakes 

Cam air brakes are used on the front and rear axles. The cam-type brake 
is an air-operated, two-shoe brake. The front brake shoes each use a one-piece 
shoe lining. The rear shoes each use a two-piece lining. Air applied to the 
brake air chamber push rod causes a cam to rotate against the rollers, forcing 
the brake shoes outward against the brake drum. For more information, refer to 
 Section 06-08D .

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air Delivery

 Inspection and Verification 

Since most air leaks occur at the fittings and connections, these areas 
should be checked before any other part is replaced. For diagnostic and 
testing procedures for individual components, refer to the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of each air brake section.

 WARNING: WHEN DRAINING THE SYSTEM, DO NOT LOOK INTO THE AIR JETS OR DIRECT THEM 
TOWARD A PERSON, AS DIRT OR SLUDGE PARTICLES MAY BE CARRIED IN THE AIR STREAM. 
HOSES WHICH CONTAIN AIR PRESSURE SHOULD NOT BE DISCONNECTED UNDER PRESSURE 
SINCE THEY WILL WHIP AS AIR ESCAPES FROM THE LINE. FOLLOW THE MANUFACTURERS' 
RECOMMENDED PROCEDURES IN WORKING ON ANY AIR DEVICE SO AS TO AVOID INJURY OR 
DAMAGE FROM PARTS WHICH, WHEN RELEASED, ARE SUBJECT TO MECHANICAL (SPRING) OR 
PNEUMATIC PROPULSION. AS SYSTEM PRESSURE IS DRAINED AND THE EMERGENCY BRAKE 
APPLIES, HANDS SHOULD BE AWAY FROM BRAKE CHAMBER PUSH RODS AND SPRING 
ACTUATORS WHICH WILL APPLY AUTOMATICALLY WITH THE LOSS OF PRESSURE. THIS ALSO 
APPLIES WHEN CHECKING SERVICE BRAKE SYSTEM. 

Reservoirs which are closest to the sources of compressed air 
(compressors or auxiliary sources) should contain a safety valve in known 
working order and sufficient capacity to limit the reservoir pressure to a 
safe maximum level. Old, used reservoirs should not be used as replacements. 
The safety valves should not reset higher than specified by the reservoir 
manufacturer, vehicle manufacturer, or code to which the reservoir had been 
manufactured. Various brake air chambers contain large internal steel springs 
that require special disassembly procedures. Note and be guided by the warning 
tags on such units.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Foot Control Valve 

 Removal 

Identify and mark or label all air lines and their respective 
connections on the foot control valve to ease installation.

Disconnect all air lines.

Remove the foot control valve from its mounting on the vehicle. For 
manifold-type valves, remove the foot control valve and manifold, intact, from 
the vehicle.

 Installation 

Install the assembled foot control valve on the vehicle.

Reconnect all air lines to the foot control valve using the 
identification made during valve removal.

After installing the foot control valve assembly, perform operational 
and leakage checks before placing the vehicle in service.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tractor Trailer Air Brake System 

The tractor trailer air brake system is available as a regular 
production option. Its function is to provide air supply to the trailer for 
its braking system and control the trailer brakes during normal and emergency 
stops. It also protects a tractor's brake system should a failure occur in the 
trailer's air system and provides operation of the trailer brakes independent 
of the tractor brakes. The following components are part of this system: 
trailer air supply control valve (also known as the MV-3 valve), tractor 
protection valve (also known as the VM-1 valve), trailer brake hand control 
valve (also known as the TC-2 valve), bobtail proportioning relay valve (also 
known as the BP-R1 valve) and the hoses, hanger and connectors. 

The trailer air supply control valve supplies air through the tractor 
protection valve to the trailer air brake system. It works in conjunction with 
the parking brake control valve to set the trailer brakes if the trailer is 
parked. The air supplied through the tractor protection valve opens the 
service portion of the tractor protection valve. As the supply pressure 
reaches a predetermined setting, it will allow service brake application on 
the trailer. The bobtail proportioning relay valve functions as a standard 
service relay valve during operation of a tractor trailer combination. During 
bobtail tractor operation, the bobtail proportioning relay valve improves 
controllability and reduces stopping distances by reducing air pressure to the 
rear brake air chambers, whose axle load has been greatly reduced. This is 
controlled by the foot control valve or trailer brake hand control valve. The 
trailer brake hand control valve can be used to apply the trailer brakes 
independent of the tractor brakes.

================================================================================
PAGE 4874
================================================================================

The trailer air supply control valve provides the following functions: 

tractor protection 

trailer service air control 

system park 

trailer park only 

trailer charge with tractor spring brakes applied (tractor park only) 

supply reservoir selection 

primary and secondary reservoir connections

 Operation 

During initial charge, with the system completely discharged, both 
buttons are out. When system pressure reaches 450 kPa (65 psi), the red button 
(trailer supply) can be pushed in and should stay in, charging the trailer 
system and releasing the trailer spring brakes. The yellow button can now be 
pushed in which will supply air to the tractor spring brakes, releasing them.

 Normal Operating Position 

With both buttons pushed in, air is supplied to the trailer and to the 
tractor spring brakes; all brakes are released.

 Automatic Application 

With both buttons in, in the normal run configuration, if the supply 
pressure to the trailer air supply control valve is reduced to approximately 
241-310 kPa (35-45 psi), the red button (trailer supply valve) must pop out, 
applying the emergency parking brakes on the trailer. If the red button is 
held in manually and the pressure decreases to approximately 172-241 kPa 
(25-35 psi), a tripper piston within the trailer air supply control valve will 
move upward, exhausting the trailer supply, effecting the required 
non-override feature. The yellow (tractor parking brake) button will pop out 
at approximately 138-207 kPa (20-30 psi).

 Reservoir Selection 

The number one service reservoir will at all times be selected as the 
primary supply source for the trailer air supply control valve. This is 
accomplished automatically by the function of the dual circuit supply valve 
contained in the body of the trailer air supply control valve. Only in the 
event of a pressure drop of more than 207 kPa (30 psi) below that of the 
number two service reservoir will the dual circuit supply valve shuttle and 
establish the front service reservoir as the supply.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tractor Protection Valve

The tractor protection valve houses three valves that serve the trailer 
and tractor braking system. It is attached to the dash-mounted manifold. The 
valves are: 

the trailer service line shut-off portion of the tractor protection 
system that operates in conjunction with the dash-mounted trailer air supply 
control valve to manually or automatically close and retain sufficient air 
pressure in the towing vehicle to stop it with its service brakes 

a double check valve that permits either primary or secondary circuit 
air pressure from the foot control valve to actuate trailer brakes 

a double check valve that permits use of a trailer brake hand control 
valve to control only the trailer brakes

[FIGURE: H3348B.gif]

—

Double Check Valves (Part of 2B200)

In addition to the ports necessary for the function of the above 
described valves, the tractor protection valve also provides ports for the 
installation of the service stoplight switch and the trailer emergency 
stoplight switch. 

The tractor protection portion of the tractor protection valve provides 
air supply (emergency) and a control signal (service) to the trailer. 

Air from the delivery line of the trailer air supply control valve, 
located within the cab, enters the tractor protection valve at the tractor 
protection (delivery) port. It passes through the tractor protection valve, 
acts upon the plunger and moves the inlet valve off its seat, thus opening the 
service line passage through the tractor protection valve.

If the trailer air supply control valve is manually or automatically 
actuated, the trailer emergency line pressure will exhaust out the trailer air 
supply control valve exhaust port, causing an application of the trailer 
brakes. The piston spring will move the piston. This will allow the inlet 
valve spring to close the inlet valve, thus closing the service line passage 
through the tractor protection valve and protecting tractor air pressure. 

There are two double check valves in the tractor protection valve. They 
work with each other to perform the following functions:

to permit the trailer brake hand control valve to be used for applying 
trailer service brakes only

to permit either the primary or secondary circuit from the foot control 
valve to apply trailer brakes if air is lost in either of the circuits

Each double check valve has two separate inlets and one common inlet, 
and the passage of air is as shown.

Double check valve A inlets are connected to the trailer brake hand 
control valve and the secondary delivery circuit of the foot control valve. If 
the trailer brake hand control valve is applied, the shuttle of the double 
check valve will move and seal off the secondary delivery passage from the 
foot control valve. Air from the trailer brake hand control valve will pass 
out the outlet port of double check valve A.

If a foot control valve application is made, the shuttle of double 
check valve A seals off the trailer brake hand control valve air passage and 
application air will pass out the outlet port of double check valve A. 

Double check valve B inlets are connected to the primary delivery 
circuit of the foot control valve and the outlet of double check valve A. The 
purpose of double check valve B is to permit actuation of trailer brakes 
should a loss of air occur in either the primary or secondary braking circuits 
of the tractor. 

When a foot control valve application is made, air from the primary 
delivery circuit enters one inlet of the double check valve and air from the 
secondary circuit passes through double check valve A and enters the outer 
inlet valve of double check valve B. Air passes out the outlet port and 
through the tractor protection valve to the trailer thus actuating the trailer 
service brakes.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Double Check Valves

Double check valves are used in an air brake system to direct a flow of 
air into a common line from either of two sources, whichever is at the higher 
pressure. They may be used for directing airflow for specific functions, or to 
select the higher pressure of either of two sources of air as a supply source. 
It is recommended that double check valves be mounted so that the shuttle 
operates horizontally.

[FIGURE: H4167D.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Inlet Port (Part of 2K119)

2

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2K119)

4

—

Body (Part of 2K119)

5

—

Shuttle Guide (Part of 2K119)

6

—

O-Ring (Part of 2K119)

As air under pressure enters either end of the double check valve 
(inlet port) the moving shuttle responds to the pressure and seals the 
opposite port, assuming it is at a lower pressure level. The airflow continues 
out the delivery port of the double check valve. The position of the shuttle 
will reverse if the pressure levels are reversed. Double check valves are 
designed so that the shuttle can never impede the backflow of air in the 
exhaust mode.

The trailer brake hand control valve is a hand-operated control valve 
which features a graduated control of air pressure. The trailer brake hand 
control valve is not intended as a parking brake control valve and should not 
be used for that purpose. The handle of the valve will remain in its position 
unless returned to the OFF position by the vehicle operator. 

When the handle is moved in a clockwise direction from the released 
position, force is exerted on the graduating spring through the action of the 
cam and cam follower. 

The exhaust seat which is in the center of the piston, contacts the 
exhaust valve and closes the exhaust passage in the piston. The continued 
downward movement of the piston moves the inlet valve off its seat. Reservoir 
air pressure flows by the open inlet valve and out the delivery port. 

If the brake application is to be held constant, the trailer brake hand 
control valve balances itself. The air pressure that flows by the open inlet 
valve also becomes effective on the bottom area of the piston. As the force of 
the air pressure beneath the piston balances the force of the depressed spring 
above, the piston lifts slightly and the inlet valve returns to its seat. The 
exhaust valve remains seated so the flow of air through the trailer brake hand 
control valve is stopped and air pressure in the service line is held. 

When the handle is moved in a counterclockwise or upward direction, the 
force above the piston is decreased. The air pressure beneath will lift the 
piston, moving it away from the exhaust valve. With the exhaust passage open, 
air pressure in the service line will exhaust out the exhaust port of the 
trailer brake hand control valve.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Quick Release Valve

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. One function is to speed up the exhaust of air from a particular part 
of the brake system. It is also used to exhaust air from brake air chambers, 
front and rear. It is mounted near the brake air chamber, to speed up the 
release of air without the air traveling all the way back to the source of the 
air. It is used in tractors to release air pressure in the service line. It is 
used in the parking brake system to provide a faster brake application and to 
eliminate the undesirable exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H4959E.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

2A095

Quick Release Valve

2

—

Supply Port (Part of 2A095)

3

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2A095)

4

—

Exhaust Port (Not Threaded) (Part of 2A095)

Its operation is very simple. When a brake application is made, air 
pressure enters the supply port. The diaphragm moves down and seals the 
exhaust port. At the same time, air pressure forces the edges of the diaphragm 
down and air flows out the delivery port. 

When air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals the 
pressure being delivered by the foot control valve (above the diaphragm), the 
diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm when the foot control 
valve application is released. The air pressure above the diaphragm is 
released back through the foot control valve exhaust. Air pressure beneath the 
diaphragm forces the diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust and allowing air 
from the brake air chambers to exhaust.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve

The bobtail proportioning relay valve is a combination of two 
individual valves in a single housing. The lower portion, or body, of the 
bobtail proportioning relay valve contains a "standard" service brake relay 
valve, which functions as a relay station to speed up brake application and 
release. The upper portion, or cover, houses a brake proportioning valve, 
which reduces normal rear service brake application pressure when the tractor 
is not towing a trailer. 

Used in tractor air brake systems only, the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve is installed in place of a standard relay valve. It functions as a 
standard service relay during operation of a tractor trailer combination. 
During bobtail tractor operation, the bobtail proportioning relay valve 
improves controllability and reduces stopping distances by reducing air 
pressure to the rear brake air chambers, whose axle load has been greatly 
reduced. The bobtail proportioning relay valve has a crack pressure of 28 kPa 
(4 psi).

 Service Application 

Brake application air enters the bobtail proportioning relay valve 
service port and is conducted through the service piston to the exhaust 
diaphragm which flexes in response to the incoming air and seals the exhaust 
passage in the exhaust piston. Air flows around the exhaust diaphragm, then 
through the center of both the blend back and proportioning pistons to the 
inlet and exhaust valve. Flowing around the inlet valve, application air moves 
through a passage in the cover to the top of the service relay piston. In 
response to air pressure, the relay piston moves into contact with the exhaust 
portion of the inlet and exhaust valve. With the exhaust passage sealed, 
continued movement of the piston unseats the inlet portion of the inlet and 
exhaust valve, allowing supply air from the reservoir to flow out the bobtail 
proportioning relay valve delivery ports to the brake air chambers.

 Service Brakes Holding 

The air pressure being delivered to the brake air chambers is also 
present beneath the relay piston. 

When the air pressure above and below the relay piston is equal, the 
piston moves slightly allowing the inlet valve to return to its seat. The 
exhaust valve remains closed. With both the inlet and exhaust valves closed, 
air pressure in the brake actuators is held stable and neither increases nor 
decreases.

 Service Brakes Releasing 

When the brake application is released, air pressure in the service 
port of the bobtail proportioning relay valve returns to the foot control 
valve and is exhausted. Air from above the relay piston flows back through the 
proportioning, blend back and service pistons to the exhaust diaphragm. If the 
service brakes are rapidly released, the diaphragm flexes in response to the 
returning air and opens the exhaust. If the brakes are slowly released, 
service air pressure will flow through the slot behind the diaphragm and back 
to the foot control valve. As air pressure is reduced above the relay piston, 
pressure beneath it lifts the piston away from the exhaust valve and opens the 
exhaust passage. Air from the service brake air chambers returns to the 
bobtail proportioning relay valve and flows out the open exhaust.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Tractor/Trailer Air Brake System

 Inspection and Verification 

 End Cap Inspection 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO KEEP THE WEATHER SEAL PLUG IN PLACE ON DOUBLE DIAPHRAGM 
SPRING PARKING BRAKE AIR CHAMBERS ALLOWS ROAD SALT AND OTHER CONTAMINANTS TO 
ENTER THE SPRING BRAKE AIR CHAMBER. THIS MAY CAUSE INTERNAL CORROSION AND 
POSSIBLY WEAKEN THE PARKING BRAKE SPRING, SPRING SUPPORT PLATE AND THE INSIDE 
SURFACE OF THE END CAP. THE CORROSION IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE OUTSIDE OF THE 
SPRING BRAKE AIR CHAMBER AND COULD EVENTUALLY RESULT IN A FRACTURE OF THE 
SPRING, SUPPORT PLATE OR THE END CAP, WHICH COULD ALSO LEAD TO PROPERTY DAMAGE 
OR PERSONAL INJURY. 

Whenever an inspection or service operation is performed on a spring 
brake air chamber, check for the presence of the weather seal plug. Install a 
new plug if it is missing.

 Component Tests 

 Trailer Air Supply Control Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

To perform the following test, an accurate vehicle test gauge is 
required. The vehicle dual air pressure gauge, if used, should be checked for 
accuracy against the test gauge prior to making these tests. 

Chock or hold the vehicle by means other than the service air brakes. 

Charge the air brake system to 827 kPa (120 psi), and check for leakage 
by coating the area between the body of the trailer air supply control valve 
and the cover plate with a soap solution. Leakage at the exhaust port must not 
exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. 

With supply pressure still at 827 kPa (120 psi), push the red button 
in. The button must stay in. Leakage at the exhaust port must not exceed a 
25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. 

 NOTE: The yellow button must not pop out before the red button. 

Slowly reduce pressure in both service reservoirs. The red button must 
pop when supply pressure drops to 241-310 kPa (35-45 psi).

Hold the red button in and continue to reduce pressure in all service 
reservoirs. Air must start to escape from the exhaust port when the trailer 
supply line pressure reaches 138-241 kPa (20-35 psi). 

Release the red button and rebuild the supply pressure to at least 827 
kPa (120 psi). Push in the yellow button; the yellow button must remain in. 
Leakage at the exhaust port should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in 
five seconds. 

With the red button out slowly reduce pressure in all service 
reservoirs. The yellow button must pop at 138-207 kPa (20-30 psi). 

Charge the system to 827 kPa (120 psi) and push both buttons in. Pull 
the red button out. The yellow button must remain in. 

Push the red button in and pull the yellow button out. The red button 
must pop out almost instantaneously. 

Install a gauge to monitor tractor brake air chamber delivery pressure. 
Apply 827 kPa (120 psi) to all service reservoirs (No. 1 and No. 2). Push in 
the yellow button. Delivery pressure should equal the pressure in reservoir 
No. 1. Reduce the pressure in No. 1 reservoir. Delivery pressure and No. 1 
reservoir pressure should descend together to 724-620 kPa (105-90 psi) at 
which point the dual circuit supply valve shuttle should switch to No. 2 
reservoir and delivery pressure should increase to No. 2 reservoir pressure. 
After the No. 1 reservoir pressure is reduced to zero, there should not be 
audible leakage at the No. 1 reservoir opening. Close the leak which had been 
created in the No. 1 reservoir. 

Leaving the yellow button in, recharge the No. 2 reservoir to 827 kPa 
(120 psi). The delivery pressure should also read 827 kPa (120 psi). Recharge 
the No. 1 reservoir to 689 kPa (100 psi). Slowly vent the No. 2 reservoir. As 
the No. 2 reservoir pressure and the delivery line pressure descend, pressure 
should stabilize at approximately 689 kPa (100 psi). 

Close all reservoir drain cocks and charge both reservoirs to 827 kPa 
(120 psi). Position the red button out and the yellow button in. Cause a leak 
in the brake air chamber delivery line and hold the yellow button in. No. 1 
reservoir pressure must reduce to zero and No. 2 reservoir pressure to 138-207 
kPa (20-30 psi). The dual circuit supply valve shuttle should cycle several 
times during this leak-down period. 

If the trailer air supply control valve fails to operate as described 
or leakage exceeds the limits stated, replace or service it using genuine 
Bendix parts or equivalent. 

Close all reservoir drain cocks and deliberately caused leakage points 
before placing the vehicle in service.

 Tractor Protection Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

Perform test as follows.

With key to run, place trailer air supply control valve in emergency 
position. The vehicle is equipped with an emergency stoplight switch; 
therefore the trailer stoplights should function. 

Charge air brake system to governor cutout and chock wheels. 

Apply trailer brake hand control valve and check at open tractor 
service hose coupling for leakage. Excessive leakage would indicate worn or 
damaged tractor protection valve inlet valve. 

Release trailer brake hand control valve and place trailer air supply 
control valve in the charged position, with trailer supply hose connected to 
trailer supply hose coupling. 

Connect tractor service hose coupling to a test gauge. 

Apply trailer brake hand control valve and note that service air 
pressure is present at the service hose coupling. If service air pressure is 
not present, this would indicate either a worn or damaged tractor protection 
valve or a worn or damaged shuttle in one of the double check valves. Check 
foot control valve exhaust for leakage. If leakage is detected, double check 
valve requires servicing. Release trailer brake hand control valve. 

With key to run, apply and hold a foot control valve application and 
note that stoplights function. Check foot control valve exhaust for leakage. 
If leakage is detected, double check valve requires servicing. 

 NOTE: When plugging line as directed, fitting and crimped copper tubing can 
be assembled and used as a plug. High-pressure air can turn loose parts into 
dangerous projectiles. Keep parts well tightened.

Disconnect line from primary circuit delivery (PCD) port. Plug end of 
line.

Make a foot control valve application and check primary circuit 
delivery (PCD) port of manifold for leakage. Leakage at port indicates double 
check valve requires servicing. Remove plug from line and reconnect to 
manifold. 

Disconnect line from secondary circuit delivery (SCD) port and plug end 
of line. Make a foot control valve application and check secondary circuit 
delivery (SCD) port of manifold for leakage. Leakage at port indicates double 
check valve requires servicing. Remove plug from line and reconnect to 
manifold. 

Make a foot control valve application and test for gasket leakage. 
Tighten bolts if necessary. 

If the tractor protection valve does not function as described above or 
leakage is excessive, it is recommended that it be replaced with a new or 
remanufactured unit, or serviced with genuine Bendix parts or equivalent.

 Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve 

 Operation Test 

During the following test, note that trailer brake hand control valves 
are preset lower than reservoir pressure. Intermediate positions should 
deliver proportional intermediate pressures. Upon release, the gauge should 
immediately register zero.

Connect an accurate test gauge to the delivery port. When the handle is 
moved to the fully applied position, the test gauge should register 552 kPa 
(80 psi).

 Leakage Test 

Locate the exhaust port or exhaust line and apply a soap solution. (It 
is common practice to connect a line from the trailer brake hand control valve 
exhaust port to a location remote from the immediate driver's area.) With the 
trailer brake hand control valve in the released position, exhaust leakage 
should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. 

With the trailer brake hand control valve fully applied, leakage at the 
exhaust should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in three seconds. 

If the trailer brake hand control valve does not function as described 
or leakage is excessive, it is recommended that it be replaced with a new or 
remanufactured unit, or serviced with genuine Bendix parts or equivalent.

 Quick Release Valve 

 Operation Test 

With the air brake system fully charged, apply the brakes. Observe the 
brake action on the wheels controlled by the quick release valve or relay 
valve in question. The brakes should apply promptly. 

Release the brakes and inspect to be sure the air pressure is exhausted 
rapidly from the exhaust port. Be sure the exhaust port is not restricted.

 Leakage Test 

With brakes applied, coat the exhaust port with soap solution and 
inspect for leaks. Leakage is not permissible. Disassemble and check for 
contamination and clean if leakage is evident.

 Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

To properly test the function of the bobtail proportioning relay valve, 
a pair of test gauges or gauges of known accuracy must be used. 

Park the vehicle on a level surface and chock the wheels or hold the 
vehicle by means other than the air brakes. 

Exhaust air pressure from all vehicle reservoirs. 

Install a "tee" at the bobtail proportioning relay valve service port 
and at one of the delivery ports, then install a test gauge in each. 

Connect the tractor service and emergency "glad hands" (hose couplings) 
to hose couplings that have been plugged, or alternatively, to a trailer. 
Build the tractor system air pressure to governor cutout and make four to five 
full brake applications. Check the air fittings at the bobtail proportioning 
relay valve for leakage. Tighten as needed. 

With the trailer air supply control valve (dash control with red 
octagonal button) and parking brake control valve (dash control with yellow 
diamond button) activated for tractor trailer operation, apply, hold, then 
release the service brakes with the foot control valve several times varying 
the application pressures while watching the reaction of the gauges installed 
on the bobtail proportioning relay valve. Note that a prompt application 
occurs and that it can be held and then promptly released. 

 NOTE: When performing the following procedure, the measured differential 
should be approximately 28 kPa (4 psi). 

Check the bobtail proportioning relay valve differential pressure by 
applying 69 kPa (10 psi) to the service port and noting the pressure 
registered at the delivery port. Subtract delivery port pressure from the 69 
kPa (10 psi) service pressure to obtain the differential. Compare the measured 
differential with the pressure specified for the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve part number.

Make and hold a full 689 kPa (100 psi or greater) brake application and 
note that full pressure is delivered to the brake air chambers. 

Activate the dash-mounted trailer air supply control valve for bobtail 
tractor operation. Then make a slow service brake application, increasing the 
pressure at the bobtail proportioning relay valve service port to 138 kPa (20 
psi) while watching the reaction at the delivery port gauge. Note that 
delivery pressure rises to approximately 34-69 kPa (5-10 psi) and remains 
constant while service pressure continues to rise to 138 kPa (20 psi). Release 
the application. 

Make another service brake application and slowly increase the pressure 
at the bobtail proportioning relay valve service port to between 413-482 kPa 
(60-70 psi) while observing the gauge installed at the delivery port. Note 
that when service port pressure rises to between 138-207 kPa (20-30 psi), 
delivery pressure begins to rise above the initial pressure noted in Step 6. 
The rise of delivery pressure should be at a proportioned rate of 
approximately 3:1. At 482 kPa (70 psi) service pressure, delivered pressure 
should be 103-172 kPa (15-25 psi). 

Make a full service brake application and note that both test gauges 
register the same pressure. 

Remove the test gauges from the bobtail proportioning relay valve. 

Build the air system pressure to governor cutout. With the dash mounted 
trailer air supply control valve activated for tractor trailer operation, 
apply a soap solution to all three exhaust ports (two in cover and one in 
body). The leakage noted should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in less 
than three seconds at any exhaust port. 

Make and hold a full service brake application and apply a soap 
solution to all three exhaust ports and around the cover where it joins the 
body. The leakage noted should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in less 
than three seconds at any exhaust port.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Trailer Air Supply Control Valve 

 Removal 

Chock the vehicle wheels and drain all air system reservoirs completely. 

 CAUTION: Note the orientation of these buttons in relation to the trailer air 
supply control valve to be sure they will be replaced properly. 

Remove the red and yellow buttons from the stems of the spools on the 
trailer air supply control valve by turning in a counterclockwise direction.

Remove and save the mounting hardware from the four corners of the 
cover plate. 

If totally removing the trailer air supply control valve from the 
vehicle, identify and remove the air lines from the back of the trailer air 
supply control valve. 

Remove the six Phillips head screws from the cover plate and carefully 
remove the cover plate from the trailer air supply control valve. Remove the 
trailer air supply control valve. 

 Installation 

Install the cover plate onto the valve body and retain with the six 
Phillips head screws. Tighten to 3 Nm (27 lb-in). 

Attach the red and yellow buttons onto the threaded stems of the 
spools, making sure they are oriented correctly. 

Reattach the trailer air supply control valve to the dash using the 
hardware removed in Step 3 of Removal. If air lines were removed during 
disassembly, reconnect to proper ports.

Remove wheel chocks.

Repeat the Trailer Air Supply Control Valve Operation and Leakage Test procedures under Diagnosis and 
Testing. Test drive vehicle at slow speed in a safe area prior to placing back 
into service.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Trailer Air Supply Control Valve

 Disassembly 

Remove the cap and O-ring from the bore of the tripper valve. Remove 
the piston, springs and check valve. These parts will all fall out of the 
cavity of the trailer air supply control valve by tilting the body forward. 
Remove the O-ring from its groove on the piston. 

Remove the two main spools from the body of the trailer air supply 
control valve by grasping the stem and pulling firmly. Remove the two springs 
from the bottom of each spool cavity. 

Pull the guide cap and guide spool over the threaded end of one of the 
plungers. Remove the O-ring from the guide cap and the O-ring from the guide 
spool. Remove O-rings and the exhaust seal from the plunger. 

Repeat Step 3 on the remaining spool assembly. 

Remove the retaining ring from the cavity of the trailer air supply 
control valve body that contains the dual circuit supply valve. 

 NOTE: If during the removal of this assembly from the body the cap dislodges 
from the rest of the trailer air supply control valve, the balance of the 
parts can be removed by the use of a bent wire. The spring, piston and O-ring 
that are internal to the dual circuit valve assembly are non-serviceable. 

Using needlenose pliers, grasp the bar in the center of the cap and 
remove the dual circuit valve assembly. Remove the three O-rings from the 
valve or from the cavity of the body, if some have remained there. Other than 
the three external O-rings, do not disassemble the piston assembly further.

 Plunger and Exhaust Seal 

[FIGURE: H5062B.gif]

 Assembly 

Lubricate all O-rings, bores and sliding surfaces of dual circuit 
supply valve with Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M13P4-A.

Install O-rings onto the dual circuit supply valve. Then install the 
assembly into its cavity in the body (small diameter to enter first). 

Install the snap ring making sure it is fully seated in its groove.

 CAUTION: The exhaust seal must be installed so that its beveled surface mates 
with the beveled surface of the plunger. 

Install O-rings and the exhaust seal onto the stem of plungers.

Install O-ring onto the guide spool and O-ring onto the guide cap. 
Place the guide cap on top of the guide spool and install entire assembly over 
the threaded end of the plunger pressing down firmly until it snaps into 
place. 

Install spring over the boss in the bottom of the spool cavity in the 
body of the trailer air supply control valve. Place the spool assembly into 
the body, keeping the spool square to the body press and turn the stem until 
the spool is fully seated in its cavity. Note the assembly is keyed and may 
only be installed one way. 

Repeat Steps 5 and 6 with the remaining components for the opposite 
spool.

Install O-ring into its groove on the piston and O-ring onto the cap. 

Install spring on the piston and spring on the boss of the check valve. 

Install the spring and check valve into its cavity in the body of the 
MV-3 valve (tapered end of check valve to enter cavity first). Make sure the 
spring is centered in the bore. 

Install the piston assembly into the cavity making sure the spring 
mates with the bore of the piston. 

Install the cap with O-ring.

Test the trailer air supply control valve for leakage and correct 
operation. Refer to the Operation and Leakage Test under Component Tests in 
the Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Tractor Protection Valve

 Disassembly 

Remove six capscrews and lockwashers. This will permit separation of 
the body, intermediate body and lower body and gaskets. 

Remove piston and piston spring from intermediate body. Remove O-rings 
from piston. 

Remove both double check valve shuttles and guides from body. 

Remove large retaining ring from lower body. Remove valve retainer 
spring and inlet valve. Remove O-ring from valve retainer.

 Assembly 

 NOTE: Before assembly, lubricate all O-rings, bores and mating surfaces with 
Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESR-M13P4-A. 

Install inlet valve. Install O-ring on valve retainer. Install spring 
and valve retainer. 

Install retainer ring, making sure it is seated in groove. 

Install double check valve guides in intermediate body and install 
shuttles in guides. 

Install spring in body. Install O-rings on piston. Insert stem of 
piston inside of spring, making sure vent is open. 

 NOTE: Locating pins match corresponding holes in gasket. 

Install new gaskets on both sides of intermediate body. Install lower 
and upper bodies with assembly in the following manner:

Tighten center two capscrews to 9 Nm (80 lb-in). 

Tighten upper right and lower left capscrews to 9 Nm 
(80 lb-in). 

Tighten lower right and upper left capscrews to 9 Nm 
(80 lb-in). 

Repeat Steps a, b, and c.

Test the tractor protection valve for leakage and correct operation as 
described in Operation and Leakage Test under Diagnosis and Testing.

1997 L-Series

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Tractor/Trailer

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve

 Disassembly 

Drive out the spiral pin and remove the handle, head, and head seal 
O-ring. 

Remove handle O-ring. 

Remote-operated type valve: remove setscrew, head and head seal O-ring. 

Remove adjusting ring lockwasher. 

Remove capscrews that hold body and cover together; separate cover from 
body. 

Remove gasket and graduating spring. 

Remove cam and cam follower from cover. 

Unscrew and remove adjusting ring. 

Remove piston and piston return spring from body. 

Remove piston O-ring. 

Remove inlet and exhaust insert screws and lockwashers, then insert 
O-ring seal. 

The inlet and exhaust valve insert can be disassembled if desired or 
necessary. 

Insert some object such as a capscrew in the supply port to hold the 
inlet valve on its seat. 

Depress the exhaust valve guide and spring; remove the exhaust valve. 

Remove stem with inlet valve from inlet seat and remove inlet valve 
from stem.

 Assembly 

Prior to assembly, lubricate the body and cover bores, cam and cam 
follower, piston O-ring, and cover top with Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M13P4-A. 

Press inlet valve on stem. A little water in the boot valve or some 
soap on the stem will make it easier to press on the inlet valve. 

Place stem with inlet valve installed in inlet seat. Insert some object 
such as a capscrew to hold the inlet valve up against its seat. 

Position spring and exhaust valve guide. 

Depress guide and spring, then press exhaust valve on stem. 

Place seal O-ring over insert seat and with capscrews and lockwashers. 
Install inlet and exhaust insert in body. Recommended torque on insert 
capscrews is 7-9 Nm (62-80 lb-in). 

Install piston return spring. 

Install piston O-ring on piston and install piston in body. 

Install adjusting ring in cover and screw it down until it is flush 
with top of cover. 

Place cam follower and cam in cover. 

Position graduating spring and gasket in body. 

Connect body to cover. Tighten capscrews evenly and tighten to 8.5-10.7 Nm
 (75-95 lb-in). 

Install adjusting ring lockwasher, head seal O-ring, and head. 

Install setscrew in head of remote-operated type valves. 

At this stage, before installing handle and spiral pin of 
handle-operated type valve, the rebuilt trailer brake hand control valve 
should be tested and adjusted if facilities are available. If facilities are 
not available, the trailer brake hand control valve can be tested on the 
vehicle.

[FIGURE: CH7993B.gif]

 Disassembly 

 CAUTION: The bobtail proportioning relay valve may be lightly clamped in a bench 
vise during disassembly; however, overtightening will cause damage and result 
in leakage. If a vise is to be used, position the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve so that the jaws bear on the supply ports on opposing sides of the body. 

Remove all air fittings and plugs from the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve. 

Mark the relationship of the cover to the body and if the bobtail 
proportioning relay valve is equipped with a mounting bracket, mark the 
relationship of the bracket to the cover. 

While holding the exhaust cover, remove and discard the retaining ring 
that secures it to the body. 

Remove and discard the exhaust cover along with both O-rings. 

Remove and discard the valve spring, valve retainer, and the valve 
assembly from the body. 

Remove and retain the four capscrews that secure the cover to the body. 

Separate the cover from the body, then remove and discard the sealing 
ring and O-ring. 

Remove and retain the relay piston from the body. 

Remove and discard the O-ring from the relay piston. 

Remove and discard the dust shield and the retaining ring from the 
valve cover, then remove and retain the exhaust piston. 

Remove and discard the exhaust piston O-ring and the exhaust diaphragm. 

Remove and retain the service piston from the valve cover, then remove 
and discard the service piston O-ring. 

Remove the spring and spring cage from the valve cover. Discard the 
spring and retain the spring cage. 

Remove and retain the blend back piston from the cover, then remove and 
discard both O-rings. 

Remove and retain the proportioning piston from the valve cover, then 
remove and discard both O-rings. 

While holding the inlet valve seat in place, remove and discard the 
retaining ring from the proportioning piston. 

Remove the inlet valve seat, the inlet valve, and the valve spring from 
the proportioning piston, then remove and discard the O-ring from the valve 
seat. Discard the valve and spring also. 

Remove and discard the exhaust cover screw and exhaust cover. 

 Assembly 

Prior to assembly, lubricate all O-rings, seals, and pistons as well as 
body and cover bores, using the lubricant provided with the Bendix maintenance 
kit. Use all of the lubricant and spread it evenly on the rubbing surfaces. 

Install the O-ring on the inlet valve seat. 

Install the small end of the inlet/exhaust valve spring over the rubber 
of the valve, making sure the spring coils rest on the valve's four tabs. 

Insert the spring and valve into the valve seat, making sure the four 
tabs are within the seat's bore. 

Insert the valve, seat and spring assembly into the proportioning 
piston, large end of the spring first. 

While holding the seat in place, install the retaining ring to secure 
it in the piston. Make sure the retaining ring is fully seated in its groove. 
Make sure the valve is straight against the exhaust seat and free to move. 

Install both the large and small diameter O-rings on the proportioning 
piston. 

Install both the large and small diameter O-rings on the blend back 
piston, then insert the small diameter of the proportioning piston into the 
small diameter end of the blend back piston. 

Carefully insert the assembled proportioning and blend back pistons to 
the edge of the bore in the cover. Do not cut or pinch the O-rings. 

With the bore of the cover facing up, install the spring cage in the 
blend back piston so that its flat side rests against the blend back piston 
(its depressed side out toward spring). 

Install the O-ring on the service piston, then install the spring in 
the cage so that its coils are within the inside diameter of the cage. 

Install O-ring on exhaust piston, and place exhaust diaphragm between 
the six posts of the service piston. 

Place exhaust piston on service piston with its six-ribbed side facing 
the service piston. Then install both pistons while pushing the proportioning 
and blend back pistons all the way into the cover. 

Install the dust shield in the cover. 

While holding the dust shield in the cover, install the retaining ring, 
making sure it is fully seated in its groove. 

Install the exhaust cover using screw to retain it. Tighten the screw 
to 1-1.7 Nm (9-15 lb-in). 

Install the valve retainer on the inlet and exhaust valve so that the 
flange of the retainer surrounds the rubber portion of the valve. Install the 
inlet and exhaust valve in the body. 

Install the inlet and exhaust valve return spring in the body. 

Install the large and small diameter O-rings in the exhaust cover, then 
install the exhaust cover in the body, taking care not to damage the O-rings. 
Hold the exhaust cover in place. 

While depressing the exhaust cover, install the retaining ring in the 
body. Make sure the retainer is fully seated in its groove in the body. 

Using lubricant to hold them in place, install the large and small 
sealing rings on the cover. 

Install the O-ring on the relay piston, then install the piston in the 
body. 

After noting the relationship marks made prior to disassembly, install 
the mounting bracket (not illustrated) on the cover. Then secure the cover and 
mounting bracket on the body using the four capscrews. Tighten the capscrews 
to 14-16 Nm (10-12 lb-ft). 

Install all air line fittings and plugs making sure thread sealing 
material does not enter the bobtail proportioning relay valve. 

Install the bobtail proportioning relay valve on the vehicle and 
perform the Operation and Leakage Tests under Diagnosis and Testing before 
returning the vehicle to service.

Trailer Air Supply Control Valve

 CAUTION: The non-metallic components which comprise most of the parts of the

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Quick Release Valve 

Clean all parts in good cleaning solvent.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve 

Using mineral spirits or an equivalent solvent, clean and thoroughly 
dry all metal parts. Do not damage bores with metal tools. 

Wash all non-metallic components being reused in a soap and water 
solution, making sure to rinse and dry thoroughly. 

Inspect the interior and exterior of all metal parts that will be 
reused for severe corrosion, pitting and cracks. Superficial corrosion or 
pitting on the exterior portion of the body and cover is acceptable. Replace 
the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if the interior of the body or 
cover exhibits signs of corrosion or pitting. 

Inspect each non-metallic component for cracks, wear or distortion. 
Replace the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if either is found. 

Inspect the bores of both the body and cover for deep scuffing or 
gouges. Replace the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if either is 
found. 

Make sure the air channel running between the top surface of the body 
and its supply port is clear and free of obstruction. 

Make sure all air channels and exhaust passages in the cover are clear 
and free of obstruction. 

Inspect the pipe threads in the body and valve cover. Make sure they 
are clean and free of thread sealant. 

Inspect all air line fittings for corrosion and replace as necessary. 
Make sure to remove all old thread sealant before reuse.

ADJUSTMENTS

Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve

Refer to the following illustration.

The trailer brake hand control valve should deliver 552 kPa (80 psi). 

 NOTE: A spanner wrench can be used to rotate the adjusting ring, but if such 
a wrench is not available, the adjusting ring can be turned with a small 
screwdriver inserted in one of the inner notches of the ring. Turning the 
adjusting ring one notch will raise the delivered pressure approximately 34 
kPa (5 psi). 

If the delivery pressure is below specified final delivery pressure, 
552 kPa (80 psi), it can be adjusted by removing the head and adjusting ring 
lockwasher and rotating the adjusting ring clockwise to raise the delivery 
pressure. 

If the delivery pressure is above specified final delivery pressure, 
552 kPa (80 psi), it can be lowered by rotating the adjusting ring 
counterclockwise.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Cam

 WARNING: DO NOT INHALE DUST FROM BRAKES, CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. 
INHALATION OF DUST CAN BE INJURIOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. COMPRESSED AIR OR BRUSHES 
MUST NOT BE USED TO CLEAN BRAKES, BRAKE DRUMS, CLUTCHES AND ASSOCIATED 
COMPONENTS. USE BRAKE AND CLUTCH SERVICE VACUUM, MODEL 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT 
EQUIPPED FOR THIS PURPOSE TO CAREFULLY REMOVE ANY DUST. ADHERENT DUST SHOULD 
BE REMOVED WITH A DAMP RAG. ANY DUST SHOULD BE CONTAINED IN A SEALED AND 
LABELED BAG FOR DISPOSAL. WEAR AN APPROVED HIGH EFFICIENCY CARTRIDGE OR AIR 
LINE RESPIRATOR AND USE EXTRA CAUTION TO AVOID BREATHING THIS DUST. 

The cam-type brake is an air-operated two-shoe brake. The front brake 
shoes each use a one-piece shoe lining. The rear shoes each use two-piece 
lining.

 Front Brake Assembly, Rockwell Q-Series 

[FIGURE: H7405B.gif]

Camshaft Bracket

As the brake pedal application is made, air pressure is applied to the 
brake air chamber. The brake air chamber has an internal diaphragm that will 
push against the brake chamber push rod with a force proportional to the air 
pressure being applied. The push rod then pushes on the automatic slack 
adjuster arm, which causes rotation of the brake camshaft. The rotation causes 
the rollers of the brake shoes to roll up the cam ramp forcing the brake shoes 
against the brake drum. When the brake pedal is released, the retracting (or 
return) spring of the brake pulls the shoes away from the brake drum, and a 
return spring in the brake air chamber returns the slack adjuster to the 
released position.

================================================================================
PAGE 4902
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 06-08D: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Slack Adjuster, Automatic 

The automatic slack adjuster design uses both brake chamber push rod 
travel and shoe-to-brake drum force to maintain proper brake adjustment. On 
brake application, the brake chamber push rod rotates the slack adjuster until 
the adjusting link engages a one-way cone clutch on the wormshaft. At this 
point, if the brake shoes are not in contact with the brake drum, the cone 
clutch will remain engaged with the shaft and the link will rotate the 
wormshaft. This shaft rotation adjusts the brake shoes by reducing 
shoe-to-drum clearance. Adjustment continues until the brake linings are 
forced against the brake drum. The shoe-to-brake drum force creates a 
resistance torque that exceeds the slip torque of the clutch, and allows the 
clutch to slip on the wormshaft for the remainder of the slack travel. During 
the return stroke the one-way cone clutch allows the link to return without 
shaft movement. The adjustment cycle will repeat until shoe-to-brake drum 
contact force occurs simultaneously with the initial link to clutch engagement.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air, Cam-Type

 Inspection and Verification 

It is important that a careful parts inspection be made before 
assembly. Check all parts for wear or damage and service or replace as required.

Check the brake backing plate for expanded anchor pin holes and for 
cracks. Replace damaged backing plate and anchor pin bushings.

Check the camshaft bracket for broken welds, cracks and correct 
alignment. Replace damaged brackets.

Check anchor pins for corrosion and wear. Replace damaged anchor pins.

Check brake shoes for rust that can impair operation, expanded rivet 
holes, broken welds and incorrect alignment. Service or replace as necessary.

On 16.5 inch brake shoes only: anchor pin holes must not exceed 25.63 
mm (1.009 inches) in diameter. The distance from the center of the anchor pin 
hole to the center of the roller hole must not exceed 324.59 mm (12.779 
inches). Replace any shoe whose measurements are not to specifications.

Check the brake camshaft for cracks, wear and corrosion. Check the cam 
head, bearing journals and splines. Replace damaged brake camshafts.

Check the slack adjusters:

For slack adjusters with "quick connect" type clevis, check the gap 
between the clevis and the collar. If the gap exceeds 1.52 mm (0.060 inch) 
replace the clevis.

Check the clevis pins and the bushing in the arm of the slack adjuster. 
Replace the pins if they are worn. Replace the bushing if its diameter exceeds 
16.7 mm (0.656 inch).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Slack Adjuster 

 Removal 

 NOTE: The spring brake must be caged to remove the push rod clevis pin. Refer 
to Section 06-08E for the Maxi II brake air chamber or to Section 06-08F for 
the MGM.

Remove the clevis pin attaching the slack adjuster to the air chamber 
push rod.

Remove the lock ring attaching the slack adjuster to the camshaft.

Mark the position of the slack adjuster on the brake camshaft, then 
slide the slack adjuster off the shaft.

 Installation

If installing a new quick-connect clevis, install the new snap nut on 
the air chamber push rod in the same location as the clevis which was removed. 
Do not tighten the jam nut at this time.

Install the clevis on the slack adjuster using the pins and cotter pins 
supplied.

Install the automatic slack adjuster on the brake camshaft using the 
original mounting hardware. If brake camshaft end play is 1.57 mm (0.062 inch) 
or greater, install an additional spacer at cam end of brake camshaft.

 NOTE: The hex portion of the snap nut must come in contact with the clevis 
for proper engagement. Incomplete or improper assembly will result in improper 
brake operation. Pull on the slack adjuster to check for proper engagement.

Rotate the adjuster by turning the 7/16-inch hex extension of the 
wormshaft in a clockwise direction until the snap nut fully engages the 
clevis. Once snapped into the clevis, the snap nut cannot be removed from the 
clevis without damage to the clevis or snap nut.

Adjust the clevis until the distance from clevis pin to the face of the 
brake air chamber is 65-67 mm (2-9/16 to 2-5/8 inches).

 NOTE: Failure to tighten the jam nut will allow the snap nut to rotate and 
change the initial position, preventing the automatic slack adjuster from 
functioning properly.

Tighten the jam nut. For 1/2-20 threads, tighten to 27-41 Nm
 (20-30 lb-ft). For 5/8-18 threads, tighten to 45-122 Nm
 (33-90 lb-ft).

Manually adjust the brakes. Refer to Adjustments in this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Brake Shoe and Camshaft

 Lining/Drum Replacement Procedure 

Special attention must be given to proper maintenance procedures of the 
automatic slack adjuster when the brake linings or brake drums are replaced.

If the axle is equipped with spring brake chambers, manually cage the 
spring brakes, following the manufacturer's recommended procedures.

Applying 69-137 kPa (10 to 20 psi) air pressure to the service brake 
chamber is recommended. This relieves the internal pressure on the adjusting 
mechanism, minimizing wear when backing off the slack adjuster.

Rotate the hex extension counterclockwise until adequate clearance is 
reached for the new brake linings or brake drum.

Release the 69-137 kPa (10-20 psi) in the system.

Proceed with the lining change or brake drum replacement.

 Clean Parts 

 WARNING: INCORRECT USE OF HOT SOLUTION TANKS OR ALKALINE SOLUTIONS CAN CAUSE 
SERIOUS PERSONAL INJURY. TO PREVENT INJURY, FOLLOW MANUFACTURER'S 
INSTRUCTIONS. DO NOT USE GASOLINE TO CLEAN PARTS. GASOLINE CAN EXPLODE. 

Ground or polished parts

Use a cleaning solvent, kerosene or diesel fuel to clean ground or 
polished parts. To prevent corrosion, do not use hot solutions, water, steam 
or alkaline solutions.

Rough parts

Rough parts may be cleaned in hot solution tanks or a weak alkaline 
solution. After cleaning, rinse and dry the parts thoroughly.

 Corrosion Prevention 

Apply brake lubricant to cleaned or new brake parts as needed. Do not 
apply lubricants to brake linings or drums.

 Parts Inspection 

Check all parts for wear or damage. Service or replace as necessary. 
Rockwell recommends replacement of springs, rollers and anchor pins each time 
the brake shoes are relined or replaced.

 NOTE: Anchor pin holes must not exceed 25.63 mm (1.009 inches) in diameter. 
The distance from the center of the anchor pin hole to the center of the 
roller hole must not exceed 324.59 mm (12.779 inches).

Check the backing plate for cracks or expanded anchor pin holes. 

Check the camshaft bracket for cracked or broken welds. Check for 
correct bracket alignment.

Check anchor pins for corrosion or wear. Replace as necessary.

Check brake shoes for cracks, heat damage, loose or missing rivets and 
loose or damaged lining. Replace as necessary.

Check the brake camshaft for cracks, wear and corrosion. Check the cam 
faces, shaft bearing journals and splines. Replace damaged brake camshafts.

Check the slack adjusters:

For slack adjusters with quick connect clevis, the clevis-to-collar gap 
must not exceed 1.52 mm (0.060 inch). Replace clevis if not within 
specification.

Replace worn clevis pins. Replace clevis pin bushings with diameter 
greater than 13.5 mm (0.531 inch).

Check slack adjusters by rotating the adjusting nut counterclockwise 
with a torque wrench. Turn the gear 360 degrees. The torque must be a minimum 
of 20 Nm (15 lb-ft) for the full rotation of the gear. 
Service or replace a slack adjuster not meeting specification.

[FIGURE: DH0175A.gif]

 WARNING: TO AVOID POSSIBLE SERIOUS PERSONAL INJURY, DO NOT INSTALL A BRAKE DRUM 
NOT MEETING MANUFACTURER'S SPECIFICATION. 

Check the brake drums.

Measure the inside diameter of the brake drum at several points with a 
drum caliper or inside micrometer. Replace if the brake drum exceeds 
manufacturer's specifications.

[FIGURE: H10254A.gif]

Check dust shields for rust or distortion. Service or replace as 
necessary.

on each anchor pin. Tighten the anchor pin lock nuts. Install the brake shoe 
hold-down clips.

Install the brake shoe retracting spring.

Lubricate the camshaft splines and install the slack adjuster on the 
brake camshaft, using the alignment marks made at removal. Install the 
camshaft snap ring.

Connect the brake chamber push rod clevis to the slack adjuster by 
installing the clevis pin in the hole of the slack adjuster 139.7 mm (5.5 
inches) from the centerline of the brake camshaft to the center of the hole 
for front or rear brakes.

Install the wheel, tire and brake drum assemblies.

Adjust the brakes as described in this section.

 Rockwell Front or Rear (16.5 x 5, 6, 7), Q-Series 

 Removal 

Secure vehicle by chocking the wheels, put transmission in neutral, 
cage the spring brake.

Rotate the slack adjuster adjustment nut counterclockwise until shoes 
no longer touch the brake drum.

Raise axle and remove tire, wheel and brake drum. 

Press down on the bottom brake shoe and remove the lower cam roller. 
Next, lift the top shoe and take out the top cam roller.

[FIGURE: H10255A.gif]

Lift out the shoe return spring which is now free of tension.

[FIGURE: H10256A.gif]

Swing the lower shoe back approximately 180 degrees to relieve the 
tension on the retainer springs, remove the springs and slip the shoes off the 
stepped anchor pins.

[FIGURE: H10257A.gif]

After removing shoes, completely inspect brake components, servicing as 
necessary.

Remove the slack adjuster clevis pins.

Remove retainer and washers on end of brake camshaft.

Remove the automatic slack adjuster.

Check the camshaft bracket bushing wear by moving the camshaft up and 
down and side to side. If the total movement is more than 0.76 mm (0.030 
inch), remove the brake camshaft from the camshaft bracket.

[FIGURE: H10292A.gif]

Use an appropriate driver to remove the camshaft bracket bushings and 
seals.

[FIGURE: H10293A.gif]

 Installation 

If necessary, use an appropriate driver and install new camshaft 
bracket bushings.

If the camshaft was removed, install new camshaft bracket seals. Use an 
appropriate driver and install with the seal lips pointing toward the slack 
adjuster.

[FIGURE: H10294A.gif]

Coat the camshaft splines, bushings and bearing journals with Ford Disc 
Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1C172-A.

Install the brake camshaft. It should turn by hand without binding.

Install the camshaft flatwasher and slack adjuster and fasten the slack 
adjuster in place. Add spacing washers to limit the end play to approximately 
1.57 mm (0.062 inch) and install a new snap ring.

 CAUTION: Always use all new springs. 

Install the relined or new shoes by reversing the procedure used to 
remove them.

Reconnect slack adjuster clevis to air chamber push rod. Lubricate the 
clevis pins with Ford Disc Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C172-A.

Reinstall brake drum and wheel and tire assembly.

Lube brake camshaft tube cavity with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or 
-K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Adjust brakes as required, as described in Adjustments, Manual 
Adjustment in this section.

MAINTENANCE

Brake, Air — Cam Type

Perform the following periodic maintenance every three months or 40,225 
km (25,000 miles).

Check the condition of the foundation brakes, including brake drums, 
shoes and linings, cams, rollers, bearings, etc.

Check for structural damage of the automatic slack adjuster and 
condition of the boot for cuts, tears, etc. Replace if necessary.

After allowing brake drum to cool to room temperature, check for 
correct brake air chamber stroke.

================================================================================
PAGE 4910
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 06-08D: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

LUBRICATION

Brake, Air — Cam Type

The automatic slack adjusters should be lubricated every 39,000 km 
(24,000 miles) or six months, whichever occurs first, more frequently under 
adverse conditions. Use the following procedure.

Locate the grease fitting on the slack adjuster. With a conventional 
grease gun, fill the inside of the slack adjuster until new grease flows from 
the grease plug hole or automatic grease relief opening.

Lubricate the slack adjuster with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Lubricate the brake camshaft splines every 39,000 km (24,000 miles) or 
12 months, whichever occurs first. Lubricate more frequently under adverse 
conditions. Use Ford Disc Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C172-A. Do not lubricate the cam 
faces.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Service Air Chamber, Front and Rear

 Disassembly and Assembly 

Because of the normal wear on other internal components, service of the 
front brake air chamber diaphragm is not recommended. If the front brake air 
chamber diaphragm is worn or damaged, replace the whole brake air chamber.

For disassembly and assembly of the rear brake air chambers, refer to 
 Section 06-08E for the Maxi-Brake II and to Section 06-08F for the MGM.

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Adjusters, Automatic

 Inspection 

Free stroke is the amount of slack adjuster movement required to bring 
the brake shoe and linings into contact with the brake drum. Check the slack 
adjuster free stroke as follows:

With the brakes released, measure and record the distance from the 
brake air chamber face to the center of the large clevis pin. Distance "A."

Using a lever, extend and hold the air chamber push rod at the point at 
which the brake shoe and lining is felt to come into contact with the brake 
drum.

Make the same measurement as in Step 1. Distance "B."

[FIGURE: H10290A.gif]

Subtract "A" from "B" to obtain the free stroke measurement. For a 
properly installed slack adjuster, with the brakes properly adjusted, the free 
stroke should be 10-16 mm (3/8-5/8 inches). A free stroke that is longer than 
specified is caused by a foundation brake concern. Inspect the foundation 
brakes for proper installation, loose, missing or broken parts. Service or 
replace as necessary.
