 Assembly 

If removed, press in a new needle bearing. 

If removed, install a new shaft seal in the housing. 

If removed, press a new bearing onto the driveshaft. Install the 
retaining ring in the driveshaft groove. 

Install the driveshaft and bearing assembly into the housing. 

Install the bearing circlip in the groove. 

Install O-ring and backup ring on the rear faceplate. 

 NOTE: The cam ring of the rotor assembly must be installed with the arrow 
pointed in the direction of rotation. Set pin is installed in location 
recorded during disassembly. 

Install the set pin, front faceplate and rotor assembly into the 
housing. 

Install the O-ring and backup ring in the rear cover housing in 
accordance with exploded view. Place the rear pressure spring in the rear 
faceplate. Position the rear cover in the housing. 

Press down on the rear cover plate and install the hook spring ring in 
the groove in the housing. 

Install the helical drive gear and Woodruff key. Install the nut and 
tighten to 80-90 Nm (59-66 lb-ft).

Section 11-03A: Steering Linkage

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering Linkage

The steering linkage on L-Series consists of right- and left-hand 
spindle assemblies attached to an I-beam front axle. Separate steering and 
spindle arms attach to the spindles. A tie rod, adjustable for toe-in, is 
connected between the left- and right-hand spindle arms. The drag link is 
connected between the steering arm on the left spindle assembly and the pitman 
arm on the steering gear. 

16K, 18K and 20K axles utilize steering gears on both left- and 
right-hand sides to reduce steering efforts normally associated with these 
heavy axles. This is known as a dual-gear system. In the case of a dual gear 
system, the steering linkage on the right-hand side is the same as the linkage 
on the left-hand side.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drag Link 

 Removal 

Replace the drag link if the ball stud at the pitman arm end or the 
steering arm end has lash or if the drag link is damaged.

Remove cotter pins and nuts from ball studs. 

Remove ball studs from arms. 

 Installation 

Position new drag link ball studs in arms with axle end installed in 
steering arm, and install nuts.

Tighten the pitman arm ball stud retaining nut and the steering arm 
ball stud retaining nut to 149-203 Nm (110-150 lb-ft). 

Install new cotter pins. Advance nut to next castellation if necessary 
to insert cotter pin.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Grease Seals 

 Greaseable Type 

 Removal 

Remove sliding seal from socket. 

 NOTE: Do not use a liquid solvent of any type to clean these parts. 

Thoroughly wipe away all grease and foreign material from around ball 
stud and throat of socket.

 Installation 

Install a new sliding seal over ball stud. Assemble ball stud into 
steering arm or pitman arm and tighten nut. 

Grease ball joint with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B until excess grease is 
pushed out from under the seal.

================================================================================
PAGE 5517
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 11-03A: Steering Linkage

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Tie Rod End 

 Removal 

If the tie rod end ball stud has lash, replace the tie rod end. 

Remove cotter pin and nut from rod end ball stud. 

Remove ball stud from spindle arm. 

Loosen clamp bolt, and turn rod end out of the rod. Count the number of 
turns needed to remove the rod end. 

 Installation 

Lubricate threads of a new tie rod end and turn it into the rod to 
about the same distance the old rod end was installed. This will provide an 
approximate toe-in setting. 

Install ball stud in spindle arm. Tighten nut to 149-203 Nm
 (110-150 lb-ft). 

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install cotter pin. 
Install new cotter pin.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Tie Rod, Front Wheel Spindle

 Removal 

Replace the wheel spindle tie rod if the end threads are stripped or if 
the rod is damaged. Do not attempt to straighten a bent rod.

Loosen both wheel spindle tie rod end clamps. 

Unthread wheel spindle tie rod until rod drops off both ends. Count 
number of turns needed to remove rod ends. The right rod end has a right-hand 
thread; the left rod end has a left-hand thread.

 Installation 

Lubricate threads on tie rod ends and turn a rod end into the tube 
about one thread. 

Start the other end and continue to turn rod until rod ends have 
entered rod to about the same distance the old rod was installed. This will 
provide an approximate toe-in setting. 

Tie rod ends should be parallel with each other and in the same plane 
within 5 degrees.

Check toe-in and adjust, if necessary. Be sure to tighten tie rod end 
clamps after adjusting toe-in. Refer to Section 04-00 .

 Removal 

Replace the pitman arm if it is bent, if the ball stud hole is

pin. Install new cotter pin.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Spindle/Steering Arm 

Replace the spindle or steering arm if it is bent or damaged. Do not 
attempt to straighten a bent spindle or steering arm.

 Removal 

Remove spindle tie rod end ball stud or drag link ball stud from 
spindle or steering arm. 

Remove cotter pin and retaining nut from arm. Remove arm from the 
spindle. Drive arm out of spindle, if necessary. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: Unique arms are used for different front axles and wheelbases. Refer to 
Master Parts Catalog for part number information.

Install a new arm in the spindle.

 NOTE: The spindle hole is slotted to align the arm with a key.

Insert key in the slot from nut side of spindle. Be sure key is flush 
with slot face of spindle. 

Install spindle/steering arm retaining nut. Tighten steering arm 
retaining nut to 733-989 Nm (540-730 lb-ft) or spindle arm 
retaining nut to 489-650 Nm (360-480 lb-ft). 

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install a new cotter pin through the nut and spindle or steering arm.

Install tie rod end ball stud or drag link ball stud in the arm. 
Install the ball stud nut.

Tighten drag link retaining nut or tie rod nut to 149-203 Nm
 (110-150 lb-ft).

If necessary advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install a new cotter pin through the nut and ball stud.

Check toe and adjust, if necessary. Refer to Section 04-00 .

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Rotary Assist Cylinder

Certain heavy truck power steering systems are equipped with a rotary 
assist cylinder to equalize power steering forces. The rotary assist cylinder 
is similar in design to the power steering gear but without the worm gear and 
valve components that attach to the steering wheel.

The rotary assist cylinder consists of a combined cylinder and gear box 
that contains a piston with an integral rack. The rack meshes with a gear 
sector that connects to a pitman arm and steering linkage similar to the 
integral power steering gear.

The piston operates from pressure supplied from and controlled by the 
integral power steering gear. When the integral gear supplies pressure to the 
top of its own piston, it supplies pressure to the top of the auxiliary 
cylinder piston. When it supplies pressure to the bottom of its own piston, it 
supplies pressure to the bottom of the auxiliary cylinder's piston.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Rotary Assist Cylinder 

 CAUTION: The rotary assist cylinder weighs approximately 36 kg (80 pounds) dry. 
Exercise care when removing, lifting or carrying the unit. 

Label hoses before disconnecting so they can be easily identified for 
reassembly. 

Refer to Section 11-02A for removal and installation of the steering 
gear.

 Removal 

Stop the vehicle in a straight-ahead position with the steering 
centered. Maintain the straight-ahead centered position until the rotary 
assist cylinder has been reinstalled for ease of correct rotary assist 
cylinder alignment. 

Thoroughly clean off all outside dirt, especially from around fittings 
and hose connections. 

Note the location of existing alignment marks on the output shaft and 
pitman arm. 

Remove pitman arm from output shaft. 

Disconnect the hydraulic fluid lines at the rotary assist cylinder. 
Identify and tag the lines to aid in installation. Plug all port and line 
openings.

Remove the rotary assist cylinder from the vehicle and drain any 
remaining fluid into a suitable container.

 Installation 

Check to make sure that steering wheel and front wheels are in the 
centered, straight-ahead direction to aid in aligning sector output shaft and 
pitman arm.

XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

the fluid.

and check the system for fluid leaks. Check fluid level and add fluid if 
necessary. 

 NOTE: In the following step do not hold the wheels against the stops for more

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Rotary Assist Cylinder

 Disassembly 

 WARNING: SOLVENTS ARE FLAMMABLE. BE EXTREMELY CAREFUL WHEN USING ANY SOLVENT. 
EVEN A SMALL EXPLOSION OR FIRE COULD CAUSE INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: WEAR EYE PROTECTION AND BE SURE TO COMPLY WITH OSHA OR OTHER MAXIMUM 
AIR PRESSURE REQUIREMENTS. 

 CAUTION: Never steam clean or high-pressure wash hydraulic steering components. 
Do not force or abuse closely fitted parts. 

 NOTE: Thoroughly clean and dry the rotary assist cylinder before disassembly. 
During disassembly of the rotary assist cylinder, clean all parts in clean, 
petroleum base solvent, and blow dry. Keep each part separate to avoid nicks 
and burrs.

Put the cylinder in a vise, clamping firmly against the housing 
mounting flange or boss. Rack piston bore should be horizontal; side cover and 
end cover are accessible for disassembly.

[FIGURE: G9420A.gif]

Place suitable container under gear, then unplug hydraulic ports.

[FIGURE: G9421A.gif]

Rotate the sector shaft until the timing mark on the end of the sector 
shaft is in line with the timing mark on the end of the housing. This will 
position the sector shaft for removal.

[FIGURE: G9422A.gif]

Remove and discard dirt and water seal from the housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G9423A.gif]

Remove any paint or corrosion from the exposed area of the sector 
shaft, using a fine grade emery cloth.

[FIGURE: G9424A.gif]

Tape the serrations and bolt groove of the sector shaft with one layer 
of masking tape. The tape should not extend onto the sector shaft bearing 
diameter.

[FIGURE: G9425A.gif]

Remove the sector shaft adjusting screw jam nut.

[FIGURE: G9426A.gif]

Remove the six special bolts from the side cover.

[FIGURE: G9427A.gif]

Remove the side cover and sector shaft assembly from the cylinder. 
Start the shaft and cover assembly removal by tapping the end of the shaft 
lightly with a soft mallet or wooden hammer handle.

[FIGURE: G9428A.gif]

Remove and discard the side cover gasket.

[FIGURE: G9429A.gif]

Remove and discard the vent plug.

[FIGURE: G9430A.gif]

Turn sector shaft adjusting screw clockwise through the side cover and 
pull the sector shaft out of the side cover.

[FIGURE: G9431A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not damage the bore or DU bushing when removing the seal. 

Clamp the side cover in a vise. Place a standard 5/8-inch or 
11/16-3/8-inch drive socket in the center of the side cover. Pry the seal out 
with a rolling head pry bar, using the socket for support. Discard the seal 
and remove the socket.

[FIGURE: G9432A.gif]

Inspect the sector shaft assembly for damaged adjusting screw threads. 
The retainer must be securely staked in place. The adjusting screw must rotate 
by hand with no perceptible end play (lash).

[FIGURE: G9433A.gif]

Mark the orientation of the end cover to the housing prior to removal 
of the end cover. Remove the four Torx® head end cover bolts 
and the end cover.

[FIGURE: G9434A.gif]

 CAUTION: The set position of poppet seat and sleeve assemblies must not be 
disturbed if the poppets are not going to be replaced or reset during 
disassembly. 

Remove the rack piston subassembly. Place the assembly on a clean cloth.

[FIGURE: G9435A.gif]

Remove and discard the end cover seal ring.

[FIGURE: G9436A.gif]

Cut and remove the Teflon® seal ring and O-ring from 
the rack piston.

[FIGURE: G9437A.gif]

 NOTE: TRW recommends that the poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies not 
be removed unless replacement of poppet components is required.

Push poppet stems. They should spring back. Push poppet seat. It should 
not move by hand. If components are bent or broken, poppet stems do not spring 
back or poppet seat moves by hand, proceed to Step 20. If poppet component 
replacement is not necessary, proceed to Step 29.

[FIGURE: G9438A.gif]

Place rack piston in a soft-jawed vise.

[FIGURE: G9439A.gif]

 NOTE: Poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies are retained by Loctite®
 applied to the threads, which makes the assemblies 
difficult to remove.

Slide service tool J36452 or equivalent over the seat of poppet 
adjuster seat and sleeve assembly and engage tool in the slots in the threaded 
sleeve. Hit the end of the tool firmly, four or five times with a 2-pound 
sledge hammer, to loosen the Loctite®.

[FIGURE: G9440A.gif]

With ratchet applied to the tool, turn one adjuster seat and sleeve 
assembly out of the rack piston. If the ratchet does not turn easily, strike 
adjuster removal tool again with a hammer. If the engaging tangs will not stay 
in place while tightening, it might be necessary to hold in place with an 
arbor press while applying loosening torque. Discard poppet seat and sleeve 
assembly.

[FIGURE: G9441A.gif]

Remove the two poppets, spring, spacer rod and push tube.

[FIGURE: G9442A.gif]

 NOTE: It is possible to reset one poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly 
for automatic poppet adjustment while it is in the rack piston, if one 
adjuster seat and sleeve assembly and poppets, spring, spacer rod and push 
tube are removed.

Remove and discard remaining poppet seat and sleeve assembly only if 
required.

[FIGURE: G9443A.gif]

If one poppet seat and sleeve assembly was left in rack piston, it can 
be reset for automatic poppet adjustment by inserting a 9.5-mm (3/8-inch) 
diameter x 152-mm (6-inch) drill rod down through the poppet seat hole at the 
opposite end of the rack piston and against the adjuster seat, to press the 
seat in until it bottoms against the adjuster sleeve.

[FIGURE: G9444A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not allow Loctite® or Locquic to get on the 
adjuster seat component of the adjuster seat and sleeve assembly. The poppets 
will not function properly. 

Carefully apply Locquic T primer or equivalent to the threads in poppet 
holes and threads on the new seat and sleeve assemblies. Allow to dry for 10 
minutes, then carefully apply Loctite® RC680 or equivalent 
to same threads.

[FIGURE: G9445A.gif]

 WARNING: WEAR EYE PROTECTION WHILE ASSEMBLING POPPETS. SPRING-LOADED POPPETS 
COULD EJECT AND CAUSE EYE INJURY. 

Place rack piston in a soft-jawed vise and turn one new poppet adjuster 
seat and sleeve assembly, with slotted end out, into the poppet hole in one 
end of rack piston.

[FIGURE: G9446A.gif]

From the other end of the poppet hole in the rack piston, install one 
poppet, poppet spring, nylon spacer rod, push tube, other poppet and the other 
new poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly. Tighten both poppet adjuster 
seat and sleeve assemblies to 25 Nm (18 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: G9447A.gif]

Remove the retaining ring that is closest to the output end of the 
housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G9448A.gif]

Remove and discard dirt seal.

[FIGURE: G9449A.gif]

Insert a screwdriver into housing bearing bore from the trunnion end 
and carefully push seal and spacer washer out of the other end of bearing bore 
without damaging the sealing area of the bore or the spacer washer. Discard 
the seal.

[FIGURE: G9450A.gif]

Inspect roller bearing in the housing for brinelling or spalling. 
Inspect retaining ring for damage. If replacement of either part is required, 
go to Step 33. If component replacement is not necessary, go to Step 37.

[FIGURE: G9451A.gif]

 CAUTION: The bearing must be pressed out from the side cover side to protect the 
seal counterbore. Be sure to use a bearing removal tool that will clear the 
retaining ring. 

If roller bearing in housing needs to be replaced, place the bearing 
removal end of the bearing and seal tool against the side cover end of the 
bearing and press it out of trunnion end of the bearing bore, using bearing 
press tool J37705 or equivalent for TAS40, J37071 or equivalent for TAS55 or 
TAS65, or J38779 or equivalent for the TAS85 steering gear. Discard bearing.

[FIGURE: G9452A.gif]

If the retaining ring that is still in the housing bore needs to be 
replaced, remove it through the trunnion end of the bearing bore, to protect 
the pressure seal bore area from being damaged.

[FIGURE: G9453A.gif]

Insert retaining ring, if it was removed, into the housing bore from 
the trunnion end, to protect sealing area. Make sure it

INSPECTION

Steering Gear

Inspect the rack piston teeth for cracks or obvious damage. If teeth 
are damaged, replace the rack piston and sector shaft.

[FIGURE: G9479A.gif]

Inspect the housing cylinder bore. Some scoring marks are normal. If 
there was internal leakage greater than 1 gallon per minute, make sure there 
are no damaged seals before replacing the housing.

[FIGURE: G9480A.gif]

Inspect the housing faces for nicks that would prevent proper sealing. 
Replace the gear housing if these nicks are present and cannot be easily 
removed with a fine-tooth flat file without changing the dimensional 
characteristics, or if depressions are located in a seal area.

[FIGURE: G9481A.gif]

Inspect side cover DU bushing for damage. Also check side cover bushing 
to sector shaft clearance. If damage exists or if clearance exceeds 0.20 mm 
(0.008 inch), replace side cover bushing assembly.

[FIGURE: G9482A.gif]

 NOTE: A service sector shaft will come assembled with the adjusting screw and 
retainer.

Inspect the sector shaft bearing and sealing areas and sector teeth 
contact surfaces for brinelling, spalling or cracks. Run your fingernail edge 
across these areas to detect steps. Remove masking tape from the shaft and 
inspect for twisted or otherwise damaged serrations. If any of these 
conditions exist, replace the sector shaft.

[FIGURE: G9483A.gif]

ADJUSTMENTS

Steering Gear

To center the steering gear, rotate sector shaft until the timing mark 
on the end of the sector shaft is in line with the timing mark on the end of 
housing trunnion.

Tighten side cover adjusting screw to 7-13 Nm (62-115 
lb-in), then back out the screw one-half turn. 

Check the torque to rotate sector shaft through approximately 20 
degrees each side of center.

Screw in the adjusting screw to provide a torque rise of 4.5-9 Nm
 (40-80 lb-in) over the previously established torque as 
the sector shaft passes through center.

 NOTE: Torque to rotate the sector shaft must not exceed 41 Nm
 (30 lb-ft) at any point in travel of cylinder.

Tighten jam nut to 54-61 Nm (40-45 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering Column 

L-Series can be equipped with one of two types of steering column 
assemblies. The fixed column is standard equipment. The tilt/telescopic 
adjustable column is optional. Refer to Section 11-04B .

The steering column assembly attaches to an intermediate shaft which 
connects to the steering gear on all L-Series (except LL and LTL). The LL- and 
LTL-9000 use an assembly consisting of the column, an intermediate shaft and a 
lower steering shaft.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Steering Column Shaft and Joint 

 Disassembly 

Cut the boot retainer strap and remove the boot from the joint. 

Bend the lock tabs that retain the six hex screws attaching the upper 
shaft to the joint. Remove the six screws and separate the shaft from the 
joint. 

Remove the cotter pin and castellated nut that retain the stub shaft in 
the joint inner race. 

 CAUTION: No further disassembly should be done on this joint. The inner race, 
ball bearings and outer race are not to be disassembled. 

Remove the stub shaft, being careful not to drop the ball bearings by 
turning the inner race relative to the outer race.

[FIGURE: G38551A.gif]

 Assembly 

Insert the stub shaft in the joint inner race. Install the castellated 
nut and tighten to 28-42 Nm (21-31 lb-ft). If necessary, 
advance the nut to the next castellation while rotating the shaft and install 
the cotter pin. 

Lubricate the joint with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. 

Attach the shaft to the joint using the six hex screws. Tighten the 
screws to 11-16 Nm (8-12 lb-ft) and bend the lock tabs along 
a flat of each screw. 

Install the rubber boot and attach securely using a new boot retainer 
strap.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Steering Shaft, Intermediate 

The intermediate steering shaft must be removed from the vehicle for 
servicing. Normally the shaft will only require servicing if the coupling 
assembly has excessive lash or doesn't telescope in and out under normal 
operation. 

This shaft on L-Series is a coupling assembly with a splined shaft 
telescoping into a reduced tube.

specification ESA-M1C75-B. 

Insert the shaft in the tube and stroke. It should stroke freely at a 
maximum pull load of 67 N (15 lbs.) at room temperature. If the load exceeds 
this specification, replace the required parts.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Steering Shaft, Lower, LL-LTL-9000 

 Removal 

Remove the bolt from the lower steering to intermediate shaft U-joint. 
Disconnect the shafts. 

Remove the bolt at the lower steering shaft and steering gear U-joint. 
Disconnect the shaft and remove the spacer. 

Remove the setscrews on the lower steering shaft at the bearing

 Installation

the spacer. 

Connect the lower steering shaft to the steering gear. Install and

the bolts to 68-95 Nm (50-70 lb-ft). 

Pull on the lower steering shaft to position the bearing against the 
spacer. There should be a slight gap between the bearing and the weld bead on 
the shaft. Install and tighten the setscrews in the lower steering shaft at 
the bearing assembly.

Section 11-04B: Steering Column, Tilt/Telescopic

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Steering Column Lower Yoke

 Removal 

Remove nut(s), washer(s) and bolt(s) and slide intermediate shaft 
upward. 

Remove lower yoke (universal joint). 

 Installation 

 NOTE: The serration pattern in the upper yoke is different from the pattern 
in the lower yoke. When installing the universal joint assembly, make sure the 
yoke serrations match the serrations in the mating shaft. 

Install the lower yoke (universal joint) on the steering gear input 
shaft or spacer shaft, if so equipped. Slide the intermediate shaft onto the 
lower yoke (universal joint). 

Install the bolt(s), washer(s) and nut(s), making sure the bolt(s) 
align with the whistle notch(es) in the shaft(s). 

Tighten the nut(s) and bolt(s) to 68-95 Nm (50-70 
lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Adjustable Column Bracket 

 Removal 

Remove the steering column. 

With an assistant, remove the adjustable column bracket retaining bolts 
and remove the bracket. 

 Installation 

Position the adjustable column bracket in the vehicle. Install and 
tighten the bolts to 42-57 Nm (31-42 lb-ft). 

Install the steering column.

Bearings

Remove retaining ring from large diameter of wheel tube and sleeve only 
if replacement is required. Press the bearings and bearing spacer off the 
wheel tube and splined sleeve assembly using suitable tubular bearing removal 
tool. Remove retaining ring from wheel tube. Discard retaining ring from wheel 
tube. Discard bearings and retaining ring.

self-tapping screws using a 5/16-inch hex socket. Remove stop cover and two 
travel stop pins from main housing assembly. Note the letters of the holes 
with stop pins as they are removed.

[FIGURE: G7213D.gif]

[FIGURE: G7214B.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not exceed 500°F or material hardness may be 
affected. 

 NOTE: Applying heat to support bracket attaching nuts with electric heat gun 
or 1000 watt hair dryer will facilitate removal of setscrews and pivot screws 
that were coated with Loctite® at assembly. Using the proper 
size thread chaser, as well as a suitable solvent, on setscrews, pivot screws 
and support bracket nuts, will aid in Loctite® removal. 

Using a 3/32-inch Allen wrench, remove setscrews from the two support 
bracket nuts. Remove the two pivot screws from main housing assembly using a 
5/16-inch Allen wrench. Remove support bracket from main housing assembly. 
Clean off the Loctite® applied to the threads in the nuts 
that are an integral part of the support bracket, the pivot screws and 
setscrews.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Steering Column Shaft and Joint 

 Disassembly 

Cut boot retainer strap and remove boot from joint. 

Bend lock tabs that retain six hex screws attaching upper shaft to 
joint. Remove six screws and separate shaft from joint. 

Remove cotter pin and castellated nut that retain stub shaft in joint 
inner race. 

 CAUTION: No further disassembly should be done on this joint. The inner race, 
ball bearings and outer race are not to be disassembled. 

Remove the stub shaft, being careful not to drop the ball bearings by 
turning the inner race relative to the outer race.

 Assembly 

Insert the stub shaft in joint inner race. Install castellated nut and 
tighten to 18-24 Nm (13-18 lb-ft). If necessary, advance the 
nut to the next castellation and install the cotter pin. 

Lubricate the joint with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or 
-K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. 

Attach shaft to joint using six hex screws. Tighten screws to 11-16 Nm
 (8-12 lb-ft) and bend the lock tabs along a flat of each 
screw. 

Install rubber boot and attach securely using a new boot retainer strap.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Steering Shaft, Intermediate 

The intermediate steering shaft must be removed from the vehicle for 
servicing. Normally the shaft will only require servicing if the coupling 
assembly has excessive lash or doesn't telescope in and out under normal 
operation. 

This shaft on L-Series vehicles is a coupling assembly with a splined 
shaft telescoping into a reduced tube. 

 Disassembly 

Remove stop bolt from end of splined shaft. 

Pull shaft completely out of tube. 

Thoroughly clean shaft and tube assembly with a nonabrasive solution. 

Inspect all parts for excessive wear and replace if necessary. 

 Assembly 

Repack splined shaft and inside surface of reduced end of tube with 
Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1C75-B. 

Insert shaft in tube and stroke. It should stroke freely at a maximum 
pull load of 44 N (10 lb). If load exceeds this specification, replace 
required parts.

 Intermediate Steering Shaft

ADJUSTMENTS

Adjustment for Elimination of Torsional Free Play of Tilt/Telescopic 
Columns

Refer to the following flowchart for the preferred method for 
performing this adjustment. An alternate method, which is referred to in the 
flowchart, follows.

 Preferred Method 

[FIGURE: G9485A.gif]

 Alternate Method 

Park vehicle with wheels straight ahead to make steering wheel 
alignment easier for reinstallation.

 WARNING: DISCONNECT THE BATTERY PRIOR TO REMOVING ANY IGNITION ASSEMBLY AND 
CABLES FROM THE COLUMN. FAILURE TO DO THIS COULD CAUSE ELECTRICAL SHOCK OR 
FIRE WHEN IGNITION ASSEMBLY IS REMOVED. 

Disconnect battery power.

Remove steering column.

Place column in a vise by clamping on one support bracket flange. Make 
sure the column is in the full up position (tilted up). Unhook the tilt 
springs from the housing without damaging the springs. Remove upper spring 
cover.

 CAUTION: The lower bearing housing and universal joint may eject under spring 
tension during this step. Hold the lower bearing housing firmly while 
releasing the bolt. 

Make sure the column is in the full extended position. Remove the bolts 
from the support bracket and the lower housing. On reinstallation the bolts 
must go back in the same locations.

Remove the lower bearing housing. U-joint assembly and spring from the 
main housing.

[FIGURE: G7206D.gif]

Remove pipe plug from slotted end of the universal joint a 3/16-inch 
Allen wrench if possible. If the pipe plug is stripped, remove with Ezy-Out®
. Discard the pipe plug.

 NOTE: If the pipe plug is tightened so the end of the universal joint is 
spread open, the shaft may not assemble into the splined sleeve correctly.

Place the new 1/4-inch drive pipe plug in tapped hole in the slotted 
end of the universal joint. Screw in to make sure threads are engaged. 
Adjustment will be made later.

 NOTE: Do not damage the serrations, threads or taper on the end of the wheel 
shaft.

Using a steering wheel as a holding fixture, place the main housing 
assembly (wheel tube end down) vertically into the steering wheel.

Note the design of the splined sleeve. Use a marker to highlight two 
separate places:

the large spaces in the sleeve, and

the shaft of the U-joint assembly beginning at one of the slots in the 
splined end and continuing 51 mm (2 inches) up the shaft. This will make 
installation easier.

Place the telescope spring inside the jacket tube in main housing.

[FIGURE: G7223C.gif]

Put clean grease on U-joint splines. Hold the lower bearing housing 
while feeding the splined end of the U-joint into the splined sleeve with 
marks aligned. Compress the telescope spring by pushing the lower bearing 
housing into position. Do not trap the tilt springs. Align the bolts in the 
support bracket with holes in the main housing assembly.

Tighten the support bracket bolts while holding the U-joint and lower 
housing in place. Tighten to 34-47 Nm (25-35 lb-ft).

Assemble the upper spring cover over the two tilt springs, then hook 
the loose ends of the springs in the holes in the main housing.

[FIGURE: G7201C.gif]

Push the column to the full forward position. Use the hex wrench to 
screw in the pipe plug until it is as tight as possible by hand. Final 
adjustment will be made when column is installed in vehicle.

[FIGURE: G72291B.gif]

 NOTE: The pinch bolt must pass through the whistle notch on the serrated end 
of the U-joint for proper alignment.

To adjust pipe plug tighten plug only enough to lock the telescope 
function then back off plug 1/8 turn and retest telescope function. Telescope 
should function with minor assistance. If not, back off plug 1/8 turn again to 
regain telescope function.

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Heat Transfer

This section gives the basic principles and service procedures that 
apply to all air conditioning systems.

Air conditioning is the cooling or refrigeration of the air in the 
passenger compartment. Refrigeration is accomplished by making practical use 
of three laws of nature. These laws and their practical application are 
described in the following paragraphs. A basic air conditioning system is 
shown in the illustration.

 Air Conditioning System, Typical 

[FIGURE: K22586B.gif]

Tighten to 12-14 Nm (9-10 Lb-Ft)

If two substances of different temperature are placed near each other, 
the heat in the warmer substance will always travel to the colder substance 
until both are of equal temperature. For example, a block of ice in an ice box 
does not communicate its coldness to the bottle of milk standing nearby. 
Rather, the heat in the warm milk automatically flows into the ice.

To determine the amount of heat that transfers from one substance to 
another, science uses the British thermal unit or BTU. One BTU is the amount 
of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of water 0.55°
C (1°F). For example, to raise the 
temperature of one pound of water from 0°C to 100°
C (32°F to 212°F), one BTU 
of heat must be added for every 0.55°C (1°F) 
rise in temperature or a total of 180 BTUs of heat. Conversely, in order to 
lower the temperature of one pound of water from 100°C to 0°
C (212°F to 32°F), 180 
BTUs of heat must be removed from the water.

================================================================================
PAGE 5556
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Latent Heat of Vaporization

When a liquid boils (changes to a gas) it absorbs heat without raising 
the temperature of the resulting gas. When the gas condenses (changes back to 
a liquid), it gives off heat without lowering the temperature of the resulting 
liquid.

For example, place one pound of water at 0°C (32°
F) in a container over a flame. With each BTU of heat that 
the water absorbs from the flame, its temperature rises 0.55°
C (1°F). Thus, after it has absorbed 180 BTUs of heat, the 
water reaches a temperature of 100°C (212°
F). Even though the flame continues to give its heat to the water, the 
temperature of the water remains at 100°C (212°
F). The water, however, starts to boil or change from the 
liquid to the gaseous state. It continues to boil until the water has passed 
off into the atmosphere as vapor. If this vapor were checked with a 
thermometer, it also would show a temperature of 100°C (212°
F). In other words, there was a rise of only 100°
C (212°F) (from 0°C to 100°
C or 32°F to 212°F) in the 
water and vapor temperature even though the flame applied many more than 180 
BTUs of heat. In this case, the heat is absorbed by the liquid in the process 
of boiling and disappears in the vapor. If the vapor were brought in contact 
with cool air, the hidden heat would flow into the cooler air as the vapor 
condensed back to water. Scientists refer to this natural law as the latent 
(hidden) heat of vaporization.

Water has a latent heat of vaporization of 970 BTUs and a boiling point 
of 100°C (212°F). This means that one pound 
of water at 100°C (212°F), will absorb 970 
BTUs of heat in changing to vapor at 100°C (212°
F). Conversely, the vapor will give off 970 BTUs of heat in 
condensing back to water at 100°C (212°F).

This tremendous heat transfer, occurring when a liquid boils or a vapor 
condenses, forms the basic principle of all conventional refrigeration systems.

For a liquid to be a refrigerant, it must also have a low boiling 
point. That is, the temperature at which it boils must be lower than the 
substance to be cooled.

R-134a is a non-CFC refrigerant used in the L-Series vehicles. Its 
temperature/pressure relationship makes it suitable for mobile air 
conditioning systems.

================================================================================
PAGE 5557
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Effect of Pressure on Boiling or Condensation

As refrigerant passes through an air conditioning system, it flows 
under high-pressure conditions, first as a high-pressure vapor between the 
compressor and A/C condenser core, then, as a high-pressure liquid between the 
A/C condenser core and the A/C evaporator core orifice. It expands to a 
low-pressure vapor between the A/C evaporator core orifice and the refrigerant 
return port in the compressor. As pressures in the closed refrigerant circuit 
vary, temperatures will also vary. As pressures increase, temperatures also 
increase; as they ecrease, temperatures also decrease.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety Precautions

 CAUTION: It is extremely important to determine which type of air conditioning 
system a vehicle has before servicing the air conditioning system. Usingg R-12 
components and refrigerant on R-134a systems will cause damage to A/C 
components. 

 CAUTION: A number of manufacturers are producing refrigerant products that are 
described as being direct replacements for refrigerant R-134a. The use of any 
unauthorized substitute refrigerant can severely damage air conditioning 
components.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Precautions

Observe the following service precautions:

Never open or loosen a connection before discharging the system.

When loosening a connection, if any residual pressure is evident, allow 
it to leak off before opening the fitting.

Evacuate a system that has been opened to replace a component or one 
that has discharged through leakage before charging.

Seal open fittings with a cap or plug immediately after disconnecting a 
component from the system.

Clean the outside of the fittings thoroughly before disconnecting a 
component from the system.

Do not remove the sealing caps from a replacement component until ready 
to install.

Refrigerant oil will absorb moisture from the atmosphere if left 
uncapped. Do not open an oil container until ready to use and install the cap 
immediately after using. Store the oil only in a clean, moisture-free container.

Install a new O-ring before connecting an open fitting. Coat the 
fitting and O-ring with refrigerant oil before connecting.

When installing a refrigerant line, avoid sharp bends. Position the 
line away from the exhaust or any sharp edges which may chafe the line.

Tighten fittings only to specifications. The steel and aluminum 
fittings used in the refrigeration system will not tolerate overtightening.

When disconnecting a fitting, use a wrench on both halves of the 
fitting to prevent twisting of the refrigerant lines or tubes.

Do not open a refrigerant system or uncap a replacement component 
unless it is as close as possible to room temperature. This will prevent 
condensation from forming inside a component that is cooler than the 
surrounding air.

Keep service tools and the work area clean to avoid contamination of 
the refrigerant system.

Suction Accumulator/Drier (Low-Pressure Vapor)

During stabilized conditions (air conditioning system shutdown), 
refrigerant system pressures are equalized on both the high- and low-pressure 
sides of the system.

When the heater blower motor is on and the function selector lever is 
in any air conditioner position, the A/C compressor clutch field coil is 
energized and the clutch plate is pulled into contact with the compressor 
clutch pulley. The clutch plate and hub assembly then rotates the compressor 
shaft.

When the compressor shaft is rotated, the pistons are alternately moved 
back and forth with respect to their cylinder bores. As each piston is pulled 
through its cylinder bore, the pressure in the cylinder suddenly reduces to a 
pressure (or vacuum) considerably lower than the refrigerant system. The 
higher refrigerant system vapor pressure overcomes the suction reed valve 
spring pressure, forcing itself through the reed valve and into the lower 
pressure (or vacuum) area inside the compressor cylinder. The spring pressure 
on the reed valve closes the valve when the refrigerant system suction vapor 
pressure and the compressor cylinder vapor pressure are equalized.

As each piston is forced into its respective cylinder bore, the 
refrigerant vapors from the suction side of the refrigerant system are 
compressed into a decreasingly smaller area, thus increasing the refrigerant 
vapor pressure and also raising the refrigerant vapor temperature. The higher 
refrigerant vapor pressure now assists in sealing the suction reed valve 
closed and also opens the discharge (high-pressure) reed valve as the cylinder 
pressure exceeds the higher pressure side of the refrigerant system. When the 
compressed higher pressure and temperature refrigerant vapor is discharged 
into the high-pressure side of the refrigerant system, the discharge reed 
valve spring pressure and the high side refrigerant pressure closes and seals 
the reed valve, thus preventing the discharge gas from entering the compressor 
cylinder. The compressor's refrigerant vapor compression cylinder then begins 
again.

The high-pressure and high-temperature compressor discharge refrigerant 
gas is released into the top of the A/C condenser core, via the compressor's 
discharge hose. The A/C condenser core, being close to ambient temperature, 
causes the refrigerant vapor to condense into a liquid when heat is removed 
from the refrigerant by ambient air passing over the fins and tubing.

Liquid refrigerant from the A/C condenser core exits from the bottom of 
the A/C condenser core and enters the condenser to evaporator tube and then 
the inlet side of the A/C evaporator core orifice located in the inlet tube. 
The inlet filter screen of the A/C evaporator core orifice removes coarse 
contaminant particulates, which may be present in the liquid refrigerant, 
before the liquid refrigerant enters the calibrated opening of the A/C 
evaporator core orifice. The outlet end of the A/C evaporator core orifice has 
a fine mesh filter with four open side slots in the body of the A/C evaporator 
core orifice, upstream from the filter. This filter removes fine contaminants 
and causes some of the refrigerant to exit through the non-filtered side 
slots. The side slots and filter act as a refrigerant flow noise suppressor.

Pressure in the A/C evaporator core is reduced as a result of air 
conditioner compressor suction. As the pressure is lowered and the condenser 
to evaporator tube pressure increases, the liquid refrigerant passes through 
the A/C evaporator core orifice and enters the A/C evaporator core at a low 
pressure and as a cold liquid. As airflow passes over the plate/fin sections 
of the A/C evaporator core, the refrigerant inside absorbs the heat and 
changes into a vapor.

Compressor suction draws the vaporized refrigerant and oil mixture into 
the suction accumulator/drier where the heavier oil-laden vapors fall to the 
bottom and the lighter vapors and oil mixture continue their path to the 
compressor via the top of the vapor return tube. A desiccant bag, located 
inside the suction accumulator/drier, absorbs and retains moisture that may be 
circulating in the refrigerant system. The heavier oil-laden refrigerant also 
returns to the compressor through a small liquid bleed hole near the bottom of 
the vapor return tube. The liquid bleed hole provides a controlled second 
opportunity for the accumulated refrigerant and oil mixture to revaporize as 
it passes through the opening to re-enter into the main vapor flow path to the 
suction side of the compressor.

 Refrigerant Systems 

The refrigerant R-134a is a hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant. R-134a is 
non-corrosive, non-explosive, non-flammable and has a slight ether-type odor. 
R-134a is heavier than air. Although it is classified as a safe refrigerant, 
certain precautions must be observed to protect the parts involved and the 
person working on the unit.

To help identify whether or not your vehicle is equipped with R-134a, 
look for the yellow R-134a tag located near the high and low side charge ports.

[FIGURE: K22587A.gif]

If a component has been used with R-12, it cannot be used again in an 
R-134a system. If used in an R-134a system, it cannot be put into an R-12 
system. Contamination can occur and performance can be adversely affected 
because each system uses a different oil designed for that system.

 WARNING: AVOID BREATHING A/C REFRIGERANT AND LUBRICANT VAPOR OR MIST. IF 
ACCIDENTAL SYSTEM DISCHARGE OCCURS, VENTILATE THE WORK AREA BEFORE RESUMING 
SERVICE. LIQUID R-134A, AT NORMAL ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURES AND TEMPERATURES, 
EVAPORATES SO QUICKLY THAT IT HAS THE TENDENCY TO FREEZE ANYTHING IT CONTACTS. 
FOR THIS REASON, EXTREME CARE MUST BE TAKEN TO PREVENT ANY LIQUID REFRIGERANT 
FROM COMING IN CONTACT WITH THE SKIN AND ESPECIALLY THE EYES. 

 WARNING: WEAR NON-POROUS GLOVES AND SAFETY GOGGLES AT ALL TIMES WHEN HANDLING 
LIQUID REFRIGERANT. SHOULD ANY LIQUID REFRIGERANT GET INTO THE EYES OR ON THE 
SKIN, IMMEDIATELY FLUSH EYES AND SKIN WITH PLENTY OF WATER FOR AT LEAST 15 
MINUTES. REMOVE CONTAMINATED CLOTHING AND SHOES. CALL A PHYSICIAN. 

 WARNING: REFRIGERANT R-134A IS ALWAYS UNDER PRESSURE. BECAUSE THE SYSTEM IS 
TIGHTLY SEALED, HEAT APPLIED TO ANY PART CAN CAUSE THIS PRESSURE TO BUILD UP 
EXCESSIVELY. TO AVOID A DANGEROUS EXPLOSION, KEEP AWAY FROM OPEN FLAMES, 
GLOWING METAL SURFACES, BLOW TORCHES, STEAM CLEANING AND WELDING. R-134A CAN 
BE DECOMPOSED AT HIGH TEMPERATURES. MAKE SURE THAT CONTAINERS ARE NEVER HEATED 
TO OVER 52°C (125°F). CONTAINERS MUST BE 
STORED AND INSTALLED IN ACCORDANCE WITH ALL STATE AND LOCAL ORDINANCES. 

 CAUTION: Use only R-134a refrigerant. Due to environmental concerns, when the 
air conditioning system is drained, the refrigerant must be collected using 
refrigerant recovery/recycling equipment. R-134a must never be removed without 
the appropriate equipment or released into the atmosphere. Use of a recovery 
machine dedicated for R-134a is necessary to reduce the possibility of oil and 
refrigerant incompatibility concerns. Refer to the instructions provided by 
the equipment manufacturer when removing refrigerant from or charging the air 
conditioning system. 

 CAUTION: When admitting R-134a into the refrigerant system, always keep the tank 
in an upright position. If the tank is on its side or upside down, liquid 
R-134a will enter the system and can damage the compressor. Refrigerant R-134a 
must not be mixed with air for leak testing or used with air for any other 
purpose above atmospheric pressure. R-134a is combustible when mixed with high 
concentrations of air and higher pressures. 

 CAUTION: A number of manufacturers are producing refrigerant products which are 
described as being direct replacements for R-134a. The use of any unauthorized 
substitute refrigerant can severely damage the A/C components. If service is 
required, use only NEW or RECYCLED R-134a.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Compressor and A/C Clutch Assemblies

When the vehicle is running and the function selector is in an A/C 
mode, the A/C clutch is energized when the A/C cycling switch, located on the 
suction accumulator-drier, closes. The closing of the A/C cycling switch 
completes the circuit to the A/C clutch and draws it into engagement with the 
compressor drive shaft.

The pressure acting on the A/C cycling switch and the ambient 
temperature existing at the temperature sensor combine their effect to control 
the A/C clutch. When both pressure and temperature are within specifications 
and the function control knob and temperature control lever is set at MAX A/C, 
NORM A/C, or either of the settings calling for full or partial defroster 
operation, the compressor will be operating. (Compressor operation during 
defrost is provided to minimize humidity in the passenger compartment). The 
compressor is mounted on the engine and is driven by a drive belt. Tension 
adjustment is obtained by moving the compressor braces away from the engine.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Refrigerant System Protection

 A/C Compressor Pressure Relief Valve 

Under extreme pressure conditions, the A/C compressor pressure relief 
valve will momentarily open, allowing refrigerant vapor to escape. This 
relieves excessive pressure that might damage the compressor. The valve closes 
as soon as pressure is lower than the relief setting. This prevents loss of 
the complete refrigerant charge. The A/C compressor pressure relief valve is 
located in the A/C manifold and tube at the rear of the compressor.

 A/C Pressure Cutoff Switch 

 Single Function 

The A/C pressure cutoff switch is used on R-134a systems.

A refrigerant containment switch is used with air conditioning to 
interrupt A/C compressor operation in the event of high system discharge 
pressures which could result in the loss of refrigerant charge. The switch is 
located in the discharge line between the compressor and the A/C condenser 
core. The switch is sensitive to the discharge pressure and functions to 
interrupt the A/C compressor operation if the discharge pressure exceeds a 
setting of 2751-3068 kPa (399-445 psi).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Condenser Core

The A/C condenser core is located in front of the radiator. The A/C 
condenser core receives compressed (therefore heated) refrigerant gas from the 
compressor.

As the hot refrigerant gas flows through the A/C condenser core, it is 
cooled by air passing over the fins. The cooled, compressed refrigerant gas 
condenses to liquid refrigerant, which flows directly to the A/C evaporator 
core through the A/C evaporator core orifice in the inlet.

================================================================================
PAGE 5564
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Evaporator Core Orifice 

The A/C evaporator core orifice is a restriction between the high- and 
low-pressure refrigerant and meters the flow of liquid refrigerant into the 
A/C evaporator core.

The A/C evaporator core orifice is located in the inlet tube to the 
evaporator and has filter screens on the inlet and outlet ends of the tube 
body. The inlet filter screen acts as a strainer for the liquid refrigerant 
flowing through the opening. The outlet screen acts to reduce the noise of the 
refrigerant flowing through the orifice tube. O-rings on the tube body prevent 
the high pressure liquid refrigerant from bypassing the A/C evaporator core 
orifice. Adjustment or repairs cannot be made to the A/C evaporator core 
orifice and it must be replaced as a unit.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Evaporator Core

The A/C evaporator core is a multi-pass plate/fin aluminum core. The 
condenser to evaporator tube (inlet) connects to the bottom of the A/C 
evaporator core and the suction accumulator/drier (outlet) connects to the top 
of the A/C evaporator core. The outlet of the accumulator/drier then connects 
to the evaporator to compressor suction line. The condenser to evaporator tube 
is fitted with an A/C evaporator core orifice to control refrigerant flow. 
This A/C evaporator core orifice can be removed from the A/C evaporator core 
orifice tube for replacement if it becomes necessary. However, a special tool 
is necessary to prevent breakage of the A/C evaporator core orifice.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Refrigerant Containment Switch

A refrigerant containment switch is used with air conditioning to 
interrupt A/C compressor operation in the event of high system discharge 
pressures which could result in the loss of refrigerant charge. The switch is 
located in the discharge line between the A/C compressor and the A/C condenser 
core. This switch is sensitive to the discharge pressure and functions to 
interrupt the A/C compressor operation if the discharge pressure exceeds a 
setting of 2751-3068 kPa (399-445 psi). This switch is serviced as part of the 
A/C compressor to condenser discharge line only.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suction Accumulator/Drier

The suction accumulator/drier is mounted on the side of the A/C 
evaporator core and attaches directly to the outlet tube. A suction service 
access gauge port valve is mounted on the accumulator/drier. Its purpose is to 
provide service access to the suction side of the refrigerant system for 
pressure readings, system diagnosis, and system charging. An inverted liquid 
diverter cup is mounted internally on top of the refrigerant vapor return 
tube, in the center of the suction accumulator/drier. Its purpose is to 
prevent the heavier, oil-laden liquid refrigerant from going directly into the 
evaporator to compressor suction line. Upon entering the inlet of the suction 
accumulator/drier, the heavier, oil-laden refrigerant contacts the liquid 
diverter cup, which serves as an umbrella, and drips down onto the bottom of 
the housing. A small-diameter aspirator tube, with approximately 3.34 mm 
(0.1315 inch) inside diameter, is placed close to the bottom of the 
accumulator at one end and to the top of the vapor return tube at the other 
end. It allows the accumulated heavier liquid refrigerant and oil mixture to 
re-enter the evaporator to compressor suction line at a controlled rate. As 
the mixture passes through the aspirator tube, it has a second opportunity to 
vaporize and circulate through the compressor without causing compressor 
damage due to slugging. A fine mesh-screened filter fits tightly around the 
bottom of the aspirator tube to filter refrigerant contaminants which may be 
in the system and prevent them from plugging the aspirator tube.

A desiccant bag is mounted inside the suction accumulator/drier tank 
assembly to absorb any moisture which may be in the refrigerant system.

Another fitting, on the suction accumulator/drier, is used to mount the 
A/C cycling switch. It has a long-travel valve stem core installed in the 
fitting opening to prevent refrigerant loss when the A/C cycling switch is 
removed.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Cycling Switch

As described previously under A/C Compressor and A/C Clutch Assemblies, 
the A/C cycling switch is mounted on a valve type fitting on the suction 
accumulator/drier assembly. A valve depressor, located inside the threaded end 
of the A/C cycling switch, depresses the valve stem as the switch is mounted 
and allows the suction pressure inside the suction accumulator/drier housing 
to control the operation. The electrical contacts are normally open when the 
suction pressure is at or below 152 kPa (22 psi); they will close when the 
suction pressure rises to approximately 276-324 kPa (40-47 psi) or above. 
Lower ambient temperatures (below 10°C or 50°
F), during cold weather seasons, will also open the contacts due to the 
pressure/temperature relationship of the refrigerant in the system. The 
electrical contacts control the circuit to the A/C compressor clutch field 
coil. When the contacts are closed, the A/C compressor clutch field coil is 
energized and the A/C clutch is engaged to drive the compressor. When the 
contacts are open, the A/C compressor clutch field coil is de-energized, the 
A/C clutch is disengaged and the compressor does not operate. The A/C cycling 
switch, when functioning properly, will control the pressure in the A/C 
evaporator core at a point where the plate/fin surface temperature will be 
maintained slightly above freezing, which prevents icing and the blockage of 
airflow.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Special Service Equipment

In order to minimize the discharge of ozone depleting 
chlorofluorocarbons into the atmosphere, the Ford Motor Co. supports the 
efficient usage, recovery, and recycling of R-134a used in vehicle air 
conditioners. Ford Motor Co. recommends the use of U.L. approved 
recycling/charging equipment such as:

Rotunda R-134a Manifold Gauge Set 176-R032A or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Low-Side Quick Disconnect 176-R0036 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a High-Side Quick Disconnect 176-R0037 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a A/C Service Center 176-00001 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Automatic Calibration Halogen Leak Detector 023-R1000 or 
equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Vacuum Pump (1.5 CFM) 176-R0126 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Vacuum Pump (3.0 CFM) 176-R0034 or equivalent.

This equipment should be used during any air conditioning system repair 
and recharge procedure that requires the air conditioning system to be 
discharged.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Climate Control System

 Inspection and Verification 

It is possible to detect problem causes by a careful visual inspection 
of the air conditioner refrigerant system. This includes broken drive belt, 
obstructed air passages, a loose A/C clutch, loose or broken mounting 
brackets, disconnected or broken wires and many refrigerant leaks.

A refrigerant leak will usually appear as an oily residue at the 
leakage point in the system. The oily residue soon picks up dust or dirt 
particles from the surrounding air and appears greasy. Through time, this will 
build up and appear to be a heavy, dirt-impregnated grease.

Most common leaks are caused by damaged or missing O-ring seals at the 
various hose and component connections. When these O-rings are replaced, 
lubricate the new O-rings with refrigerant oil. Be careful to keep shop towel 
lint from contaminating the internal surfaces of the connection. Leakage may 
occur at a coupling if the wrong O-rings are used at the coupling. Use only 
the O-rings listed in the Ford Master Parts Catalog for the coupling.

If the system contains no refrigerant or is extremely low on 
refrigerant, the A/C clutch will not engage for compressor operation. A rapid 
cycling A/C clutch is usually an indication that the system is low on 
refrigerant. Also, cycling will normally not occur when the engine is 
operating at curb idle speed.

Prior to diagnosis and testing, make sure the battery is fully charged 
and that sufficient coolant is present in the heating system.

Various tests to check heater system operations are included in this 
section. In addition to these tests, visual inspection of all heater system 
components including fuses and connections can be made to make sure the system 
is operating properly.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Refrigerant System Tests 

Poor air conditioning system performance can be caused by a plugged A/C 
evaporator core. Airflow is restricted. 

This condition can be detected by checking the center register 
discharge temperature. An abnormally low temperature indicates air is spending 
more time in the A/C evaporator core and is very cold when discharged, 
although the airflow volume is not enough to cool the vehicle properly.

Additional cause components are listed at the bottom of the Refrigerant 
System Pressure and Cycle Timing Evaluation Chart for poor compressor 
operation or a damaged compressor condition.

These diagnosis charts provide the most direct and sure way to 
determine the cause of any condition in a poorly performing refrigerant system.

After servicing and correcting a refrigerant system concern, take 
additional pressure readings and observe the cycle rate while meeting the 
conditional requirements to be sure the concern has been corrected.

To diagnose a condition in the refrigerant system, note the system 
pressure (shown by the gauges) and the clutch cycle rate. Then compare 
readings with the charts.

The system pressures are low (compressor suction) and high (compressor 
discharge).

A cycle is the time the A/C clutch is engaged plus the time it is 
disengaged (time on plus time off).

Cycle times are the lengths of time (in seconds) that the A/C clutch is 
on or off.

To achieve accurate diagnosis results in the least amount of time, use 
the following procedure and refer to the charts.

 NOTE: The test conditions specified at the top of each of the following 
charts must be met to obtain accurate test results.

Connect a gauge set to the system.

When system has stabilized, record high and low pressures as shown by 
gauges.

Determine cycle rate per minute (ON time plus OFF time is a cycle).

Record OFF time in seconds.

Record ON time in seconds.

Note center register discharge temperature.

Determine and record ambient temperature.

Compare test readings and appropriate chart.

Plot a vertical line for recorded ambient temperature from scale at 
bottom of each chart to top of chart.

Plot a horizontal line for other test readings from scale at left side 
of appropriate chart.

If the point where the two lines cross on each chart falls within the 
dark band, the system is operating normally. If the lines cross outside the 
dark band on one or more of the charts, there is a condition and the specific 
cause must be determined. Refer to the Refrigerant System Pressure and Clutch 
Cycle Timing Evaluation Chart.

 NOTE: The following five system operating conditions are indicated by where 
the lines cross on the chart:

System high (discharge) — pressure is high, low or 
normal.

System low (suction) — pressure is high, low or normal.

Cycle rate is fast, slow or A/C clutch runs continuously.

ON time is long or short.

OFF time is long or short.

Match these conditions to the conditions shown in the five columns 
toward the left in the System Pressure and Cycle Timing Evaluation Charts. All 
five system conditions will be indicated on one line. The most likely 
component or components causing the condition are listed in the right column.

 Service Access Gauge Port Valves 

These valves are unique to R-134a refrigerant systems. The 
Schrader-type valves found in R-12 systems are not used. The service valve in 
the A/C compressor to condenser discharge line, allows access to the 
high-pressure side of the system for attaching a service hose and pressure 
gauge.

The service valve on the suction accumulator/drier allows access to the 
low pressure side of the system for attaching a service hose and pressure gauge.

The refrigerant system has a high-pressure (discharge) and a 
low-pressure (suction) gauge port valve. They provide access to both sides 
(high-pressure and low-pressure) of the system for service hoses and a 
manifold gauge set so system pressures can be read. Rotunda R-134a High-Side 
Quick Disconnect 176-R0037 or equivalent is required to connect a manifold 
gauge set or charg

SERVICE PROCEDURES

A/C Evaporator Core and/or A/C Condenser Core

 On-Vehicle Leak Test 

 Evaporator Core 

Verify that the manifold gauge set is capable of holding vacuum with 
the following procedure:

Connect the RED and BLUE hoses together using a 1/4-inch flare coupling.

Connect the gauge set YELLOW hose to a known good vacuum pump. 

Turn the vacuum pump ON and open both gauge set valves.

Operate the vacuum pump for one minute and close both gauge set valves. 
The low side gauge should indicate approximately 30 inches of vacuum.

Allow the gauge set, with vacuum applied, to set for at least 30 minutes.

If the gauge reading drops during that time, the gauge set hose 
connections, gauges, or valves are leaking and must be repaired before 
proceeding with the leak test.

Discharge the A/C system. Refer to System Evacuating in the Service 
Procedures portion of this section.

Disconnect the liquid line and suction accumulator/drier from the 
evaporator core tubes. DO NOT leak test an evaporator core with the suction 
accumulator/drier attached to the core tubes. Refrigerant outgassing from oil 
and desiccant bag in the accumulator will indicate a false leak condition.

Clean the evaporator core tube fittings.

For threaded connections wipe any dirt or debris from sealing surfaces 
with a clean, lint-free rag.

For this particular test procedure, it will be necessary to use a 
manifold gauge set for an R-12 refrigerant system, as the manifold gauge set 
for the R-134a refrigerant system cannot be attached to the leak test adapters.

Connect the appropriate test fittings from A/C Test Adapter Set 
D88P-19703-B or equivalent to the evaporator tube connections.

 NOTE: The automatic shutoff valves on some gauge set hoses do not open when 
connected to the test fittings. If available, use hoses without shutoff 
valves. If hoses with shutoff valves are used, check to make sure the valve 
opens when attached to the test fittings or install an adapter which will 
activate the valve. The test is not valid if the shutoff valve does not open, 
as only the hose will be tested.

Connect the RED and BLUE hoses from the gauge and manifold set to the 
test fittings on the evaporator core. Connect the YELLOW hose to a known 
quality vacuum pump.

Open both gauge set valves and start the vacuum pump. Turn the A/C 
system blower on low and allow the vacuum pump to operate for a minimum of 30 
minutes after the gauge set low-pressure gauge indicates 101 kPa (30 in-Hg). 
The 30-minute evacuation is necessary to remove any refrigerant from oil left 
in the evaporator core. If the refrigerant is not completely removed from the 
oil, outgassing will occur and degrade the vacuum and appear as a refrigerant 
leak.

If the low-pressure gauge reading will not drop to 101 kPa (30 in-Hg) 
when the valves on the gauge and manifold set are open and the vacuum pump is 
operating, close the gauge set valves and observe the low-pressure gauge. If 
the pressure rises rapidly to zero, a large leak is indicated. Recheck the 
test fitting connections and gauge set connections before replacing the A/C 
condenser core.

If the low-pressure gauge reading rises 10 or more inches of vacuum 
from the 101 kPa (30 in-Hg) position in 10 minutes, a leak is indicated. If a 
very small leak is suspected, wait 30 minutes and observe the vacuum gauge. If 
a small amount of vacuum is lost, operate the vacuum pump with gauge valves 
open for an additional 30 minutes with the system blower on low to remove any 
remaining refrigerant from the oil in the evaporator core. Recheck for loss of 
vacuum as outlined. If a very small leak is suspected, allow the system to set 
overnight with vacuum applied and check for vacuum loss.

A leaking fitting, gauge set or hose connection will appear as a 
leaking A/C condenser core.

If the A/C condenser core does leak, as verified by the above 
procedure, install a new A/C condenser core.

 Condenser 

Verify that the manifold gauge set is capable of holding vacuum:

Connect the RED and BLUE hoses together using a 1/4-inch flare coupling.

Connect the gauge set YELLOW hose to a known good vacuum pump.

Turn the vacuum pump ON and open both gauge set valves.

Operate the vacuum pump for one minute and close both gauge set valves. 
The low side gauge should indicate approximately 30 inches of vacuum.

Allow the gauge set, with vacuum applied, to set for at least 30 minutes.

If the gauge reading drops during that time, the gauge set hose 
connections, gauges, or valves are leaking and must be repaired before 
proceeding with the leak test.

Discharge the A/C system using the procedure outlined in System 
Evacuating in this section.

Disconnect the high-pressure line and discharge line at the condenser. 
Plug the lines leading to the compressor and evaporator.

Clean A/C condenser core fittings.

For threaded connections wipe any dirt or debris from sealing surfaces 
with a clean, lint-free rag.

For this particular test procedure, it will be necessary to use a 
manifold gauge set for an R-12 refrigerant system, as the manifold gauge set 
for the R-134a refrigerant system cannot be attached to the leak test adapters.

Connect the appropriate test fittings from A/C Test Adapter Set 
D88P-19703-B or equivalent to the evaporator tube connections.

 NOTE: The automatic shutoff valves on some gauge set hoses do not open when 
connected to the test fittings. If available, use hoses without shutoff 
valves. If hoses with shutoff valves are used, check to be sure the valve 
opens when attached to the test fittings or install an adapter that will 
activate the valve. The test is not valid if the shutoff valve does not open; 
only the hose will be tested.

Connect the RED and BLUE hoses from the gauge and manifold set to the 
test fittings on the evaporator core. Connect the YELLOW hose to a known 
quality vacuum pump.

Open both gauge set valves and start the vacuum pump. Turn the A/C 
system blower on low and allow the vacuum pump to operate for a minimum of 30 
minutes after the gauge set low-pressure gauge indicates 101 kPa (30 in-Hg). 
The one-half hour evacuation is necessary to remove any refrigerant from oil 
left in the evaporator core. If the refrigerant is not completely removed from 
the oil, outgassing will occur and degrade the vacuum and appear as a 
refrigerant leak.

If the low-pressure gauge reading will not drop to 101 kPa (30 in-Hg) 
when the valves on the gauge and manifold set are open and the vacuum pump is 
operating, close the gauge set valves and observe the low-pressure gauge. If 
the pressure rises rapidly to zero, a large leak is indicated. Recheck the 
test fitting connections and gauge set connections before replacing the A/C 
condenser core.

If the low-pressure gauge reading rises 10 or more inches of vacuum 
from the 101 kPa (30 in-Hg) position in 10 minutes, a leak is indicated. If a 
very small leak is suspected, wait 30 minutes and observe the vacuum gauge. If 
a small amount of vacuum is lost, operate the vacuum pump with gauge valves 
open for an additional 30 minutes with the system blower on low to remove any 
remaining refrigerant from the oil in the evaporator core. Recheck for loss of 
vacuum as outlined. If a very small leak is suspected, allow the system to set 
overnight with vacuum applied and check for vacuum loss.

A leaking fitting, gauge set or hose connection will appear as a 
leaking A/C condenser core.

If the A/C condenser core does leak, as verified by the above 
procedure, install a new A/C condenser core.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

A/C Compressor

 External Leak Test 

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

A/C Pressure Test Adapter

T94P-19623-E

If the compressor is on the vehicle, discharge the system using a 
service center to recover, recycle and recharge. Remove the compressor from 
the vehicle. Observe all safety precautions.

Remove the retaining bolt and remove the A/C manifold and tube from the 
rear head of the compressor. Install A/C Pressure Test Adapter T94P-19623-E on 
the rear head of the compressor using the existing attaching bolt.

Connect the high- and low-pressure lines of a gauge set to the 
corresponding fittings on the pressure test plate.

Attach the center hose of the gauge set to a refrigerant container 
standing in an upright position.

Using the clutch hub, hand-rotate the compressor shaft ten revolutions 
to distribute the oil inside the compressor.

Open the low-pressure gauge valve, the high-pressure gauge valve and 
the valve on the refrigerant container to allow the refrigerant vapor to flow 
into the compressor.

Using Rotunda R-134a Automatic Calibration Halogen Leak Detector 
023-R1000 or equivalent, check for leaks at the compressor shaft seal and the 
compressor center seal.

If a shaft seal leak is found, install a new shaft seal. If an external 
leak is found at the center joint of the compressor, install a new compressor 
assembly.

When the leak test is completed, close the gauge valves (both high and 
low) as well as the valve on the refrigerant container.

Slowly remove the gauge set hoses from the pressure test fitting tool. 

Install the compressor on the vehicle.

Leak test, evacuate and charge the system. Observe all safety 
precautions.

 Rotating Torque Check 

Check the rotational torque of a used compressor if excessive 
compressor drag is suspected.

Discharge refrigerant system. Observe all safety precautions.

Remove refrigerant hose and A/C manifold and tube from compressor. Use 
care not to allow dirt to enter compressor.

Remove the compressor from the vehicle. With the A/C clutch disengaged, 
rotate the compressor shaft one complete revolution and note the torque 
required to rotate the shaft another complete revolution. 

If the rotational torque exceeds specification 13.0 Nm 
(9.6 lb-ft), replace the compressor assembly.

If the rotational torque is less than specified, excessive drag does 
not exist in the compressor. Install the A/C manifold and tube and leak test, 
evacuate and charge the system.

Check the system for proper operation.

Thermal Protection Switch Test

If installed on vehicle, disconnect air conditioning compressor 
connector (gray color) from main wiring harness.

Disconnect air conditioning compressor clutch connector (white color) 
mounted on the rear side of the compressor body.

Jumper across the two terminals on the male end (harness side) of the 
white clutch connector.

Orient the gray, compressor harness connector and locate the power, 
ground and indicator light terminals.

Using a continuity tester, place one probe on the power terminal and 
the second on the ground terminal. If continuity exists between the power and 
ground terminals, the switch is good. If no continuity exists, replace thermal 
switch.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Refrigerant System

 Refrigerant System Identification 

Several refrigerants are used in today's air conditioning systems. The 
refrigerants are not compatible. While system operations and procedures are 
the same, the equipment is unique and cannot be used interchangeably.

The label stating A/C refrigerant use in the vehicle is attached in the 
engine compartment so the proper service procedure and equipment can be 
referenced in the service manual. An R-134a refrigerant system will have gold 
R-134a NON-CFC tags in addition to the refrigerant charge tag.

[FIGURE: M4526A.gif]

If a component has been used with R-12, it cannot be used again in an 
R-134a system. If used in an R-134a system, it cannot be put into an R-12 
system. Contamination can occur and performance can be adversely affected 
because each system uses a different refrigerant oil designed for that system.

 Special Service Equipment 

 CAUTION: Use extreme care and observe all safety and service precautions related 
to the use of refrigerants. 

The refrigerant used in this refrigerant system is HFC-134a 
(tetrafluoroethane-CF 3 CH 2 F), which is a 
hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant. HFC-134a, also known as R-134a, is 
non-corrosive, non-explosive, non-flammable and has a slight ether-type odor. 
R-134a is heavier than air. Although it is classified as a safe refrigerant, 
certain precautions must be observed to protect the parts involved and the 
person working on the unit.

Use only R-134a refrigerant and R-134a compatible refrigerant oil. Due 
to environmental concerns, when the air conditioning system is drained, the 
refrigerant must be collected using refrigerant recovery/recycling equipment 
meeting SAE-J1991 and J2210. R-134a must never be removed without the 
appropriate equipment or released into the atmosphere. Use of a recovery 
machine dedicated for R-134a is necessary to reduce the possibility of oil and 
refrigerant incompatibility concerns. Refer to the instructions provided by 
the equipment manufacturer when removing refrigerant from or charging the air 
conditioning system.

Ford Motor Company supports the efficient usage, recovery, and 
recycling of R-134a used in car and truck air conditioners. Ford Motor Co. 
recommends the use of U.L.-approved recovery/recycling equipment such as:

Rotunda R-134a Manifold Gauge Set 176-R032A or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Low-Side Quick Disconnect 176-R0036 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a High-Side Quick Disconnect 176-R0037 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Mobile Recycling Center 023-00150 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Automatic Calibration Halogen Leak Detector 023-R1000 or 
equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Vacuum Pump (1.5 CFM) 176-R0126 or equivalent.

Rotunda R-134a Vacuum Pump (3.0 CFM) Pump 176-00127 or equivalent.

This equipment (or equivalent which meets SAE standard J1991) must be 
used during any air conditioning system repair and recharge procedure that 
requires the air conditioning system to be discharged.

Refrigerant recovery systems and recycling stations are in use in an 
increasing number of automotive air conditioning service facilities. The use 
of such equipment makes possible the recovery and use of air conditioning 
system refrigerant after contaminants and moisture have been removed.

If a refrigerant recovery or recycling station is used, refer to Refrigerant Reclaiming/Recovery/Recycling Equipment 
 for general procedures, in 
addition to the operating instructions provided by the equipment manufacturer.
