DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Audible Warning and Shutdown Activation

When the engine alarm/shutdown module receives a fault signal at one or 
more of its three inputs, it immediately sounds the audible warning. After 
approximately 30-40 seconds, it opens the circuit that provides battery 
voltage to the fuel shutoff relay coil. The fuel shutoff relay then opens the 
voltage supply to the fuel shutoff solenoid and the engine is shut down.

The fuel shutoff solenoid is used to allow the vehicle to run or be 
shut down. This solenoid moves the fuel rack into the fuel on and off 
positions. Power for the solenoid is controlled by the ignition switch and 
fuel shutoff relay in the system.

The fuel shutoff solenoid is comprised of two coils within one housing. 
A powerful pull-in coil is used to pull the fuel shutoff lever to the open 
position. The pull-in coil is fed from the switched side of the starter motor 
relay, so it is energized whenever the ignition switch is in the start 
position. At the same time, a much less powerful hold coil is fed from the run 
circuit. When the ignition switch is released to the run position, the pull-in 
coil drops out and the hold coil is left energized to keep the fuel shutoff 
lever in the open position.

 CAUTION: The pull-in coil draws a considerable amount of current while it is 
energized. Do not allow it to remain energized for longer than 30 seconds, or 
damage to the coil can result. 

The fuel shutoff electrical system consists primarily of the following 
components:

Fuel shutoff solenoid, located next to the fuel injection pump.

[FIGURE: K19637A.gif]

Fuel shutoff relay, located behind the instrument panel, near the 
circuit breaker panel.

Engine alarm/shutdown module (on vehicles with engine shutdown), 
located on brake and clutch pedal support.

 Engine Alarm/Shutdown Module, Brake Low Air Pressure Buzzer and Low 
Coolant Module — Except Cummins ECI, CAT C10 and C12, CAT 3406 
PEEC, and DDC Series 60 Engines

A

Disconnect for item 6. Connect together for items 4 and 5.

 Start 

With the ignition switch in START, the fuel shutoff solenoid pull-in 
coil is energized by Circuit 669 (R/BL) from the starter relay.

The fuel shutoff relay coil is energized by the ignition switch through 
Circuits 16 (R/GN), 69 (R/GN) (without engine shutdown) and 932 (BL). This 
closes the contacts in the relay and the fuel shutoff solenoid hold coil is 
energized through Circuits 37 (BK/Y) and 69 (R/GN). The solenoid pulls the 
shutoff lever to the open position and the engine will crank and start.

If the vehicle is equipped with the engine shutdown system, the run 
signal from the ignition switch is routed through Circuit 16 (R/GN), through 
the engine alarm/shutdown module to the fuel shutoff relay. The bypass 
connector is not connected.

If the vehicle does not have the engine shutdown system, the bypass 
connector around the engine alarm/shutdown module is connected and the harness 
connectors to the engine shutdown module are not connected.

 Run 

After starting, the ignition switch returns to RUN. This de-energizes 
the starter relay and the fuel shutoff solenoid pull-in coil. The fuel shutoff 
relay remains energized by the ignition switch through Circuits 16 (R/GN), 69 
(R/GN) and 932 (BL). The fuel shutoff solenoid hold coil remains energized by 
Circuits 37 (BK/Y) and 69 (R/GN) through the closed contacts of the fuel 
shutoff relay.

 Shutoff 

When the ignition switch is moved to OFF, current to the fuel shutoff 
relay coil is cut off and the relay contacts open. This de-energizes the fuel 
shutoff solenoid hold coil and the shutoff lever returns to the off position, 
fuel flow is cut off, and the engine stops.

Turning off power to the engine alarm/shutdown module (key off) resets 
the system, and the sequence of events repeats if the engine is restarted.

 Automatic Shutoff with Engine Shutdown System 

If the engine alarm/shutdown module senses low oil pressure, low 
coolant level or high coolant temperature, the module will interrupt battery 
voltage to Circuit 932 (BL) to the fuel shutoff relay after a 30-40 second 
delay. This de-energizes the relay, cutting off current to the fuel shutoff 
solenoid hold coil. The shutoff lever moves to the off position and the engine 
stops running.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Prove-Out Mode

The prove-out function is activated while the engine is cranking. All 
warning indicator lights except parking brake, low air and oil pressure will 
illuminate.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Oil Pressure Detection

The oil pressure switch is normally closed. The presence of adequate 
oil pressure opens the switch, thereby turning off the oil pressure warning 
indicator lamp and the audible warning. When oil pressure is insufficient, the 
oil pressure switch closes, grounding the oil pressure warning indicator lamp 
circuit and the engine alarm/shutdown module circuit. The indicator lamp 
illuminates and the engine alarm/shutdown module sounds a warning signal. If 
equipped, and the circuit is activated (grounded) for 30-40 seconds, the 
engine alarm/shutdown module opens the battery voltage supply for the fuel 
shutoff relay and causes engine shutdown.

================================================================================
PAGE 5744
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 13-09: Engine Protection System

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

High Coolant Temperature Detection

The coolant temperature switch is normally open. When the coolant 
temperature is excessive, the switch closes, grounding the coolant temperature 
warning indicator lamp circuit and the engine alarm/shutdown module circuit. 
The indicator lamp illuminates and the engine alarm/shutdown module sounds a 
warning signal. If the circuit is activated (grounded) for 30-40 seconds, the 
engine alarm/shutdown module opens the battery voltage circuit for the fuel 
shutoff relay and causes engine shutdown.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Coolant Level Detection

The engine alarm/shutdown module monitors the low coolant level sensor 
circuit. When the coolant level drops far enough so that the sensor is no 
longer submerged, the engine alarm/shutdown module senses an open condition 
(air has a much higher resistance than coolant). After a short delay (1-3 
seconds), the engine alarm/shutdown module grounds the coolant level warning 
indicator lamp circuit. The coolant level warning indicator lamp is 
illuminated, and the engine alarm/shutdown module sounds a warning signal. If 
the low coolant level sensor circuit is open for 30-40 seconds, the engine 
alarm/shutdown module opens the battery voltage circuit for the fuel shutoff 
relay and causes engine shutdown.

 NOTE: The resistance value of pure antifreeze (without water mix) is high and 
the low coolant level sensor may indicate a low level reading if it is 
submerged in pure antifreeze. During a system refill, if the coolant supply 
tank is filled with pure antifreeze, the low coolant level sensor may have to 
be jumped to allow the engine to run long enough to mix the antifreeze with 
the coolant (water/antifreeze) in the system.

Section 13-10: Gauge, Warning Indicator, Brake Operation

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Warning Indicators, Dual Brake

The direct air pressure indication systems consist of a dual air 
pressure gauge with dual pointers mounted in the instrument cluster, two-way 
check valves and air tubes connected at the pressure pickup point on the 
vehicle. As the system's air pressure increases, the Bourdon tubes in the dual 
air gauge deflect, causing the pointers to move. The two air pressure 
indicating systems measure the air reservoir's pressure (standard) and the 
application air pressures where equipped.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Pressure Gauge 

 Removal 

 CAUTION: The instrument panel finish panel assembly is retained by a wire 
assembly. Handle with care to avoid damage to the wires. 

Remove six screws on left instrument panel finish panel assembly. 

Pull instrument panel finish panel assembly toward steering wheel and 
rotate out of way. Refer to Section 13-01 .

[FIGURE: K10520E.gif]

Drain primary and secondary air tanks prior to removing the air lines.

Disconnect air lines.

Remove two nuts retaining dual air pressure gauge to the instrument 
panel finish panel. 

Remove dual air pressure gauge from vehicle.

 Installation 

Install dual air pressure gauge into instrument panel finish panel. 
Install two retaining nuts. 

Connect air lines.

Position instrument panel finish panel assembly to the instrument panel 
and install six retaining screws. 

Check operation of dual air pressure gauge.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Double Check Valve 

 Removal 

Exhaust air from the system and block the wheels to prevent the vehicle

Remove the double check valve from the line.

 Installation 

Place Teflon® tape or equivalent around the check 
valve threads to act as a seal.

Install the double check valve in the air line.

Charge system with air and check for leakage.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Low Air Pressure Switch

Two low air pressure switches are mounted to the foot brake valve. One 
switch monitors the primary supply and the other monitors the secondary 
supply. The low air pressure switches close to operate a warning buzzer and 
light when low air pressure is detected.

 Removal 

Turn the ignition switch to OFF and exhaust the air from the air brake 
system.

Disconnect the wire at the low air pressure switch.

Unscrew the low air pressure switch and remove it.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Charge the system.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Battery and Charging System

 Inspection and Verification 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES AND CLOTHING. SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN OR EYES, FLUSH IMMEDIATELY WITH 
WATER FOR A MINIMUM OF 15 MINUTES AND GET PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION. IF ACID IS 
SWALLOWED, CALL A PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY. 

 WARNING: BATTERIES NORMALLY PRODUCE EXPLOSIVE GASES THAT CAN CAUSE PERSONAL 
INJURY. DO NOT ALLOW FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED SUBSTANCES TO COME NEAR THE 
BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR WORKING NEAR A BATTERY, ALWAYS SHIELD YOUR FACE AND 
PROTECT YOUR EYES. ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION. 

Verify the vehicle owner's original concern by operating the engine to 
duplicate the concern.

Inspect to determine if one of the following mechanical or electrical 
concerns apply.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Electrical

Before attempting to test a battery. Give it a thorough examination to
determine if it has been damaged.

Batteries are tested to determine the state of charge and ability to
crank an engine. The result of these tests is to show that the battery is
either good, needs recharging, or must be replaced.

Preliminary checks to the charging system should be made regardless of
the fault condition. These checks include:

Check the fuses/fuse links to the generator to make sure that they are
not burned or damaged. This condition, resulting in an open circuit or high
resistance, can cause erratic or intermittent charging system concerns.

Check battery posts and cable terminals for clean and tight
connections. Clean the posts and the cables to ensure good electrical contact.

Check for secure connections at the generator output, generator
regulator and engine ground. Also check the connection at the load
distribution point.

Check the generator drive belt to ensure proper tension and no slip
between the generator pulley and the drive belt. Refer to Section 03A-05 ,
 Section 03B-05 or Section 03C-05 

Check battery for full charge as outlined.

Before performing charging system tests on the vehicle, note conditions
such as: slow cranking, discharged battery, charge indicator lamp stays ON
with engine running, charge indicator lamp does not illuminate with ignition
switch in RUN and engine not running, etc. This information will aid in
isolating the part of the system causing the symptom.

When a relatively new battery is discharged, test for current drain.
The following are some of the most common current drain concerns:

Glove compartment lamp stays on with the door closed.

Engine compartment lamp stays on constantly.

License plate lamp or interior lamp stays on constantly.

Other electronic component damage.

Battery, starting system, and lighting system concerns can be caused by 
poor charging system performance. The charging system can also cause an 
overload in other areas of the electrical system. 

To correctly identify the area where the difficulty lies, isolate the 
battery, the charging system, and the electrical circuits. Check the battery 
before any electrical system diagnosis, to see if it has the ability to accept 
and hold a charge. Refer to Section 14-01 . If the battery is good, check the 
charging system to see if it can keep the battery charged. 

If the battery cannot meet specifications, it must be replaced. 

If the battery meets the required specifications, it must be fully 
charged before proceeding with the diagnosis of other electrical system 
components. 

Before testing any of the individual charging system components, 
perform general Component Tests in this section. 
The component tests will determine which components require servicing.

Perform Pinpoint Test A 
using Rotunda Inductive Dwell-Tach-Volts Ohms Tester 164-R0254 or equivalent. 
Be careful when using the ohmmeter near hot circuits. The component to be 
checked should be disconnected from the circuit or the battery terminals 
should be disconnected. Use Rotunda Charging/Starting Analyzer 164-R0251 or 
equivalent for testing the charging system. Test instructions are provided 
with the analyzer. 

 CAUTION: Damage to the component being checked can occur during testing if it is 
not disconnected from the circuit, or if the battery terminals are not 
disconnected. 

Continue through the Diagnosis and Testing until service has been 
completed. Test the system again to see if the service has corrected the 
system.

 Component Tests 

Perform the following tests using Rotunda Inductive 
Dwell-Tach-Volts-Ohms Tester 164-R0254 or equivalent, a jumper wire and a test 
lamp (12 volt). The meters should be calibrated once a year and the date of 
calibration stamped on the meter face. This practice should be followed by all 
technicians to maintain their meters at acceptable accuracy. 

Troubleshooting or diagnosis is required before performing electrical 
system service. Even where an obvious fault makes the replacement of a unit 
necessary, find out why the unit failed. If a problem is diagnosed correctly, 
unnecessary service is prevented, the time the vehicle is out of operation 
will be decreased, and the service performed will be permanent.

When performing charging system tests with a voltmeter, turn off all 
lamps and electrical components. Place the transmission in neutral and apply 
the parking brake.

 Battery 

Before performing charging system tests on the vehicle, verify the 
concern, such as slow cranking, battery dead or voltmeter shows excessive 
charge at all times or no charge. This information will aid in isolating the 
part of the system causing the symptom. The Rotunda Alternator, Regulator, 
Battery and Starter Tester (ARBST) 010-00725 or equivalent will simplify 
on-vehicle tests. Refer to Section 14-01 for battery warnings and cautions.

Connect the test block to the generator as shown in the following 
illustration.

ADJUSTMENTS

Regulator Output, Delco Generator 

Remove the access pipe plug from the integral charging system. 

Turn the adjusting screw one or two notches clockwise to raise the 
voltage setting and one or two notches counterclockwise to lower the voltage 
setting. 

Replace the access pipe plug. 

After adjusting the setting, check for an improved battery condition 
over a service period of reasonable length. If adjusting the setting does not 
correct the battery condition, remove the generator for service. 

Remember that if the battery state of charge is low, the regulator 
might not be limiting the voltage, and turning the adjusting screw will show 
no change on the voltmeter. However, turning the adjusting screw will change 
the voltage setting to a new value, which will be indicated by the voltmeter 
when the battery state of charge increases.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Battery

LN-7000 vehicles are equipped with two 93 or 96 ampere-hour, 
maintenance-free batteries. L, LN, LS-8000 vehicles are equipped with two or 
three 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. LA-8000 (Aeromax 8000) 
vehicles are equipped with two or three 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free 
batteries. LT, LN, LTS-8000 vehicles are equipped with two or three 93 or 96 
ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. L, LN, LS-9000 vehicles are equipped 
with two, three or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. 
LA-9000 (Aeromax 106) vehicles are equipped with two, three or four 93 or 96 
ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. LT, LNT, LTS-9000 vehicles are 
equipped with two, three or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free 
batteries. LTA-9000 (Aeromax 106 tandem) vehicles are equipped with two, three 
or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. LL, LLS-9000 
vehicles are equipped with two, three or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, 
maintenance-free batteries. LLA-9000 (Aeromax 120) vehicles are equipped with 
two, three or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, maintenance-free batteries. LTL, 
LTLS-9000 vehicles are equipped with two, three or four 93 or 96 ampere-hour, 
maintenance-free batteries. Vehicle application and equipment determine 
battery type and quantity.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Battery

 Removal 

Remove hex nuts and battery cables from battery terminals (negative 
first). 

Clean cable terminals with an acid neutralizing solution and terminal 
cleaning brush. 

Remove hold-down clamps. 

Test battery and determine if it should be: 

placed back in service

recharged before being placed back in service

replaced with a Motorcraft or equivalent battery

 WARNING: WHEN LIFTING A PLASTIC-CASED BATTERY, AVOID PUTTING EXCESSIVE PRESSURE 
ON THE END WALLS, WHICH CAN CAUSE ACID TO SPEW THROUGH THE VENT CAPS, CAUSING 
PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE OR BATTERY. LIFT WITH A BATTERY 
CARRIER OR WITH YOUR HANDS ON OPPOSITE CORNERS. 

Remove battery using a suitable battery carrier.

 Installation 

Clean cable terminals and hold-down clamps with a wire brush. Replace 
all cables or parts that are worn or frayed. 

[FIGURE: J6320A.gif]

Clean battery tray with a wire brush and scraper. 

Place battery in tray with positive and negative terminals in the 
original positions. 

Install battery cable hex nuts and bolts. 

Assemble and tighten hold-down clamp so battery is secure. Do not 
overtighten.

Secure cables (positive first) to proper terminals. Do not overtighten. 
Apply a small quantity of Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
grease meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to terminals.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Battery Charging

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES. BATTERY CHARGING CAN BE DANGEROUS. WHILE BEING 
CHARGED, THE BATTERY PRODUCES A POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE MIXTURE OF HYDROGEN AND 
OXYGEN GASES. KEEP SPARKS, FLAMES AND LIGHTED CIGARETTES AWAY FROM BATTERIES. 
REMEMBER, IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH LARGE AMOUNTS OF WATER. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION. 

 WARNING: BATTERIES NORMALLY PRODUCE EXPLOSIVE GASES THAT CAN CAUSE PERSONAL 
INJURY; THEREFORE, DO NOT ALLOW FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED TOBACCO TO COME NEAR 
THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR WORKING NEAR A BATTERY, ALWAYS SHIELD YOUR FACE 
AND PROTECT YOUR EYES. ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION. 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES, OR CLOTHING. SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IF ACID CONTACTS SKIN OR EYES, FLUSH IMMEDIATELY WITH WATER FOR A 
MINIMUM OF FIFTEEN MINUTES AND GET PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION. CALL A PHYSICIAN 
IMMEDIATELY. 

 NOTE: Perform battery tests to determine battery state of charge and capacity 
or ability to crank an engine. The ultimate result of these tests is to 
determine if the battery is good, needs recharging or must be replaced. 

Before attempting to test a battery, it is important to give the 
battery a thorough examination to determine if it has been damaged. 

Remove negative battery cable, then positive cable.

Check for dirty or corroded connections.

Clean terminals and clamps, if necessary.

Check for loose battery posts. If posts are loose, replace the battery.

Check battery cover by first removing hold-downs and shields.

Check for broken or cracked case or cover. Replace battery if case or 
cover is damaged.

Perform battery capacity test if current battery appears to be in good 
shape. Use a high rate discharge tester with a variable rate control or a 
fused rate tester with meter compensation for different electrical sizes. 
(Follow instructions supplied with tester.)

 NOTE: Recommended discharge rate at 27°C (81°
F): one half the cold cranking amperage.

Voltage readings at 15 seconds for a good battery are shown on the 
following chart.

 BATTERY VOLTAGES

Approximate Battery Temperature

Minimum Load Voltage

27°C (81°F) and above

9.6

21°C (70°F)

9.6

16°C (61°F)

9.5

-1°C (30°F)

9.1

-7°C (20°F)

8.9

-12°C (10°F)

8.7

-18°C (0°F)

8.5

Wait two minutes and check the open circuit voltage (OCV). Measure OCV 
with a digital voltmeter capable of reading 1/100 volt.

Battery is OK if minimum load voltage and OCV measure above 12.40. If 
battery measures below 12.40, charge for 20 minutes @ 35 amp. Repeat battery 
capacity test. If battery OCV measures above 12.40, but failed minimum load 
voltage, replace worn battery.

Before recharging a discharged battery, inspect and service the 
following conditions, if they exist: 

loose generator belt

pinched or grounded generator or voltage regulator wiring harness

loose harness connections at the generator or voltage regulator

loose or corroded connections at battery, starter relay or engine ground 

excessive battery drain due to hood, glove compartment and courtesy 
lamps remaining on (damaged or misadjusted switch, etc.)

The state of charge for Motorcraft Heavy-Duty batteries is determined 
by comparing the measured battery terminal voltage with the Voltage/State of 
Charge table. 

 VOLTAGE/STATE OF CHARGE

Measured Voltage

State of Charge

Specific Gravity

100%

12.45

75%

1.230

12.30

50%

1.200

12.15

25%

1.170

Cold batteries will not readily accept a charge. Therefore, batteries 
should be allowed to warm up to approximately 5°C (41°
F) before charging. This may require four to eight hours at 
room temperature depending on the initial temperature and battery size. 

A battery that has been completely discharged may be slow to accept a 
charge at the normal charger setting. When batteries are in this condition, 
charging can be started by using the dead battery switch on chargers so 
equipped. 

To determine whether a battery is accepting a charge, follow charger 
manufacturer's instructions for use of dead battery switch. If switch is the 
spring-loaded type, it should be held in the ON position for up to 3 minutes.

After releasing switch, and with charger still on, measure battery 
voltage. If it shows 12 volts or higher, the battery is accepting a charge and 
is capable of being recharged. However, it may require up to two hours of 
charging with batteries colder than 5°C (41°
F) before the charge rate is high enough to show on the charger ammeter. It 
has been found that all non-damaged batteries can be charged by this 
procedure. If a battery cannot be charged by this procedure, it must be 
replaced.

 Procedure to Charge a Known Good Battery 

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES. BATTERY CHARGING CAN BE DANGEROUS. WHILE BEING 
CHARGED, THE BATTERY PRODUCES A POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE MIXTURE OF HYDROGEN AND 
OXYGEN GASES. KEEP SPARKS, FLAMES AND LIGHTED CIGARETTES AWAY FROM BATTERIES. 
REMEMBER, IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH LARGE AMOUNTS OF WATER. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION. 

 NOTE: If excessive gassing or electrolyte spewing occurs during the charge, 
discontinue charging. The battery has reached serviceable charge. If the 
battery will not accept at least 5A after 20 minutes of charging, replace the 
battery.

A rapid recharge procedure has been developed for recharging batteries 
that have passed the preceding battery capacity test and only need a recharge.

The battery can be rapidly recharged by using either of the following 
methods: 

Perform a two-hour charge using 20A constant current (manual setting on 
charger). 

Perform a two-hour charge using a constant potential (automatic setting 
on charger).

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Battery Cleaning 

Keeping the battery top clean and dry reduces the need for service and 
extends battery life. Make certain the cable clamps are tightly fastened to 
the battery posts. If corrosion is found, disconnect the cables and clean 
clamps and posts with a wire brush. Neutralize the corrosion with a solution 
of baking soda and water. After installing cables, apply a small quantity of 
Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent grease meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1C75-B to each battery post to help prevent corrosion. 

[FIGURE: J6321A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tools 

Using properly designed tools can prevent damage to the battery, 
battery cables and hold-down bracketry. They can also reduce potential hazards 
to both technician and vehicle being serviced. 

Tools and equipment manufactured for servicing batteries have parts 
insulated to help prevent arcing. This feature can reduce potential component 
damage and fire hazards if tool is dropped and shorts the battery terminals. 

 Pliers 

Battery pliers have jaws specifically designed to grip cable clamp 
bolts securely. Exercise care when removing or replacing the cable clamp bolts 
to make sure that the battery terminal is not subjected to any excessive 
lateral or twisting forces. Such forces could cause major damage to the 
internal components of the battery, and result in leakage at the terminals. 

 Clamp Puller 

Use a clamp puller to remove a cable clamp from the battery terminal. 
The jaws exert a force on the top of the battery post to remove the clamp. 
Proper use of this tool prevents the damaging lateral or twisting forces that 
result when using a pry bar or plier. 

[FIGURE: J3889A.gif]

 Clamp Spreader 

The spreader is used to expand the cable clamp after it has been 
removed from the terminal. The cable clamp can then be easily placed in its 
correct position on the terminal. 

[FIGURE: J3890A.gif]

 Terminal Cleaning Brush 

The terminal cleaning brush is designed to clean both the threaded 
battery terminal and the mating surface of the cable connector. 

[FIGURE: J6320A.gif]

 Carrier 

Use a suitable battery carrier for lifting and transporting the 
battery. The illustration shows a clamp-type carrier used to grip the 
sidewalls of the container just below the lip of the cover. The carrier is 
used on the sidewalls, rather than the end walls, since the sidewalls have 
additional strength from the inner cell partitions. This is particularly 
important with polypropylene-cased batteries that have flexible end walls. 

[FIGURE: J43371A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The Motorcraft 95 ampere generator is belt-driven from the engine. 
Field current is supplied from the voltage regulator mounted on the rear of 
the generator to the rotating field of the generator through two brushes and 
two slip rings.

[FIGURE: J3170B.gif]

The generator produces power in the form of alternating current. The 
alternating current is rectified to direct current by six diodes. The voltage 
regulator automatically adjusts the generator field current to maintain the 
generator output voltage within prescribed limits to correctly charge the 
battery. The generator is self-current limiting.

If equipped with a warning lamp, the regulator voltage control circuit 
is turned on when the ignition switch is in RUN and voltage is applied to the 
regulator I terminal through a resistor in the I circuit. When the ignition 
switch is in OFF, the control circuit is turned off and no field current flows 
to the generator.

On warning lamp equipped vehicles, the warning lamp is connected across 
the terminals of a 420-ohm resistor at the instrument cluster. Current passes 
through the warning lamp when the ignition switch is in RUN and there is no 
voltage at terminal S. When voltage at S rises to a preset value, the 
regulator switching circuits stop the flow of current into terminal I and the 
lamp turns off.

System voltage is sensed and generator field current is drawn through 
terminal A. The regulator switching circuits will turn the warning lamp on, 
indicating a system concern, if terminal A voltage is excessively high or if 
the terminal S voltage signal is abnormal.

A fuse link is included in the charging system wiring harness on all 
models. The fuse link is used to prevent damage to the wiring harness and 
generator if the wiring harness should become grounded, or if a booster 
battery is connected to the charging system with the wrong polarity.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Generator

 WARNING: BATTERIES NORMALLY PRODUCE EXPLOSIVE GASES THAT CAN CAUSE PERSONAL 
INJURY. DO NOT ALLOW FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED TOBACCO TO COME NEAR THE 
BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR WORKING NEAR A BATTERY, ALWAYS SHIELD YOUR FACE AND 
PROTECT YOUR EYES. ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION. 

 WARNING: WHEN LIFTING A PLASTIC-CASED BATTERY, AVOID PUTTING EXCESSIVE PRESSURE 
ON THE END WALLS, WHICH CAN CAUSE ACID TO SPEW THROUGH THE VENT CAPS, CAUSING 
PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE OR BATTERY. LIFT WITH A BATTERY 
CARRIER OR WITH YOUR HANDS ON OPPOSITE CORNERS. 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES, OR CLOTHING. SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IF ACID CONTACTS SKIN OR EYES, FLUSH IMMEDIATELY WITH WATER FOR A 
MINIMUM OF FIFTEEN MINUTES AND GET PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION. CALL A PHYSICIAN 
IMMEDIATELY.

generator front housing only when adjusting belt tension. Refer to Section 03A-05 , Section 03B-05 or Section 03C-05 depending on type of engine.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Generator

 CAUTION: When rebuilding an integral generator, use only high-temperature 
bearings. Use of standard parts will result in generator failure. 

 NOTE: Depending on generator application, certain components are separately 
serviceable, while other components are not and could require generator to be 
replaced as an assembly.

Wipe the stator, rotor and front bearing with a clean cloth. Do not 
clean these parts with solvent.

Rotate the front bearing on the drive end of the rotor shaft. Check for 
any scraping noise, looseness or roughness. Look for excessive lubricant 
leakage. If any of these conditions exist, replace the bearing.

Inspect the rotor shaft rear bearing surface for roughness or severe 
chatter marks. Replace the rotor assembly if the shaft is not smooth.

Place the rear bearing on the slip ring end of the rotor shaft and 
rotate the bearing. Make the same check for noise, looseness and roughness as 
was made for the front bearing. Inspect the rollers and cage for damage. 
Replace the rear bearing if these conditions exist or if the lubricant is lost 
or contaminated.

Check the slip rings for nicks and scratches. These can be removed by 
turning down the slip rings. Do not go beyond a minimum diameter of 31 mm 
(1.22 inches). If the rings are badly damaged, replace the rotor assembly.

Check all wire leads on both the rotor and stator assemblies for loose 
or broken connections. Check the windings for burned insulation. Replace parts 
that show signs of burned insulation.

Check the pulley and fan for excessive looseness on the rotor shaft and 
for cracks or other damage. Replace any pulley or fan that is loose, cracked 
or bent.

Check both the front and rear housings for cracks, particularly in the 
webbed areas at the mounting ear. Replace a damaged or cracked housing.

Wipe the heat transfer grease from the rectifier assembly base and 
rectifier mounting area of the rear housing with a clean cloth.

Replace the brushes if they are worn shorter than 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) 
from the shunt.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The electrical charging system is a negative ground system consisting 
of a generator, voltage regulator, charge indicator lamp (optional), storage 
battery, wiring and cables. Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting 
Manual, City Delivery or Fleet 
and Full, for schematics and locations of components and wiring.

[FIGURE: J6211B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

10334

Slip Ring End (SRE) Housing

2

10336

Stator

3

10333

Drive End (DE) Housing

4

—

Adjustment Lug (Part of 10346)

5

10A310

Fan

6

10344

Pulley

7

—

Mounting Lugs (Part of 10346)

The only difference between the 100 and 115 ampere generators is the 
drive pulleys installed on each. The 100 and 115 ampere generators are 
one-wire systems (the minimum number of lead wire connections necessary at the 
generator for proper operation). With a one-wire system, there is residual 
magnetism in the rotor at start-up. As the generator rotor begins turning, the 
residual fields around the rotor induce voltages in the stator windings. The 
faster the rotor turns, the higher the voltage induced in the stator windings 

Once the speed and output are up to specification, the voltage 
available at the diode trio becomes sufficient to supply field current for 
normal operations. If an indicator light is connected in series with the I 
terminal, the light will be on while the generator comes up to speed. The 
indicator lamp will light due to a voltage imbalance between the battery 
voltage on one side of the light and system voltage coming from the diode trio 
on the other side of the light. Once the generator output voltage equals the 
battery voltage, the voltages are balanced on both sides of the indicator 
light. With no difference in potential, the light turns off.

Once the system voltage exceeds 14 volts, the voltage regulator will 
turn off the field current to prevent the voltage from rising any higher. This 
causes the magnetic field around the rotor to collapse, which reduces the 
generator output voltage. As the voltage falls below the battery voltage, the 
voltage regulator turns the field current back on, which allows the magnetic 
field to build up again. This cycle is repeated many times a second, so 
quickly that the output voltage is steady for all practical purposes and the 
indicator light cannot turn on and off fast enough to keep pace and so stays 
off unless a prolonged voltage imbalance should occur. The system voltage is 
used to control the output, which eliminates the need for extra sense wiring.

[FIGURE: J6212A.gif]

Section 14-02B: Generator, 100 and 115 Ampere Delco

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Generator

The 21-SI series Delcotron® generator is a 
high-output integral charging system with built-in rectifier and voltage 
regulator that produces DC current. The 21-SI generator can be operated in 
either a clockwise or counterclockwise direction at continuous speeds of up to 
10,000 rpm (intermittent speeds of up to 12,000 rpm are also acceptable). The 
ambient temperature range for proper operation is -34°C to +
93°C (-30°F to +
200°F).

The B+ terminal has 1/4-inch threads, as does the ground 
terminal hole.

================================================================================
PAGE 5782
================================================================================
1997 L-Series

Section 14-02B: Generator, 100 and 115 Ampere Delco

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Voltage Regulator

The voltage regulator is a solid-state integrated circuit-type with a 
nominal regulated voltage setting of 14.0 volts. In addition, the voltage 
regulator features flat temperature compensation, low parasitic draw and low 
turn-on speed with improved radio frequency interference (RFI) suppression 
capability and load dump protection from voltage spikes. The voltage regulator 
limits system voltage by switching the ground circuit for the rotor field on 
and off.

================================================================================

Section 14-02B: Generator, 100 and 115 Ampere Delco

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Generator Circuit

 Circuit Description 

The generator output or B+ terminal is connected to the 
battery positive terminal. The ground path is through the generator housing 
and mounting back to the battery negative terminal. When the voltage regulator 
switches the ground circuit on, the battery voltage passes through the 
rectifier bridge and into a diode trio, which passes the voltage to the rotor 
through a brush and slip ring assembly located on the rotor shaft. This will 
cause a magnetic field to build up around the rotor windings. The voltage 
regulator also receives battery voltage that it uses to compare with the 
voltage produced by the generator. When the generator voltage exceeds 14 
volts, the voltage regulator switches off the ground circuit going to the 
rotor, which collapses its field and reduces the output momentarily.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

[FIGURE: J6262A.gif]

The 26-SI, 30-SI series Delcotron® generator is a 
brushless, heavy-duty integral charging system with built-in diode rectifier 
and voltage regulator, producing DC current for battery electrical systems. 
The 26-SI, 30-SI series is designed for use on large and mid-range diesel and 
gasoline engines in over-the-road service, as well as for off-road, 
agricultural, and construction equipment.

With its brushless construction, the 26-SI, 30-SI has substantially 
increased service life over brush-type units. The absence of moving electrical 
connections eliminates sparks from brush/slip ring contact.

The integrated-circuit regulator is designed for low parasitic draw and 
features a low turn-on speed. A special diode-trio/capacitor assembly provides 
superior radio frequency interference (RFI) suppression. The electronics are 
protected two ways. Standard load dump protection guards the generator against 
voltage spikes caused by loose connections or interruptions in the charging 
line, and total environmental sealing protects against dirt, road salt, and 
other corrosives.

The generator can be operated in either clockwise or counterclockwise 
directions (external fan may require changing to reverse rotation) at 
continuous speeds of up to 10,000 generator rpm. Intermittent speeds of up to 
12,000 generator rpm are also acceptable. The ambient temperature range for 
proper operation is -40°C to +85°
C (-40°F to +185°
F).

The solid-state, integrated circuit voltage regulator built into the 
generator limits system voltage by switching the ground circuit for the rotor 
field on and off. When the ground circuit is on, field current passes from a 
diode trio through the stationary field coil. Nominal regulated voltages of 
13.8, 14.0, and 14.2 volts are available for 12-volt systems, 27.8 volts for 
24-volt systems.

For a 12-volt system, an output rating of 85 amperes is standard. For 
24-volt systems, output ratings of 50 or 75 amperes are available. For output 
ratings of specific 26-SI models, refer to the Specifications portion of this 
section.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Integral Generator/Regulator

The 26-SI, 30-SI Delcotron® generator is designed for 
a one-wire charging system configuration. One-wire refers to the minimum 
number of lead wire connections necessary at the generator for operation and 
requires only that the generator output terminal be connected to the battery 
positive terminal and that a ground path be provided between the generator 
housing and the battery negative terminal.

Some applications use an I terminal circuit to power an indicator light 
or to lower the engine speed (rpm) at which the generator will turn on (begin 
producing current). Such a system is commonly referred to as a one-wire system 
with I terminal or, occasionally, as a two-wire system.

I Terminal (Part of 10346)

External connections to the generator are made to terminals. The 
standard output terminal is a female type with insulated output terminal bolt 
and charge lead cable with a special connector. When properly installed, the 
electrical connection is sealed from moisture and there are no exposed parts 
with B+ voltage. The output terminal bolt head is normally 
stamped NO VOLTS to indicate the insulated type.

Some 26-SI, 30-SI models use a 1/4-inch threaded stud type of output 
terminal. With this type of terminal, the exposed metal parts are not 
insulated and will have B+ voltage when connected to a battery.

[FIGURE: J6266A.gif]

Optional connections to the 26-SI, 30-SI series include either an R 
(relay) or I (indicator light) terminal, and a ground lead connection to the 
generator's rectifier end housing.

An R or relay terminal is located on the side of the generator opposite 
from the output terminal. This terminal may be used to operate some types of 
charge indicator, an ADLO system, a tachometer, or similar device by providing 
voltage pulses at about half of system voltage and at a frequency of one pulse 
for each 7.5 revolutions of the generator. The current draw of the accessories 
being powered through this terminal must not exceed 4 amperes. R terminals are 
normally of the unthreaded pin type.

When an I terminal is present it will be located on the side of the 
generator opposite the output terminal, in place of the R terminal. An I 
terminal is connected internally to the field circuit. An indicator light 
connected in series with this terminal will be on whenever there is a voltage 
difference between the positive side of the field circuit and the system 
voltage at other side of the indicator light. During normal generator 
operation, the light will be off since the diode trio output voltage equals 
the system voltage. A side benefit of this circuit is that current is passed 
through the field winding during engine start-up, resulting in a lower 
generator turn-on speed. If an indicator light is not required, a diode or 
resistor can be used in place of a light bulb. Up to one ampere of current may 
be passed through this circuit to aid in generator turn-on. An I terminal is 
normally a threaded-stud type with a 10-24 thread.

A threaded 1/4-inch hole (with screw and lockwasher) in the rectifier 
end housing between the output and R or I terminals is provided to connect a 
ground lead if used; otherwise, the ground path is through the mounting 
hardware and brackets to the engine. On replacement units, a paper tag is 
present identifying the ground screw, remove and discard the tag. The screw 
and lockwasher should be installed in the housing regardless of whether a 
ground lead is connected, to prevent entry of dirt and water.

All electronic parts of the generator are sealed in a compartment to 
keep out moisture and dirt, and the generator is inside-cooled by air drawn 
through a baffled inlet in the rectifier end cover and exiting from the drive 
end frame behind the fan.

A generator is a voltage-creating machine. The voltage regulator limits 
the maximum voltage that the generator will produce at the output terminal by 
controlling the magnetic field present in the stationary field. The output 
voltage, induced in the stator and rectified by the diodes, allows current to 
flow to satisfy the electrical loads placed on the system, up to a maximum 
current that is characteristic of the generator design.

With the generator rotor turning, a magnetic field around the 
stationary field coil is conducted by the rotor poles to induce voltages in 
the stator windings. The faster the rotor turns, the higher the induced 
voltage will be.

 Generator with R Terminal 

[FIGURE: J6267A.gif]

Capacitor

The initial voltages at start-up are generated by residual magnetism in 
the rotor. On applications with an I terminal in use, this magnetism will be 
boosted by a small amount of current flowing through the field from the 
indicator light circuit. As speed and output increase, voltage available at 
the diode trio becomes sufficient to supply field current for normal 
operation. When the output voltage exceeds the battery voltage, the generator 
begins to drive the system voltage. If the wiring system includes an indicator 
light, the presence of system voltage at the diode trio equalizes the voltage 
on both sides of the indicator light and the light goes out.

While the system voltage is below the voltage regulator setting, the 
voltage regulator turns on the field current and allows the generator to 
produce as much output as possible for the generator speed (rpm), temperature 
and system voltage. When the voltage setting is reached, the voltage regulator 
turns the field current off. When the field current is turned off, the 
magnetic field in the rotor collapses and the generator output voltage begins 
to fall. The falling voltage causes the voltage regulator to turn the field 
current back on and the magnetic field to rebuild. The switching action of the 
voltage regulator continues rapidly, keeping the output and system voltage 
very close to the voltage setting. This will continue unless the electrical 
demands of the system cause the system voltage to fall below the voltage 
setting. Should this happen, the voltage regulator will again allow full field 
current to flow so that the maximum output of the generator at the given 
speed, temperature and system voltage is realized.

An internal sense lead installed between the output diode heat sink and 
regulator stud, is used for voltage control.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Generator

 WARNING: HYDROGEN AND OXYGEN GASES ARE PRODUCED DURING NORMAL BATTERY OPERATION. 
THIS GAS MIXTURE CAN EXPLODE IF FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED SUBSTANCES ARE 
BROUGHT NEAR THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR USING A BATTERY IN AN ENCLOSED 
SPACE, ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION AND SHIELD YOUR EYES. 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING. ALSO, SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH WATER FOR A MINIMUM OF FIFTEEN MINUTES. IF ACID IS SWALLOWED, 
DRINK LARGE QUANTITIES OF MILK OR WATER, FOLLOWED BY MILK OF MAGNESIA, A 
BEATEN EGG, OR VEGETABLE OIL. CALL A PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY.

Disconnect the battery ground cable. 

Loosen the pivot bolt and the adjusting rod-to-generator nuts, and 
remove the drive belt from the generator pulley.

Remove the pivot bolt and the adjusting rod bolt, disconnect the 
generator wire and remove the generator.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Radio Reception

 Antenna Position 

The AM and FM stereo antenna has a range of about 32 km (20 miles) 
before interference noises are heard. This means that in areas with tall 
buildings or hills, it is necessary to select the strongest possible station. 
The electronic radio automatically tunes to the center of any given station, 
eliminating the need for manual fine tuning.

 Antennas and Mobility 

Although an automotive radio antenna will give outstanding mobile 
reception, it cannot provide the continuous reception of home audio 
components. The home receiver is not limited by the vehicle operating 
characteristics and certain geographical effects, as is the mobile unit. For 
example, for the best FM reception, the automotive antenna should be designed 
like a TV antenna and pointed in the direction of the station. The best AM 
antenna is a long piece of wire; the higher the wire, the better the 
reception. However, because of design necessity, the automotive antenna is 
restricted in size, height and direction and must receive both AM and FM 
stations. This means that a limited amount of the station's signal reaches the 
vehicle radio.

 Tuning 

Fine tuning is not required for the radio chassis. The electronic radio 
chassis automatically tunes the radio chassis to the center of the station 
where it will obtain minimum noise and best possible reception.

 Tone Control 

Favoring the rear radio speakers in noisy areas will help to reduce 
noise.

 FM Flutter 

Flutter can best be described as repeated pops and hissing bursts heard 
in the radio speaker during an otherwise good broadcast. Usually this 
condition exists while traveling in the fringe area of the station. Flutter 
will become more severe beyond approximately 40 km (25 miles) of the station. 
The signal loss becomes greater away from the station, until finally noise 
takes over and reception becomes impossible. Flutter can also be noticed near 
the station because of the line-of-sight characteristics of FM radio waves. 
This condition can occur when a building or large structure is between the 
radio receiver and the station being received. Some of the FM signal bends 
around the building, but certain spots have almost no signal. Some of these 
signal losses are only a few inches wide and if the vehicle is parked in one 
of these dead spots, you will only hear noise from the radio speaker. After 
moving out of the shadow of the structure, the station will return to normal. 
Flutter will not occur on AM because the AM radio waves are much longer than 
FM waves.

 FM Multi-Path Cancellation 

Another effect caused by the line-of-sight characteristics is called 
cancellation. This condition exists when the radio waves are reflected from 
objects or structures. The noise produced by cancellation is similar to 
flutter, with the addition of distortion in the program. A more familiar 
description of cancellation is its similarity to the multiple ghosts and 
picture jumping that occurs on television when a low flying plane passes. The 
same condition exists in the vehicle, except that the vehicle is moving and 
the reflecting structure is stationary. The reflected signal cancels the 
normal signal, causing the antenna to pick up noise and distortion. 
Cancellation effects are most prominent in metropolitan areas, but can also 
become quite severe in hilly terrain and low-lying roadways.

 FM Strong Signal Capture and AM Overloading 

FM capture is an unusual condition that occurs when traveling in the 
vicinity of a broadcast tower. If listening to a weak FM station when passing 
the broadcast tower, a stronger station can interfere without changing the 
tuning control. When passing the tower, the station may switch back and forth 
a few times before returning to the station originally tuned. When several 
broadcast towers are present (common in metropolitan areas), several stations 
can overload the receiver resulting in considerable station changing, mixing 
and distortion. Fortunately, this condition is localized and it will not harm 
the receiver. Some overloading can also be noticed on AM, but usually to a 
lesser degree.

 Receiving FM Stereo 

Because more data is carried in the FM stereo waves than in the 
monaural FM broadcasts, flutter, cancellation and capture are even more 
noticeable. The FM stereo noise-free broadcast range is approximately 8 km (5 
miles) less than that received with the monaural FM radio. The AM/FM stereo 
radio might never encounter any of these troublesome conditions, as they are 
more prominent in metropolitan areas, hilly terrain and low-lying roadways. 
However, when diagnosing FM stereo concerns, it is recommended to tune to the 
strongest FM stereo station.

 Stereo Indicator Inoperative or Flickering (AM and FM Reception Are OK) 

A weak or distant signal can cause the stereo indicator to flicker. 
Tune radio to a nearby FM stereo station. If reception is good, but stereo 
indicator is still intermittent, remove radio chassis for service.

 Radio Tests 

Internal diagnostic examination of the radio chassis should be left to 
the authorized radio service center. However, the automotive technician should 
be able to analyze and isolate radio chassis reception conditions to the 
proper area or component causing the condition. All radio chassis conditions 
can be isolated to one of five general areas:

antenna system

radio chassis

speaker system

radio noise suppression equipment

radio amplifier

 Interfering Noise 

The vehicle ignition system is a possible source of radio interference. 
This high-voltage switching system produces a radio frequency electromagnetic 
field that radiates at AM, FM and CB frequencies. Although components have 
been designed into the vehicle to minimize this concern, the noise is more 
noticeable if the radio is tuned slightly off-channel for FM programs. Vehicle 
electrical accessories and owner add-on accessories also contribute to radio 
interference. Furthermore, there are many noise sources that are external to 
the vehicle. These include power lines, communication systems, ignition 
systems of other vehicles, neon signs, etc.

Noise or static can result from many causes. Three of the most common 
sources of radio noise are ignition noise, missing or poor grounds, and 
missing or damaged noise suppression components.

 Missing or Poor Grounds 

Check bond strap grounding effectiveness by wedging a large file 
between metal parts, such as between the tail pipe and body, or between the 
fender and frame, to ensure proper ground while the radio chassis is playing 
and the engine is running. Listen for a decrease in the objectionable radio 
noise. If a reduction in radio noise is noted, first try tightening body and 
exhaust system clamps and brackets. Then, if necessary, install a new bond 
strap between the two metal parts to ensure proper ground.

 Missing or Damaged Noise Suppression Components 

Refer to the description for Missing or Poor Grounds.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Audio Systems

 Inspection and Verification 

 NOTE: Many customers do not understand the limitations of FM reception. Refer 
the customer to the owner guide for information about the limitations of FM 
radio performance.

If AM reception is extremely poor and FM reception drifts or appears to 
have trouble holding stations, make sure the antenna and antenna connectors 
are properly mated. If the antenna connectors are properly mated but the 
reception is still poor, refer to the symptom chart in this section.

If only FM reception is poor, it is unlikely that the antenna is at 
fault. Remove the radio chassis for service.

If the tape player malfunctions (radio operating properly), check 
operation of the tape player by using a known good cassette/cartridge. 

If the condition is not corrected by the substitution of a known good 
cassette/cartridge, the radio chassis must be removed and sent to an 
authorized service facility for service. 

 Symptom Chart — Audio Systems 

Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for the 
connector numbers in the pinpoint tests.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cassette Tape Player Head

 CAUTION: Excess alcohol on the swab may run down the capstan and damage the 
bearings. Do not use carbon tetrachloride. 

The playback head and capstan in the tape player can accumulate tape 
coating residue (oxide) as the tape passes over the head. This accumulation 
needs to be periodically removed as part of normal maintenance if it causes 
weak or wavering sound. It is recommended, for best performance, that the 
player be cleaned every 10 to 12 hours of playing time using a Ford cassette 
player cleaning cartridge or equivalent. An alternate method of cleaning is to 
hold the player door open and clean the playback head with a cotton swab, 
slightly moistened with alcohol. To clean the capstan, trip the on-off switch 
at the slot with eraser end of a pencil and hold the alcohol-moistened swab 
against the rotating capstan.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radio Chassis

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Radio Removing Tool

T87P-19061-A

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable. 

Disengage sun visor ends from edge of radio housing retaining slots. 
Remove four radio housing retaining screws. 

Swing radio control housing down from radio mounting plate and bracket. 

Insert Radio Removing Tools T87P-19061-A, one on each side of the 
radio, into the access holes in bezel until a click is heard. Apply an outward 
pressure on the sides to release the locking tangs and slide the radio from 
the dash. 

Disconnect the radio power lead, antenna lead-in cable and the speaker 
lead wires at the radio. 

Remove the support bracket from the back of the radio. 

To disengage radio removing tools from AM/FM stereo radios, depress the 
retaining clips on side of the radio while applying slight inward pressure on 
the tool and pull tool out of access holes. 

 Installation 

Connect the radio power lead, radio speaker wires and the antenna 
lead-in cable to the radio. 

To install AM/FM stereo radio, slide radio into dash opening until 
retaining clips lock. 

Position radio housing and install four retaining screws. 

Connect battery ground cable.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Radio Speakers

The radio speakers used in all vehicles have 3.2 ohms impedance. The AM 
radio speaker is mounted to the right side of the radio in the radio chassis 
housing. The FM stereo radio speakers are mounted in the doors.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radio Speaker, Instrument Panel

 Removal 

 CAUTION: Do not operate the radio when the speaker is disconnected. 

Remove the radio chassis housing from the roof panel. 

Disconnect the speaker plug connector.

Remove the four speaker mounting nuts. 

Remove the speaker. 

 Installation 

Position the speaker on the radio chassis housing speaker mounting 
screws. 

Install the four speaker mounting nuts. 

Connect the speaker electrical connector. 

Install the radio chassis housing on the roof panel.

Section 17-01: Lighting, Exterior

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Headlamps 

L-Series vehicles are equipped with one of two non-aerodynamic headlamp 
arrangements — single rectangular, or dual rectangular. In the 
single rectangular arrangement, the high-beam and low-beam filaments are both 
contained within the one headlamp. In the dual rectangular arrangement, a 
high-beam filament is contained within the inboard headlamp and a low-beam and 
high beam filament is contained within the outboard headlamp. The single 
rectangular headlamps are protected by a 15-amp circuit breaker. The dual 
rectangular headlamps are protected by a 22-amp circuit breaker.

 Aerodynamic 

The aerodynamic headlamp lens is contoured to fit the aerodynamic shape 
of the body. The high-beam and low-beam filaments are both contained within 
one headlamp. In all arrangements, the lamps are halogen lamps. The headlamps 
are connected to the battery supply circuit through a circuit breaker, 
headlamp (safety) relay switch terminal and the headlamp dimmer switch. The 
headlamp switch energizes the coil (+) terminal of the headlamp (safety) 
relay. The aerodynamic headlamps are protected by a 15-amp circuit breaker.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Headlamp Switch

The exterior lamps, except stop, turn and backup, are controlled from a 
single switch module located to the right of the steering column. All switches 
are the toggle type that are moved up or down to turn lights on or off.

 Panel Dim Switch 

The panel dim switch is located under the toggle switches to the right 
of the steering column. The instrument cluster illumination can be dimmed by 
turning the panel dim switch fully clockwise.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lamps, Fog/Road

Fog lamps and road lamps are mounted in the front bumper below the 
radiator grille. Fog and road lamps are a mutually exclusive option for 
L-Series vehicles. Fog lamps contain a yellow lens and road lamps contain a 
clear lens.

The fog/road lamp circuit operates through the fog/road lamp relay, 
which is fed by the headlamp dimmer switch. The headlamp switch must be in the 
HEAD position and the headlamp dimmer switch must be in the LO position in 
order to energize the fog/road lamp relay coil (+) terminal. The fog or road 
lamp switch can then be actuated to the ON position, illuminating the fog or 
road lamps. The fog or road lamp switch is located on the instrument panel, to 
the right of the steering column.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Stoplight Switch 

Vehicles with hydraulic brakes have a plunger stoplight switch mounted 
to the brake pedal arm. When the brake pedal is at rest (brakes not applied), 
the stoplight switch plunger contacts a stationary stop that depresses the 
plunger. In this position, the stoplight switch is open and no voltage is 
supplied to the stoplamps. When the pedal is pressed (brakes applied), the 
stoplight switch moves with the pedal arm away from the stationary stop. This 
allows the stoplight switch plunger spring to extend the plunger and close the 
stoplight switch contacts, illuminating the stoplamps.

 Vehicles with Hydraulic Brakes 

[FIGURE: K22953B.gif]

The L-Series air brake system has two stoplight switches, one for the 
service line and one for the emergency line. The stoplight switches are 
threaded into elbow fittings that are threaded into pressure ports of the air 
brake manifold. The manifold is mounted on the engine side of the dash panel.

 Vehicles with Air Brakes 

[FIGURE: K22954B.gif]

1997 L-Series Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lamps, Parking, Tail and Marker

The parking lamp system includes all external lamps except the 
stoplamps, turn signal lamps, backup lamps and headlamps. When the headlamp 
switch is in the HEAD position, the marker/tail lamp relay is energized, which 
illuminates the lights. 

The rear stoplamps are operated by either two air pressure stoplight 
switches (air brakes) or a plunger stoplight switch (hydraulic brakes). When 
the foot brake is applied, the stoplight switches are closed (air pressure or 
plunger) and the stoplamps are illuminated.

 Tail Lamp 

[FIGURE: K22955B.gif]

All vehicles are equipped with five roof marker lamps, and some 
vehicles are equipped with mirror marker lamps operated by a toggle switch 
located to the right of the steering column. The switch also has a blink 
function. When the switch is pressed upward from the ON position, the lamps 
will go off. When the switch is released, it spring-loads back to the ON 
position. 

On city delivery vehicles, the circuit is protected by a 20-amp circuit 
breaker. A 25-amp circuit breaker is used on fleet and full instrumentation 
vehicles. From the fuse and switch feed all lamps are connected at a common 
splice. From the roof lamps, the ground circuit is wired to common splice with 
a single ground connection. The mirror marker lamps are wired to individual 
ground connections.

 Roof and Mirror Marker Lamps 

[FIGURE: K22956B.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lamp, Trailer Hookup

The trailer lamp is mounted on the back of the cab and provides light 
for connecting or disconnecting a trailer under low light conditions. The 
interior dome lamp and trailer hookup lamp are operated by a common toggle 
switch located on the instrument panel to the right of the steering column. 

On city delivery vehicles, the dome and trailer hookup lamps are on a 
common 15-amp fuse. A 25-amp circuit breaker is used on fleet and full 
instrumentation vehicles.

From the fuse/circuit breaker and switch, the circuit is wired to an 
instrument cluster indicator lamp that alerts the driver when the light is on. 
A jumper wire from the indicator light connector connects the switch to the 
hookup lamp circuit.

The ground side of the circuit is through the lamp housing and body.

Lamp, License

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lamps, Backup

The backup lamps are actuated by a switch on the transmission. When the 
ignition switch lock cylinder is in the RUN or ACC position and the 
transmission is placed in REVERSE, a switch on the transmission is actuated 
and illuminates the backup lamps.

On vehicles equipped with an Allison MD or MT automatic transmission, 
the backup lamp circuit operates through the vehicle interface module. When 
the module receives a transmission in reverse input signal, it outputs a 
voltage to turn on the backup lamps.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lamps, Cornering/Parking

The cornering lamps are fed from the turn and emergency signal switch. 
When the turn and emergency signal switch is activated, the cornering lamps 
are fed with pulsed voltage from the flasher. The same lamps are also 
activated by a steady voltage when the headlamp switch is actuated to the PARK 
position.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Turn Signals

The fixed steering column is equipped with a turn signal switch mounted 
in the column under the steering wheel. The tilt and telescoping steering 
column is equipped with a turn signal switch that is externally mounted on a 
steering column bracket.

Pull the turn indicator lever downward to signal a left turn, or push 
upward for a right turn. With the lever in either position, the corresponding 
signal lights outside the truck and on the instrument panel flash on and off 
to signal a turn.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hazard Warning Flasher Switch

 Fixed Steering Column 

The hazard warning flasher switch is located on the steering column. 
Push the switch inward to start the flashers. Pull the switch out to stop the 
flashing action. It can be used with the ignition switch lock cylinder in the 
RUN or OFF position. Be sure the turn signal lever is in the OFF (center) 
position before turning on the warning flasher system.

[FIGURE: K42131A.gif]

 Tilt/Telescoping Steering Column 

 NOTE: Flasher will not operate with brake pedal depressed. 

With the turn signal lever in the center (OFF) position, pull the 
hazard flasher warning switch to activate the hazard warning system. To turn 
the hazard flasher off, move the turn signal lever to the right or left turn 
position and then back to center (OFF) position.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Indicator Flasher

A combination turn signal/hazard warning flasher unit is used on 
L-Series vehicles. On Fleet vehicles, it is located on the left side of the 
brake pedal support bracket. On City Delivery vehicles, it is located in the 
top right corner of the fuse panel.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Lighting, Exterior

Common point diagnosis should be used to isolate problems in a 
multiload circuit (a circuit with more than one operating component) without 
making any tests. If one system functions properly but another does not, the 
problem must be in the part of the circuit unique to the inoperative system. 

If more than one circuit does not operate, check for blown fuses. 

Before performing any lighting system tests, make sure the battery is 
in a fully charged condition and all battery cable connections are clean and 
tight. 

A visual inspection is an important part of the lighting system test. 
Check for wires with frayed or damaged insulation, loose connections and 
proper harness routing.

Correct any concerns found by the visual inspection before performing 
further tests of the lighting system. For example, a loose ground strap 
between the engine and body dash panel cause an intermittent operation of the 
lamps and gauges. Inspect and tighten (if necessary) the ground strap 
retaining screws at the back of the engine and the body dash panel. 

If a No. 10 screw is required, use Part No. 42367-S36 hex washer head 
tapping screw.

 Component Tests 

 Turn Signal Switch 

 Turn Signal Flasher Power Test 

Turn ignition switch lock cylinder to RUN or ACC position. 

Connect 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the wire connection at turn signal flasher 
Circuit 383 (R/W). If test lamp illuminates, power flow to turn signal flasher 
is good. If test lamp does not illuminate, power is disrupted between turn 
signal flasher and power source. Service feed circuit. 

 Turn Signal Switch Power Test 

Turn ignition switch lock cylinder to RUN or ACC position. 

Connect 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the wire connection at Circuit 44 (BL). If 
test lamp illuminates, power flow to turn and emergency signal switch is good. 
If test lamp does not illuminate, power flow is disrupted between turn signal 
flasher and turn and emergency signal switch. Service Circuit 44 (BL), or 
replace turn signal flasher. 

 Turn Signal Switch Power Out Test 

Turn ignition switch lock cylinder to RUN or ACC position. 

Position turn and emergency signal switch lever to ON position for left 
and right turns as required. 

Connect 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the wire connection at the switch to check 
for continuity to the following turn signal lamps: 

left front — Circuit 3 (GN/W).

left rear — Circuit 283 (Y/BK). 

right front — Circuit 2 (W/BL). 

right rear — Circuit 282 (GN). 

If the continuity through switch is not OK, service or replace the turn 
and emergency signal switch as required. 

 Turn Signal Switch Test by Substitution 

The turn and emergency signal switch can also be checked by installing 
a known good unit into the main wiring harness. 

Operate the controls to determine whether the circuits (including the 
hazard flasher) function. If not, service or replace the turn and emergency 
signal switch as necessary. 

 Bulb Socket Power Test 

Turn ignition switch lock cylinder to RUN or ACC position. 

Position turn and emergency signal switch lever to ON position for left 
or right turn as required. 

Connect 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the wire connection at the bulb socket to 
check for continuity to the following turn signal lamps: 

left front — Circuit 3 (GN/W). 

left rear — Circuit 283 (Y/BK).

right front — Circuit 2 (W/BL). 

right rear — Circuit 282 (GN). 

If the continuity to bulb socket is not OK, service circuit(s) between 
turn and emergency signal switch and bulb sockets. 

 Bulb Socket Ground Test 

Turn ignition switch lock cylinder to RUN or ACC position. 

Position turn and emergency signal switch lever to ON position for left 
or right turn as required. 

Connect 12-volt test lamp to ground strap on bulb socket. 

Contact test lamp probe to the wire connection at the bulb socket to 
check for continuity to ground. 

If test lamp illuminates, ground is good. 

If test lamp does not illuminate, ground circuit is incomplete and must 
be serviced. 

 Hazard Warning Flasher Lamp Switch 

Connect a 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the feed circuit wire connection at the turn 
and emergency signal switch. 

If test lamp illuminates, power flow to turn and emergency signal 
switch is good. 

If test lamp does not illuminate, power flow is disrupted between the 
flasher and the turn and emergency signal switch. Service feed circuit or 
replace flasher. 

To operate the turn signals, the ignition switch lock cylinder must be 
in either the ACC or RUN positions. The hazard flasher system is operated 
independently of the ignition switch by activating the hazard flasher switch. 

 Hazard Warning Flasher Power Test 

Connect a 12-volt test lamp to a good ground. 

Contact test lamp probe to the feed circuit wire connection at hazard 
flasher socket. Hazard warning flasher in vehicles with City Delivery 
instrument panel is located in fuse panel without tractor package. Flashers on 
all other models are mounted to instrument panel near fuse or circuit breaker 
panel. 

If test lamp illuminates, power flow to hazard flasher is good. 

If test lamp does not illuminate, power flow is disrupted between fuse 
and flasher. Service hazard flasher feed circuit as necessary.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Stoplight Switch

 Air Brakes 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable.

Disconnect wire connectors at the stoplight switch.

Unscrew stoplight switch body from the pressure port.

After installing the wire connectors, coat the entire stoplight switch 
and connectors with Caulking Cord D6AZ-19560-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G32-A.

 Installation 

Screw the switch body into the threaded pressure port and connect the 
wire connectors.

Reconnect the battery ground cable.

 Hydraulic Brakes 

 Removal 

Disconnect wiring from stoplight switch.

Thread stoplight switch out of pedal bracket retainer.

 Installation 

Thread stoplight switch into retainer until it contacts pedal mounting 
bracket.

Connect wiring.

Thread stoplight switch in or out until brake lights come on when pedal 
is pressed lightly.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Headlamp Bulb, Aeromax 

 Removal 

 WARNING: THE HALOGEN HEADLAMP BULB CONTAINS GAS UNDER PRESSURE. THE BULB CAN 
SHATTER IF THE GLASS ENVELOPE IS SCRATCHED OR THE BULB IS DROPPED. HANDLE BULB 
CAREFULLY. GRASP BULB ONLY BY ITS PLASTIC BASE. DO NOT TOUCH THE GLASS 
ENVELOPE. KEEP BULB OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. ENERGIZE THE BULB ONLY WHEN 
INSTALLED IN THE HEADLAMP. 

 NOTE: A properly aimed headlamp normally need not be reaimed after 
installation of this bulb. A burned out bulb should not be removed from the 
headlamp reflector until just before a replacement bulb is to be installed. 
Removal of a bulb for an extended period of time can allow contaminants (dust, 
moisture, smoke) to enter the headlamp body and affect the performance of the 
headlamp. When servicing the headlamp bulb, energize the bulb only while it is 
contained within the headlamp body. 

Check that headlamp switch is in OFF position. Open hood and tilt 
forward. 

Remove bulb access cover from back of headlamp assembly. 

Disconnect electrical connection at bulb. 

Remove bulb retaining ring by rotating counterclockwise. 

Carefully pull bulb straight backward out of socket in headlamp 
housing. Do not rotate bulb during removal.

 Installation 

Place new bulb in headlamp housing. Turn base slightly to align grooves 
with locating tabs and push firmly into socket. 

Install bulb retaining ring by rotating clockwise. 

Connect electrical connector at bulb. 

Replace bulb access cover at back of headlamp assembly. 

Turn headlamp switch on and check lamps for proper operation. 

Close hood.

 Bulb, Fog and Road Lamp 

 Removal 

The fog and road lamp assembly uses a halogen bulb. In the event of a 
bulb failure, the following procedure must be followed. 

Remove the lamp stone cover and the two screws retaining lens assembly 
to the lamp housing.

[FIGURE: K16297C.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Housing (Part of 15200)

2

15237

Wire Harness Assy

3

15200

Fog Lamp

4

—

Self-Tapping Screw (Part of 15200)

6

Stone Cover (Part of 15200)

Remove the lens and body assembly from the lamp housing and turn it to 
gain access to the rear of lamp body. 

Release the bulb socket retainer from the locking tab. 

Remove the lamp and socket assembly from the lamp body.

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Do not touch the new lamp with bare hands or oily cloth. The stains 
will cause contamination of the quartz, which can result in early failure of 
the lamp. Do not remove the protective plastic sleeve until the lamp is 
inserted into the socket. Be sure the circuit is not energized. If the quartz 
was inadvertently handled, wipe it with a clean cloth moistened with alcohol 
before installing. 

Insert the new lamp into socket assembly. Install socket into the lamp 
body and secure it with the retainer. 

Position the lens and body assembly right side up (as indicated on the 
lens) into the lamp housing. 

Secure the lens assembly to the lamp housing with the two screws and 
test the lamp for proper operation. Install the stone cover.
